summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, had reported that the sample was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and I am of the opinion that the same is adulterated due turbines, as defined in section 2(1)(f) of the Act. The Food Inspector found that the food articles were adulterated dueto insect filt, that it was adulterated because it was not adulterated within the meaning of sub clause (f) and therefore adulterated. He accordingly convicted the respondent under section 7 read with section 16 of the . On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the Food Inspector had reported the matter to the Public Analyst and that the appellant Corporation had failed to establish further that the article was unfit for human consumption. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the absence of any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section 2 (1)(b) of Act, is not attracted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was clearly wrong in its inter pretation of section2(1) of section 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. [473B] 2. In the instant case, the Food inspector had reported to the Food Analyst that the quantity of adulterated article was not fit for human use and therefore the appellant corporation had failed in proving further that it had not established further that there was any other cause of food for human health. The report of the Public analyst did not support the case that the Lal mirchi powder was adulterated, for the Public Food Inspector was not examined by the Public Laboratory. [474C D] 3. In view of the construction of section 7(1), it is clear that the High court was clearly right in its interpretation of section 8(1). [473D] 4. The appellant Corporation has not established by satisfactory evidence that thelal mirchi was adulterated for the public Analyst 's report.

The appellant was an agriculturist and he was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3(2) of the order. The Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him under section 5(1)(a) of that Act. On appeal, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence on the ground that the presumption in his case could not be drawn against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that he was an agricultural dealer and that the appellant was not liable to penalty under the law because the presumption under para 3(1) could not have been drawn. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the burden of proving innocence can be based upon them. [901 F] (ii)The words "carrying on the business" in the context of the Act postulate a course of conduct and continuity of transactions. The word "business" in section 2(2), means a course which is not a mere device to conceal or suppress material facts. It is obvious that sub para speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a trader and that is the essence of the Order. [936 B C] (iii) The word 'business ' in section 3(3) could only mean a course or conduct which would be relevant for showing that the transactions about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation. If that be so, then he is an agriculturist, and it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. [951 F G] (iv) The expression "carried on the trade" in clause 3(4) could never be drawn. It could only be rejected if there was something intrinsically wrong with that evidence.

The plaintiff respondent was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit premises. The rent was determined by a notice to quit and the defendant became a tenant from month to month under section 106, Transfer of Property Act. The appellant filed an application for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had been in arrears of rent for two successive periods, but on the expiry of the second yearly lease, the respondent ceased to be a tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendant was not entitled to recover possession of the land from the plaintiff. On appeal the High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that he was a permanent tenant in the land in suit and therefore the tenancy from month lo month was determined under section 116 of the Transfer of property Act, and that by reason of the payment of rent to the Receiver, the defendant ceased to have any right in the lands by prescription or otherwise. The High Court also held that as the Receiver had no authority to receive them, he was never a tenant in possession of land in respect thereof and therefore no tenancy could be created by the two payments of rent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the defendant appellant that the suit was based on the terms of the Kabuliyat executed by him on 24th December 1924 and the suit had been rightly decreed by the trial court, that the High Courts were wrong in holding that as a tenant had no power to receive rent from the Receiver he could not be created under section 108 Transfer of the Property Act, even though the Receiver was appointed by the Court. Held: (i) The appellant was entitled to claim the amount of rent from month and not from month till its inception in 1924. The suit was not one for ejectment but for arrears of land revenue and therefore could not have been created by section 116 Transfer of Goods Act, because the Receiver did not acquire any permanent right in it. (ii)The appellant had no jurisdiction to recover the amount from him as rent from him. It was not open to him to contend that he could claim the same on the basis of a lease for one year only. The mere fact that the Receiver accepted rent in 1925, would not make him a tenant of land within the meaning of section 116, Transfer Of Property Act and the mere fact of payment of arrears of revenue does not make it a tenant. (iii)The High Court was wrong in treating the appellant as a permanent tenancy from year to month. The question whether the rent was payable by the Receiver for one month or more could be decided on the facts of this case, because, the appellant did not have any authority to accept the rent and therefore he was not liable to pay the rent.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income Tax Officer issued notices under Section 139(1)(b) of the Act calling upon him to furnish information in respect of the assessment year 1964 65, and also to produce evidence in support of his claim that he had no knowledge of the said documents filed by him during the assessment proceedings before an income tax Officer after April 1, 1964. The assessee contended that since the Income Tax officer did not record any material on record, the order of assessment was vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of Section 138(1) (b). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the contention and held that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to assessment proceedings for 1964 65 was not a bar to the exercise of jurisdiction by the courts to summon the production of documents. The High Court, however, allowed the assessee 's appeal and set aside the orders of the Income tax Officer. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after the repeal of Section 137 of the 1961 Act by Act V of 1964 there is no longer any impediment left in the way of a court to summon production of certain documents filed before the income tax authorities after April l, 1964 for assessment years 1965 65 onwards and that the jurisdiction of the courts under section 138( 1)(b), was not confined to cases where the information etc. were not available on the date when the IncomeTax Officer issued notice under Section 138 (1) or Section 138 of the 1922 Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finality attached by Section 137 is limited to the cases where information etc., as contemplated by the section is called for by any person other than a court of law by a judicial order. [562D] 2. In the instant case, the finality which has been attached to the order passed under Section 137(1), is not confined only to cases when the information or information is available in the Court and that it would have been possible for the Incometax authorities to summon such documents from the income Tax Authorities after April I, 1964 relating to assessment years. [563E] 3.

The appellant was married to Seinaba on April 7, 1944. The father of the appellant 's minor daughter, who had attained majority in 1955, without leaving any issue, filed a suit for partition and possession of the property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the gift by the husband to his minor daughter was valid and that the appellant was entitled to get possession on her behalf. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the gift made by the father in favour of Seinama was not a valid gift, because the gift was by a registered deed no question in this behalf can arise; (ii) the transfer was by way of gift and therefore the gift must be accepted on her own behalf. HELD : (i)(a) The gift is by a Registered deed no questions in this connection can arise. It is not necessary that there should be a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of the donor 's part to the donee. [550 F] (b) The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's mother when the gift is from the husband, to his father or his executor or by his guardian, is one of fact and not in accordance with law. [552 G H] (c) The intention to make the gift, was clear and manifest because it was made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammotty to his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. [553 B C] (d) The fact that the father is living at the time of the gift in the house of his mother does not make any difference because it is made by another deed which is registered and retained by the mother in Law.

The appellant was a religious institution of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments, Madras, passed an order under section 100(1) of the Act directing the Commissioner to make a provisional assessment of contribution for the year ending March 31, 1952. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Commissioner had not determined the cost of audit fee and that audit fee demanded by him was without determination under section 76(2) of Act, and therefore, the demand for contribution was illegal. HELD: (i) The Commissioner has to determine the fee for auditing the accounts of the religious institution and to submit its report to the High Courts. It is not necessary to decide whether there is a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions. [920 D] (ii) The appellant had not fixed any fee in truth for audit of the accounts. The amount was levied for meeting the cost and audit fee. The High Court has not examined the question whether there was a reasonable relationship between the expenses incurred by Government for giving effect to the provisions of the statute or its scheme. [936 D] H. C.I.T., Madras vs K. M. T. A. V. Visvanatha Sastri, ; , referred to. (iii) The High Courts have not investigated the question as to whether there has been a reasonable nexus between the expense incurred by it for providing service and the amount intended to he collected from its income for which the contribution is to be levied.

The appellant was convicted under section 19(1) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court for quashing the proceedings on the ground that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right from any kind of order made by the High court in the proceeding by issuance of a notice. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to be proceeded against for committing contempt of the High Courts under section 20 of the Act and directed the issue of notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded with for committing an offence under section 15. A preliminary objection raised on behalf of the respondents was also rejected by the trial court. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of the trial Court. The Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that no second appeal lay to this court as a question of right under section19(1). In the appeal to this Supreme Court it was contended on behalf the appellant that no further appeal lies against the order passed by the learned single judge, and that the High COurt had jurisdiction to pass an order in respect of the proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The preliminary objection that no Appeal lay to the Supreme Court under section 18 is not maintainable because it is a matter which of right, from any other point of time, can be asked for in such an appeal. [512C] 2.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment and also enhanced the fine. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) section 6 (1 A), as amended by the Amending Act of 1949, did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the amending Act of 1948, and (ii) the amendment of section 6 of the 1952 Act was not retrospective in operation. HELD : The amending Act was repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952, which came into force on the date of the alleged commission of the offence. [619 D] (i)(a) The amending Acts were intended to provide for a different situation, namely, the repeal of an earlier Act, and it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. The amendment of the Amending Acts was not intended to affect the continued operation of the amended provisions. It could not be said that section 6 was retrospective in effect. [719 F] (b) Section 4 of the 1958 Act was a saving provision, and the amending Acts did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The amending statute was repealed when the Amending Ordinance of 1949 was passed by the legislature. [700 G H] (c) The amendment made the said section in the 1952 Amendment Act of 1950, was retrospective and did not validate the amendments made by it. [750 B] (d) Section 6(2)(a), introduced in the Act of 1933, removed it in the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and redundant. [751 G H; 751 A] (e) The Amending Act was passed with a view to bringing into force the new enactment by the repealing Act of 1939, which was repealed on the repeal. It was not necessary for the legislature to have retrospective effect. The amended section 6A was intended to be prospective in operation and it could not therefore be said to have been retrospective in its operation. [751 C] (f) Section 7(1A) of Act XIII of 1949 is a saving clause which takes away the operation of other enactments in which the repealed enactment has been applied, incorporated or referred to. The words "anything done or omitted to be done" in section 6 A are comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmissionter, the section does not prohibit possession of any wireless apparatus and therefore it cannot be said, that section 4 of Act I of 1952 was retrospective.

The appellant was the proprietor of a private limited company. The estate vested in the Court under section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1913. In execution of the decree the properties were sold and the property was sold. The appellant filed an application under section 37 (6)(a) of that Act for reopening the decrees and in working out the rights of the parties to the suit, the Court could not go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decree holders on record were in fact benamidars for another person. The court held that the appellant was a mere benamidar for her husband and that the properties sold were not liable to be attached under section 35(2)(c) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Subordinate Judge and restored the decree passed by the courts below. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the court had no jurisdiction to go behind a decree and the execution proceedings were not barred under section 34(2). HELD : (i)(a), The High Court was right in holding that the order for restoration of possession made by both the courts was illegal. [991 B] (b) The object of restoring possession of the properties in favour of the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled and in case of default in payment of any one of the instalments, the properties are returned to the decree holder purchaser. [995 B] The object was to restore possession of property to the judgment debtors and there was no proof of the debt being in fact benami for another. [996 C D] (c) The order for restoring possession made under section 38(2), is not a nullity because it does not affect the rights which could be protected by clause (b). [995 E F] (d) The High Courts were right in setting aside the orders of the courts on the ground that they had no power to restore the properties to the order passed by them. [948 G H] (e) The sale itself was not annulled, and in the absence of any proof of a decree holder being in possession of it either by themselves or through Oramba Sundari, the appellant could not be said to have advanced any right which could he protected under clause (c).

The appellant, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton and yarn. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of Rs. 1,000/ as arrears of rent from the date of the said decree. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to execute the decree as he had not executed the deed of assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, r. 16. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the document in question did not contain any provision for transfer of the decree by an assignment in the writing within its meaning of order XXI, rule 16. HELD : (i) The words "decree holder" in Order XXI Rule 16(old section 232 do not mean a transfer or an agreement to transfer. It is only when the terms are clear that the words "judgment holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that the language of Order 21, rule 17(1) does not exclude the transferee from being transferees of the decrees by an assignor. [847 C D] (ii) The word "decreeholder" in O. XXI, Rule 16 means a transfer of or an agree ment to transfer a decree for execution of the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. It does not mean that the transferee is entitled to apply for execution. [947 C] (iii) The expression "decree" in r.16 means a decree which is transferred before the transfer can be passed in future. The words 'decree holder ' in O, XXI, R. 16(1), do not include a party to the suit. The word 'decree ' does not include any person who in law has no interest in the property of the judgment debtor.

The respondent was a manufacturer of steel doors, windows and other goods. The contract provided for the supply of materials to be supplied by the respondent. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing the same and also agreed to fix the price of the materials supplied. The appellant was informed that the contract was to be completed within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the notice. The Superintending Engineer, however, did not give any charge for the service. The Deputy Commissioner, Excise & Taxation in appeal held that the respondent had no right to claim the amount agreed to be paid by it and that the price was received by the appellant as a consideration for the contract. The High Court held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts were not decisive and the respondent could not claim the amounts agreed to by him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contract between the respondent and the Executive Engineers was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. The question whether the contract is in substance one for work and labour or one for the sale of chattel would depend on the facts of each case whether the object of the party sought to be taxed is that the object must be gathered from the terms of the contract, and the circumstances that the parties intended to be served are not conclusive. [505C D] (ii) The question as to whether the appellant was liable to pay sales tax under the Sales Tax Act, was one for works contract or for rendering service in connection with the fixing of those windows. If the windows were not properly "fixed" the contract would not be complete and the parties could not get the benefit of the agreement. [511D] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the appellant had agreed to and did supply "motor bus being one for sale of goods for consideration, and that it was only upon the "fixing" of the windows that the doors were under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution of the work.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. for having committed an offence punishable under section 420 I. P.C., read with Section 120B IPC. The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 the appellant was found in a taxi and demanded the price of the goods from him. On November 16, 1967, the appellant made an application to the Magistrate for quashing the charge against him. The Magistrate rejected the application holding that the appellant had not been able to prove his innocence. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution case is that on the date when the respondent was arrested he was not an agent of the accused; and (ii) the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to try the charge under section 120 B I.p.C.; (iii) the High Court erred in interfering with the judgment of the High court as it was not a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat the complainant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar was not admissible in evidence against him and the charge framed against him were accordingly quashed. [280D] 2. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by the Police. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar Agarwalla was that he was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought a car from Ram Avtar and demanded payment of the price. It was then agreed, would be sent through Shanker Lal. [279F] 3. The charge under sections420, 468, 471 and 471 I. p.C was framed against all the three accused. The entire evidence as disclosed by the report was lodged before the Magistrate. The whole evidence as stated by the High Courts is not admissible under section 114 of the Evidence Act. [278H; 279A] 4. The statement which was made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar was that it was present alongwith Shanker Lal, when the former brought washer plates in a car and demanded price of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then stipulated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. [ 279A B] 5. The fact that the name was not mentioned of the names of Raj Chandra Kumar Agarwal did not make any mention of his name of the person who had been examined by the police. The parts which were attributed to the appellant wereher plates. The rest of the evidence as pointed out by the trial court would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Kumar too was a party, to any criminal conspiracy to cheat or cheat Ram Avtar. [277B] 6. The mere fact that it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Chandra Agarwalla came on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the Report cannot be a ground for interference with the Judgment of the trial Court as it is not a matter for this Court to interfere.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for implementation of the directions given by this Court in the case of M/s. P.K. Gopalan vs Union of India & Ors., ; , which was dismissed by this court on the ground that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional obligation, adequate safety and order by the Railways, adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. The petitioner challenged the validity of the aforesaid directions in a writ petition under article 32 of Constitution contending that the Railway in this case is not a "public utility" within the meaning of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitu tion and that it was not a 'public utility ' within the expression "public purpose". It was further contended that the petitioner had denied the assertion in the counter affidavit that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in the Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Railways Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It is not necessary that this Court should have regard to the nature of the service should improve. [321E] 2. The policy of the Railways Act, and the rules under it, must be strictly complied with.[322F] 3. The quality of the services should improve the established means of communication in this Country. It has been lodged in the Judges and if they have to fulfil their function as Judges, it would hardly be lodged elsewhere. [330G] 4. The Railway Administration is directed to ensure that the requirements of the Railway Act and Rules under them must be comply with. [328A B] 5. The principles of natural justice are not only in issue but also in issue, is not prudent and we do not, therefore, propose to issue directions. [332F] 6. It may be that the rates and fares should cover the total cost of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations, if any. [333B] 7. The nature of service should be improved by providing for such level crossings at their cost in view of the accepted position that the rate and fares shall cover the entire cost of services which would he equal to operation, interest thereon, interest at 6% per annum.

The appellants were prosecuted for non prosecution under section 13(1) of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The appellants contended that since the orders passed by the Collector in appeal were not within 30 days from the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration were barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the appeals holding that the applications made by the appellants were barred under Regulation 21 of the Jagirs Abolition Act which was applicable to them, and that the application for restoration was barred by time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since they had not filed any appeal in time, the applications were within 30 day of the receipt Of the order dismissing the appeals as time barred under regulation 21 was not barred by Limitation. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has no power to dismiss an appeal for non Prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits and to record its decision even though there is default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal. [143 D] (ii) The order passed by a Collector under Regulation 20 was not within time as the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21 had expired. It could not be said that the Tribunal had no power under Regulation 19(1). [144 E F] (iii) The word "Decide" in Regulation 19 is wide enough to include an application for review of an order passed on merits even though it may have been made after the expiry of 30 days of receipt of such order. It is not obligatory on the Tribunal to decide an appeal on merit and to give a hearing to the respondent. [144 G] (iv) The expression "Decided" in section 17(1), means "decide". In the context of section 20, it is clear that under Regulation 18(1)(a) the legislature has no powers to dismiss or amend an appeal except on merits. It follows that Regulation 19 (1) and 19(2) are not exhaustive. [145 A B] (v) The words "decides" in regulation 19(i) mean "Decree". In view of the express language of section 17, it cannot be said to include in its scope and ambit an application under Regulation 23 for restoration of an appeal or application made under regulation 20. It must be held that Regulation 21 applies to the present case and the period prescribed by the Regulation being 30 days after the receipt thereof is not within the period Of limitation prescribed under Regulation 22. [146 B C] (vi) The power given to the Tribunal under Regulation is wide and conclusive and not to be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any court. It can only be exercised on merits, even though the order passed in appeal is final and conclusive. [147 E F].

The appellant was the owner of a temple in which he had been installed by his father. The appellant 's case was that the village Telibandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swami, who was the manager of the temple and that the said temple was dedicated absolutely to the deity in the temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The High Court held that the dedication of the village was not proved and that it was not necessary for the appellant to establish that the land was given in full ownership to the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is well settled that a person who has been appointed as a manager of a public temple or whether he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute title of the public. The fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion the award suffered from any infirmity. [421 D] (ii) It may well be that Ramsaran Lal was himself led by the terms of the Bagchi award into thinking that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the temple. The mere fact that the appellant used to credit the income from Telihoo in the trust did not make an absolute dedication of his village to the public, and did not give any indication as to how the property or the income of Teli Dasi was dealt with. [416 D E] (iii) It would be open to the High Court to consider the several other issues which had been framed in the suit and without deciding which the suit cannot be properly disposed of. The question whether a particular property belonged exclusively to the Hindu family with merely a charge thereon for the expenses of the family or that he made some alienations of it to meet the expenses, would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellants were the President of the Uttar Pradesh High Court. The appellant was a member of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he was guilty of contempt. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associated with the pass ing of the Resolution which contained defamatory remarks about Chief Justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment and order of the High Court are set aside. [602C] 2. The Chairman of action described as contempt is a matter of regret that the apology is unfortunate. The contempt is not proper. It is true that the High court referred to the contumacious conduct of the appellant but the High Courts did not wish to proceed against the appellants. The reasons given by the High 'Court for discharging the notices are not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. [613D] 3. The language used by them was unfortunate. It was a matter which is of regret, that the judgment and Order of the Court were not proper or it should have been pass in that way. [625E F] 4. The words "indiscreet" by itself are unfortunate. [600F] 5. The appellants rightly discharged their notices. The notice was discharged.

The appellants Nos. 5, 6 and 7 were the sons of respondent No. 1. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge for registration of the award on 28th of November, 1983. On or about 11th of August, 1978 the arbitrators made a reference to the Court of Sub Judge, Hooghly at Chinsurah to return the award to the arbitrators. The Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitration proceedings on 24th July, 1981 and fixed the date for filing the award. On 14th of September, 1983 the arbitrators gave an application to the parties and made an order directing the appellants to file a fresh award in accordance with law. On 25th November, 1982 the arbitrators filed an application under section 30 of the . The Sub judge ordered that the arbitrators ' application be kept pending and be heard when the injunction order was vacated. On 26th of February, 1983, the arbitrators again made an applica tion before the sub Judge for making a fresh application to return back the award, but did not direct return of the same. On 24th of July, 1984 the arbitrators passed an order that the appellants would be given liberty to file the same before the Court for registration. The appellants filed an appeal against the said order before the High Court which was dismissed by the Sub judge on 25th of June, 1985. The High Court ordered that a fresh injunction should be granted in favour of the appellants and directed the appellants not to return their award within four months from 28th January, 1978. On 23rd of August 1978 the appellants filed a petition under section 151 C.P.C. for setting aside the order of the Sub Registrar, Arambagh on 24.7.1978. The learned Sub Judge ordered that if the arbitrators were not available to them, they would have to file fresh award within 4 months from the date of the order. On 28th November 1983 the appellants made an appli cation before the Subordinate Judge for cancellation of the said award. The sub Judge directed that the parties should be given notice of the filing of the application and also to give a hearing to them. On 27th of March, 1981 the arbitrators sent back the matter to the Sub Court for registering the award in terms of section 15 of the Act. On 29th November 1982 the appellants moved an application for setting out the reasons for its order dated 28th August, 1983 and prayed that they be registered as the Registrar and not the Sub court. The Subordinate Judge allowed the applications holding that the limitation for registration was not applicable to the case and that the period during which judicial proceedings were pending was a period of 4 months. On appeal by the appellants, the High COurt held that the Limitation Act did not require a person to do that which he could possibly perform and an act of the Court shall prejudice no man would apply with full vigour in the facts of this case and if that is the position then the award as it stood was in the custody of the court. On the question whether the limitation prescribed by section 15(1) of the is a period within which the period of limitation for filing an application can be taken to have been excluded in view of the principle laid down under section 15. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 15(2) of The Act does not require that a person should be allowed to do so unless he has done so. [693C] 2.1 In the instant case, the parties are directed to pay and bear their own costs. [6594D] 2:2. The award was in court and this order was passed on 28.11.1983.

The respondent was the owner of a building. The respondent gave notice to the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, to show cause why he should not be evicted from the premises on the ground that he had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub letting as a personal right for his benefit. The appellant contended that the respondent had waived the right under section 15 of the Act and that the notice was invalid because of the provisions of section 13 (1)(a) of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates Act, 1948, which prohibited the tenant from subletting the premises. Held, that the suit was not brought for the enforcement of the agreement which recognised sub letting but was a provision for the protection of private rights. The right to sue for ejectment on the grounds of subletting being a personal rights cannot be said to have been conferred by section 15(1) (e). The respondent had no right to enforce his right under the agreement. The suit was brought under section 12(1), (e) and (g) of Act, which provided that " notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, no tenant shall be entitled to recover possession if the Court is satisfied (i) that the tenant has, since the coming into operation of this Act. The protection of a statutory provision was not available to a person who had waived it as he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not evict him under section 14(1). Held further, that section 13 of the Contract Act did not apply to a case where the respondent was a public servant and the appellant had waived its right in respect of the prohibition. The provisions of the section were intended for protection of the private rights of the landlord and unless there is in the Act itself any provision to the contrary such rights as far as they were personal rights may be parted with or renounced by the landlord, it was not open to the court to take notice that the trustees under this Act had waived them as he did not waive it as a statutory right.

The respondent Board was appointed as a sub inspector of the Bombay Municipal Corporation. The respondent Board, after considering the objections filed by the respondent Board and after considering all the objections, passed an order on January 30, 1991 directing the appellant Board to take action against the respondent for violation of the provisions of the Act. The appellant Board challenged the said order before the High Court which allowed the appeal holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent was guilty of any misconduct and that the impugned order was vitiated by non compliance with the principles of natural justice, and that it was not a case of no evidence and the conclusions were reached on the basis of the admission made by the respondents. The High Court held that the findings recorded by the Standing Committee were correct and quashed the order of termination of the respondent 's services. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Standing Committees had not applied their mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and that they were not justified in taking into consideration the evidence adduced before them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The findings recorded on the question of the validity of the Standing Commit tee 's order are set aside. [799B] 2.1 The High Courts have no jurisdiction to quash the impugned notification and the impugned notifications. It is not open to the High Courts under article 226 or Article 136 to itself to itself evaluate the evidence and to interfere with the findings of fact recorded by them. [789C D] 2:2 In the instant case, the Standing committee did not apply its mind to all the relevant factors and the conclusion reached by the authorities that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or the guardian is based on the evidence on record. The finding recorded by it was based on appreciation of the evidence. [788G H] 2 :3 In dealing with question as to whether the Committee was justified in arriving at its conclusion against the appellant, it would not be reasonable to exclude from consideration the findings and to quash such an order merely on the ground that different view could possibly be taken on the materials available on record.[799C D; 789A] 2(a) The finding arrived at by the High court that the examination of the witnesses was done after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board at Bombay and before thoiversities were able to evaluate the evidences and to see whether the witnesses were reliable or not, is based upon the evidence produced on record and whether the evidence was sufficient to support such conclusion reached. [781C D E] 2.(b) The High court has no jurisdiction under article 136 to interfere in an appeal against the order merely because it is not supported by any evidence or if the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of law or in violation of principles of Natural Justice, the Court has no jurisdic tion to quash that order merely upon the ground of different view. [780D] 2 (c) The findings arrived at on the facts found by the courts below are not perverse and are liable to be set aside on the grounds of non compliance of the principles laid down in the Supreme Court 's decision. [779E F] 2nd respondent Board is a public body governed by the provisions contained in the Act, and it is open to it to interfere only with the finding and to examine the witnesses on its own merits. The conclusion reached on such evidence is not perverse or vitiated by any material or if it is based solely on the appreciation of evidence or is based purely on inadmissible evidence or on irrelevant considerations. [783E F; 784A] 3.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellants were guilty of criminal misconduct and were convicted by the trial court. The High Court acquitted them but convicted them under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the offence as defined in section 5 (1) of Prevention of criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal breach of trust was not a single act of bribery within the meaning of section 5 of the Act and (ii) the intention of the legislature was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single acts of bribery. Held, that the words "any public servant" in section 21 of the Penal Code are wide enough to include a person who is charged with criminal misconduct under section 4(1) and therefore the offence under section 6(2), read with section 5, of the Criminal Procedure Code, must be held to be one which was committed by the public servant. The words "for any purpose" in the section mean that every railway servant shall not be deemed to be a public servant for any of the purposes of that Act except those mentioned in Chapter IX. The word "for" used in section 2(d) does not come with the same meaning as in section 3(2). The words 'for any other purpose ' are wide and they have been used in the sense in which it is used in a particular sense. The expression "for the purposes" in cl. (d), of section 6, is in these terms: "For the purposes Of this Act, public servant shall be deemed not to be public servant". The words used in el. (e) are wide a meaning and they are intended to include all kinds of persons who are charged with the offence mentioned in Ch. IX of the Code. The definition of "public servant" is given in section 6 of the General Clauses Act, which is in the nature of a general term. The object of the Legislature was to provide for the protection of public servants and not to prevent private defence from being used as a weapon of criminal offence. The intention of legislature was that it should be presumed that the accused person was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe by threat or promise proceeding from the public servants or otherwise abusing his position as a public Servant. The section does not apply to cases where there is no offer to give an d acceptance of a bribe by a public officer. The fact that the appellant had given a request to Madan Lal to hush up the potato case pending against him when the talk about the bribe took place, did not make any offer to the appellant. The offence as contemplated in cl.(d) was not one under section 21 and therefore it could not be said that he was interested. The appellant had no intention to give or attempting a bribe for hushing up the case pending before him when he was asked to hump up the trial. The case of Madan Lal all the three accused were not covered by cl.(d). The appellant did not commit any offence under s. 161 I P.C., but was convicted under section 165 B, read with sections 5(1), 5(3) and 5(4) of that Code.

The appellant, a surety, was appointed as the surety in respect of certain securities. The surety executed two promissory notes in favour of the Bank and the surety. The appellant 's suit for recovery of Rs. 76,36804 P. towards security was decreed by the trial court. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the date of the contract of guarantee and the bond executed by the principal debtor in favour thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Bank was completely negligent and had not exercised such care as a prudent man would in the circumstances of the case, which resulted in loss of security. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Bank was fully justified in taking the view that the creditor having lost one security, namely, the pledge of goods and the personal guarantee of the surety, the surety was discharged to the extent of the value of the security. [83G] 2.1 In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the debtor had taken more than one security from the principal debtors at the time when the contract was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the Principal debtor, if the creditor lost or without the consent of the sureties parts with the other security. The guarantee given by the surety is not discharged to any extent as provided by section 141. [84A B] 2:2 In order that a creditor may take more than two security from him, it must appear that the principal creditor had offered security by way of pledge of the goods and that the personal bond was discharged in the event of the creditor losing or without his consent of surety parts with other security the surety would be discharged to extent of his value of security.[84C] 3.1 The surety himself agreed to give personal guarantee on the clear understanding that the Principal creditor had offer security by means of pledge, of goods, and the goods were to be in the custody of the debtor bank. [85E] 2 :3 In orderto attract section 139 it must he shown that there was a breach of contract or an obligation to pay any debt which the creditor has against the principal, at the date when the Contract of guarantee was entered upon and irrespective Of the fact if the surety did not accept his personal guarantee. [86E] 3:4 In order tO the surety 's case is that the security given by way Of pledge of good faith was offered by him to the Bank. The sureties in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee, on the express understanding that he would offer security for the advance and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities.

The appellant was the holder of a jagir in 1943. He was granted a lease of certain lands to his wife and children. The appellant 's father died in 1920 leaving behind him a widow, who had no right to resume the land. The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for possession of the lands on the ground that he was not entitled to hold the "patelki inam" lands as defined by section 2(2) of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not liable to pay the rent and that the respondent No 1 had no locus standi to resume his land and regrant the lands in question. The High Court on appeal held that the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for the services rendered by him as a member of the family rendering service and therefore, the appellant could not claim as of right that he had a share in the emoluments. Held, that the grant was not a service grant but a grant of land burdened with service and so long as the service is performed by any member of his family, the lands are joint family properties subject to partition and settlement between the parties. The grant was made by way Of remuneration or pay for the service rendered by the patel and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied. The right to resumption of the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the Jagir was a grant made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag.

The appellant was a Cutchi Memons. He was born to him in Madras and later on in Madras. The appellant 's father died leaving behind his widow, the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties by metes and bounds. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question as to who was born before 1948 was whether the deceased husband had become entitled to succeed to the property by birth in the property held by her father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. [234 B] (ii) The High Court was right in its view that since the Khojas and the Cutchi memons were governed by the Hindu Law of inheritance, they could not be said to have been excluded from the operation of the Hindu law of inheritance. [235 E F] (iii) The Act came into force on November 1, 1948. Under section 3(1) of the , all Cutchi Merger became a part of the joint family property and its devolution by survivorship is governed by that Act. The Act was not applicable to the case of a Hindu Law which was in force at the time when the Act came to be passed. [236 G H] (iv) Section 3(2) of Act, provided that all Cutch Memons shall in matters of succession and inheritance be governed by it. The definition of "Hindu law" in section 3 is not exhaustive but only inclusive. It does not include any provision which could be made for the purpose of succession. [237 G H; 235 A] (v) Section 4(1)(a) provides that all cutchi Memon shall, in matters Of succession and succession, be governed under the Mahomedan law. The provisions of section 3 are applicable to a case where there is no provision in the Act for succession and the inheritance by survivorship. [238 G H].

The appellants are manufacturers of different types. They manufacture fabrics in different kinds. The appellants were manufacturing fabrics from different varieties. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, they filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of excise duty on the yarn which was produced at an intermediate stage. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the goods which are produced at the intermediate stage of the integrated process of weaving of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of any other commodity in the same place, were liable to payment of excise duties in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that under section 3(1) of the Finance Act 1982, amendments made to rules 9 & 49 have been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force, that is to say, from February 28, 1944, it has been held that the amendment made by section 5 will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The language of rule 9(1), inter alia, provides that commodity obtained at an intermediary stage of manufacture in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises as mentioned in sub rule (1) thereof. [707C] 2. Under section 3 of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944 the expression "place of removal" has been given prospective effect by virtue of section S l of the said Act. The words "place or premises of production" have been defined in the Act to mean a factory or any other place or place of manufacture or manufacture or sale of any goods in the form of an integrated process, and includes a factory, factory or other premises of manufacture. It is not disputed that under Section 3(2) of Central Excise Act, the taxing event is the production or manufacturing of the excisable goods. [0708C D] 3. The expression " place of removal", has been defined to mean any place where the excisable articles are manufactured or produced or manufactured but any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified in sub section (1), as the case may be, whether for consumption, export or manufacture, of the goods. It has been already noticed that the taxing statute has not been made applicable to the facts of this case. [1008D] 4. The definition of place of 'place of manufacture ' is a factory and any other Place or premises where the excise duty is payable would be deemed, but rule 9 does not contain any definition of "place" in the Central Act. [1109E F] 5. The description that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises incidental to the manufacture or production of the dutiable goods. In other words, if a commodity which is manufactured in such place and is used for the manufacture of another item, then it will be a case of removal for the purpose of payment of duty. [110D] 6. The specification is not required to be given by the collector. It does not require that the excisable article must be produced or produced before him. In the instant case, the appellants are liable to pay excise duty as they were notized for the purposes of weaving the same into fabrics. [1010E] 7. The notification dated February 28. 1944 has been issued under section 5 of the Income Tax Act and the notification is valid. [1002D] 8. The Notification No. 9(i) does not provide that commodity purchased at an earlier stage of an inter state process of manufacture of other goods, is liable to the payment of Excise duty.

The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for stay of the hearing of the suit till disposal of a special leave petition. The petitioner moved an application under section 68 C.P.C. for staying the hearing on the ground that it was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction restraining the respondent from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme and acting upon it after it was published. The Civil Judge passed an order directing the parties to proceed with the suit until disposal of the special leave petitions. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. In appeal by Special Leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The procedure laid down for the preparation and approval of a scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D of the Act. Section 68 C of the provides for the publication and approval or modification of the scheme. [545C] 1.2 The procedure to be followed at the hearing is contained under section 69 C of Act. It is not open to a civil Court to issue an order of injunction restraining any hearing or approving the Scheme either with or without modification. When the scheme is approved or modified under section 70 D of Act, such approval or modifications are required to be published in the official Gazette and on such publication it becomes final. [544D] 1:3 The procedure prescribed for preparation and approve of the schemes is contained therein in sections 69 C and 69 D of Chapter IVA of the , which provides for preparation of the Scheme is contained In sections 68C and 68D of the . [546E F] 1 :4. Section 69 C. P.C., provides for publication and approve or modification. The procedure provided in section 68C of the is mandatory. [541F G] 2:1. The jurisdiction of State Government (the Hearing Authority under section68 D) of the U.P., Act, is exclusive in character and it is not subject to any limitation. [543E F; 545A] 2.2. Section 70 C.p.C, provides for a complete scheme and approval by the State Government. The power of the State Govt. under section 71 D of that Act is exclusive.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellant used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. On August 29, 1963, the appellant went to the house of the respondent and asked him to come to the village where she was living. The appellant asked for a bribe from the appellant and told him that he had not paid anything to him. The police officer refused to give any bribe. The respondent 's case was also that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel Nathaniel. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 4(2). In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The order of sanction in the present case satisfies the requirements of section 6 of the Act. [184 E] (ii) The appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money from RusselNathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The conviction of the appellant was not excessive. [185 G] (iii) The High Court erred in holding that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from the Russel, it cannot be said that the accused had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act or for showing or forbidding to do anything in the exercise of his official functions.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that the sanction accorded in this case was not a valid one. Held, that the question whether or not there was a proper sanction in the case was a question serious enough to justify the granting of a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution. The sanction given by the appellant was not merely an administrative order but also an administrative act and it was not for him to decide what he had done. The fact that the sanctioning authority did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for the connected claim cases or find out as to how they stood. Held further, that a sanction granted by the Government under section 6(c) was not valid and it could be said that the appellant should have applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The order granting the certificate was not an administrative one but only an administrative direction or reward for showing favour to someone else. The sanctioning authority had no power to grant a certificate. The Government did not act in the interests of justice, nor did it exercise its discretion in the matter of granting a certificate and that the decision of the High Court was not correct. The appellant could not be convicted under s 161 of Indian Penal code and section 5(2) of Act II of 1947, but he could not have been convicted under the , for an offence of having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents tenant on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants under section 14(1)(b) of the Act on the grounds of demolition and reconstruct. The appellate authority allowed the appeal of the appellant and set aside the order of eviction. In second appeal, the High Court held that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises and that it was inherent in such a life interests that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b) as grounds for eviction were not bona fide. The appellant tenant appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act with which the Act was dealing with the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K.S.N. Chamarbaugwala, ; , referred to. 2.1 The expression "landlord" is defined under section 2(6) of that Act as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants. It is not necessary for the landlords to invoke the provisions of the Rent Act to evict the tenants on these grounds. [512C D] 2.2 In the instant case, the landlord has only a right to evict his tenant on these ground. The landlord has merely a life estate in the property and he cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the landlord against his tenants under the provisions Of the Act. Such questions as are raised in this appeal by the tenants are, therefore, irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and others who are not his tenants. [612E F] 2:3 The expression 'landlord ' is defined in section 2 (6) as meaning "tenant" as meaning any person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent if the building were let to a tenant". In the present case, there was no question of any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man. [625E F; 626A] 2 :4 The Act does not contemplate that the landlords should be evicted only on the basis of the building which is available to him under the Act and that they shall submit affidavits in this Court undertaking to vacate the premises by the aforesaid date within two weeks from the date of the order. [613E F, G] 3:1. The expression landlord 's own right under the Rent Control Act is outside the ken of this Act. It does not mean that a tenant with a lifeinterest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se be not bona fides. [600F G] 2(a) The expression `landlord ' has been defined under Section 2(1) as a person who holds a life or interest in a premises and who admittedly has been on his own right to enjoy the property for his life.

The respondent was a tenant of a grove. He was in possession of the land and had been dispossessed by the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against him on the ground that he was not entitled to any compensation under section 6(h) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section 6 (h)of the Act read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. The High Court dismissed the appeal and held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964, the respondent was entitled to recover possession of his land from him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the right of the mortgagee to get possession of land in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The position taken by the respondent decree holder is that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution would have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by him was correct. [860 B] (2) Section 18(1)(a) of Act provides that an appeal shall lie to the mortgagee if he has not filed any suit or proceeding in respect of any part of bhumidhari rights, execution should have proceed against trees. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the "land".

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The Trial Court convicted them under section 326/149, 323/149 and 324/149 but acquitted the other accused. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction of the first appellant under Section 326/34 IPC. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the prosecution had caused injuries with a chopper and those injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; (2) the injuries were not sufficient in ordinary course to cause the death of the deceased, and (3) the offence under section 302 IPC was not permissible. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction of appellants 2 to 4 for an offense under Section 307/149 is not permissible as it has been done by the High Courts in exercise of their power under Section 149 IPC. [89G] 2. The injuries caused by the first accused with a sharp edged weapon were sufficient to cause his death. The intention to cause such bodily injury was not to be inferred from the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no evidence that any one of the accused individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused in the course of the same occurrence, nor was there any evidence to show that they had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause murder of the appellant. [90G H] 3. The nature of weapons with which they were armed and nature and seat of the injuries, it is not possible to hold that all the four appellants had shared their common intention with the others. There was no evidence to prove any particular injury caused by them according to the postmortem report. It could be said that all these appellants had given a common intention to kill Suku. The fact that some of the injured persons were armed with deadly weapons, did not make any difference. [91A B] 4. The prosecution case was that the injuries on deceased had been caused by all the accused persons and that the death had occurred due to receipt of multiple injuries. There were no injuries on any of the three appellants. There could be no doubt that the injury was inflicted by the second appellant with the chopper, but there was no injury on the body of the second accused. The offence under s 302 IPC is not impermissible. [92C D] 5. The High Court rightly convicted each of the two appellants for an act under section 325/149 I.P.C. and sentence them to suffer simple imprisonment for two years. His conviction was set aside by the Division Bench of the High court on the ground that no specific charge had been framed against him for the substantive offence of murder punishable under Section 324 IPC. The appeal filed by the appellants 2 and 3 is, therefore, dismissed.

The assessee, a resident in the State of Madras, was assessed to income tax for 1967 68 and 1968 69. The assessee claimed deduction of the amount paid by it on cash receipt basis under Section 5(2)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim holding that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 69 and 1968 70. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that since the Indian Company had credited to the assessee in its books of the Indian company, it did not actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The amount of royalty amounts paid under Section 4(2) (a) cannot be said to have been received by the assessee. [105B] 2.1 The assessee could be said that the assessee had received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. In the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own books at Coventry. It is not necessary to express any opinion on the question whether there was any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(1) and section 145 of the Act nor is it necessary to give any reasons for the conclusion reached by the High Court that there is no conflict or repugnancy between section 4(1)(a), and section 6(2). [105E F] 2:2. The method of accounting adopted by the appellant for all its income was on cash payment basis, and since it did so, it could not have been said that it had received it in U K. Section 145 was applicable to the case. [106F G] 3.1 In the instant case, the assessee did not say that the method of accounts adopted by it for all the years 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1969 70 to the effect that it was maintaining its accounts on cash based on cash credit account. The High Court was right in holding that there was no conflict between section 6 (2) and Section 145 of Act. [107F G; 108A] 2 :3. In view of the fact that the appellant did not state that the mode of accounting followed by it was maintained by the Indian Companies, it cannot be held that the amount was not actually received but the assessee firm was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a), cannot apply. [108F G].

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence of an accomplice is not admissible in law as it is not sufficient that there is corroboration of the approver 's story. It is only when a conviction based on uncorroborated testimony of an approver is proved that he is telling a story which is untrue. [834 B] (ii) In the present case, the approver had no motive to convict him on the evidence of his accomplice. The fact that the appellant was got prepared by accused No. 1 did not make any confession of his own or even if it be accepted as true. It could not be said that there was corroboration of an pardon given by an accomplice. [873 B] Bhuboni Sahu vs King, A.I.R. , Emperor vs Emperor, A I. R. and Emperor vs Ram Krishna, A, I.R., , referred to. (iii) The conviction of the appellant on the testimony of the accomplice is no corroboration of his story because the knife was got manufactured by him from the deceased. [872 C] Bhurba Singh vs King (A.I.,R. and Bogoni Sahu v Emperor, L.R, , referred. (iv) In view of section 133 of the Evidence Act, it cannot be said to be a corroboration of evidence of the accused in material particulars and qua each accused. [871 C] (v) The fact of the confession is not a rule of law but a rule which requires some independent evidence, implicating the particular accused, is not an accomplice but only an accomplice, and in the absence of corroboration in material details it cannot form the basis of conviction. [878 E F] Bhoboni Sahu & Ors. vs Emperor (A I.L.R , approved.

The appellant was charged with the offence of having committed an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the defence version was put forward by the appellant in his written statement. The trial court found that the appellant had been guilty of the offence because he was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code and therefore, he was liable to be convicted under section 161 I.P.C. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The appellant could not be deemed to be a public servants within the definition of section 2(12) of that Act. [694 B] (ii) The words "public servant" in section 21, cl. (12) are wide enough to include every officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a Government company as defined in section 617 of the . [695 C D] (iii) The word "public servants" in the definition clause is not confined to public servants. It includes every officer, in the serv ice or pay, of a Local Authority or of the Government company, as defined by section 2 of the Act. Therefore, a person taking a bribe could not he said to be an officer within the purview of section 3 of the prevention of Corruption act. [625 E F] (iv) The expression "public Servant" in cl. 12 of the definition is wide enough and includes every officers in the services or pay. In the present case, the appellant was a public officer within his meaning of the second clause in section 2, Indian Penal code. He was an officer in service or paid the Government money to the Government and he was attached to the office of the Superintendent of the Salt Department. [613 E F]. (v) The mere fact that the respondent had been convicted as a public Servant under the Prevention Of Corruption Act does not make him liable for the offence.

The appellant was convicted under section 3(1) of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1964 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the order of forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appel lant was legal; (ii) the seizure of the same was without jurisdiction because it was not made in accordance with the law contained in section 114 of the Act and (iii) the High Court had no power to forfeit the juars. HELD : The order of the High court maintaining the order was ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law embodied in section 113 of the Indian Evidence Act. Rule 141(2) is in the following terms: "141 (2) If in the course of any judicial proceedings a question arises whether a person was duly informed of an order made in pursuance of these Rules, compliance with sub rule (1) shall not preclude proof by other means that he had information of the order, (ii). The fact that the rule is contrary to law contained under section 114 does not matter because section 43 of the Defence of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act. [273 E F] The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The Rules cannot be said to be ultra vires since it lays a rule contrary to an existing act does not matters because section 3 (1 ) is within the powers conferred by sub section (2).

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and acquitted him. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court in favour of Shri Ram. The State Government did not pay enough attention to the fact that he was a friend of the deceased who was also in charge of the murder of his brother. The Sessions Judge rejected the contention and convicted him under section 307 I. P.C., but acquitted him on the ground that he had no authority to give any evidence against him. The appellant contended before this Court that Sia, Ram and his companions were carrying guns and hockey sticks and therefore they could not be identified in an identification parade. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The circumstances that the Sessions judge did not accept the prosecution case of the appellant are wholly irrelevant. [10 D] 2. The fact that the appellant had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified, in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour. It is not enough if he was aware that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [11 E] 3. The circumstance that Siya Ram and the companions were carried by the appellant in a prosecution arising out of the crime, is not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the accused. [12 C D] 4. The mere fact that Siolet informed Sia Singh that he knew Sia Sia was not in any way concerned with the deep seated enmity between the appellant and the deceased would not make him a false statement. It may be that Sian Sia had voluntarily given the call. But it is not necessary that an identification of Siya Sia should have been made by the prosecution or by the accused before the court. [13 E F] 5. The evidence of SiO. P, who was riding on the Bicycle in the company of the respondent, Kunwar Singh did not implicate him. He could not say who had seen the appellant at the time when he was supposed to have appeared for the complainant in the particular case. [14 E F; 15 A] 6. The prosecution has failed to prove that Siyolet was real and valuable. It would be difficult to hold that the evidence of the witnesses was not sufficient for convicting the accused under section 107 I.p.C.[15 D] 7. The trial court had rightly relied on the evidence in order to hold otherwise.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted accused 2 on the ground that it was doubtful whether any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted him under section 304 Part I, read with sections 34, 34, and 34 of Indian Penal code.
