In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) It is well settled that a person who is charged under section 307 read with s 34 of that Code must be tried along with other persons named or unnamed, for committing the said offence. The object of the section is to prevent the commission and not to commit the same offence. [682 D] (ii) In the present case, the High Court found that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were acquitted by the trial court, they did not participate in the offence. They were convicted under s 302 readwith section 34, of the Penal Code. The conviction was therefore bad in law. [683 E F] (iii) It would be open to the High Courts to consider whether the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried will not necessarily displace the charge under section 149 because along with the two or three others convicted were others who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so had not been named. [684 F G] (iv) The High Courts should not be justified in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the High court by holding that the acquittal was not justified.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron ore, was granted import licence for Rs.20, 12,729 in favour of M/s Metalic metal Indus tries. The petitioner filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution before the Customs Authorities claiming that the goods were not liable to be released. The Assistant Collector of Customs and the Assistant Collector rejected the application on the ground that the petitioner had failed to prove that it was a violation of the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1)(b) of the Constitu tion. The Collector, however, dismissed the writ petition. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the rate of duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force; (ii) the petitioner was not entitled to claim the benefit of the notification under Article 31(1) of Constitution. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court HELD: 1. The relief under Article32 is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. [629G] 2. The remedy under Article 226 of the Consti tution is entirely different from the one under which the goods are cleared from a warehouse under section 68 on the date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation under section 51; (iii) The rate of customs duty, ifany, applicable, to any import goods shall he the rate, and valuation, in force on the dates on which such goods are actually removed from the warehouse. [625B C] 3. In a matter of this nature where liability of a citizen to pay a particular duty depends upon interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of the Act would breach fundamental right which entitle a citizen under Article 19(2) to seek recourse to Article 32. [613E] 4. The claim of the respondent for refund of duty is not maintainable in view of the decision of this Court in Union of India vs M/S Metalic Industries Ltd., ; and Union of lndia vs Union of indus trial, ; , relied on.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the Karta of a Hindu Undivided Family. The father died in 1947 leaving behind his widow and two sons. The property was sold to the appellant 's son who had been receiving a monthly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in execution of the payment order. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the joint family property but the trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale was under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, and that the property was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the father. The High Court in appeal held that the entire estate including the share of the sons was sold in pursuance of the decree passed by the trial Court and therefore the sale could only be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The liability of the son to discharge his debts of his father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the appellants to discharge them. [1901 E] (ii) The right of the appellant to make an order for partition under section 156 of the Act was a matter of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale and not the personal law of the parties. The liability to pay the debt of the deceased father which is not tainted by immority or illegality was based on pious obligation. [2001 E F] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that it was not necessary to implead the sons or to bring another suit if severance of status between the members of the family and the father was not an avyavaharika debt as it could not be termed as "partition" within the meaning of section 155.

The petitioners in this case were charged with offences under sections 8 B and 8B of the Delhi Administration Act, 1958 for having committed offences punishable under section 178 I.P.C. The petitioners contended that they had been denied the opportunity to cross examine the witnesses who were similarly placed at the end of the inquiry as opined by the Committee itself. The Committee submitted its report on the basis of the material available on record and other peculiar features of the case. The committee considered all the aspects of the matter and passed an order directing that the petitioners be given a hearing to them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Committee had not been properly constituted in accordance with section 8 B of the Act, who had to be examined at the close of the enquiry as opined. In the special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B and that they never intended to show any kind of discourtsey to the Committee in view of the facts and circumstances of the present case, all those persons to whom notices under section 8 had been issued were to be examine at the beginning of the Inquiry. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The report of the Committee dated 29th June 1988 after it was asked by this Court by its order dated June 2, 1988 to reconsider the whole question relating to the order in which the witnesses had to he examined is not a proper one for the petitioners to have been examined at that stage. [522C] 2. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section8B of Act. The Court has to consider whether the Petitioners were entitled as persons covered by section 7 B of Act, before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end Of the inquiry. If three persons are not examined at all, they would have been asked to get their evidence before the Committee. [525D] 3. The question whether a party has the right of cross examination or not is a matter which can be decided by the committee in accordance therewith. It is obvious from the order of the committee that the inquiry should have been held at the conclusion of the proceedings and the Committee should have taken its decision on the whole matter. [500E] 4. The inquiry has to be conducted at the stage of the inquiries and the witnesses are required to be cross examined before the Com missioner. If two persons are found covered under section 7B, then obviously they would not have been called upon to get an opportunity to get a witness for being examined till that stage of inquiry. [506F] 5. The enquiry is not envisaged in section 8(B) of the . It is only after the inquiry has been held that the enquiry should be completed within two months from the date of inquiry and if the Committee has found that the petitioner were covered under Section 8 B, then certainly he would have to be dealt with accordingly. [511F] 6.

The petitioners were carrying on business in motor vehicles and were plying the buses of the State of Rajasthan. They challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, as amended by the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles (Taxation) Rules, 1959. The petitioners contended that the Act was ultra vires the provisions of the Act and the notification issued thereunder and therefore the tax was beyond the competence of the legislature. Held, that the impugned Act is intra vires and void. The Act does not authorise payment of tax on fares and freights but only lays down what the amount of fare and freight charged. The tax is still on passengers and goods, though the amount is payable in lieu of tax calculated on actual fares and the maximum, it cannot be said that the legislature has imposed a tax on passengers. The proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 is extra territorial in nature because it makes the tax payable on fares or freights as the case may be. The word "tax" in the Act means the amount which is to be paid by the owner of a motor vehicle, and not by the person who pays it. The words "tax payable on fare or freight" are not admissible because tax on goods and goods though the measure of the tax is furnished by the amount, the amount cannot be regarded as a tax. The expression "tax on fares" in section 3(3) means the sum which is payable for the whole quarter immediately preceding any of the aforesaid dates. The State Legislature has no power to impose a tax under the Entry, and therefore it is beyond the legislative competence of Parliament.

The appellant company was retrenched from service on the ground that it had been retrenched by way of retrenchment. The Labour Court held that retrenchment was invalid for reasons found by the Labour Court and the workman were entitled to reinstatement with continuity of service. The management appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated. If after such a protracted time and energy consuming litigation during which period the workman was directed to be reinstated, the employer could not shirk his responsibility of paying the wages which the workman had been deprived of by the illegal or invalid action of the employer. [567D] 1.2 The Labour court has also awarded full back wages to the workmen on its finding that retrenchment is bad and the workmen continue to be in service. [568F G] 1:3. The award of the Labour court was directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August, 1974 with full back salary for the period of one month. The appellant company did not even have any notice of hearing before the Labour Judge and the respondent were given full back Wages. [569F G; 568A] 4. The Tribunal has also award awarding full back wage to the workman to be paid in two equal instalments. It is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad, and the employer can not shill the management 's responsibility of payment of wages which he had been depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised. [565F G].

The accused was married to Churi deceased in the village. The village was about 10 p.m. and at about 8 a.m., he went to the house of the accused and told him that he had been murdered by his wife. On the day of occurrence, the accused came to the village and started beating the deceased with a knife. The accused was also beaten by the accused. The deceased died on the night of occurrence. The prosecution case was that the deceased was married in the house during the night between 7th and 8th June, 1960. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302 I.P.C. but acquitted him. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that (i) the evidence on record established beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of Churi was recovered from the house where the deceased had been killed; (ii) the accused were not given any opportunity to explain the circumstances which led to his death and (iii) the High court erred in holding that the prosecution case against the accused was proved beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i)(a) The evidence on the record established that the accused had gone to see film show at Kotkhedkar of Chri and that the murder of the deceased took place after the accused left for the house. It is not necessary that the police was aware of the murder. The fact that the relations of the appellant with the deceased were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. [1039 C D] (b) The High Court was right in holding the accused guilty under section 304 Part I. P.C., and sentenced him to death. [1140 G] (c) The statement of the prosecution that he was taken by the police to the police post from the bazar cannot be accepted because there is nothing to show that the Police was aware about the murder and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi dead staying with him without the child. [1241 B] (d) The fact of the recovery of the dead bodies from the possession of the co accused can thus be established by evidence. [1342 C] (e) The prosecution has failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Churi died on account of which he was murdered. It cannot be said that the appellant had gone inside the house when the deceased came to know of it with the murder, and that he did not have a natural affection for the child and it was difficult to hold that he could have insisted on Churi 's presence at the place of occurrence in the residence of the other accused. [1442 C D; 1343 A] (f) The mere fact that Chri deceased was with him at the time of occurrence does not make any difference.

The plaintiff sued for a declaration that the properties mentioned in Schedule A 'A ' were liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was not maintainable under section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82. [195 H] (ii) The plaintiff 's only remedy is under section 93 of the Act read along with section 83. The suit must be dismissed as it did not fall within section 92. [196 A B] (iii) The words "subrogation" in section 82 are wide enough to include a claim on a mere techni cality of pleading when the substance of the thing is there and no prejudice is caused to the other side, however, clum sarily or inartistically the plaint may be worded. [197 B] The words 'subrogatement" have been used in section 92 only for the purpose of determining whether a particular property is liable to pay the whole of the balance of the property to the extent of the value of the interest, and in default of payment, limiting the liabilities of each item of property to that extent as it had been asked for. [198 B C] (iv) The expression 'subjective ' has not been defined in section 2(1)(a). It is only when a person has not used the word "subjec tion" he has asked in substance to give him a right to redeem the whole or part of the amount due on it under section 82, Transfer of property Act.

The appellants were appointed as Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka by notification dated 4th April, 1985. The appellants applied for the post of Asstt. Engineer (Civil). They were selected on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that they had not been selected in the merit list as they had secured more than 150 marks than the appellants. The High Court dismissed the petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The rules are clearly in violation of the ratio laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. SCC 491 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Haryana & Anr., ; , referred to. 1.2 In view of the fact that the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, it is clear that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of the total marks, the appellants before us were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merits list than the appellant. In view Of the fact the result was of the respondents ' case, the Rules are clearly not in violation or in violation thereof. [497B C] 1.3 The rules clearly in contravention of the decision of this Court on 4th September, 1991 and that the selections were made according to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the said selections. [498C D] 1:4 The rules have clearly in breach of the judgment of this court in Ashok Yadav & Anr. vs Union of India & Ors, ; , and Mohinder Singh Garg vs Union Of India & Anr, ; ; , followed.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the prosecution has failed to prove conspiracy because the deceased was a member of the family of the deceased; (ii) the evidence of P.W.4 is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial; and (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with Section 120 B I.P.C. is not sustainable. [415D] 2.1 The confession of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [413F] 2:2 In the instant case, the prosecution witnesses have not spoken about any confession. They have stated that they were meeting the deceased with his wife that day, the story of bribing the jail officials was not present when the deceased went to the jail. The prosecution has also led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadhan, Yadav was taken into custody following the raid on the Ashram. The appellant had been convicted under Section 302 readwith section 120B I. P.C., and sentenced him to death under section 120 A I.p.C.; and he was acquitted by the High court. [414F G] 2 :3 In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in the hands of the other accused persons. The trial court has also lead evidence to prove the complicity by the prosecution. [416C D] 2(a) In a criminal case involving murder of a person, the Court cannot start with the conclusion that the accused had established his guilt beyond all reasonable doubt and his conviction is not warranted. [411D] 3:1 The High Courts have failed to appreciate the evidence in every case but they have come to the con fession of the prosecution from the very beginning. It has also been pointed out that the evidence on record does not show that the appellant had an interview with his husband and his wife. In such circumstances, it is difficult to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [409E F] 2.(b) The prosecution case has been established by cogent evidence and there is no reliable evidence to establish that the deceased had an interviewed with his wives that day.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of textile mills. The factory was closed down on the ground that it had not been able to maintain its own accounts and that the factory was not in existence at all. The Tribunal found that the workmen were working as such in the same industry and therefore, there was no justification for fixing the wages. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the Tribunal erred in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wage scales and dearness allowance. HELD : (i) The Tribunal had not taken into account all the relevant factors including the total pay packet of comparable concerns. It was not correct to say that the total wage packet fixed by the Tribunal was too low as compared to the total wages of comparable concern with which the Tribunal had made comparison. [365 E F] (ii) The appellant company is a small scale industry and has been working in the different industries. In doing so, it would be just for the workmen to fix the same rates of dearness allowance for clerical and subordinate staff. It may be that the Industrial Tribunal should have taken into consideration all the factors including those which are relevant to the matter. But if the Tribunal has considered what is already prevalent in these concerns and also taking into account the trend in that region, can be successfully challenged so far as clerical and inferior employees are concerned. [366 E F; 367 A B] (iii) The Industrial Tribunal had no where considered what was prevailing in these two concerns. The tribunal had not specifically considered what the total amount of dearness allowances fixed by it as the maximum instead of 15 months which was usual so far the wage packet of the comparable concerns were concerned. It has therefore to be held that the average wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and dearness allowances. [367 E F, 368 A] (iv) The award in question is not based on any principle or principle. The appellant had no such power to fix a higher rate than the minimum. The fact that the wage for these categories in comparable concerns was that there were different scales of pay and dearness Allowance would be the same as compared with the total salary packet of similar concerns. [368 E] (v) The tribunal has not specifically taken into consider what was already prevalent at the time when it came to the conclusion that the industry was not a better wage than in comparable concern. It is true that the appellant company had been working as a manufacturer and there was nothing to show that the entire industry was being managed by the other three manufacturing concerns. But, in doing so the Tribunal must, when making comparisons take into account what was earlier prevailing in those concerns and not the total number of workmen. [369 E F]. (vi) The fact of the appellant 's case is that there are different scales for comparable concerns and the Tribunal should be given a liberal construction which would lead to the anomalous result.

The appellants were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa. The appellants filed a suit against the appellants for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances and for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage deed. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the appellants had not the right to redeem the mortgage. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants were entitled to redeem annappa 's share by adverse possession and the appellants could not claim redemption of the mortgaged property by adverse Possession. [601 F] (ii) The High Court was in error in holding that even if the mortgages were subsisting, the respondents could not acquire title by adverse posses sion. [700 G H] (iii) The right to redemption is a creature of statute and it cannot be said that the legislature intended to confer on the court power to grant or refuse to grant leave to appeal against an order passed by the subordinate Court. It was not correct to say that the Legislature intended to give such a new case. [701 G] (iv) The word "transfer" in section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as Shiddppa ' did not mean, in the absence of any specific pleading and cogent proof, that a notice of relinquishment given by the registered occupant must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than one. [750 B] (v) The words "transfer", in section 73 of the Act as Shreedappa 's name are not intended to convey title in the occupancy. The word 'transfer ' is used in the context of the document itself and it is not meant, in its absence, that the registered occupants must be given by a registered occupant. [751 C] (vi) The mere fact that the notice of the relinquishment was not made by the registra tioned occupant must be presumed to have been duly signed by the original occupant. That does not mean that the registration of the occupant must also be a valid notice on its behalf and, therefore, the registered owner cannot claim redemption by adverse title.

The respondent was a manufacturer of paper falling within the purview of Item 42 in the First Schedule to the Notification No. 1 of 1948 issued under section 5(1) of the Act, and was assessed at the rate of 2 per cent ad valorem for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 6, 1967. The respondent challenged the levy of tax on carbon paper under item 42 in a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. In appeal by certificate it was contended that carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that it could not be subjected to sales tax at the time of assessment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact that the word 'paper ' is used in the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 does not lose their character as a paper as defined in the Act or the Rules. [838 B] 2.1 The mere circumstance that the words "popular sense" are not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. It is only when it is held that the meaning which people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [8838 C] 2:2 The mere existence of a word in the statute or the rules, does not ipso facto lead to the conclusion that the article was paper as ordinarily understood. [939 D] 3.1 In popular parlance, the word "paper" has been used in common parlance and in common sense, it is used for printing, writing or packing purposes. It cannot be said that the expression 'paper other than hand made paper ' as used in Notification No 1 of 1962 is not decisive. [8939 D E] 3:2 In popular sense, the words are used in a wide sense. The word " paper" has to be construed in its popular sense and not in a technical sense. It must be given the meaning of the word in common usage or in the context in which it is understood. The dictionary meaning of 'paper" is not conclusive of the fact that it is an article used for packing, writing, or packing. [90B C] 3 1.3 In popular meaning, paper is not a part of a type writer but a small scale of paper. It may be a part and parcel of a bus in the same way, ribbon is not one of the type writer though it may not be possible to type out any matter without it. The use of the words 'poptical sense ' in common popular sense is not determinative of the questions whether the articles are paper as well as paper. [91C D] 4.1 It is a cardinal rule of construction that in popular parlance the word `paper ' means paper which is used as a medium or medium. The meaning of a particular type of paper is to be given to it, and not to be read in its ordinary popular sense. [92D E] In popular usage, paper does not mean paper as commonly understood as a whole but as a small piece of paper, which is intended for printing. It does not include paper as contemplated by Entry 2 of the said Notification. [93E F] 4:2. The expression ' paper ' in the common parlance or in its context in common law means paper used for paper and paper. The words "paper other wise" are used for the printing, sign or packing purpose. It has to include paper which may be used for making, writing and packing purposes, but not as a piece of substance. [94F] 4 3.3 The mere absence of the name 'paper in the definition of paper ' does not make it a paper. There is no force in the contention that carbon papers are not paper as envisaged by Entry 42 in First Schedule. [95G H; 996A] 4 4.4.

The appellant company was a private limited company. The appellant company had its registered office at Hapur and it had been running only one factory at Hapur. On February 2, 1955 the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents from service on the ground that they had disobeyed his orders of transfer and thus they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. 1 of 1956. The respondent contended that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents had not been given any opportunity to show cause against the termination of their services, they were properly dismissed by the management. Held, that the appellant company could not be transferred from one concern to another because it was not an express term of the contract of service between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant has the right to transfer the employee from one post to another, he must have been given a notice of termination of his employment. The question whether the appellant had the right or interest in the service of the respondents either express or implied that the employer had the inherent right to transferred the employees to another concern is really to make a new contract between them. The mere fact that the employee has the inherent power to transfer his employee to another does not prevent him from transferring an employee if he has the rights to do so under the contract or under any statutory provisions. The present case was one of law and was not one of substance. The case of the appellant was that there was no express agreement between the parties that the employees had been employed by the appellant with a view to injuring him and that it amounted to alteration in the conditions of employment.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. The appellant company had its registered office at Ahmedabad and it had its factory at Ahmedabad. It had its factories at Ahmedabad, Ahmedabad and Ahmedabad. In the year 1964, the appellant company made contributions to the provident fund of the employees ' State Insurance Fund which was utilised for the benefit of the workers. The contribution was not paid by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various other social welfare legislations. The employees ' union of India, a registered society, had its own funds and the employees were also members of the said fund. The company made contribution to the Provident Fund in respect of the provident Fund. The Employees ' State insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provisions for certain other matters in relation thereto. Section 28 lists the purposes for which the Fund may be expended are: (i) payment of contribution under the Act; (ii) payment or contribution under any other law; (iii) payment by an employer of contributions of the nature of those contemplated by the for the benefits of the employee. The Provident Fund was to be utilised for payment of provident fund and gratuity, and (iv) payment to employees under the , as well as the provident funds were not in force. The respondent company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the contribution payable under Chapter V A by the appellant Company for the period, May 31, 1969 to March 26, 1973 was illegal and ultra vires. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the contributions were not made in connection with any delayed benefit from the date of the notification issued under section 28 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contribution payable by the respondent company for the periods, May 30, 1969 and March 26. 1973 to March26, 1973 is illegal as the Act does not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant. [1089G] 1.2 The contribution under Chapter IV A by a employer of Provident Fund which is to be utilized for the purposes of the benefit to employees is not a tax and the Government cannot go on levying employers ' contribution under section 2(1) of the , on the basis of the very benefit itself and its connection with the levy. [1189G H] 1:3 The contribution paid by an employee under the Provident Funds Act constitutes only a fee and not a fee. The employer 's contribution under Section 2(2) is a fee, and not tax. The Government cannot come on levying employer ' contribution in respect thereof. [1290A B] 1 :4 In the instant case, the contribution paid to the employer by the company for these years was a fee which was a tax. It was not capable of any controversy that services and benefits were indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer in due course when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. [1390B] 2:1 The Provident Funds Scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they are, in the cases of employers who straightaway receive the benefits under the Insurance Scheme, their rate of contribution is lower. This contribution goes to a fund known as the Employees 'State Insurance Fund. [1490C] 2.2 In the present case, it was not possible for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect to which contributions are made, the employees would be entitled to receive the benefit under the scheme. The Act constitutes merely a fee but not a levy and not an tax. [1591G] 3:1. The liability of the employer to pay contribution under s 2(3) is not dependent upon any delayed payment from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the said Fund only.

The petitioners, who were working as daily rated workmen in the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. and their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The respondents challenged the order of absorption by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years even though there is no work for them; and (ii) since there was no work at all, there was a vacancy in the establishment to absorb the petitioners and the accumulated loss to the establishment as on 31st March, 1988 is Rs. 10,29,40583. Allowing the writ petition, this Court HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regularly workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same works is taken from him. [610G] 2. The principles of regularisation are of no assistance to the petitioners. The doctrine of regularisation has been evolved by this Court in several cases and there is nothing on record to show that there are no vacancies or work available in the Establishment for absorption of the employees and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid in spite of the fact being no work available for them. [625B C] 3. The petitioners are not regular employees, but are working on rolls. They are entitled to be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely on humanitarian ground so far as they are concerned. [613C D] 4. The Court has rightly rejected the petitioners ' claim and came to the following conclusion that there were no vacancies nor work available at all.

The appellants were the appellants in a suit for possession of certain properties. The appellants claimed title to and the recovery of possession of the property from them by virtue of a decree obtained by them against them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their title to the property and that they had not been estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by them under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that in view of the fact that the sale in execution of the decree obtained was not registered, the appellants were precluded from challenging the validity. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there had been no transfer of title to or possession of any portion of the interest in the property. In appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by 0. r. 12(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the trial court had erred in law in holding that even if the sale was held to be real, the full owner of the properties could not be said to have been an ostensible owner of a portion of it as the property was not affected by the proceeding in suit. Held: (i) The suit was maintainable under 0. 12 (i). The suit had been filed on the basis of a sale deed exhibit 12(ii) and the sale made by the High Court was not a valid one. The suit could be dismissed only if it was instituted within two years from the date of the sale, i.e., the date when the sale deed was effected and Pir Baksh who was examined as a witness admitted that the property conveyed under exhibit 12 (ii) with impunity was not the full owners of the land. The sale in question was not made out and was real. The mere fact that there was no mutation in the revenue records when this sale was effected, would not affect the validity or effect of the title of the parties being real and intended to pass title. (ii). The High Courts were right in holding on the evidence that the transaction was a genuine one and that it was not possible for the High Courts to hold that the deed was a valid document.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 173(4) and 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, for having committed an offence punishable under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and section 207A(3) of the Indian Penal Code. The trial resulted in conviction and sentence of the appellant. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 207 A(3), and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the provisions of sections 173, 207A and 207 A were not mandatory and they were not complied with. Section 173(1) was intended to be directory and it was only after the conviction and sentences were passed that the accused person had been prejudiced in his defence. The words "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 207 and sub section(3)(a) of that section are mandatory but not mandatory. The word "shall", used both in the sub section, is directory and because an omission by a police officer to fully comply with the provisions Of section 173 should not be allowed to have such a much reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. The use of the words "may" in sub s.(4) (a) and (b) of s. 207A, is not mandatory but only directory. The provisions of section 537(4)(a), (b), (c) and(d) are mandatory and must be complied with by a person who has been prejudiced by the omission to fully complying with the requirements of the code. In the present case, the trial had not been vitiated by any substantial compliance with the provision of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The appellant was the owner of a factory in which he was working as a contractor. The appellant filed an application under section 153A(1) of the , for permission to carry on the work of the factory and for the discharge of the effluent in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Special Officer rejected the application holding that the existence of a nuisance was not established by the appellant, but only a notice requiring him to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharged of the effluents in such manner as may have been previously approved by the Government and as mentioned in the notice so that rendering saline or corrupting the water of the wells, tanks, pondents etc. would be rendered nugatory. The respondent filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said Act on the ground that it contravened article 19(1)(C) of Constitution because it would be a reasonable restriction within the meaning of article 19 (1)(c) of that Constitution and was not reasonable in the circumstances of the case. Held, that the provisions Of section 153 A of the Indian Penal Code are to be read together and construed as including sections 153A and 153A of the Code of Civil Procedure. The provisions of section 153B of the Bombay Act are intended to give effect to the object of the enactment and not to affect the rights of a citizen under article 19 of the constitution. The scheme under section 154 is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence or otherwise of a public nuisance, and the provisions relating to the manner in which the discharge is to be discharged are not intended to operate as res judicata. The Act does not require that a judicial officer should act fairly and properly so as to give him an opportunity to show why he must not be ordered to arrange the discharge. The section does not contemplate any enquiry into the question whether a nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) exists or not but only to the direction as to what extent the discharge would be justified by the statute. The provision is intended to protect the interests of the community and it is not necessary that a Judicial officer should be given an opportunity of being heard before he can be called upon to comply with the requisition in the manner specified by the notice. The purpose of section 154A is to enable the subjective opinion of the municipality as to its existence or character of a Municipality, and it would not require a judicial officers of the rank of a District Judge to enquire and report only as to whether a particular nuisance was being carried on.

The appellant was a railway servant in the Railway Stores. He was found to be unauctionable and that he had purchased the property of the railway stores. The appellant 's case was that the goods were being actually used or intended to be used for the construction of railway stores, and that the railway articles were mixed with other goods in the bags. The prosecution alleged that the appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. The trial court convicted him under section 3 of the Railway Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles were being used or was intended to have been used for construction or operation of a railway. HELD : (i) The prosecution must be shown that the article was not in fact purchased or intended for use in the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. [192 G] (ii) The appellant failed in proving that the items were being taken by him for sale to Jullunder. The evidence showed that the respondents were 'brand new ' and that they were parts of an engine and that railway articles are mixed with others in the sense that they belonged to any particular railway administration. [195 G] In the present case, the prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. [196 G] The prosecution has failed to establish that the Articles were not 'goods ' within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. [197 B C] (iii) The evidence in this case was not called upon to prove the articles seized from the appellant. There was no evidence before the courts below to show whether the articles are being actually sold or intended by the railway administration and that it was only when they were found to have purchased the same day by the appellant for consignment to Jullund under the contract. [198 G H] (iv) The High Court erred in holding that the charges against the appellant were not proved.

The appellants leased the demised premises to Smt. Anandi, wife of the first appellant and the mother of the second appellant. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the ground that they had no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction would be passed against them. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal, but the High Court reversed the findings of the courts below and decreed the plaintiffs ' suit for eviction. In the second appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Smt. A. Anandia, wife, had leased out the demised property to her husband and the father of the appellant and she had no legal right to remain with him in possession since the termination of the contract of tenancy was by virtue of the provisions of the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of land and he is entitled to continue to remain In possession even thereafter. Dismissing the appeal this Court, HELD: 1. The right of a contractual tenant even after the determination of his contractual tenancy is by virtue Of the provisions contained in the Rent Act not liable for eviction as a matters of course.

The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The appellant Board, however, refused to grant the benefit of the Provident Fund Scheme. The Board 's financial capacity to implement the Provident Funds Scheme was not disputed by the appellant. The Tribunal held that the employees had the same and similar benefits and that they should be taken into consideration while deciding matters regarding benefits to be made available to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board 'Save as well as the fact that the burden of payment of gratuity and provident fund is on the employer like any other expense including wages and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Tribunal has rightly held that interest should be paid to the Government by the Board and should not be taken to be a part of it under the Act. [47 C] The Provident Fund scheme is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion while it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. It will certainly result in some reduction in profits; but if the industry is in a stable condition and the burden is calculated and it was pointed out that the interest of provident fund and gratuity did not result into loss to employer, the Board would have to be taken in view while deciding the matters regarding benefit to be given to its employees.

The respondent husband was found to be impotent and was unable to discharge the wife. The respondent filed a complaint against the respondent for an offence under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1973, alleging that she had been impotant and that her husband had been suffering from serious illness. The Magistrate held that the husband having been found to have been imporent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. In revision before the High Court, the respondent contended that it was now well settled by a long course of decisions of various courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse the wife 's consent to live in her husband and hence she was entitled to maintenance. The High Court accepted the contention and set aside the order of the Magistrate. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution, it is well settled that a husband can refuse to reside with his wife if there is a just reason for doing so. [707E] 1.2 The High Courts have not been able to compel the wife not to live at the time of refusal to live. This Court has also not been justified in interfering with the order passed by the Magistrate, and it is not open to any stretch of imagination that where a husband refuses to live without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a proper ground for refusal to reside in the husband. [607G H] 1:3 The High court has not been right in refusing to live separately with the husband merely because she is forcing her in a situation where her physical and mental well being might be adversely affected, as there was no intention on the part of the wife for refusal of live with the wife, nor that the conduct and acts of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife [708A B] 1 :4. The courts cannot compel the husband not to stay with the petitioner in a proceeding under the section to prove, not indeed cruelty as a ground for separate maintenance, but the conduct or acts of her husband from whom the Court can draw the presumption of neglect and refusal to provide an adequate relief to live together with the spouse. [700C D] 1 5. The Courts cannot compel a wife to stay in a proceedings under the Section to prove not merely that she is impotently, but also for divorce.

The plaintiff was the owner of a plot in the city of Bhavnagar. The plaintiff had been in possession of the said plot on 1st January, 1964. He had also prayed for damages for wrongful occupation in respect of the suit property. The Trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the plaintiff had not shown actual possession of any portion of the property and the defendants were entitled to mesne profits from the date of dispossession. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been filed within 12 years from the commencement of the Act, and that the period of 12 years had expired in 1963 when the suit came to be filed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The suit is for possession based on title to the suit land and the defendant has denied title to it. [222B] 2. It is not necessary either to deal with the argument of the defendants that the vesting was made in the Municipal Board or the State Government. In the instant case, the plaintiff has not shown any actual possession as a trespasser. The fact that the property was handed over by the Government of India to the State Govern ment only on 7th July 1952 and not on 7.7.1952 does not make it obligatory either to sell the land as representing the Government but also to take the income therefrom, shall be enjoyed by the Municipalities subject to the condi tions mentioned in the letter of the Government dated 10th August, 1965. [223C D] 3. The High Court was right in holding that possession of a portion of property was not taken by the Municipal Committee at any time. [225F] 4. In view of the fact that possession had been made to the plaintiff on 7/7.7, the suit is barred by time and that it was not necessary for the Court to give a finding on title of the plaintiff even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession. [226G] 5. The mere fact that some portion of land was with the defendant does not mean that the Municipality was formally handed over to the Government. It cannot be said that the municipality was actually handed over.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. He was employed as a labourer in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was thus performing a public duty. The appellant was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of Act II of 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under section 6(1) (d) of that Act. He pleaded guilty and was convicted by the trial court. The High Court held that the appellant was not an officer within the definition of public servant as defined in section 21 of the Act and therefore he was not a public servants within the purview of that term as used in section 2(9). Held, that the word "officer" in section 6 (1) of this Act includes a person who is appointed to any office for the performance of some public duty; but it does not include a person employed to exercise the duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is an officer of the Government. The words "any officer in the service or pay of Government" in the section mean "any person employed by him to whom he has entrusted with the performance, and includes any person employed in any office or pay or of Government". The word "office" in s. 21(1), Indian Penal code, means a person appointed to an office for performing any duty. It is not necessary that a person should be in the pay or service of Government to whom the duties are immediately auxiliary. The word 'officer ' in section 3 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II Of 1947 is one who was appointed to some office for performance of certain functions and duties immediately superior to those which he performed, though he may not be an officer.

The Respondent was granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69 by the Excise and Taxation Department of the State of Punjab. The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala C, being Civil Appeal No. 2944 of 1980 against the order of the Sub Judge. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not entitled to recover any amount from him under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The High Court dismissed the appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 59 of the code do not apply to an attachment and sale in execution of a decree. [975D] 2. The expression "such attachment or sale" in the said proviso refers to attachment and sales in any proceedings other than in execution thereof. The words "such attached or sale "in execution of such a decree" refer to the attachment and the sale mentioned in sub section(1) and that is, to attachment, sale in executing of such an order. [936E] 3. Section 60 provides for attachment and Sale in execution. The opening words of sub section 2(i) of section 60 are "the following particulars shall not be liable to such attachment or sales" as the case may be". The opening expression "any attachment or any sale" is "the same as the exempted by the said Act". [936F] 4. Section 59 provides that where a person has been granted a licence for carrying on business in any place outside the State, he shall be deemed to have purchased from him and had no other residential house and such building attached to it. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the said section and the half share of the Respondent in the property was not in execution or sale. [947F G] 5. Section 61 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not apply where there is a wrong law in deciding the appeal, but only where a wrong Law has been applied. The provision of section 59 of that Code does no apply to attachment. [948G H; 975A B] 6. The language of sub s.(1) is clear and unambiguous. The sections of section 61 are not applicable to an attached and sale under any of the statute made expressly applicable thereto. The two provisions of section 62 are not attracted to an attach and sale. The properties, if any, which are exempt from attachment and sold in revenue recovery proceedings under the said enactment would be only such properties as are so exempted by that Act. [943B C] 7. Section 58 is not applicable where a property is exempt from attached and sold. It is clear that section 60 of Code applies to attachment or Sale in any proceeding other than execution of decree of a civil court. The provi sions of section 63 of the Cr. P.C. do not make the provisions applicable to attachment as they are so exempt by the aforesaid Act. The effect of sub sec.(1 ) is that section has no application to attachment & sale in any proceed ings other than under execution of the decree of civil court, and the proviso thereto applies only to execution of decrees of a Civil Court.

The appellant, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1957 58 and 1959 60. The respondent claimed compensation in respect of the lands acquired by him under section 59(a) of the Act. The Assistant Collector held that the land had been undervalued on the basis of the valuation made by the Special Deputy Collector. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued to him under s.59(a). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had no locus standi to challenge the said notice and that the same was not maintainable as it was being prosecuted by the heirs of the deceased and Land References were pending in Civil Court at the relevant time. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had wrongly decided the issue against him and that he had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the respondent has merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Civil Court. [334E] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that it had wrongly held that there was escapement of assessment to duty because the land acquisition proceedings and Land references were pending before the Special Dy Collector. In the instant cases, the respondent did not estimate the market value of lands on the date of death of the respondent. [330F] 2:2 The High COurt has attempted to differentiate between the two categories of cases which are covered by the decision of this Court in State of Andhra Pradesh vs M/s. A. V. Valluri Kotayya & Ors., ; , and the High Courts had attempted to classify the lands as having been acquired for the purpose of determining the market price on the dates of death, but what is done was not a mistake apparent from the record of the case and as such the impugned notice was liable to be quashed.

The appellant was elected as Director of the Bank from the Brewery, Chandrapur District Cooperative Bank. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was declared elected on 18.8.1986. On 8.1.1987, the Deputy Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act, 1960, calling upon him to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of the bank as per provisions of Section 73FF(2) of Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act. The Deputy Registrar passed an order removing the appellant from the Committee of Directors. On appeal by the appellant, the District Deputy Registrar held that the appellant was defaulter under section 73FF (1) and (2). The appellant 's revision petition against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar on 30.8 .1989. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that Section 73F became applicable from 6.8, 1986 as per the Government Notification dated 18.4.1986 and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21.10.86, on 18th August, 1986, he was defaulter in presenti on the date of notice under section 77(1). The High court allowed the appeal holding that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter could not be considered to have ceased to be a member of the Committee and therefore the appellant ' s election as Director was not a defaulter. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 73 F(2)(b) is inserted by Maharashtra Act XX of 1986 with effect from 12.5.86.

The respondent was in service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. He filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the Government 's order dated December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to him by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government ' s order dated January 13, 1982 on the ground that the State Govern ment had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the action of the High court in reducing the pension by 50% was without jurisdiction and that the order of punishment was unauthorised and illegal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government has power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the said Rules. [33B] 2. The power to reducing or withhold the pension conferred on the Government servant under Rule 189 of the Act is not challenged either before the Court or this Court. It is only when a Government Servant retired from the service that he has committed while in service and the Government was entitled to withhold or reduce the pension granted to him. [34C] 3. The validity of Rules 188 and 189 of Bombay Civil Service Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules cannot be questioned either before a High Court or before this Court.[33D] 4. The order of the respondent 's authority reducing the appellant 's pension by fifty per cent was wholly harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against him. The Government had power to enhance the amount by 50 percent in excess of the penalty imposed to the respondent. [35E F] 5. The effect of the reduction of pension by a 50% is very harsh and excessive. The appellant has been given an opportunity to show cause against the order. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188, and 189. [36F G] 6. The action was taken for determining the respondent "s pension" and not on the proceedings which were initiated for determining his pension. The authorities were taken into consideration by the State Govt. for determining him 's Pension. The orders of the appellant dated December4, 1982 and December 4 1982 and directed that since the respondent had already retire from service a lenient view should be taken and reduction in pension to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made. [37F G; 38A] 7. The exercise of power by the Government under Rule 186 is not questioned either in the High Courts or before the Supreme Court. The impugned order reducing the respondent from 50 per month to 50% would seriously affect his living. [38E F, 39B] 8. The reduction of the pension is too harsh and commensurate to the charges proved against the Respondent. The decision of the government 's power to reduced or withhold a part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was in serv ice and the reduction in the pension to him after he had retired from his service. [39C] 9. The respondent has been deprived of his right to receive pension by way of pension, which he may have committed during the period of his service and that he had not been given any opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure prescribed in Rule 188.

The appellant landlord filed a suit against the respondent for ejectment of his tenant on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises and that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) was invalid in law. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant 's suit was incompetent as it was not maintainable in law, and so he came to the conclusion that the respondent 's action was without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that section 3 (4) read with section 16 of the Act did not apply to a case where the District Magistrate had acted illegally or with material irregularity or had wrongly refused to act. [563 E] (ii) Section 3(4) provides that before a District Magistrate can pass an order on an application made by the landlord for permission to bring a suit, he must satisfy two conditions: (i). The first condition is that the Commissioner should hear the application and give him an opportunity to represent his case before the application of the landlord was disposed of; (ii). In the absence of such a statutory provision, if it is held that the proceedings before the appropriate authorities contemplated by section 3 are in the nature of quasi judicial proceedings and they must be tried in accordance with the principles of natural justice. [564 E F] (iii) The words "the Commissioner shall hear the applications" occurring in section 3 of the U.P. Act, 1947, mean that the order passed by the District Magis trate is final under sub section (4). It must be made clear that in a given case an order has been passed without notice to the party affected by such order, it would be open to the said party to contend that an order passed in violation of the principles laid down in section 16(3), was invalid. [565 E F; 565 A B] (iv) The word "order" occurring therein must mean a final order and not final. It is only when it is shown by a party challenging the validity of the order that the authority concerned may pass an appropriate order. If it is found by a person who is not a District Magistra trate, the order in question would be a nullity and such a nullity. [567 E F]. (v) The language of section 3 is clear and unambiguous and it must be held that it must have been intended to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner.

The petitioner, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as an Assistant Secretary to the Government of Punjab. He was appointed on September 30, 1983 as an Additional District Judge. The petitioner challenged his appointment by means of a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that before making the reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of the alleged misbehaviour of the petitioner. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of dismissal passed by the President under Article 317(1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That is why the order of removal can be passed after the Supreme Court has on inquiry held in accordance with law. [642C] 2. The power of the President to make a reference to this court under Article 318(1), is not open to question as to whether the misbehaviour is of such a nature as to warrant the removal from his office. It is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme court and not by a Court of first instance. [643D] 3. The expression "the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commis sion" in article 317(2) of the Constitution means the Chairman or such other member as the case may be. It does not mean that the Chairman, or any person of a public service Commission can only be removed from his duties on the ground of misbehaviour after the President has passed an order under Article 316(1). [644E] 4. The word "the Chief Minister" in Article 317 (1) means the Secretary to Government of the State who is required to do so by the order or the President on the grounds mentioned therein. [6445G] 5. The words "the person concerned is not defined in the Act. They are not defined as a person who has been convicted for an offence under section 161, I.P.C. and he will have to suffer a decree for damages in a civil court. [6546A B] 6. The mere fact that the witnesses of any particular witness are recorded by the learned Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. [674B] 7. The High Court has rightly held that the order passed by President under article 317 (I) is without jurisdiction and it cannot be interfered with by a criminal court of the charge of assault because he had incurred the displeasure of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the hostility of the complainant. [665C D] 8. It will not be conducive to justice to decide the reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. The Court will therefore, record its findings which the parties lead before him within the constraints of the following guidelines: (1 ) The opinion of the High Courts is final and conclusive; (2) the opinion is final; (3) the reasons for the order made by the Governor are not relevant to the question as regards whether the opinion was proper or not. [684C D, F] 9. It would be open to the President in a reference under Article 319(1)(c) to make an reference to the Supreme Bench of this Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded and found on by the Court will be forwarded to the Registrar (Judicial) who shall have the opinion that the facts found by the Chief Justice are not sufficient to warrant his conclusion.

The appellants plaintiffs filed a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 for the declaration that the endowment was not a private one and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the trust was of a public nature and the idol installed in a temple was merely a family idol having no right to worship at the shrine of the deity. In appeal, the High Court held that the dedication was of private character and the temple being a public one, it must be held that there was no question of any religious endowment or a private trust. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact that members of the public were allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members of a family had a right to idol in the deity and that extensive properties are dedicated for the maintenance of the temple belonging to the founder himself. [833C] 2.1 The mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the endowment. It is manifest that when a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed therein, the worship of the idol is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the trust. [883E] 2:2 In the instant case, the question as to whether the religious endowment was of public nature or of a private character has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application. [934F G] 3.1 It is not necessary that every dedication should be made by a person who has no right, title or interest in the property or in the hands of the founders or their descendants. The fact that the founder of the institution did not make any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made on behalf of members of public to the temple cannot be said to be irrelevant and decisive. [900G H] 3:2. In a public endowment the dedication is for the use or benefit of the community, that is to say, whether the right to property is exercised as of right or not.

The appellant Bank was a contractor to the military and other authorities. The contract provided that the appellant would pay to the appellant bank out of his monies due to him under the contracts. The appellant bank then entered into an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The agreement was executed by the appellant with the Government in various departments on condition that the money due to the contractor would be paid out of the monies receivable under the contract. The respondent bank thereupon filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that there was no equitable assignment of the moneys due under the bills and amounted to an equitable assignment. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The agreement between the lender and the borrower was that the debt owing to the lender would be payable out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. [778 D] (ii) The contract with the appellant was that of borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. It was not necessary to mention in the agreement that the amount payable under the bill was attached by the Government. The document was produced before the court on July 19, 1948. [777 D] In construing the power of Attorney General it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and the Bank was that Of borrower and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. The words "any other person" in section 2(g) of the Act are clear enough to include a equitable assignment by the creditor. [779 E] (iii) In construing a document the intention of the parties must be gathered from the surrounding circumstances, that the relation of the party is that of the one and of the other. The relationship of both parties, two, is that the contract between the debtor and the creditor is that between the creditor and the debtor that the debts owing to him would be pay out of such funds. [780 G] (iv) In interpreting the power conferred on a person by law it is not necessary that he must have a right to attach it. The intention of parties is that there should be an agreement between them, and the relationship between them is that they are the principal and the principal. If the contract is one and the other, the relationship is that which is the principal or the principal, the principal is the main object of the contract and the relation is that it is the primary object of a contract. [781 E F] (v) The words 'any person ' in section 3(g), are clear and unambiguous. In construing an instrument the intention must be given its natural meaning. It is not possible to say that the agreement between a debtor and a creditor is one which is a principal or a principal, but it is only when there is a contract of agency that the creditor has to act in connection therewith. [783 E F; 784 A] (vi) The intention must have been that the parties were the principal object of each other.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuth not and Co. Ltd., The said company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the receipt in question was profits in lieu of salary. On further appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipts in question were profits 'in lieu of the salary ' and therefore the same was his salary as defined in section 17(3)(ii). The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the income from business property was not exempt from tax under section 14 of the Income tax Act, 1961. HELD: (i) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary because undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(1)(iv) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax under the head "income from other source" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 (ii). [441 B] (ii) The receipts of Rs 27,949/ by assessee in tho relevant accounting years cannot be treated as salary though undoubtedly that was an income and the same cannot be said to be either interest on securities. income from house pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. [442 C] (iii) The income in question is not salary and the amount cannot be held to be salary although undoubtedly that may be a income.

The petitioners, who were the owners of a large number of buffaloes and cattle, challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it infringed their fundamental rights under article 19 (1)(g) and was not reasonable in the interests of general public and that the impugned Act violated articles 14 and 19(1)(f) and (g). Held, that the provisions of the impugned Acts were valid. The Act did not contravene article 19(i)(g), but it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right to slaughter of animals and calves. The impugned Act was therefore void as it contravened article 19 of the Constitution. The petitioners had no fundamental right under article 14 of the Constitu tion, and they could not be said to have infringed their rights under articles 19 (I) (g), 19(2) and 31(3). The provisions of section 19(l)(g)(b) and section 19 (6) were valid in so far as it prohibited the slaughter of cows of all ages and calveves of buffaloes, male and female. The provisions Of section 19 were not unreasonable and did not offend article 14. The restrictions imposed by the impugned legislation were reasonable and valid. Held, further, that a total ban on the slaughter was justified in the interest of generalpublic and the Act violated article 19. The restriction imposed by section 19 was not unreasonable or excessive. The entire provision was not void as no reasonable restriction could be imposed on the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 31(1) (f). The impugned Acts infringed articles 14, 19(I)(g). The restrictions were not reasonable within the meaning of article 19 and were therefore invalid. The State of Bombay vs R. C. A. No. 63 of 1956 decided on December 12, 1956, followed.
