The respondent was a public limited company carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton and textiles. The Company had its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, and it had its head office at Jabalpur. The respondent was employed as an employee under the appellant company. He was served with a notice terminating his services by an order dated September 26, 1956, terminating his service. The appellant challenged the validity of the Standing Orders on the ground that they contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they were not employees within the meaning of the Act and were therefore violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the constitution. Held, that the Standing Order No. (e) did not apply to the respondent because it was an employee within the definition of 'employee ' in section 2 (1) of that Act and an employee who had no ticket was outside his purview. The Standing Orders were not applicable to him as they did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket number included in the departmental muster, he was not an essential characteristic of an employee. The definition of an 'employee" is not a term of employment for the purpose of the standing orders but it includes all persons employed by the employer or the workman as defined in the Standing order. The expression "workman" in section 3 (1)(e) means such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen by the management and under Standing Order NO. (f) the definition clause in Standing Orders is not applicable.

The appellant company was a company in the year 1964 65. The workmen of the respondent company claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1948. The Company claimed bonus for the years 1965 66 and 1965 67 on the ground that the Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment for purposes of section 16 of the Act. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project was a distinct establishment and therefore it was not liable to be treated as a separate Establishment for purposes for computation of bonus under the Act, but the Tribunal took the view that only one unit of the Company would be a separate establishments. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because alloy Steel project was owned, controlled and managed by one single company and, therefore, the point raised has to be decided on the basis whether under the proviso to section 3 of the Alloys Project is a separate unit for purposes. [640 F] (ii) The expression "any other establishment" in section 16(1) must be construed as including all units of a Company like Hindustan Steel Ltd., and, consequently, the question raised has no substance. [741 G H] (iii) The proviso to sub section (2) of section 3 is not attracted at all when the Act itself is inapplicable in view of the provision contained in section 1(2). [642 C D] (iv) The word "any" in the proviso means a separate and distinct establishment. It is only where there is no separate establishment that the Tribunal has to take into account the actual profit and loss earned or incurred by the company itself. [643 F G] (v) The words "any one unit" in sub section 2 of section 4 are wide enough to include all units which are not part of a single establishment for purpose of computation of profits under the .

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of rayon grade pulp a base material for manu facturing of synthetics or man made fabrics. The cess is payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column 1 of Schedule II to the Cess Act. The appellant company filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the levy of cess on the ground that the industries which were covered by Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Act must be construed as understood in common parlance and it should be given its popular sense meaning. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products" and not "processed vegetable products". The High court also held that sugar factories would come under Entry 15 only if they are covered by Item 15 of schedule I to Schedule II. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'vegetable product ' means product of or made of or out of vegetable. [526C] 2. The word "vegetables" is used in common sense and it must be given their popular sense. It is not a dictionary meaning but a dictionary. It has to be understood in the context in which the word 'veg etable ' is used. [525D E] 3. The sugar manufacturing activity does not, therefore, come within entry 15 of the Schedule I. [ 526E] 4. The Sugar manufacturing industry do not, however, come under Item 15. The question for consideration was whether the industries in which sugar manufacturing was covered by item 15 of Sch. 1 to the cess must be interpreted as understood by common parlance or that it should have a wider meaning. [25F G] 5. The term 'vege ment ' is defined in the Act as including any process, processing and processing. It includes any process incidental or ancillary to the manufacture. In order to bring an industry within any of these categories, the sugar manufacturing itself is not an industry for certain purposes and hence it comes within Entry No. 15. [26F G; 526A] 6. The notification dated 1st March, 1979 issued under the Cess act was intended to control water pollution and since the object of the Pollution Act and the Cess Acts were intended to regulate water pollution, the levy is not attracted. [27G] 7. The industry manufacturing sugar itself is a 'processing product ' and it cannot be given the meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining table for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. It would be difficult to say that the industry manufacturing industry does not come within the purview of Entry 15. Therefore, construction of sugar manufacturing industries do not come under entry 15. There is no question of any such interpretation. [28F G].

The respondent was a tenant of the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller passed an order directing eviction of the appellant from the premises. The respondent filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of his tenant on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that he had been using the premises as a residence and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up; (2) that the respondent bona fide required the building for carrying on the profession as a lawyer. The appellant contended that the practice of profession was 'business ' within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, and therefore, the respondent could not seek eviction of him on the basis of his requirement under section 10(1) (a)(ii). The Rent Control Tribunal held that the appellant was a 'business" within the definition of 'business. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the profession of an Advocate was not business within the ambit of Section 2(iii) (b) (iii) and, therefore, he could not be sought to evict his tenant under section 7(3) (c). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'business " is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of any person. [11C] 2. The word 'business means that it includes an activity which is carried on by an Advocate but not by an advocate. It does not mean that the word ' business ' has been defined in the Act in which it occurs and not in the context of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context. [12E] 3. The definition of "business" in section 10 (3) is used as inclusive of the term "business". It does, however, include any profession. [13F G] 4. The words 'business of an advocate ' are wide enough to include any business. The meaning of the word may be different from that of a profession. In the context in which the expression occurs and the word is used there must be something more than one. It is not possible to hold that all the provisions of the Act including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and section 10 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings ( Rent and eviction) Control Acts, 1960 are intended to include a profession of lawyers. [14H; 15A] 5. The term 'business includes any profession ' within its meaning. In a wide connotation so as not to include an profession, it is not necessary that the expression ' business should be construed in the light of the context or other statutes. [15B C] 6. The High Court was right in holding the word "business", and the High court erred in treating the words ' business" as a commercial one. [16C D] 7. The use of the words "business ' in section 2(3), (a) (ii) and (iii)(b) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease and Eviction ) Control Act 1960, the same meaning that the term may include any trade or business within its ambit.

The respondent, a partnership firm, was the managing partner of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 with interest at 6/9 per cent from the date of its dissolution till realisation. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the use of the word " deposit" in the roznamcha or in the letter dated 29th September, 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not be decisive of the question whether it was a case of deposit of the sum of Rs 4,000 and (ii) the suit was barred by time. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that there was no express demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 because the money was deposited under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. [577 B] The mere fact that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners, of India Supplies would not make it a case where the amount was deposited with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course. [578 C] (ii)(a) The words "any sum of money which may be in deposit with them" in section 2(g) of the Indian Contract Act are wide enough to include a claim for return of the money immediately. The expression "amount" is not defined in the Act. It is not necessary that the amount should be paid in the ordinary course of business. [576 C] In the present case, the respondent was not a party giving loan to the appellant for the obvious reason that the history of the transactions between the appellant and the appellant showed that it was the intention of giving the sum to the respondent.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under sub section (1) of section 3(1) read with section 3 (2) of the , on the ground that he had confined his arguments to one point settled in the writ petition. The petitioner challenged the validity of the detention order before the High Court which dismissed the writ peti tioner 's petition. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioner that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, and since the detenu was already in custody at the time of his arrest, he was not in jail at the most one day. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive detention. [845G] 2. The question whether a detention order can be passed against a person in detention if the detaining author ity is satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of detention was necessary for put ting him back in jail, does not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention.[846A B] 3. The mere fact that an accused in certain offences involving serious offences which are punishable under section 3 of the Act is not conclusive evidence cannot be taken away by the detaining au thority in making the order or detention. It is thus clear that the fact that a detenu is already in detention and yet he was sub jected to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided since it arises squarely in this case. [ 846A] 4. The facts of the instant case, there is no warrant for holding that summons under section 108 of the Customs Act was in existence. [873B] 5. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there were no summons or the detenu having been orally ordered to attend office by authorities concerned the authorities, it cannot be said that summons and detention had been validly made. The detaining authority was aware of the fact as to whether the detenu 's detention was in jail for a period longer than one day and he was also subse quently satisfied that the detention was not necessary. [872C D] 6. In this case, the petitioner is al ready in detention. He has been remanded to judicial custody on the 27th of February, 1986 with direction to be produced before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the 28th of Febru ary, 1986. The order of remand was made by the Additional District Magistrate and before the actual service of the order was served on him. [871D] 7. In these circumstances, there was sufficient cause for holding the detention of the petitioner in the higher forum. [870E F] 8. The detenu is al just to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining autho risedly satisfied the court that his detention was neces sary.

The petitioners are working as casual labour in the Telegraphs Department. They were engaged on daily wages for the last ten years as casual labourers, and they have been denied the benefits of the scheme. The petitioners contended that even though many of them had been working for the first ten years, they were not entitled to any benefit under the scheme, since they had been employed in regular employment of the Posts and Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have not been denied their benefits. The Union of indus trial contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour, they are entitled to the same privileges as regular employees of the Telegraph Department. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners belong only to the categories of casual labourers and are not being regularly employed on daily wage basis. They are not entitled for the same benefits which the regular employees are enjoying. [608B] 1.2 In respect of categories (ii) and (iii) i.e., for those who have been continuously working for more than six months, the revision is done as and when DA/DA/added. The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to the casual labourers who are employed on regular basis. [613C D] 1:3. In respect to categories (iii), and (iv) i the above arrangements of enhanced rates of regular wages will be without prejudice to absorption of casual workers in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period of more than 6 months. These enhanced rates are applicable to the semi skilled/skilled labour who strictly conform to the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210 270 and Rs.260 as the case may be and that there should not be any variation in the respective job. [625E F] 1 :4. The arrears of wages payable to the workmen who are working for a period more than one year in the Posts & Telegraphs Departments at the rates equivalent to the minimum pay in the pay scales of regularly employed workers in the corresponding cadres but without any increments with effect from 5th February, 1986 on which date the first of the two petitions, was filed.

The appellant, a registered firm, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessment proceedings were started against the appellant for the assessment year 1950 51 and 1951 52. The appellant filed returns in respect of the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52 and 1952 53. The Income Tax Officer held that the appellant had failed to file a return within the time fixed by the notice under section 22(3) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer but the Appellate Tribunal upheld the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since he had submitted a return under section 24(2), the assessment proceedings commence either with a notice under s 22(1) or with the filing of a return showing an income below the taxable limit, and that the notice must be treated as a return of taxable income. HELD : (i) The notice under the section was issued within the period prescribed by section 24 (2). The notice was not filed within the prescribed time fixed under section 23(3), but only filed on the date when the notice was served. [120B] (ii)The appellant had submitted his return showing a non taxable income at the relevant time and that he had no opportunity to file it before the assessment was completed. The notice must therefore be treated in as a notice of demand under section 34(1)(a). [120C D] (iii)The notice under sub section (1) of section 24 is served on a person who thought that he has a taxable income and therefore a return should have been filed within time. [122E] (iv) The appellant had not submitted a proper return in accordance with the notice issued under section 25(2). [123F] (v)The word "assessment" in section 24 of the Indian Act means a return which is made by an assessee for the purpose of filing a return and not a return filed under that section but filed under section 26(1). The assessment proceeding commenced either with the return or with a return called for under section 27(2) or even under section 29(3). [122G] (vi)The words "assessment", in the context, mean "assessment". In the case of any person whose total income is, in the Income Tax officer 's opinion, of such an amount as to render such person liable to income Tax, the IncomeTax Officer may serve a notice upon him requiring him to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days. [123H] (vii)The expression "assessment " in section 22 (1)(b) means assessment made by a person on whom he has no taxable income or profits and gains chargeable under that Act but is assessed on the basis of his total income. The word " assess" in the section means assessment of an assessee, whether filed within a period not exceeding sixty days, and the Incometax Officer may give notice to him of such assessment.

The Central Government framed the Employees ' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952 for the establishment of a nationalised bank. The Central Government by its notification dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued under Section 9 of the Employees Provident Fund Act, 1948, appointed one Director of the Reserve Bank to function as the Regional Controller of the respondent bank. On 30.3.1984, the Central Government issued an order dated 23rd August, 1984 (Annexure B) appointing the employees of the appellant bank as its employees on the basis of their choice between the two modes of appointment and the choice between them. The appellant bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act contemplates both election and nomination of members of the Board of Directors and the option to choose the representatives of the employees, and that the choice of the mode of appointment is left to the Central Govern ment as well as the choice by the choice. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the scheme envisaged both election or nomination must be such as would be furtherance of the object of the legislature as to the composition of the Boards and the determination of their respective choice in the selection of their representatives, and the method of appointment was not such as to restrict the choice to the three persons specified on the panel furnished by the representative union. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme envisaged by Section 9 is a statutory provision and it must be reasonably exercised so as to give effect to the true intent of the Legislature as to composition of Board of directors. [561C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Act requires the Central Govt. to make a scheme in consultation with the Reserve bank for the constitution of the board of Directors so as not to appoint the true representatives of employees and other speci fied categories. The mode of election or nominations must be by way of nomination, and if election were to be construed to give the best form of repre sentation to every category of persons mentioned in the Act. [560D E] 1:3. In view of the legislative intent as disclosed by the Act, the scheme contemplated both election, and nomination, it is not possible to hold that the Scheme would be a mere formality. The scheme contemplated by Section 10 of the Act must be so construed as to include representatives of all employees mentioned in section 9. [559E] 1.(4) It is open to the State Government to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it was incumbent upon it to continue the present scheme in such a way as to provide the best mode of choosing the representatives. The Act also provides that the Central government may make rules for the purpose of constituting the Board and the procedure for appointment of members is to enable it to reasonably exercise its discretion in such manner as to render the provisions of the statute ineffective.

The respondent was imposed penalties under section 255(6) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the penalty but the Appellate Tribunal held that the Tribunal had no power to stay the proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the absence of any express provision in sections 254 and 255(5) of Act, the Income Tax Officer could not stay the recovery proceedings as he did not appear at all before him. HELD: The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. [682 D] In the absence Of any express provisions in sections 255 and 255 of the Act, no such power can be exercised by the Tribunal except on certain specified grounds. It is not necessary that an order should be made more than one way or the other. The High Court was right in holding that the Appellate Assistant Commission had the power under section 256 to stay proceedings relating to recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. [625 E F] In a case where the appeal is pending before the Appellate Tribu nal, it may well be said that when section 254(6), as it stood at the relevant time, confers the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as would prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory.

The respondent was officiating as a Sub Inspector of Police in the District Magistrate, Gonda. He was charged with having committed offences under section 7 of the Police Act and was convicted by the Sessions Judge, Gonda, under section 5(1) (a) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his petition for quashing the order of dismissal on the ground that the respondent had been officiating as Sub Inspector in the discharge of his duties and was therefore not liable to be proceeded with by a police officer senior in rank to a Superintendent. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court was right in holding that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect of the matter which was the subject matter of the departmental trial. The order of discharge passed by the District Magis trate was only administrative orders and not judicial orders. The mere fact that in the course of the enquiry the respondent was incharge of the police station, did not affect the validity of the order. The State of U.P. vs Ram Chandra Singh, ; , followed. Held, further, that there could be no doubt that the departmental inquiry was only a preliminary inquiry and the departmental enquiry was only an administrative inquiry and not a judicial enquiry. The departmental inquiry is only a continuation of the disciplinary proceedings and it does not affect any question whether the departmental proceedings were in the first instance received by the Magistrate and forwarded to the police for inquiry. The fact that the Superintendent of Police gave at first a good certificate to the respondent, in respect whereof he had been charged, was not a matter which could be said to have been committed by him.

The appellant was appointed as a Deputy Director of Health Services in November, 1965. He was promoted to the post of Deputy Director, Health Services and later promoted to that post on December 8, 1971. The appellant challenged the promotion before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that since he had been promoted to supertime grade II by conversion of one post from unspecified Specialists ' Grade I to a specified post in the cadre of Deputy Directors, it was not open to him to challenge the promotion as being violative of article 16. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion on the basis of his appointment to the said post and that he should have been promoted from that date. In appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the order promoting him to super time grade II was made in November 1965; (ii) the promotion of Dr. P. Sen was not made in accordance with the relevant rule; and (iii) the post was not a teaching post in any particular cadre but was a teaching cadre which meant specified in the speciality in which a need had been felt from amongst those in the specialists ' grade or general duty officers ' grade. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was fully qualified for being promoted to this post. He must be considered eligible for promotion from that year. [53E] 1.2 In passing a contention of the appel lant that all 28 posts which were deducted from the strength of permanent posts in Specialists" grade or specialists" posts were treated as "extime grade" and not "ex time scale". The appellant had been fully qualified to be promoted to such post. [54F] 1:3. In passing the impugned order, the appellant would be the senior to Dr. Sen and was fully eligible for being considered for the post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for promo tion to super hoc grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists. [55F] 2.1 In passing of a contention, it would be open to the appellant to challenge that order if some one who is already in that grade is transferred to the newly created post and the post vacated by such transferred employee is offered by way of promotion which in fact was done in this case there is any violation of the rule. [56F] 3.2 The appellant would not have been qualified for promotion to super Time grade II in February 1971 from the date he claim as being considered by him. He would be eligible for appointment on that account alone, if he had put in 10 years of serv ice in the post held by him and was given the benefit of promotion at the time when Dr. D. Sen became available.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) was enacted to provide for the acquisition of land in excess of the permissible limit. Section 19B(4) provides that no person shall acquire any land by inheritance or bequest or gift from his own source, except under a registered deed or settlement any land held by him as an heir by inheritance. The Act provided for the compulsory acquisition of lands in excess thereof and section 19B provided for payment of compensation to the heirs of the deceased son or wife. Section 10A provides that the Collector shall be competent to utilise any surplus area for the resettlement of tenants ejected, or to be ejected under clause (i) of sub section (1) or section 9. The appellants who were displaced from West Pakistan filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the land inherited by them and later transferred to their sons and wife was not hit by section 10A and section19B(2). The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the lands inherited by the son or husband were not hit under section 10 A and section 9B had no application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Act did not provide any machinery for determining surplus area and since by gift to the son, the land acquired by him and later transfer to his sons and husband were neither hit by the ceiling set out in section 19 B(4). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1954 is to see that no one held in excess than the permissible area and as such there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [632E] 2. Section 9B provides for compensation for the surplus area. It provides that if after the commencement of the Amending Act, any person acquires any land under section 19A(1) he may acquire any right or interest in any land and which with or without the lands already owned or held by such person exceeds in the aggregate the permissible extent of the available area which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. The provision is not intended to give some time to the heir to ascertain the assets he has inherited, made the choice of his 'reserved area ' which he wishes to retain. [732G H] 3. Section 18B provides that any person who has been allotted land within a prescribed period shall be ignored. The section does not provide for any time to be determined by the Collector. It is only when after the coming into force of the amending Act, April 15, 1953, any persons acquires any right by inheritance, gift or gift which, with the lands previously held by them exceed in the permissible limits, that is, the surplus pool will be ignored and the surplus land acquired will not be affected by the prohibition contained in section 10 B. [700H; 700A] 4. The object of the legislation is to give certain time to a person who acquires any property by inheritance from his source. It does not make any difference whether he has acquired any right, title or interest which he can have been declared as surplus land. The legislature has provided for an exception to section 19(B) and it is not necessary that the provision should be made in the Act. [ 700A B] 5. Section 20 provides for the payment of the compensation to a heirs of a deceased son, who has acquired the right of inheritance or gift, which with the land already held by the deceased, is entitled to make a declaration of his lands within a period prescribed time. The purpose of the statute is that the provisions of the Land Act are not intended because the legislature has used the words "for the benefit of the heirs" and it cannot be said that the legislature intended that the Legislature should have intended that such a provision should have been made in respect of the surplus lands. [750B C] 6.

The appellants, who were the eldest member of the family of the appellant, filed a suit for possession of the lands in dispute on the ground that they had been dispossessed by the defendants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were entitled to the estate of the deceased father and that the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari land was binding on the plaintiffs. The High Court held that the suit was barred by section 14 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the Governor dated August 30, 1951, declaring the appellants as the successor on the death of the appellants was not a nullity and the decision was binding upon the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the decision could be filed within two months from that date. [334 B] (ii) The High Courts were in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded to the appellants. The order dated August 3, 1951 set up by the appellants did not operate to deprive the plaintiff of the right to those lands or compensation payable in respect thereof. [328 C D] (iii) The decision of this Court in Ram Narain Singh vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. (iv) The suit was not barred by the decision on the question of title. The decision was based upon a rule of primogeniture and it was not open to the High Court to interfere with the decision unless there is some evidence to show that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of the power conferred by section 3 of the , as required by section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in dispute. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of rent from the appellant on the ground that he had been using the premises as a licensee and had not paid the rent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenancy was not governed by the provisions contained in section 12(3)(a) of the Act, but that the suit was governed by section 12 (3) (a) and (b). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 12 were applicable only to a dispute raised within one month from the date of service of notice under section 12. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay High Court in Ambalal 's case held that the dispute as to standard rent is to be raised within two months from the service of the notice and therefore the suit is governed by sections 11 and 12(1) (b) of Act. [630B] 2. Section 12(2)(a), (b), (c) and(b) are not confined only to the dispute raised in the suit but also to the question whether the suit has been filed within one year from the time of service. The provisions contained therein are as follows: "In any case where there is a dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act, the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2) he makes an application to the Court under sub section(3) of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount of rent or permit increases specified in the order made by the court. The Court may make an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court forthwith such amount of the rent as the Court considers to be reasonable, if he is satisfied that the tenant is withholding the rent on the grounds mentioned in sub s.(2) of s.11. [ 630B C] 3. Section 11(4)(a)(b) is not limited only to an dispute raised by a landlord and it is not enough to raise a dispute for the first time in the written statement. The Act does not contemplate any dispute as regard standard rent. It is only when there is dispute as between the parties that the question of standard rent arises. [ 631B] 4. Section 13(3), (a), and (c), are not limited to a disputed dispute raised under one month before the date on which notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute, as contemplated in section 11(2) (d). The Act is intended to give the tenant a right to dispute the standard rent in the event of a suit and if the tenant raises a dispute in answer to a suit, he will be entitled to raise the dispute. [625E F] 5. Section 10(4) (c)(a). does not require that the landlord must make an application within one months from date of the service on the tenant. The landlord can claim protection from the operation of section 13(1)(b), and he is bound to pay or tender rent in court immediately such amount as the court considers to have regard to the provisions under section 11 (4) and section 12, and it will be open to him to make an appropriate order directing that the tenants shall deposit in court forthwith such amounts as the trial Court may specify.

The respondent company was a director of the respondent company. The respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the company and the appellant as its directors. The directors of a company were appointed by the Board of Directors of the Company to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd., and the respondent was appointed by them as directors of that company. In exercise of the power conferred by article 105 of the Constitution, the respondent issued a notice under section 21 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 read with section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to the appellant for being declared an insolvent and on his failure to make any such declaration, the directors of respondent company nominated by the Aluminium Company as directors. On the question whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the directors were entitled to a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of that Act. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to the controlling interest of the appellant in the respondent 's shares held by him in the company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the Respondent company and as such, he could not apply either of the tests mentioned above, be said to have a controlling interests in the Company when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority of the shares which under the articles of association of the companies, carry the right to vote. The appellant was entitled to have the controlling interests of the respondents in the appellant 's company.

The respondent was promoted as Accounts Superintendents on the basis of seniority cum merit. He was promoted to that post with effect from 1st November 1956 and he was confirmed in the post of Accounts Superintendent on the ground that he had not passed the examination. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969 which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the resolutions and holding that the respondent was exempted from passing the examination and therefore he could not be denied on the grounds of delay and laches. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Resolution dated 5th January, 1970 is not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the resolution it cannot be said that the allottees are exempted from pass ing the Departmental Exami nation. [512C] In the instant case, the Resolution was passed by the Board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Government referred to in the Resolution itself. The Resolution did not apply in the present case as the Regulations framed under section 79(c) were not applicable to the allottees and mere because the allotment was made prior to that date would continue to be insisted in future also, and if passing of the said Resolution was not challenged by the appellant, it is incumbent on him to pass the Departmental Examination. [511C D] The resolution did not refer to the Regulations which were framed under Section 79(a) of the Act.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the death sentence on the ground that the death penalty imposed by it had been grossly disproportionate to the value of human rights and that the petitioner 's father, who was a citizen, was entitled to compensation for the loss of his life. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the State had failed to prove its liability to pay compensation in this case since it was found to be a custodial death. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the judgment of the Supreme Court in Rudul Sah and others vs State of Bihar and Anr., ; relied upon. The State has not disputed the liability of the State for payment of compensation in respect of the loss suffered by the petitioner. It is also submitted that the High Courts have not committed any error in law in awarding compensation to the petitioner, since it had not been established that the deceased was a custodial life and that award of compensation was grossly disproportionate. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The relief of monetary compensation as exemplary damages for contravention of human right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution is a remedy available in public law by way of penalising the offender. [608C] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioner was not entitled to any compensation in view of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitu tion. The payment of compensa tion in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental right of the citizen. [625D E] 2:2 The compensation is in the nature of exempellary damages. It does not mean that the amount of compensation is to be determined by way or by way off a civil suit or criminal proceedings. This Court and the High courts being the protectors of the civil liberties of the citizens, have not only the power and jurisdiction but also an obligation to grant relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of the Consti tution. [613E F] 2 :3 The compensation in such a case is not the same as it may be available as a defence in public interest.

The petitioner, a prisoner in Jail, was convicted by the Chief Justice of India for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death for an alleged offence under s.302 Indian Penal code and the petitions filed by him to the President of India were dismissed by the President on the ground that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution was not an absolute right nor indeed did it confer any right on the press. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court. The High Court held that the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19(i)(a), of the Constitu tion, which includes the freedom of the Press and the right to free speech and to free expression was not absolute right but only limited to the freedom conferred by Article 14 of the constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the right claimed by the petitioner is not the right of the press but the right guaranteed under article 19 (1)(c) of Constitution which includes freedom of press and that the freedom guaranteed by article 14 of that Constitution, which include the freedom to speech and order, must be restricted to the free speech. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right claimed in the petition is not a right to express any particular view or opinion but the rights conferred by articles 19(l)(a). [1187D] 2. Article 19 (i) of our Constitution which provides for a search of the person who wants to interview a prisoner, does not require that the press should be interviewed. The right is not absolute and cannot be restricted only to the right conferred by the Press. It does not provide that no newspapermen will be allowed. [1188E] 3. Article 14 is an absolute one and is not an unlimited right but is an unfettered right. [1102D] 4. The fundamental right of freedom of expression conferred under article 14 is not only a right but also a right which is guaranteed by the Constitution. It is not, therefore, open to any person to express his views on the subject or the right asserted in the grounds of detention. [1089F] 5. Article 21 of the Consti tution does not contemplate that no pressmen will he allowed to be interviewed and, indeed, if it were to appear that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be selected, it would have been impossible for them to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed to interview the two convicts. [1012G] 6. The petitioners are entitled to freedom under article 21 of our constitution. They are free to move freely and without any justification. [1003B] 7.

The respondent was the owner of a tea garden. The appellant filed a suit against the Receiver and the appellant praying that the receiver should furnish security for the amount due under the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but the High Court in revision set aside the decree on the ground that the Receiver had no jurisdiction to enforce the surety bond executed by the appellant as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office nor the assign of the District Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the order for recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the receiver could be executed against the appellant only when the Receiver took possession of the property. HELD: The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond were pending before him. [360 F] The surety bonds were executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending at the date when the receiver took possession. The surety 's liability to make good the loss caused to the tea garden by fire was also a part thereof. The sureties bond was executed in the same manner but it was impossible to accept the contention that the appellant had committed default in payment of the mortgage and therefore the order was not binding on him. The bond was not executed in accordance with law. [361 F G] The bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the presiding officer of the court. But the Subordinate Judge was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the bond as the District Court himself.

The appellant was a dealer in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller, Uttar Pradesh. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants and rejected the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. The High Court held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of the U .P. Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "sale" in section 2(h) of the Act means the money consideration for sale of goods and includes all other sums received by a dealer as may be authorised by him in that behalf. [581 F] Ram Bilas Ram Gopal vs State of U. P., ; , followed. (2) The definition of 'sale ' in section 3(h), is wide enough to include the price paid for goods, and it includes all sums received from the seller to the buyer. The expression 'sale" has been defined in the U P. Sales tax Act. [580 F] (3) The word 'sale " in section 4(h)(f) means a sale of property in goods, or a transaction in which goods are to take place at a future time or subject to some condition thereafter to be fulfilled. The definition is wide and covers all kinds of transactions including the price for delivery of wheat on hand, and he has also to supply to the State Government 50% of the quantity of wheat procured or purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of the Order until such time as the State Govern ment otherwise directs. [583 F G] Rameswar Ram Gopal 's case (3 ) The definition in section 5(h). does not justify the view that even if the liberty of contract in relation to the fundamentals of the transaction is completely excluded a transaction of supply of goods pursuant to directions issued under a conciliator, it would be open to the assessee to contend that even though the liberty was given by the latter, the tax payer was under the control of the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the definition of the word 'Sale ' in Section 2(g) of U P . Sales Tax. Act, and not pursuant to the directions issued thereunder. [584 F G; 584 A B] Ram Dhani Ram Gopal & Ors. vs State Of U.p. ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Advisory Board had not been constituted within three months of the date of detention and hence the detention should be upheld. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The report of the Advisory Boards is more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order of detention, though it was within three weeks from the date when the order was made. [206E] 1.2 In a habeas corpus proceeding, it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date on which the report or its opinion regarding suffi cient cause for detention was required to be obtained within three month of the first order of the second order of deten tion. [207E] 2.1 In a case where a detention order has been made under the Act, the State Government shall, within three days from the first date of the third order of detain ingly detain him on June 23, 1986 and thereafter submit a report of its opinion about suffi sition for the detention. [208E] 3.2 The Advisory Board is more or less than three months after the date o f the second detention. If the report of such an Advisory Board has been obtained within the period of three months from the said date, it will be no answer to that contention. [209F] 4.3 In a writ petition filed by the detenu under Article 226 of the Consti tution, the High Court was not confronted with the present situation at all. The report is not made within three years from the second date of his first order. If a reference to an Advisory Boards has been received within three calendar months from that date it is no answer either to say, that the report though not obtained within 3 months, was made before the hearing of the case. [210F G] 5. The fact that the opinion of the advisory Board is not taken into account does not affect the validity of the detention order. It is not necessary to allow the appeal and quash the order.

The petitioner, the father of respondent No. 1, was a minor. He filed an application for setting aside the award on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to defend himself and that the entire responsibility of the arbitrator will lie on him and that he has taken the responsibility. The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had failed to prove his case beyond the period of limitation, and that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In the special leave petition filed against the order of the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the notice was given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, (i) the notice dated 20th January, 1977 in respect of which the award had been made was not set aside under section 30 and (ii) the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. Allowing the special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to arbitration. [540D] 2. The petition for setting out the terms of the contract was signed by two parties, about which there was nothing in the agreement to refer them to arbitration, and therefore, the award is not liable to be set aside. [541E] 3. The judicial Committee held that the conduct of both the par ties that there were an arbitration agreements and by sign the award the respondent had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20.1.1977 in respect thereof. It was clear from the recitals of the agreement that there had been an arbitration clause and by signed the award itself, it could not be said to have committed any breach of contract. [543E] 4. The Judicial Committee held in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case can certainly be construed to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of Act. But in the present context it is clear that the course in which the proceedings under the Act are conducted and without an exception to the provisions of section 3(a), has made lawyers laugh and legal philosophers weep. With respect to which there is no factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the party had agreed upon refer the disputes to arbitration of the named arbitrator. [544E F] Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Shri Kali Nath, ; , referred to.

The appellants were the mortgagees of certain properties in suit No. 1, who had mortgaged some of the properties in favour of the appellants. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from them on the ground that they had not received any notice under section 28 of the Act and that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the application made by the appellants to the Subordi nate Judge was incompetent as the appellants were not parties to the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The words and that they have not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of section 28 make it clear that in exercise of the powers conferred on the court or to be exercised either in any suit to which the Act applies, the Court has reason to believe that the exercise of one or more of the power will give relief to the borrower. [586C] (2) The expression "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the commencement of this Act" does not mean a proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of Section 2(22). [596E F] (3) The word "suit" is used in section 2(23) as amended by the Calcutta High Court. It is clear from the language of the said section that it is not intended to include a proceeding which is pending before the court. [591C D] (4) In the present case, the appellants had no right to claim exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section (1). The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in the passage quoted above are clear and unambiguous. [606E] (5) The language of section 2 (22) is plain and unambiguous and it is clear that the words and the words "any suits or proceedings instituted or pending on that date" are not intended merely to include any suit or proceedings which are pending before that date and includes a proceeding relating to the same matter. [616E G] (6) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent as sub mortgagee was an assignee of the mortgage debt and of the mortgagor 's right to recover the debt from the original mortgagor.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. He transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint family. The appellant 's father died in 1949 leaving behind his widow, his wife and children. In 1947 he executed two deeds in favour of the appellant and his three sons. The properties were not divided by metes and bounds but were sold by the respondents to the respondents. The respondents filed suits against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents were invalid as they were hit by section 6(h) of the , and were void. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the transfers under exhibit A 1 and A 2 were not supported by any consideration or gift, but were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transfer was without consideration or for immoral purposes and was therefore void. HELD : (i) The properties gifted under exhibit P 1 andA 2 were in reality gifts made in consideration of past illicit cohabitation and therefore those gifts were invalid, the court rightly held that past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers. [157 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that past transactions were void because they were supported by no consideration or consideration for their subsequent promises to transfer the properties to their concubine. The property gifted under the two deeds was without any consideration and was, therefore, not hit by sec. 6(a). [157 E] (iii) The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gift and as such were void, the Court is entitled to take into account the subsequent promises for their future services. [158 G H] (iv) The gifts were not hit under section 6 (h) because they had been made in pursuance of past transactions. They were therefore invalid.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the State of Bombay, was carrying on business as an agent of the respondent company. The company had been running its own business as a dealer under the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The appellant company was registered as the sole selling agent of certain companies. The Company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice dated 5.12.75 issued by the I.T.O. to the L.I.C., and also the order dated 5 12.75, directing the company to revoke the notice issued by it under section 226(3) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of section 226 (3)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961, and that the company was not making the payment to the respondent. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the notice under section226(3)(vii) of Act, 1922, was not applicable to the case because in spite of the LI. C.I.,C. itself had taken the stand throughout that the money due under the policies were held by it for and on behalf Of the assignee and not the defaulter; and that there fore, the LlI.c. itself has taken the view that the respondent was entitled to make the payment due against the policy to the company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question of revoca tion of the notices under section 227(3), 1961, by the L I. T.O., did not arise because in the instant case, the award of interest was made by the appellant and there fore it could not be said that writ petition when the IT.I Act had made the requisite statement on oath under section Writ Petition. [114G H] 1.2 The question whether a part of the amount is due to the assessee or any of its officers to personal liability has to be decided by the Court in the light of its own facts and circumstances of each case. [115E F] 1:3. In the instant cases, the delay in making the requisite statements on oath was not made since it involved the likelihood of exposing the L to the risk of the company 's business. The delay in filing the return under section 22(3). [116F G] 2.1. The question as to whether a particular amount is payable only to the assignee, does not arise from the assessee inasmuch as it was payable only on 5. 12. 75 which led to revocation of the said notice by the l.T., or a reasonable time, without objecting to the demand by denying its liability to the asses see in the manner prescribed in clause (vi) thereof, instead of in doing so. [116G H; 117A] 2:2.2.3 The delay is not fatal because it was not done when the L1.C. had taken a stand throughout. It was not possible for the assignee of the policies to obtain revocation of notice by him. There was no reason why the delay should not be condoned. [117H; 118A] 3.1 In the present case, there is no material on record to show that the delay was due to any undue delay in giving the requisite information under section 26(3); and the delay could not have been condoned by the respondent in the way of refusing to accept its liability. The conduct of the assignee or the assignee as a result of which the company had to be wound up, is not sufficient to justify the inordinate delay in taking the requisite steps for obtaining the requisite return. [118A B] 3:2 In the circumstances, the inordinate and unexplained delay in passing the requisite statutory obligation by theL.I C.T./C. was the result of misconstruction of the provision and misappreciation of its liability thereunder.

The appellant, a resident of Madhya Pradesh, was assessed to sales tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant filed an application for refund of the amount paid by him on the ground that he had not been able to pay the tax due from him in respect of the assessment year 1951 52 and that the claim was barred by limitation. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the application holding that the period of limitation prescribed under section 29(2) of the Act was not applicable to the case, but held that the appellant was entitled to have the benefit of the provisions of section 29 (2)(a). On appeal the High Court set aside the order of the Assistant Commissioner and restored the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the first part of section 5(1) of Act, which provides a period of one year from the date of the commencement of the Limitation Act, is not attracted because of the non compliance with the provisions contained in section 29. HELD : (i) The second part of sub section (2) is concerned only with proceedings under the Code of Civil Procedure and not under the first schedule. It does not contemplate that a period prescribed for an appeal or application by any special or local law must be of a kind similar to that prescribed by the First Schedule. [143 E] (ii) The first part is intended to cover cases where the second part is not so provided in the First schedule. The first limb of sub s.(2) does not include a suit, appeal or applications for a period exceeding one year. It is only when the special or Local law prescribes for any suit, Appeal or application a period Of limitation different from that prescribed for any such appeal or appli cation by any Special or local Law. [144 E] In the present case, the first limb was not satisfied with the second parts of sub sec.(2). The first portion was intended to include a claim for refund and that therefore, cl. (a) would apply only in so far as it related to suits filed under the First part of the section.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, was running a bus stand at Mathura. The route was to be run by the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district. The appellant challenged the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate under section 76 of the Act on the ground that the route was a bus stands vested in the Regional transport authority having jurisdiction to fix the places for the bus stand. The High Court held that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus stood at Mathura and therefore the order made under section 77 of the , was unassailable. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Regional Authority had passed the impugned order in question with the object of establishing a bus standing stand for purposes of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Magistrate has no power under section 68(2)(r) of the . [710C] 2. Section 76 of Act provides that the State Government may make rules for the purpose of the purpose for which a bus scheme is to be framed and the Regional Road Transport Authority has jurisdiction over any area or area. The Regional Transport Authorities have no power in respect of such area as are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the State Govern ment under section 75 of the Motor Vehicles Act. [711D] 3. Section 68(1)(r), which provides for the control of transport vehicles, confers the power on the State Transport Authority to make rules regarding the conditions of a permit and the conditions thereof. The power to issue a notification fixing a bus Stand stands vested with the power to make Rules for the purposes of that chapter. [11D E] 4. Section 77(2) of Act which provides that no person shall be deemed to have any right to ply his vehicle in question unless he has authority to do so under section 64 A by the Central Government. Such a power should be given specifically by the statute and that the power could be exercised only by the authorities specified therein. [1011E] 5.

The appellants were charged with offences under sections 3(a) and 4(1)(d) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1955. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the High Court set aside their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export within the meaning of Para 2(a). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) There is no evidence on record to show that the appellants were attempting to commit an offence under section 7 of the Act. The fact that they were not attempting to export paddy outside the State of Punjab in this case does not make any difference. [667 B] (2) The fact of the first information report was not a mere attempt to commit it. It is only a preparation on the parts of the accused and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt to export. [67 G] (3) The mere fact that the first Information Report was lodged at the relevant point of time at about the 18th mile from Delhi would not make the offence punishable under Para 2 (a). [667 C D] (4) There has been no attempt to committing the offence by the appellants in this Case. It could not be said that there had been an attempt on their part to commit a offence. The mere omission of the appellant to send the report to the police did not amount to any attempt to cause the offence.

The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on business as a dealer in shares and shares. The Managing Agency Agreement provided that the managing agency agreement would be effective from 1st April, 1948, subject to the provisions of section 5(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Under the terms of the agreement the managing agent was to pay to the company the remuneration or commission which was payable to the Managing Agents under the terms and conditions of the Managing Agency Agreements. The appellant company paid the commission to the appellant on the termination of its agency agreement. The company filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from the appellant in respect of the same. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the agreement was not binding on the appellant and that it was not open to the respondent to raise any question as to whether the remuneration paid by the company was an income bearing asset which had accrued to them during the chargeable accounting period. Held, that the terms in the agreement were not intended to be a business and the remuneration for the entire year was the income of the appellant. The agreement did not create any right or interest in the property of the respondent but merely created a liability on the part of the assignee to pay the entire sum of money as per the Managing Agent 's Agreement. The terms of an agreement were intended to give effect to the terms which were agreed upon by the parties and that the appellant was entitled to receive the entire remuneration for each year. The managing agency agreements did not depend on any specific term between the parties but on the fact that what was transferred was an asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that fell due after the date of assignment. Held further, that though the agreement did create a liability in respect thereof, the remuneration could be said to have accrued to the assignee, and the appellant could not therefore be treated as an income arising out of the transaction during the relevant accounting period, because, it was a mere clause in the Managing agency Agreement which was the source of income. The payment of the managing Agency agreement did no affect the character of the remuneration and the payment of commission was not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to be paid for the whole year 's remuneration.

The appellant was employed in the Lucknow, and his wife was living with her. The deceased was living separately from the house of the appellant. He was found guilty under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The evidence in the case is circumstantial. It is not possible to say that it is extra judicial confession. It may be used only as a corroborative piece of evidence. But, there is no reason why the statement implied in the confession should be given (1 ) to another. If that be so in the present case, fully established, the conviction could certainly be proved as a confession of guilt. [890 F G] (2) The circumstances found by the High court are consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. [889 D E] (3) The circumstance that the accused must have committed the murder is not a conclusive evidence. It can be used merely as a substantive piece of Evidence. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an admission or a confession and the weight to be attached to it. [891 F G; 892 A] (4) The High Court was right in holding that the conviction was not an extra judicial confessions.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary employee in the respondent 's service. He was confirmed on probation with effect from 1st April, 1976. The services of the appellant were terminated by the appellant 's order dated 4th September, 1976 and he filed an application before the Central Government under section 7 of the Act for reinstatement. The Central Government rejected his claim. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of termination on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to any relief as it had been denied by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not competent to terminate the services of an employee under Rule 8, and that the order was invalid because the appellant did not have any such vesting and could not be said to have been made in accordance with the rules. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the Board of Directors had no power to terminate his service by tendering one month 's salary in lieu thereof, and therefore, the order terminating the services was invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Board of Management did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of the appel lant. [ 224A] 2. The respondent had the right to dismiss an employee, under Rule 9 of the Rules. He could not have the power to dismiss him under Rule 5 for misconduct in the manner prescribed in the Rules.[225B] 3. The order of the Board was construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation. [226C] 4. The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's Service whether permanent or temporary, which should be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice in writing of his intention to do so. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in a way which would make the provision or the Rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [225D] 5. The word "in" has been used in the context of the expression "under the Act". It is not necessary to define the meaning of the word "underthe Act", as defined in the Act. [227E] 6. The words "in any case" have been defined in section 2(g) of the , and the words "on the date of the order" are capable of that interpretation. But from the facts, it is clear that the board of Management does not abolish post but only directs that the post would be abolished. [228F] 7. The power to appoint a permanent employee by giving one month"s notice or pay in lieu of notice is an incident which may be taken into account while the employee is occupying the post.

The Orissa Excise Act, 1915 was enacted to provide for the establishment of a distillery in the State of Orissa. Section 2(1) of the said Act provided that no person shall be entitled to any privilege under section 22 of the Act except on the written permission of the Collector of Mayurbhanj to manufacture and sell liquor. The appellant who was the highest bidder, filed an application before the Excise Commissioner for re auctioning the license and declared that he was a licensee under the Bihar and Orissa Excise (Orissa) Rules, 1915. The Excise Commissioner rejected the application holding that the licence was not granted for an exclusive privilege under Section 22 of Act. The State Government issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 under section 29(2) of Act No. 1802 of 1970 directing the Collector to re auction the license in accordance with the provisions of the amended section 29 (2). The appellant filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order and also the order of the Excise Commis sioner. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the petitioner was the lowest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the bid register and the entry was signed by the petitioner, he was not entitled to the grant of an exclusive right under section 2(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that as the petitioner had been highest bidder on the date of the re auction, his name could not be considered for an independent licence under section 7 of the Amending Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of a Excise Commissioner dated April 15, 1970 was valid and the grant was valid. [785B] 2. Section 6(a) of Amending Ordinance No. 17 of 1970 provides that no licence shall be granted for any privilege to manufacture or sell liquor except on written permission from the Collector. The expression "any privilege" in section 22 means a right which is not contemplated by the Act and includes a right to manufacture, sale or purchase. [777C] 3. Section 7(a), of the amending Ordinance No 1802 1970 provides for the grant or renewal of an unvi sion under section 20 of the Bihar & Orissa Excise Rules. The word "any" in the amended clause means "any right to sell or dispose of any privilege". The expression 'any privilege ' is not defined in the Act. [779D] 4. Section 3(a)(b) of that Act provides for a licence for sale and sale of country liquor. It does not provide for an additional privilege under the Act, as the primary purpose of the statute was to restrict the manufacture and sale. The power of the State Government in that respect has been delegated to the Board of Revenue. [780E] 5. Section 4(a). of the Amendment Ordinance No 17 of 1971 is a provision which provides for grant of exclusive privilege to the manufacture, sell or purchase of liquor. Section 5(b) provides for an appeal against any order made under that Act by virtue of section 6(c) and the order made thereunder. The proviso to sub section (1) lays down that no licensee shall be allowed to manufacture any privilege except on a written permission granted by the Collector, or by the Excise Officer in writing. [781E F] 5(a ) The expression `any privilege under s 22 of this Act ' means a privilege which is an essential ingredient of the offence and includes any right to carry on business in liquor.

The appellant was a son of accused No. 2 and his wife. The prosecution case against him was that the deceased was the son of the deceased and that he had been falsely implicated by the police in the murder of the appellant. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. but acquitted him. On appeal, the High Court reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the accused that there was no corroboration of the evidence of the two witnesses and that the conviction could not be sustained as the appellant had been convicted under section 304 Part B of the Indian Penal Code. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that there is sufficient corroboration of evidence of an eye witness in material particulars in regard to the connection of the crime and in regard of the conspiracy as well as the common intention. [623 A] (2) There was no evidence to connect accused No 2 with murder of his wife after he had left the house of accused Nos. 3 and 4. The evidence of PW 1 that the appellant and his son were seen alive in the company of accused NO. 2, and that they were guilty of the offence under section 201 read with Section 34 I P.C., [624 B] (3) There is no evidence that the two persons were present at the time when the deceased came to know of the murder. The fact that the accused was seen alive does not make any difference in view of the death of the wife. [625 E] (4) The evidence regarding the body of the dead body and the common intent of the assailant is not a reliable witness and it is proved that the person who had seen the dead bodies was present at that time when he came to see the house. It is also proved that there were some other persons who were present in the house where the deceased had gone to the house and gave the key of the godown to accused No 1. The discovery of articles in the godown of PW 2 and the other circumstances show that the dead articles were given by accused No 3.

The appellant 's case was that the Town Planning Officer had no power to make a scheme under section 68 of the Act. The Town Planning officer, after making a declaration under section 32(1) (iii), made a scheme for the area in respect of which the declaration has been made and published in the prescribed manner. The appellant ' s contention was that since the appellant had not filed any objections to the scheme as required by section 64(1)(f) of the Town planning Act, the Town Plan should be approved under section 65 (1). The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to a higher rate than the original plots and not the final plot.
