In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the scheme is not appealable under section 66(1), because the Town Development Officer had power to fix the rate of compensation in respect thereof, and that the High Court was right in holding that the Act specifies a principle of compensation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 68 are similar to those of section 64 (1) of Bombay Town Planning Act, 1948. Section 69(1 ) provides for the determination of the amount of compensation payable on each plot by the Town Committee. Under section 67(1). the Town development officer is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner of any property or right which is injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of Section 69. [84G H] 2. The High court was right, in holding (i) that the provisions are similar and not identical; (ii) that section 68(1 )(f), which provides for determination of compensation is not applicable to the case because the market value of the original plot is determined on the basis of the market price of the plot at the date of declaration of intention to make the scheme. [85A B] 3. The scheme is as follows: (i). Under section 68, the owner is required under section 71 to estimate compensation to he paid to him by the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties; (iii) the market rate of the land at the time of declaration is determined according to the provisions contained in section 69. The market value has to be determined on a basis of market value, and the market rates have to be fixed on the market valuation. [86C D] 4. The principle for determining compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not; compensation is payable on the principle that an owner is entitled to compensation from section 71 of the , which says that the net amount of loss shall be payable to him, by the Local Authority in cash, or in any other way, as may he agreed upon. [87D] 5. The principles for determining the compensation are the same as those of sections 68 and 69. Section 70 provides for a uniform rate of interest on the original land at rates fixed by the Government from time to time. Under clause (xiii) the Town Improvement Officer is required, to estimate, the compensation payable to the owners of any land or right acquired from any person benefited or partly from the local authorities and partly from such person as the Town improvement officer may in each case determine. The rate of compensa tion is the highest. In determining the difference between the total value of original plots, the market values are determined by the market valua tion of the plots at the rate fixed by Government. [88G H; 89A] 6. The Court has to see whether the principles laid down in the Act are applicable to all lands covered by the scheme and not to the final plots.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama. He died in 1934 leaving behind his widow and three daughters. The appellant 's brother, Seetharaamma, filed a suit for partition of the properties in 1934. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the will was not admissible as it had been executed by the testator and that the gift was altogether void for uncertainty. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "he shall deliver possession of the remaining properties to the children as and when they become major" in section 89(1)(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1908 are clear and certain things which would lead to the inference that the testator intended that the daughters should get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The words used in the will are not different from those used in section 90(2). [857 B C] (ii) The intention of the testator was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the selection. The intention was clearly intended to give the gift to the daughters. [858 E F] (iii) The will is not a mere writing but an oral or documentary evidence which would support the inference, that the legatee intended that daughters should have been given to them before taking into consideration the good, bad quality and utility of the property. There are no words in the Will which show that the legatee was nominated by the legatee to make the selection and give the devised land to the two daughters. It is not possible to say on the construction of a will that the bequest should be given in India also and the decision in Narayanasami Gramani 's case (supra) is correct. [884 H] (iv) The language of the will shows that it was intended to have left the choice to the legatee. It was not possible for the testator to say that the words were used by him to make a gift which could be made certain by selection. There were no express words in section 88(1) (c).

The plaintiff appellant, a co sharer of the land in dispute, was allotted to him by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The respondent 's name was recorded as a co co sharers in the consolidation proceedings. The names of the plaintiff were entered in the revenue records in the name of the defendants. The respondents filed a suit for joint possession of the plots in dispute on the ground that they had been wrongly included in the khewat and the entire property was mutated in the record in the Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953. The trial court accepted the allegations of the respondents and dismissed the suit. The District Judge held that the plaintiff 's names were not recorded as co sharees but only as co co co shares. The High Court further found that the name was wrongly entered in a khewat. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the defendants were in separate possession of land or plots in question and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The possession of defendant No. 2 was never given to him. It is not open to the High Court to interfere with this finding of fact in second appeal. [867G] 2. The mere fact remains that the District Judge has come to a clear finding of facts after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the defendant were sought to be extinguished. [886E F] 3. The plaintiff ' s plea of fraud must have been pleaded or proved by the plaintiff and the right of the respondent would be deemed in law to be the possession of plaintiff. [881F G] 4. The fact remains the same as the District Court has come into a clear findings of fact after consideration thereof. It cannot be said that the possession was not given to the plaintiff by the respondents as the defendants had been co sharors. The finding of the District judge is not sustainable in law and the judgment of the High court cannot be allowed to stand. [878F G; 867A] 5. The findings of the trial Court are not sustainable. It has been repeatedly held that there was no evidence on record to prove that the appellant was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of holdings Act, 1951 or that the respondents were co sharants of the lands. [877G] 6. The plea of the appellants that they were in possession of their land or plot No. 201 and plots Nos. 201 & 274 are not correct. It was never the case of the plaintiffs that any fraud was practised on the consolidation authorities. What she had stated in her plaint and in her evidence was that the defendant had practised a fraud on her by giving her an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. [876E G] 7. The suit was barred by section 49 of the Act. [879F] 8. The contention that there is no evidence to prove the plaintiff was not tenable in law, and the High Courts erred in holding that the present suit was within time.

The petitioner, a Minister of India, was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister in the year 1964. He was later promoted as Deputy Chief Minister and was posted as Deputy Minister. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to defend himself by filing a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the oath administered to him as Deputy Ministers was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the constitution and that his appointment was invalid. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. Dismissing the petition, this Court HELD: 1. The oath administered by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Ministers along with his other submis sion. [868C] 2. The expression "the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [886E F] 3. The words "any power of the Prime Minister" in section 173 read with Form VII A are one, namely, that the person taking a oath or make the affirmation will bear true confidence and allegiance, to the constitution. [876G] 4. The prescribed oath must be divided amongst two parts, one which contains a sub stntial part and the others which contains it is a mere device or error. [896E] 5. The requirement of Article 75 read with Rule VII A was that the persons taking the affirmation or making an affirmation would have true faith. It is not necessary to refer to any other form even for the Prime Ministers. [906G H] Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a factory in Calcutta and its workmen were paid wages for the period from 1st November 1948 to 31st March, 1948. The management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on 1st October, 1948 amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the Factories Act, and that the management was justified in its decision that the continuity of service of the workers was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike. The appellant contended that the discontinuance of the work was not a lock out and did not amount to a strike and did no longer require any break in the continuity. Held, that the action of the management amounted to a lockout and the workmen were entitled to leave for the night shift when a half a day 's leave was granted to the day shift workers. The stoppage of the working on 1th November 1948 was not an illegal strikes but only an illegal lock out. The strike was not illegal because no notice had been given to the management, nor was it possible to take any action against the appellant for the reason that the strike was a lock up and the workers were entitled under the Factories (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1947, to leave the night of 1st December 1948. Held further, that in view of the facts and circumstances of the case the stoppage was not justified as there was no break in continuity of their service by the stoppage caused by illegal strike or by illegal strikes and the appellant was entitled to privilege under section 49 B(1) of the Act.

The appellant, a film producer of films, was granted by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious or any material to quash the proceedings. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by an authority under the (for short), it is not open to the court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 79 of the Penal Code does not confer any right on the Court to examine the accused in question as to whether the certificate issued under section 5A(1) of the Act is groundless or not. The absence of such certification may constitute an offence under section 292 I.P.C. notwithstanding anything contained in the Act, namely, by some other provision, then section 79 of that Act does not require any prosecution for a public exhibition. [503B C] 1.2 In the instant case, the trial court when itars the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under section S(1A) of that Code and section 79 I. P.C., resolves the apparent conflict between section 5 A and section 80 I.p.C, and section 81 of the Indian Penal Code. [511D E] 1:3 The trial court while it is a judicial body, has to consider, before certification, all the points section 292I.P.,C. is general, the is special. After considering the evidence adduced by the prosecution, the Court is satisfied that the certificate of the Board of Censorcates, acting within their jurisdiction and on an application made and pursued in good faith, sanctions the public exhibition, the producer and connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 79 does not empower the court, to discharge or discharge the said accused as a charge, unless the ground covered by the two laws be different. [506D E; 507A B] 1 :4 In the present case, there is no evidence that what was merely certified as suitable for show by a law may not go the length of holding that it is justified by law. The trial Court when it isars the accused may appropriately apprised about the certificate and its effect that the Certificate of the board of Cen dents would be protected because Section 79 doesnot confer any power on the court in certifying the public exhibiting the film. [500E F] 1 5. In the absence of a certificate under Section 5A, it is open to a Court to discharge an accused as he has no right to examine him as the charges is groundless and that he entertained a mistake of fact and in good conscience believed that he was justified by Law in doing so. [525F G] 2:1 The trial Judge when it wasars the suit may be suitably apprised of his certificate under the Act and, in the light of the observations made by this Court, it fills the bill under section 79. [504G H] 2 :2 In view of the decision of this Court in State of Madhya Pradesh vs M/s. Ram Gopal Sharma & Ors., ; , the trial Court while itars a case may appropriately be apprised of its certificate under s 5A (1) and its impact on the combined operation of section 5B of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the 'grounds section 292 1.P C. is groundless, and the trial Judge has no jurisdiction to discharge him as he had not been able to show by any evidence that he had been justified by the law in doing it. [ 509A B; 510B] 2.3 The prosecution is unsustainable because section 80 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not authorise the court for its reception or discharge, but only requires a prosecution to satisfy the 'lay" magistrate that there was sufficient ground for the reception or discharging the accused.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an Advocate by the High Court. He was appointed to be an advocate on remuneration paid from the public exchequer. The petitioner challenged his appointment before the High court under article 136 of the Constitution in a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner 's client 's claim as the sole representative of Government Pleader was not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government pleader. The petition was allowed by the Division Bench on the ground that the Government Pleader had failed to sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf, and that his client 'S ' was only an agent of the Government pleader who was appointed by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code. The Court held that the Advocate General was only a person who had a crowd of cases to be conducted, his services were not required to be terminated and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Courts should have been slow in interfering with the decision of the High 'Court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The practice of the State Pleader is that his duties are only to the Government who are his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that the Court must also be concerned with the quality of the product or service control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the people who are the third world clients. [766C] 2. The State Pleader, Madras is only an independent and responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. It is not necessary that the State pleader should sacrifice the expeditious conduct of the case by not appointed a number or more than one world clients, in the absence of a specific provision for recording any finding on the nature of the circumstances of the present case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [766E F] 3. The duty of the Court is not to act as a public officer within the meaning of a thing which he has a stake in the litigation. It does not mean that the court should be given an opportunity to explain why the Government Advocate should not be appointed to perform the duties of the court. [776G] 4. The time has come to examine the quality and nature of his work, control the prices, floor, to ceiling etc., control the cost of the administration of justice oriented on basic social justice so that the profession may flourish without wholly hitching the calling to the star of material amassment immunised by law from the liabilities of other occupations. [756G H] 5. The Government Pleader and, in a sense, every member of the legal profession has a higher dedication to the community. He is only a representative of the government pleader who is appointed by State Government as an advocate. [746H; 766A] 6. The Advocate General is only one person who has a crowd or a group of persons to be appointed by a State Government. It cannot be said that he has been appointed by any other person.

The appellant held shares of the Bank of India in the year 1943, and a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the appellant. The appellant filed an application before the High Court under section 66(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the respondent to allot the shares to its nominees. The High Court held that the distribution of the right to apply for and obtain two shares was not a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act, and that the transfer of the share in favour of the shareholders amounted to distribution of "dividend" within the definition of "cividend". The High court held that it was not justified having regard to the form of the question which expressly related to the distribution amongst its shareholders. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the allocation of the rights to apply under section 2 (6A), in enlarging the scope of the questions and in answering it in the light of its ordinary meaning. [588 E] (ii) The expression "dispute" in section 2 of the Act is an inclusive and not an exhaustive definition, and even if the distribution is a mere device to distribute the right of the shares of a bank of India, it would be taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. [589 G] (iii) The word "daccend" in s 2(1A) was an inclusive one and not a exhaustive definition. It was not intended to include any dividend within section 2.(6A). [588 H] (iv) The definition of 'dividends ' in section 3(6 A) is an exhaustive and not exhaustive definition and even though the distribution may be made by the company of shares, it does not necessarily mean that the shares are distributed amongst its members as dividend. It did not also take the form or a part of the definition in s.2(6B).

The appellant was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had not been given permission to examine himself as a witness in the list under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The High Court rejected the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to examine the witnesses who were not examined in compliance with the order XVI Rule 1A of the Code of civil Procedure and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to refuse to examine such witness as it thought fit. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the provisions of sub rule 1A are mandatory; (ii) the requirement of sub section (1), of Rule I of Order XVII is directory and not mandatory; and (iii) the High court had no power to refuse the application for examination of a witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Court has no jurisdiction in refusing to examine a witness who is present in the Court on the short ground that the name of the witness was not mentioned in the List envisaged by sub rule(1) and who can be produced without the assistance of the court. [534C] (i). The requirement of section 87 of the Act is that the party to a proceeding does not wish to have the assistance or to produce documents which are mentioned in sub rule 2 of Rule lA of Order XVIII, but he can do so under Rule 1 A of order XVI only if he has been able to produce them before him on the date fixed for recording his evidence. [540D] (ii). The proviso to section 87 is mandatory and not directory. It is not obligatory on the party tendering such a copy as he may be required by the Court to do so. If it was implicit in Rule 1 that it only enables the party who has failed to produce the witnesses without the help of the Court, it can do otherwise under Rule l(3) to procure the presence of a person who is not shown in the lists filed under sub section(1). [540E F] (iii). The provision of sub r. 1A is mandatory. It does not require that the witness should be examined by the party on the first day fixed for the recording of evidence, but if on the dates fixed for record the evidence, the party is able to keep his witnesses present there would be no necessity to examine him. [541F G] (iv) The proviso thereto provides that the Court shall have the discretion to refuse an application for examining any witness whose name is not mentioned therein in the Schedule to sub rule l(1), and who could be produced after the evidence of the party was able to kept his witnesses without being summoned by the court, it is not necessary to provide in Rule l A that the parties should be allowed to examine them and to produce such documents through the witnesses. [543F G; 541A] (v) The requirement under sub r.(1) is mandatory but if the party would be able to do the work of a Court without the aid of the trial court it can render the evidence ineffective for procuring the presence or appearance of a party and the court has no power in that behalf to refuse such examination. [544F] (vi) The provision under sub Rule 1(3), is mandatory, but not directory and cannot be construed as directory. [542G H] (vii) The provisions of section 47 of the 1951 Act are mandatory and do not require any further investigation by the trial Court. [546A B] (viii) The High Courts have no jurisdiction under sub rr. 1(1)(a), 1(2) and 1(4).

The appellant was appointed as Principal of a College in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The order contained an order of the State Government appointing him as Principal. The appellant challenged the appointment by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of appointment made by the Managing Committee of the College was not valid and that the Selection Committee had no power to make any appointment, and therefore the appointment of the appel lant was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the selection committee had no authority to make the appointment. [982F] 2.1 The order dated April 27, 1981 contained an Order of the Government appointing the appellant as Principal and the Director of the institution. If the order contained any power to appoint a Head of the Institution, it would not be open to the Selection Commis sioner to make an appointment. It is not open to him to contend that the Committee of Management had no powers to make appointment. The effect of this order is that the recommendation made by a committee of management in exercise of its power under section 9 of the Act, the second contention of the respondent that the appellant was not entitled to be appointed as Head of an Institution in contravention of the provisions of the . [983G H; 984A] 2:2. The appointment of appellant was therefore valid and must be quashed. [89E F] 3.1 It is true that on April 7, 1981 the order was made by an authority to appoint the appellant but it could not be said that the Government or the Committee had any power on the part of the Committee to make appointments. The State Government could be said to have rescinded that power under the Act. [1989F] 3:2 It is well settled that the appointment made in exercise or purported to be made by it without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind the regulation or make any other order consistent with the provisions contained in the Act as it deems necessary and in particular, may by such order modify or cancel such appointment and pass such consequential orders as may be necessary. [90G H] 3 :3. The power to making appointment was not conferred on the State Govern ment without making an reference to Board to making, modification or rescind any regulation or makes any other provision in the statute. It could not therefore be said, that the power of the committee of Management having been delegated to it by the State government, without making a reference to it to the board to make its appointment and hence ineffective though it may not be invalid. [91G H, 92A] 4. The Government could not have exercised its powers under section 10 of the , in exercise thereof.

The petitioners, manufacturers of tyres and other goods manufactured by them, were assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the , on the ground that they manufacture "textile" and also that it serve as part of raw material for what ultimately also goes into the manufacture of a fabric. The petitioners contended that the products manufactured by the petitioner were not "end product" within the meaning of section 2(g) of the . Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the goods under consideration constitute the "end products" and not any other kind of fabric. [594C] (2) The word "end" used in the Act means "a textile". It is a technical question which can be decided by this Court on its own facts. [500D E] (3) The words "textiles" are wide enough to include all kinds of cloth. The expression "end goods" has been defined in section 2 (g) as meaning "any kind of cloth". The word 'end product ' is used in a sense which includes cloth. It is not so much the point of manufacture at which the Mills sell their own products which determines the nature of goods which are entitled to exemption, but it is the stage reached by this product, in the process of manufacture of the same kind of fabrics. [525E F] (4) The expression 'end products ' has been used in section 3(g). It does not mean that the word "and" has to be understood as a word or a word. [25F G] (5) The definition of "totton" given in the Oxford Dictionary, is a wide enough and includes all kinds or varieties of cloth which are known as cotton fabrics. The meaning of the term "t silk" given by the legislature is that it should be understood in its popular sense. It must be understood to mean something more than what it has been done. [26F G; 26A] (6) The dictionary meaning of 'textiles ' given in section 4(1)(d) is that a textile fabric which is a textile must be regarded as an "fabric" or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. It does, therefore, mean something different from the one which has been put into the hands of the first petitioner. [27F G]. (7) The meaning given in sub section (1)(a) is not to be accepted. [28G] (8) The question whether the product for which the Delhi Cloth Mills claims exemption is a "end commodity" or not in the final manufacture of an other fabric was quite irrelevant. It has been urged that so far as the Delhi cloth products are concerned, the goods are under consideration constituting the "t Silk" and therefore, they fall within the definition of 'end commodity '.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal from the appellant company. The Company was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. The appellant company had been running a coal mill and it would be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court, Patna. The Government of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the appellant made an order transferring the case from the Labour Court Patna to another Labour Court Ranchi. The said order was challenged by the appellant before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the company that the Government had no jurisdiction to transfer the case to the Labour court, Patna and transfer the proceeding to the labour court, Dhanbad for speedy disposal from stage at which the case was transferred. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of transfer in that case was one of a Senior Supervisors in the appellant 's Establishment at Dhanbad and it was not possible for him to attend the Labour Courts, Patna to have given an opportunity to the management to explain his reasons when any order to the prejudice of the normal procedure laid down in section 64(1) and (2) of the Act is sought to be made against him. [294C D] 2. The object of transfer is to provide for speedy settlement of disputes between employers and employees. It is not necessary that the parties should give an opportunity of being heard before any order of transferring the cases is passed by the Labour Commissioner or the Central Board of Revenue, as the case may be. [295D] 3. The power vested in the appropriate Government to withdraw any proceedings pending before a labour court or Tribunal under section 5(7A) of Act, 1961, transferred an application for transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna. [296E] 4. The reason given by the Government for transferring the Case is another question to be considered. It would be prudent if the principles of natural justice are followed in dealing with a case. [293F] 5. The reasons given by Government for transfer are not such as to act fairly and reasonably. The procedural standards which are implied by the duty to act judicially, are not so much to act arbitrarily or capriciously. [292G] 6. The Court has no power to interfere with an order of the Tribunal on the ground that it is passed in a case where administrative officers are concerned. It may also be made to appear before the Labour Appellate Tribunal at Patna and the Labour Board or the State Board of Reve nue, as it may be necessary to record reasons in making the order of transferred after affording a reasonable opportunity of having been heard to the assessee in the matter. [ 294E] 7. The High Court was right in holding that the reasons given for transferring cases were not bona fide or the honesty of an assessee and normally the income tax authorities would not be justified in refusing to transfer them.

The appellant company was a registered office of the appellant and its workmen as its employees. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the reference was incompetent and two grounds were given out in support of it, namely (1) the employer who was the management of the hotel was not a party to the reference; (2) the reference did not indicate how many of the workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The appellant contended that the union could not be made a party under the , and (3) the dispute was vague as it did not specify what number of workmen employed by the hotel, and (4) the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make a reference. Held, that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was one of general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the names of particular workmen who might have been responsible for the dispute; and (5) the question whether the reference in this case was incompetent merely because it was mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the present case. The fact that in the order of reference the words "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " were added to the definition of " workmen" in section 2 (k) of the Act as meaning " any dispute or difference between employers and workmen". The word "as representing 36 workmen" used in section 10(1) of that Act means a dispute which is referred for arbitration.

The appellant imported certain goods from the customs authorities under the Customs Act, and cleared the same. The Collector of Customs, after giving an opportunity to the appellant, passed an order on May 12, 1986, granting part exemption from payment of duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaftones imported by the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Notification grants exemption in part from payment to the extent of Rs.2 lakhs and not under Heading No. 84.06. The appeal was also dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of the engines, mentioned under Heading 84.07, but it also mentions the 'parts thereof ', that is to say, parts of such engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, and not a few parts thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The Notification will apply to parts of engines mentioned under heading No.84.06, but only refers to parts thereof, namely, parts thereof and not to parts whereof they are parts of their engines. [227D] 2. The words "parts" in Heading No 84.09, by necessary implication and in the context of the Notification, it includes the parts thereof must be the parts which are parts constituting a engine or engine, as mentioned under Entry No. 83.06 and not the parts whereof are parts thereof.[227E] 3. The intention is clear and manifest that the words "in respect of which the exemption is claimed" in the Notification are not readily understandable. [228F] 4. The object of the notification was to provide for the use of the engine, such parts must be only those parts constituting an engine or machinery, and also the parts therein. So, though the parts are not mentioned under Chapter 84.05, by appropriate implication and, in the absence of any specific provision to the contrary, it is difficult to hold that the part of the equipment which have been imported by them are parts or parts thereof [228G] 5. The notification will apply only to parts or portions thereof. It cannot be said that the components of the machinery or engines mentioned in Heading 8406.06 are excluded from the benefit of the exemption granted by the Notification. In view of the finding that the Notifications were not applicable to parts, the intention of the Customs authorities was clear enough and manifest. [229F] 6. The appellants have been able to show that the tyres which were imported by it were parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading Nos. 8406,06. It is also apparent from the context in which the Notification granted exemption to the parts mentioned in paragraph 2 of column (2) of the Table appended thereto. [230G] 7. The expression "part ' has been defined in the notification as including parts thereof". The intention of Notification is clear that parts of a engines, described under Heading NO. 8407, will get the benefit thereof as provided by the notification, irrespective of the fact whether they or any of them have already been included under Heading 82.06 or under any other heading. [231A] 8. The exemption would be granted in respect to parts and not for the parts or any one of them having already been excluded under Heading (2). [230C] 9. The contention that the appellants were parts and they were parts thereof cannot be accepted.

The plaintiffs, who were the descendants of the first respondent, filed a suit for declaration that they had been in possession of the said properties and also for mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove ouster on the basis of any oral evidence and that the defendants had not proved ouster of Fathima Bee from the suit property. On appeal, the first appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, it was held that the appellants were entitled to a share in the offerings in the Dargah and even if they were entitled under the provisions of the Muslim Law, they would be entitled to any right of Mujawar as the right was given only to the male members and not to the females. The High Court also held that there was no question of any knowledge about the ouster of the appellants on the ground that their father did not claim any right till her death. In appeal by special leave, it is contended for the appellants that the High Court was wrong in holding that they were estopped from claiming any right to Mujawar and that they could not be allowed to raise a plea of estoppel against the appellants. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the rights of Fathi Bee had become barred by limitation is a mixed question of law and fact. [526C] 2.1 In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathita Bee, it must be shown that the said judgment and decree were not binding on Fathim or the plaintiffs. The onus was on the appellants to prove affirmatively that they asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment of any share in them. [525D] 2:2 In order that a person claiming through female members of a Muslim Law must establish affirmatively, it should be shown by evidence that she had asserted hostile or hostile title against the other party. The burden is on the plaintiffs who are not entitled to claim any share. [500E F] 3.1 The onus is on them to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt and the burden of proving affirmatively rests upon them. It is also clear from the evidence that the defendant had asserted that she was being ousted from her right or share in any portion of the offerings. [511F G] 2 :3 In order of convenience it may be stated that both Fathibir and the plaintiffs were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim law were not entitled, as such, to claim no right of management or possession in a Dargah. The defendants were carrying on the business of offering offerings to the descendants and the descendants. [506F G; 506A] 2(a) In order for making out a Case of ouster from the right or claim of any portion thereof, it would be necessary to prove that she has asserted hostile possession of F.athima or the defendants. The mere fact that she is being ousted by her will cannot be said to be an adverse inference against F.I.R. [ 506F G]. (b) In the instant case, the plaintiffs have not claimed any right in the management or share of the Dargah.

The appellant was a licensee under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. He was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled to any house rent allowance. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the house rent from him on the ground that the house rate was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the terms of the contract between the parties include the rule quoted above and therefore the respondent was not liable to pay any house allowance. Held, that the rule is inconsistent with some of the terms and conditions of the agreement between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one of those places would be entitled to house rent allowances; but it does not make the grant in such absolute terms. The rule is consistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Bombay Rent Act, which provides for payment of house allowance as part of his salary. It is clear from section 7 that a person who has been allotted railway quarter of a specified place would be eligible to house allowance if either the Government provides accommodation to the employee in question or the employee refuses to occupy the accommodation so offered to him. The rules do not make any grant in favour of the employee, but only provide for payment to an employee of a particular category but the rules do no more than prescribe the grant. The appellant was entitled to recover the house allowance from him under the rules. The terms of contract between them were not included in the terms as defined in section 2 (vi) and section 11 of Act.

The detenu was detained under section 3(1) of the , by an order dated February 18, 1980 purporting to have been made under section 4(1), of the (for short called COFEPOSA). The grounds of detention were served on him on April 3, 1980. On March 25, 1980, the detenu was arrested and detained under the provisions of the . The grounds were served upon the detenus on April 23, 1980 and they were served with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds of Detention. The detenu made a representation to the State Government requesting him to furnish the copies of certain statements to enable them to make an effective representation. The State Government rejected the same on March 25. The order of detention was challenged before the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the grounds were not supplied to the detenu and that the detenu had been deprived of the opportunity of making an effective representa tion. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The delay of more than three weeks in supplying the copies to the detenus has vitiated the detention. [348E] 2. In the instant case, the detaining author ity did not have authority to pass the order of preventive detention. It was on the direction of the Central Government that the State Govern ment would supply the copies thereof to the petitioners. The detaining authority without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies were supplied to them. [349G] 3. In view of the fact that the copies had been supplied to detenus, the detention order was not vitiated because the concerned Minister of the State did not apply his mind to his nature of those documents and the copies supplied to him were not furnished to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. [350G] 4. The grounds are not vague or indefinite. It is on the face of it, that the detaining au thority could have made an order under clause (6) of Article 22 withholding the supply of those portions of statements after satisfying itself that their disclosure would be against the public interest. In such a situation, the delay of nearly three weeks was not justified. [351A] 5. The detention is on account of the failure to apply its mind in the nature and circumstances of the case. It has been on the part of the detaining authorities without applying their mind to these facts. There was thus an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply to the detenue, all the basic material relied on or referred to in those "grounds" must be supplied to detenu with reasonable expedition to enable he to make the full and effectively representation at a earliest.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court held that the joint appeal against all of them was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A joint appeal to the High Court by several persons jointly tried and acquitted by a common order, but if an appeal by persons jointly committed jointly tried or convicted is competent, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability of one appeal by the State against several accused persons jointly. [419 F] (2) The question of competency of a joint appeal by several accused person jointly tried jointly and severally cannot be decided in view of section 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [420 G H] (3) A combined reading of sections 258, 410 and 414 shows that each one of them is guilty of an offence by the state against whom separate trial has also to be held not to be contrary to any provision of the code and therefore not legally prohibited. The question whether a joint appeals by several or more accused persons are jointly tried together cannot be determined in view Of section 419. [411 G H; 411 A] (4) In the present case, the joint appeals were filed against several other accused persons who were acquitted at one trial. The State could not have the advantage of arguments on behalf of several accused. [413 E F] The Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court rightly distinguished and explained this decision. [414 G H].

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in foreign territory. The income tax officer assessed the appellant to income tax under the 1918 Act, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that in the case of business carried on in foreign country the business as such was not liable to tax under section 3 of the 1918 act because the assessee was only taxed on remittances received from the profits of the foreign business and there was no tax on the foreign income. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act, and accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. In appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant that the foreign trade of the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions of the Act because the income from the house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. HELD: (i) The question whether the foreign company is liable to pay tax under this Act is one of fact and not one of which is business. [912 D] (ii) The assessee was entitled, therefore, to relief thereunder. [936 G] (iii) The income from house properties held by the appellant in respect of his activity styled as foreign firm could be assessed under the 1922 act only if it was income derived from the foreign partnership and not from the Indian business itself. [948 D] In the context of these facts the foreign concern must be taken that there was an assessment to tax on foreign business within the meaning of section 25 (3) Of the 1922, and it must therefore be taken, upon the facts found by the appellate Tribunal in this case that the assessee is entitled to exemption under section 10(3).

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln. The contract was to be executed by the appellant with the public Works Department. The contractor had agreed to pay Rs. 1,000 per year as royalty on the materials supplied under the contract and the applicant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The respondent assessee paid the amount in accordance therewith. The assessee filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount from the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the transaction was a works contract, and not a works contracts. The High Court held that the contract was a contract of sale and not an execution of contract. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the agreement in question was a work contract and not merely a works Contract. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the Government was a matter which could be decided by the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act. [163C] 2. The agreement in this case is a contract for sale and cannot be said to be a works contractor. It is not necessary that the parties should have agreed to enter into an agreement with the Contractor at his own cost. If, however, it is found that the materials had been sold by him to private parties or other bodies, he shall have to pay to Department at the rate of 10% of the value of materials at the tender rates. [164D] 3. The appellant was not entitled to claim any compensation for the loss suffered by him on account of the collection of the materials and on the material being approved by the Government. [165E] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of Bihar, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a member of the Lok Sabha, was declared elected to the Rajya Sabha. The President of India passed an order on March 25, 1977 by which the President of the State of Jammu and Kashmir was either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation on March 26, 1977. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency dated March 25th June, 1975 issued by the President on March 27, 1977, under Article 356 of the Constitution. The petition was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court on August 3, 1976. In the writ petition filed before this Court it was contended that the proclamation of Emergency was invalid because the Proclamation had been validly issued and the proclamation was not published in the official Gazette of the Government of India. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The proclamation of emergency dated March 26th June 1975 was passed by Parliament both the Proclamations of Emergency as required by law and that actually the proclamation had been revoked by the two Houses of Parliament. [434E] 2. The Proclamation of emergency was in force on March 24, 1977 and the Proclamation was not issued in the Official Gazette of Parliament until it was revoked by a resolution passed by the House of the People (Extension of duration) Act 1976. [441G] 3. The two Proclams of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions passed by both Houses of the Parliament. The period of five years (being the period for which the House was to be taken into account is not a period of one year at a time. [442E] 4. The effect of the proclamation dated March 27th June. 1975 was that the Proclamation would remain in force till the expiration of two months from the date on which each of them was issued as the resolutions of the Houses of Legislature approving the two resolutions were duly published in official Gazette. [443F] 5. The resolution passed on 3rd December, 1971 was not challenged by any of the petitioners. It is only after the proclamation has been revoked that the two Pro cams of emergency were kept In force and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period of the House. [444G H] 6.

The appellant was the owner of a property in dispute. The property was sold by public auction and purchased by the respondents. The appellant filed an application for leave to appeal to this Court under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the property was not a private or public temple but was a public temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951, and that the appellant was entitled to leave under section 133(2). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was right in holding that the properties were private property and set aside the decision of the authorities. HELD: (i) The question whether a property is a public trust or a public religious endowment depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The question as to whether the property is an private or a private one has to be determined with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property in question was not inalienable and was a private property of the family, it was incapable of valuation. [157 D] (ii) The High court was right on the assumption that the respondent was a Public temple within its meaning. The appeal must be allowed. [158 E] (iii) The appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property capable of alienation, and therefore was incapable or could not be said to be a public Temple. [156 G] (iv) The property is the private properties of the said family and it is incapable of valued. It is open to the appellant to establish that the private temple is not a public deity but a public place. [155 B C] (v) The suit was filed by the respondent in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 650 of 1882, and the High court had rightly held that it was not right in assuming that the land was a 'public temple ' within the definition of Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 Of 1951.

The appellant was a workman in the category of clerks above the clerical staff. He was employed as clerks on a monthly salary of Rs. 100 per day and he was paid Rs. 10/ per day. The appellant 's workmen were paid Rs, 900 as bonus for the period from 1st July 1960 to 31st March 1961. In 1956 the appellant made an application before the Industrial Tribunal under section 33(1) of the , claiming that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical Staff should be paid as bonus in lieu thereof. The respondents contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make an award in respect of the cash allowance for the appellant 'S 's employees, that the Industrial Tribu nal was not justified in making an award on the ground that the impugned decision is erroneous in law. Held: (i) The Tribunal has rightly granted the second claim and has directed that it should be directed to pay the clerical and other allowances as bonus. The fact that the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations, does not make any difference. The Industrial Tribun al had no material bearing in dealing with the question whether the impugned order is erroneous or unjustified. The facts of this case showed that the appellant had throughout been making provision for the t he clerical staff and the correspondence between the parties on this subject shows that the respondents felt that the policy adopted by the appellant was not fair and justified. The dispute raised by the respondents was one relating to the claim made by the res pondents in respect Of tiffs who were paid wages for the periods during the period 1960 to 30th March 1961, and the respondent represented to the State Government that though the company gave assurances to its employees that re employment would not be resorted to on a liberal scale, those assurance were disregarded and the practice was being followed in many cases. The question whether there was any unfairness or unjustified could have no material before the Tribunal.

The appellant was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He applied for transfer of his provident fund and claimed immunity from attachment under the , as he had not been authorised by the Central Government to receive payment of the amount on his behalf. The Union of India, however, applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment. The appellant contended that the moneys were not liable to be attached. The High Court held that the amount represented provident Fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune under section 4(1) of the . Held, that the appellant was not a trustee for the subscriber of the money. Section 3 of , does not require that the accounts Officer should send the amount through a bank for payment at the place at which payment is required. The Bank was in respect of the provident fund in the position of a trustee who had been authorised to receive the Provident Fund amount from the Reserve Bank. The Reserve Bank was, as already stated, the agent of the Railway Administration for conversion of the amounts into sterling and was not the agent or of Browne to receive any payment on his own behalf. Under section 3 Of the , the Central Board of Revenue is in respect to the provident funds of the person who has been authorised under section 3 to receive it from the Bank. When the money remained under the control of the railway Administration as provident fund fund money, it was exempt from attachment and sale under the law and that the payment was required either under the first intimation at Liverpool by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of 'Browne at Birmingham. The Central Board was in the nature of a trust for the benefit of the public. The respondent was a trustee of the subscriber to a Provident Fund Account in sterling if the country in which it is to be paid, the rupee is not legal tender.

The appellant was employed in the respondent 's establishment. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from serv ice with effect from 1st January, 1971. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal and also the validity of the termination of his services. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that the termination was mala fide or unfair labour practice. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination is a colourable exercise of power, the employer must disclose to the court the grounds of his order; (ii) the appellant has failed to establish that the order was mala fides or unfair Labour practice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the action of the management was not bona fide and therefore the termination could not be sustained. [497 F] (i)(a) The power of the Court to go behind the form of the order is preserved there. But if it came to the conclusion that the impugned order was a colourable or mala fide, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [498 G] (b) The High court was satisfied that the reasons given by the Labour Appellate Tribunal were not bona fides. If it came before the finding that the dismissal was a wrongful exercise of the power or was a result of victimisation or unfair work, the Industrial Tribunal would have jurisdiction to interfere and set at naught such termination.[498 G H] (c) The order of termination was not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order made by the management. [500 A B] (d) The finding of the Labour Court that the respondent had lost confidence in the employee was essentially one of fact aad this Court should not disturb the finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point.

The petitioners, who were working as a sublive nent in Uttar Pradesh, arranged and conducted the training programme for the treatment of doctors. The petitioners, however, did not participate in the inquiry conducted by the Deputy Director (Eye treatment) and the Sub Divisional Magistrate, U.P., and the District Magistrate, appropriate follow up action was contemplated by the Government against those responsible for the tragedy. The Committee recommended that the doctors should be given some monitary relief to the victims. The State Government also recommended that they should be paid a sum of Rs.5,000 by way of interim relief. The District Magistrate rejected the recommendations and directed that the petitioners would be entitled to receive the additional payment from the State Government. The Petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the orders of the Committee and the direction for payment of additional amount. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the State should have been given some interim relief by the State Govern ment. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The State would approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to be made by the state Government. [256G] 1.2 In addition to the sum of RS.5 lakhs already paid by way Of interim relief, the State Govt. shall pay a further sum of rupees one lakh by way off the interim relief and the amount shall be deposited as directed by the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of the interim Relief. [257A B] 1:3 The petitioners would certainly be willing to render help to the victim within the constraints of its resources. They would have to be given an opportunity to the injured victims within the stipulated period and, therefore, they should pay a sum as those who had the benefit of the interlocutory relief of Rs 5,000 already paid. [255C] 1 :4 The State should also take up this issue and process the claims of the victims for such other bene fits under any of the existing schemes now in force in the State, their cases shall be considered for such benefit. [260E] 2:1 In addition, if any of these matters would have been decided by the Court and the limited scope of the proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine of State action. The Court is not concerned with the merits of the case. It is only in exceptional cases that the victims should be afforded some monaster relief by a State Government, but would also look upon them as a compa ny which must, accordingly, be held vicariously liable. [262C D] 2.2 The State shall take up the issue and proceed with the claims for such benefits under any existing schemes so that the claims may be consid ered in accordance therewith. [263G H] 3:1. In addition thereto, if the victims are, otherwise, eligible for any benefit of pension under any other scheme then, eligible to any benefit under any such scheme. The victims shall also be considered as a provi sion of the schemes providing for aid to the aged, the disabled, and the destitute, sub ject to the condi tions. [264G H; 264A] 3.2.

The petitioner No. 1 was the President of the Assam State Assembly and elected to the Legislative Assembly. The petitioner No 2, who was the Secretary of the State Assembly, challenged the action taken by the respondent No. 3 in the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the impugned order was violative of article 19(1)(c) of the Constitu tion as it was passed without any authority or authority and that the said order was ultra vires the provisions of Article 19(i)(c). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner No 1 that the Act was enacted by the Legislature in exercise of emergency powers under article 19 (1) (c) and (d) of Constitution and as such the provisions were ultra vires. Dismissing the Writ Petition, HELD: The impugned order is valid. [171C] The Act does not provide for an Act to provide for temporary transfer of management and control of affairs of a Samiti. It is only when that was challenged by a suit, an ordinance was brought taking over the Samiti as a whole specially replaced by the Act and it was made clear that the Adhiniyam was a temporary measure in fact, the Act does no more than have been taken away. [172D] The word "may" has not been defined in the Act. It has been used to mean "may". In the instant case, the impugned Act is not violative of Article 14 of the Consti tution. [173E F] The impugned Act was passed by the legislature and it had no power to enact it. [174F] The State Government had no desire to restore the Samiti and therefore the Act did not have any effect whatsoever.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of a Hindu wife, was married to the respondent on May 10, 1938. The respondent 's father, who was the son of the appellant, made an application under section 14 of the Indian Succession Act for a declaration that the marriage was void and not binding on her. The trial court held that the appellant had no right to make a gift of the four houses at Asansol in favour of the respondent. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent was competent to execute a deed of gift in favour Of the daughter of a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband to her daughter as she had not been given any right to execute the deed of gifts. The question whether a Hindu woman could make a valid gift for or at the time of marriage, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Held further, that in view of section 14 Of the Indian Evidence Act, it is open to a Hindu female to adopt a son who has been married to her husband irrespective of the consideration whether she made a gift for the purpose of the deed or not. The mere fact that the gift was made some two years after the marriage could not make a declaration under section 15 of the Act. Held, further, also that the question whether the respondent had any right in the properties given to her as a marriage dowry in pursuance and fulfilment of an ante nuptial agreement, even though the gift is made some one after the other, was not a valid transfer for or At the time when the marriage ceremony was performed.

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The election of Tej Singh was challenged by the first respondent in a petition under section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 on the ground that he had committed corrupt practices punishable under section 77(1)(a) of that Act and that he was guilty of committing corrupt practice. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove the corrupt practice alleged by him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the first Respondent (appellant) that the allegations of corrupt practices were vague, and that the posters were printed in the newspapers and were printed not by Ruplal but at the instance of Tej Kaur. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The poster alleged to have been published by Tej Singh had been clearly proved. [416D] 2. The posters said to have be read as a whole and that all the voters who would have voted for the poster were not invited to vote for Ruplals. It is also clear from the evidence that the poster was printed at the behest of Tejinder Singh. [417E F] 3. In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between the defeated and returned candidates, it is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in these elections. [414F] 4. The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh has actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and with the consent of Tej singh. It was also clear that Tejinder Kaur had withdrawn and any vote given to Tej Singh would be considered as a vote given by Tejinder singh. [413F] 5. The pamphlet was not published in the newspaper but at a later stage, it was necessary to extract some portions thereof from the newspapers. [411G] 6. In the circumstances, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Kaur had actually paid the posters for the printing of the poster which were issued by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign. [420A B] 7. The evidence on record shows that Tej singh was known to him as a person who could have voted in favour of Tej Sing Singh and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered. [409C D] 8. In other words, the effect of the posters was that all those voters who had come to his printing press and informed him that he (Tej. Singh) would be sending some work for the printed poster which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement. The result is that the election of the appellant would have gone to the appellant 's printing. [405D] 9. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that Tej Sing had actually made any attempt to prove corrupt practice particularly when the printing was done by or with the permission of Tejpal Singh. Therefore, it could not be held that Tejpal had actually received the posters from Tej Singh and Tej Singh. The conclusion is that can only be arrived on that basis.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was appointed as an officer to be an Additional Chief Minister. The Chief Minister of the State was appointed to officiate as an Additional Secretary to the Government. On his appointment he was appointed on probation for one year and later on he was confirmed with effect from 1st January, 1978. He was confirmed in that post on 1st February, 1978 and he was promoted to the rank of Additional Chief Secretary. The appellant challenged the order of confirmation before the High Court by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the application for contempt against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High court in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt, section 19(1) is inapplicable and the appeal is incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 215 of the Constitu tion is to punish a person for contempt. When no punishment is imposed by the Court it is difficult to say that the HighCourt has exercised its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215. [893G] 2.1 The High Courts exercising their jurisdiction or powers are not competent to punish any of them under section 19 (1) of the Act.

The appellant was the owner of a house in Bombay. The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment against him on the ground that he had committed breach of contract by the tenant and that as the plaintiff did not approach the defendants and no demand for rent was made, no forfeiture occurred. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the notice was necessary before the lease could be terminated. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 111(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, were not applicable to a tenant of the description given in the notice as it then stood. Held, that the provision in sub section (g) Of section III of the Act was intended to apply only to cases where there was a forfeiture by denial of landlord 's title to the property and for enforcing the forfeiture in case of non payment of rent, and even in other cases except where statutory provisions were made to the contrary. The provisions of the section are not intended to be applied in this case as it stood before 1929 and to leases executed after 1st April, 1930, the principle of equity and good conscience was applicable to the facts of the present case. The provision in section 111 (g), which is a statutory recognition of a principle of justice, equity and bad faith, must be construed as a whole and not merely a procedural law but also a substantive rule of justice. In the instant case, the provisions in sub s.(g) were intended to cover all leases and no notice as required by section 111 was necessary for terminating the lease.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Industrial Tribunal. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the dismissal of his services on the ground that he had been denied an opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of the order of dismissal as required by Standing Order 17(2) of the Madhya Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1960. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to a workman at the conclusion of the enquiry into his misconduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment of dismissal was imposed on Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that Standing Order No. 17 provided for second opportunity being given to the workman to showcause against the action proposed punishment of dismissing him as required under the Standing Order. The Labour Court held that the procedure laid down in Standing Order 22(2), namely, (i) the enquiry was vitiated by not affording him an opportunity of showing cause against proposed punishment; and (ii) the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer were perverse and therefore no distinction on the basis of the said Standing Order was justified. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The first part of Standing order No.17 provides for second chance being given by a workman to offer his explanation. It is true that the Arbitrator has undoubtedly taken the view that the opportunity spoken of by para 3 does not refer to the further opportunity being afforded to a workmen at the stage of enquiry into their misconduct and it is not possible to say that if no such second opportunity is contemplated by it then the only ground on which the inquiry has been held to be invalid by the Arbitrator and the High court would disappear and the Arbitrator could not have entered into merits of the case or interfered with the punishment. [368C D] 2. The word "dismissed" in Standing order 17(1) means dismissal, removal or reduction from service. It does not mean dismissal or removal from service but only termination of services simpliciter. The second part of the Standing order deals with two different stages concerning disciplinary proceedings and the third part deals with the penalty of dismissal and for that punishment alone makes a special provision that no order awarding that punishment will be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity, to show explanation. [369D E] 3. The words "any other kind of misconduct" in section 2(2)(a) of Madhya Pradesh Road Transport Act, 1960 are wide enough to include dismissal or discharge from service and for this purpose it is necessary that the workman should be given a second opportunity to offer any explanation. The third part of sub clause (1) deals with three stages viz., disciplinary proceedings against a delinquent, first holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of natural justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to the delinquent to show that he has been guilty of misconduct. [370E F] 4. The only ground for interference with the order passed by the Labour Court is that when the enquiry is held to have been invalid having disappeared it must follow that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to enter into the merits of case or interfere with the punishments of dismissal inflicted upon him. [371F G] 5. The mere fact that the respondent was given an opportunity being taken to show a second notice, does not make any such assumption and, therefore, the finding recorded by him that the delinquent is guilty of conduct which is to be explained by him and not the proposed penalty of dismissing or removal on the other hand cannot be interfered with. [372F G; 371A] 6. The expression "dismissing" in sub clause 2(1)(a), means dismissal or dismissal or termination of service.

The Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 was amended by the Kerala Land Reform (Amendment) Act, 1969. The Amendment Act provided that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law, custom or usage or usage, or in any contract, custom, usage or custom or custom, or usage of land custom or practice or usage etc., or in the any contract or usage. Section 7D of the Act provided for the acquisition of rights of tenants and sub sections (1) and (2) of section 52 were made applicable to such lands as were acquired by the State Government under the Kerala Estates Abolition Act, 1964. The appellants who had been cultivating land for not less than ten years prior to the commencement of the Kerala Agricultural Lands (Amendment Act, 1970, filed a suit claiming that they were entitled to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything contained in section 52 or any other law, and that they should be deemed to have been tenants notwithstanding any order of court. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had not acquired any right of occupancy rights but had acquired title by adverse possession. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondents were entitled only to the benefit of section 7D. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act is a piece of legislation and it is not intended to be enacted with a view to protect tenants from eviction. [112B] 1.2 The Act does not contemplate any particular kind of legislation but only provides for certain types of legislation. It is not necessary that the legislature should have intended to provide for such legislation. The legislature has also provided for certain classes of legislation which are not exhaustive. The Legislature has also prescribed a procedure for the determination of disputes between the parties. [111C D] 1:3. In the instant case, the Act does contemplate acquisition of land by the Government or by an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. The Act provides for the compulsory acquisition of lands and sub section (2), which is in pari materia with section 52, provides that the acquisition shall be deemed always to be tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land on the 11th day of April, 1957. [ 112E F] 1 :4. The object of the legislation is to provide a speedy remedy for eviction of tenants from lands and to make suitable provision for their rehabilitation.
