It would not be possible to lay down any rigid formula or inflexible rule that the Act should be construed as a whole and it would be impossible to lay out any particular method of construction which would render the provisions of the statute invalid. [114F G] 1 5. The purpose of the enactment is to ensure that the tenants are protected from eviction by the Act. If the legislature has intended to give effect to the policy of the law, it would have been impossible to do so. It was not possible to say that the Legislature had intended to make a provision for the protection of tenants against eviction. The intention of the legislature is to give such protection to tenants from ejectment and to avoid eviction by resorting to any other method of interpretation which will defeat the object of legislation, if it were otherwise permissible to do. [115G H] 6.

The appellant was found in possession of a consignment of goods. He was convicted under section 135(b) (ii) of the . The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had not produced evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods in question were actually smuggled and therefore they could not be said to have been smuggled or imported into India without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory; that the appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. HELD: (1) The appellant had not been able to know where the goods came from or when the goods were imported or that duty, if leviable was not paid on them. [557 B] (2) The fact that the person who is found in Possession of the goods and the writing on boxes in which they were kept, for proving the place from which they came, or when they were questioned, would not lead to any inference that they are smuggled goods; but it was immaterial whether the goods actually were smuggled or brought into India. [541 C] (3) The High Courts had rightly convicted only under section 136 of the Act. It is true that the High Court has held that the appellants were found in posses sion with full knowledge of what the goods had actually been, and brought into the country without payment thereof. But it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the articles were legally brought into or sold by the appellant. [542 D] (4) The mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable the prosecution, to apply section 106 of the Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where they came from. It was immaterial that the accused had knowledge of the possession of the articles and the manner in which he was brought into his country. [543 G] (5) The onus of proving that the article was smuggled or was imported into the territory without payment or knowledge of it is on the person from whose possession the goods are seized. It may be that the said article was found to have not been seized under the Act, as provided by section 123(2). [543 F] (6) The burden of proving the articles in question was upon the person to prove the existence of the article and the nature of the evidence adduced by him.

The appellants were the President of a Association, Budhar. The members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of the goods and the profits on the sales thereof shall be according to the capital shares of the members of that Association. The appellants filed a suit for accounts of the income from the sale proceeds of the said goods and also for accounts. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the suit was not maintainable because the provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, were not applicable to the case. Held, that the appellants had a right to bring a suit under section 4 (2) Of the Rewa States Act, 1934, and the suit for account of the profits was maintainable. The suit was therefore maintainable for recovery of the contributions made by the appellants and also in respect of accounts of an illegal association which was dissolved in February 1948. The provisions of sections 4(1)(a) and 69(3)(a), (b) and (c) of section 69(2A) of that Act were not attracted. The object of the Act was to prevent the abuse of the process of the court by a person who is guilty of any offence under the law declared to be illegal, and therefore, the suit must fail. The general principle of res judicata is that in order that illegality may be a defence, it must affect the contract on which the plaintiff is compelled to rely so as to make out his right to what he asked.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420 and 471 IPC read with section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0.1986 they along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 1, who was a member of the mob. The respondents were prosecuted under section 9(1)(a) read with Section 5(2) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1955 for having committed offences punishable under sections 161, 165 and 120B IPC. The Trial Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against the respondents. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed against the three respondents. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the order passed by the Magistrate would not be binding on him. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The test is that taking the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High court will be justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. [463C] 1.2 In the instant case, the charge sheet was filed on 8th June 1986 and the Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of summons to the respondents for being tried on the basis of the complaint or the charge sheets do not in law constitute or spell out any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of the process of the court or not. [464D] 1:3 The test was whether taking the allegation and the complainant as they were, without added or subse quently, a case of conspiracy or conspiracy can be made out against them. It is not necessary that the ingredients of an offence under section 499 IPC should be established before the Court can take cognizance of an alleged offence. [465F] 1.(4) The test in such cases is whether taking cognizance is taken on the police report or the chargesheet do not disclose any offence or make out a case against the accused. If the Magistrate is satisfied that there was prima facie evidence and the allegations made in the charge or the charges are true, then the Court will be entitled to take cognizance under section 482 of Cr. P.C. [467F G] 2.1 In the present case, there were no prior conviction and the order dated 1.7.1986 passed by a Magistrate taking cognizance was not challenged before the High Courts. The High Court was in error in quashing proceedings of the Magistrate on the facts of this case. [468G H; 468A B] 2:2. In view of the fact that the two offences are substantially "the same offence" and "same offence", the question whether the ingredients mentioned in the first part of section 9 (1) read together with Section 50(l) of Act, on the other hand, constitute an offence ' under the IPC and at the same time constitute an offense under the Indian Penal Code. [470B C] 2 :3. The test for determining whether jurisdiction is to be exercised by a Court only on the report of the police officer is not satisfied with the allegations, whether those allegations are made out or not, and whether those averments are true and substantially the same as Section 50 (l) and (2). [470C] 2 4. In cases where the acts alleged to constitute contempt of court are punishable under section 5 (1)(b), it is necessary that there should be a prima facie case for quashing the proceeding in exercise thereof.

The petitioner was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to release the accused without bail or on his own bond; (2) the police had failed to produce the relevant documents before the courts in criminal cases; (3) the High Court had not correctly exercised its discretion in quantifying the amount of bail and (4) the public exchequer has to bear the cost of maintaining him in the jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law which is now being followed in the report of a Committee with Judges, lawyers, members of Parliament and other legal experts, cannot be said to have been violated by the procedure prescribed by law. [343G] 2. The practice which is being followed by the courts is that either the poor or the poor should not be released on bail or their release on his personal bond without bail, i.e., surety, cannot he conditioned to attend at the appointed place. [344A B] 3. The Magistrate has no power to release on bail in a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs. He is prevented from taking any steps to secure his release. [345B] 4. The discretion of the court to release him on his self bond without surety, is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deter mination against release. If a Magistrate is Satisfaction that the accused has his roots in the community and is nor likely to abscond, he can safely release the person on his bond without a bail or even on his behalf. [346C] 5. The courts have not been justified in imposing conditions on release on one 's own bond. It is imperative that the magistrate should be given an opportunity of being heard before he is released on his application for bail. If he is in confinement, that be released from jail custody, actual or potential, may be released by the court, to further the ends of justice and nothing in section 389(1) which reads as follows: "The accused shall ordinarily be released at any time on his furnishing a personal bond with or without sureties". The Magistrate should also have been given an option to apply for bail before he can appear or on behalf his pleader. [347D E] 6. The object of the Act is to protect the poor and indigent 's rights, and not to release them on their own bond without any bail, even if they are deprived of an opportunity to work to support himself and his family with the result that burden of his detention falls heavily on the innocent members of the family, (3 ) The Magistrate must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the Criminal Procedure Code. [349G H] 7. The power of the Court to release an accused without surety is not absolute and unfettered. It does not mean that an accused should be released only on his 's personal bond, with orwithout sureties. [350A B].

The assessee, a registered firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. The Tribunal held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it had proceeded on an assumption that in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52 the income from 'Castle ' had not been computed and included in the computation of the capital invested for the purpose of section 15 C. The High Court, however, held that a question of law did not arise out of the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner refusing to state a case for an order directing the Tribunal, to state it, and referred it to it. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) Section 66(2) invests the High Courts with jurisdiction to require the Tribunal on questions of fact, if there is some evidence to support the finding. But the refusal of the tribunal to state any case for the opinion of the High court on a question whether the finding was one or not would be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. [440 D] (ii) The Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at its conclusion and in refusing to do so, it did not consider the other questions on which the Appellate Tribunal had relied. [ 431 B] (iii) The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal is based upon some evidence ignoring other relevant matters on which it was founded and ignores other relevant factors on which that finding is founded and overlooked other relevant considerations on which such conclusion is founded, and its effect has to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which a finding is based. [427 C] (iv) The High Courts have jurisdiction to call upon the Tribunal for the reasons stated by it to state its case and to refer it, if the Appellate Court had refused to state that the case was one which was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion of the income of 'Cantastle" in the assessment of the appellant may have been a relevant circumstance.

The respondent was appointed as a party to the writ petition. The Minister of the State Government, who had been impleaded as a respondent in the writ peti tion filed by him, filed an application for impleading the respondent as a defendant in the petition. He also filed an affidavit stating that he had not been heard and that he should be impleaded as an opposite party in the Writ Petition. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the Minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties and thereafter pass necessary order in the matter. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to be impleaded in the appeal because he had acted as a witness in the case of the writ petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a person was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of his allegations made in the election petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. [972C] In the instant case, the Minister had not filed any affidavit in regard to the allegations made against the Minister. The respondent was directed to file his affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister to decide in the light of the allegations contained in the application and thus, to afford the appellant an opportunity to rebut those allegations if he otherwise deemed proper, [973D] In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not possible to interfere with the order made by the respondent. The direction regarding impleading of a Minister as an party was given in the present petition.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed an application under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 for recovery of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent and buildings. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in revision affirmed the decision of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the view taken by the High court was erroneous. HELD: (i) Section 259 of Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1913 is not applicable to a case where the Act or the Rules made thereunder are silent as to what they do. The provisions of section 259 are intended to be applied in cases where the provisions of the Act have been made applicable to the case and the rules framed thereunder. [347 B] (ii) Section 260 of the Municipal Act is not attracted because the provisions relating to rent of land or buildings under the management of the Board do not apply to rent on land and buildings let out by it even by suit if the rent in the section refers only to rent directly claimable under the Act. [346 C] (iii) The provisions contained in section 259 do not affect the operation of section 260 of that Act. Section 259 does not confer any right on the Board to recover rent due to the appellant in the manner provided for in the Act, and the Rules which empower the Board or the Municipal Officer under the provisions thereof. [349 E] (iv) The words "claimable by a committee under this Act" and that it was not any sum that could be described as rent or fee which could be recovered under section 260. [348 G H] (v) Section 258 of the is not intended to apply in cases of rent or fees which could have been recovered under summary provisions of that section. The words 'claimable ' are not meant for recovery and therefore, neither could a reference be made by the Sessions Judge to the High Courts under section 438. [350 G H; 347 A] (vi) Section 264 does not affect any question of law arising out of the provisions contained therein. It is only when the Act has been passed that the provisions in section 260 apply to cases where rent of lands or buildings are not payable by a landlord, and if such rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under this section or the rules made thereunder, the Rules would be applicable.

The appellant was appointed as a Section salesman in the State of Rajasthan. The services of the respondent company were terminated from service on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The appellant challenged the order of termination by a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of the services of respondent company was legal and justified and if not to what relief he was entitled to, the reference was incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Labour Court has given findings in favour of the employer on the question whether the termination itself was illegal. [474G] 2. The finding of the Tribunal that the appellant was not a 'workman ' is not correct. The High Court has held that the order was incompetent and the reference, therefore, was incompetent.[473A B] 3. The scope of the Act and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's services were terminated, the employee has to be 'under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the section i.e. manual, skilled and/or clerical nature and that the provisions of the Industrial Dispute Act are not applicable to the termination in the instant case which was long prior to the enactment of this Act. [473D E] 4. The question whether a workman is a ' workman ' or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The employer has to show whether he is a workman employed for manual, unskilled and/ or clerical nature. If the employer has no such power, he cannot be said to have been in employment for manual work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. [476F G] 5. The definition of 'workman" under the industrial Disputes Act is not applicable. The object of this enactment and the employee covered by it also go ting to show how persons employed in the shop of the wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell the products of the company and to collect the amount of sale. [477G] 6. The management has to pay an amount equivalent to three years salary at the rate he was drawing when the appel lant 's appointment was terminated, in addition to whatever amount they were paying during the pendency of the appeal under orders of this Court. [478A B; 478B] 7. The work involved in the case is not a workman. It is not necessary that the employer should pay some compensation to the workman for manual labour and labour. The wages involved by the appellant are not the same as those employed for sale promotion normally. The workmen are not employed for any particular purpose. [479C] 8. The Tribunal has given finding on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour Court. It cannot be interfered with that finding unless there is some evidence to show the intention of the legislature or the employee to justify such a conclusion. [480G H] 9. The findings of the Labour court are not binding on the appellant.

The respondent was a company registered under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950. The Company was a statutory tenant under the M.P. Land Revenue & Tenancy Act. The company was not a Government lessee within the meaning of section 181 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue Act, 1951. The State Government issued a notification dated 1.10.1977 in exercise of its powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 182 of the M P. Land Reforms Act, Samvat 2007 (for short, the Act). The Company filed an application before the Additional Collector for eviction of the company on the ground that it was not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182 of Madhya Bharat Act, 1961. The Additional Collector held that the land was not covered by Section 181 of M. P. Act and was therefore not liable for being proceeded against. The appeal filed by the Company before the High Court failed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Company was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the Code as it had not become a "pakka" tenant under Section 54(vii) of the Act and therefore, the company could not be evicted by summary proceedings provided for under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has found in the earlier proceeding that the company was neither a "Pakka ' tenant" nor a "Ghatka" as found by the High court in the previous proceeding held that it could not have recourse to the proceedings prescribed under section 182 Code. [179F] 2. Section 181(1) and (2) of Madhya Pradesh Act, 1958 are clear from the provisions of the two Acts. The expression "Pankka" is defined in the Madhya Pravat 2007 as meaning "a Government lessee". It is not and cannot be disputed that the original lease was obtained from the predecessor State and the Company continued to remain in possession of the land under the newly stipulated terms agreed upon between the parties to enable the company to remain In possession of land under a new lease or holding, upon termination of that lease, under and in terms thereof. [180F G] 3. The finding of the High Courts to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [181G] 4. The view taken by the Additional Collec tor is correct. The findings of the trial court to the same effect are set aside and the order of the Additional collector is restored. [182F] 5. The question whether or not the Company has been holding over under the old lease or under the new lease, the Company had been at all material times a Government lessees in respect of the lands in dispute at any time prior to the coming into force of the said Act No. 66 of 1950 is a question of fact and cannot arise. [183F] 6. The order of High Court dated 20.9.1980 in case No. 8.1.1977 was passed by the Assistant Collector on 1. 10.1977 for eviction from the land in question.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964 was passed by the Orissa Legislature in exercise of its powers under section 1(3) of the Act. By a notification dated October 17, 1960 the State Government declared that the provisions of the Orissa Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1965 were not applicable to the lands which were within the ceiling limit applicable to them under any law for the time being in force. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was inconsistent with or takes away orabras any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution and as such was void. The High Court held that section 47 incorporated by Act 15 of 1965 did not apply to the land which could be acquired and that the petitioners were entitled to compensation under the Act for the acquisition of their proprietary interest. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 47 incorporated in the Orissa Act 16 of 1960 was not extended by a notification issued under section I(3). The Act was therefore in force on July 1, 1949. [319 A] (2) The impugned notification did not contain any provision for compensation for the property which may be laid only if the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus land which is within the Ceiling limit applicable in him under any laws providing for the compulsory acquisition by the State of any estate. [328 B] (3) The Act did not provide for compensation to the landholders for extinguishment of their interests but only provided for compensation at a rate which shall be determined and given. The Act had no application to the case because section 47 was in force when the Act came into force. [330 C D] (4) Section 1(1) of Act 16 Of 1960 is not applicable as it stood before the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act 1964. It is only after the power is exercised by the Government that the State Govern ment has to make a declaration under section 47 that the Act shall come into operation. [332 E] (5) The notification issued in exercise thereof was valid and the notification was not saved by section 1 (3). [330 G] (6) Section I(1)(a) of Orissa Land reforms (Amendment), Act, 1963 is undoubtedly a law in force but until the power was exercised by State Government to issue an appropriate notification, the provisions Of Ch. IV of the principal Act were not extended to the areas which were covered by any law providing for acquisition by State of such land.

The widow of her husband 's estate was in the same way as that of an alienee from her husband. She died leaving behind a widow and two daughters. The widow filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that she had no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of the properties to her husband and that the widow 's right to claim the property was not extinguished by adverse possession. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) as the widow had no title left in the widow, she could not have any interest left with her and therefore the widow could not be surrendered to the reversioner; (2) even assuming that the husband had acquired by adverse Possession the limited interest of a widow was really an act of adoption by her, the widow would not be entitled to claim compensation for the property which she had herself made; (3) even if the alienation was valid, it could not affect the rights of the reversioners in the sense that they got the inheritance even during the widow"s lifetime. Held, that the right of a reversioner to enforce his title by adverse posses sion is not extinguished and the widow has no interest in the property at all and therefore could not claim compensation under section 12(1) of the Act. The right of the reversioner to challenge it was not affected by the surrender made by her. The transfer by a Hindu widow to her father was not an alienation but an alienation made subsequently by the widow. The gift by a female in favour of the widow was not a voluntary act on the part of the husband and she was under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate.

The appellant company was a public limited company. The Cotton Mills Company was incorporated in the State of Uttar Pradesh and its registered office was situated at Kanpur. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 169 of the U.P. Government Industrial Undertakings (Development and Regulation) Act, 1958, the Central Government issued an order dated February 1, 1985 directing the appellant to treat the said notice as a special notice under section 169(2) of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the power of the Collector under section 17A was not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of a Receiver under the Land Revenue Act, and that the order passed by the Collector was without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Mills company had ceased to have the rights of a member of the Polytex Company by reason of the appointment of the Receiver under section 170(2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed under section 171(2)(a) of U. P. Government Industries (Development & Regulation)Act, 1958 is not the general meeting of the Board of Directors of the company and therefore the order of the Collec tor is not a nullity. [177C] 2. The power to issue a notice under the Act in respect of the shares of a company without more cannot be taken away by reason or otherwise deprive the holder of the share which he has acquired as an issue at the next meeting. [179D] 3. The powers of the Commissioner under section 18AA (1) (a) are not the similar to those of the Cotton Mill Company. It is only when a receiver has been appointed in respect thereof that he has no right to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under Section 169 of Act. [180F] 4. The Deputy Collector, Kanpur, was not entitled to call the meeting in accordance with the notice issued under section 168 of the Land revenue Act. He could not be treated as the holder 's share in the Poly Mills Company 's shares. [181G] 5. The Custodian General of Uttar pradesh is a statutory body and its members are not required to act independently or otherwise. It has no bearing on the case before him. [182F] 6. The Assistant Collector, the Deputy Commissioner, Kanpur was not competent to issue notice under s 169 of U P. Act. There is no provision in the Act which provides for the appointment or a Receiver. The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pra desh, does not make any difference between the case and the case. [183F] 7. The Collector was not empowered to issue notices under section 172(2), but only to call upon the meeting of a Board of directors of the Company or to give notice under sec. 169 of that Act. It was also not necessary for him to call a meeting in compliance with the said provision. [184G] 8. The Commissioner, the Collector, is not competent in law to issue any notice under Sec. 169(1)(a). He may be given an opportunity to the Board to show cause why he should not be removed from the meeting. If he so desires he may give a hearing to the Chairman of the Committee. [185G] 9.

The petitioners filed a suit in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others. The suit was dismissed by the trial court on the ground that the suit property belonged to the Panchayat and it had no sort of right in the suit. The petitioners filed an appeal before the Additional District Judge which was allowed by the Additional Sub Judge. The revision petition filed by the petitioners was allowed. In the Revision Petition, the High Court held that since the question involved in the Suit was merely one of title to the suit and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit was shamlat deh or not, and that the land had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Gram Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The High Court also held that the question raised in the Civil Suit was simply one of fact and that it was necessary to determine whether the property in question was sham plot or not and whether the land was sham ly or not. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act and therefore he held that it could not be said that the property was sham land in question. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiff who claimed to be the owners along with others of the Suit land had failed to prove that the plaintiff was a shamlat lord. It is no doubt true that the plaintiffs who claimed the suit lands were not shamlat ments but they had, however, questioned the correctness of entries in the Revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the same. The Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The Panchayat in fact did not claim a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the plaintiff land belonged to it or that it did not belong to the Village Panchayat. [837C D] 2. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration, that the lands in question belonged to them as shamlat t. They had no right or title in it. It was not possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration under section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act 1961. [889C D]. 3. The defendants cannot by merely raising the plea that the disputed land belonged exclusively to them or that they belong to them. They have, however. questioned the validity of the entries in revenue records and not by the Civil Court. [899D] 4. The question whether a suit is shamlat or not is essentially one of law and fact. It will not be possible in this case for the Civil court to give a declaration as to the nature of the land in dispute. [909E] 5. In view of the provisions of section 12 read with Sections 13A, 13B and 13 B of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation), Act 1961, the jurisdiction of civil courts to try such suits had been taken away. The Civil Court has not been given any right or possession in it, nor is there any ground to interfere with the judgment of the High court of Punjab and Haryana against which this petition is filed. [919E F] 6. The respondents cannot by taking their plaint say that the civil suit was not maintainable because they had no title or interest in it; but they have only challenged the correctness or validity of entries made therein. They are, therefore, not entitled to claim a decree for possession. [929G H] 7. The trial court has rightly held that there is no ground to interference with the judgments of the courts below.

The appellants, a public limited company, had entered into an agreement with the Board for supply of electricity to its consumers. The Board was to supply electricity to the consumers at the rate of 2% per annum on the security deposit. The Electricity Board was also to pay interest on the amount deposited by the consumer with the Electricity Board in terms of clause 20 (a) and (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. The appellants, however, did not pay interest for the period from 1st April, 1986 to 31st March, 1987. The consumers filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the demand on the ground that the Board was not justified in imposing a unreasonable restraint on the power of the Board on the consumer in respect of the validity of consumption security deposit and the conditions on which it is supplied being statutory, the provisions under the conditions of supply that the Electricity Supply shall not pay any interest on such security deposit, as they were not guaranteed at the time of supply. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the appellants had no power to impose a reasonable restraint on their right to carry on business in respect thereof and that the demand of interest on security deposit was not only a deposit in cash to safeguard recovery of electricity dues for the energy supplied to the consumer on credit but also a security towards payment or satisfaction of any money (for example, theft), which may become due and payable to the Board by the consumers. In these appeals it was contended that the power to fix the conditions under the terms and conditions of the supply is not only an additional security deposit but also an additional charge for the purpose of supply of energy. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The demand of the Electricity Boards on the consumers in respect the validity or otherwise of consumption of electricity is not unreasonable. [557E] 2. The power to levy a reasonable restriction under Article 19 (1) (f) and the terms of supply is an additional condition of supply which has direct bearing on the operation of the Act. It is not necessary that the conditions must be complied with before imposing any amount liable to be paid by the licensee to the Electricity board for violation of any conditions of supplies in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tampering with the meters and such other methods adopted by the Board. [511B C] 3. The condition of supplying electricity to consumers at their own cost is not a condition precedent for the supply of electrical energy. It does not contemplate appropriation of the amount of interest payable on the amounts due to the licensee. [506D] 4. The conditions of Supply are such that it represents the moneys of the consumer and the Board must be satisfied before imposing a penalty. [525C D] 5. The terms of the agreement are not only in the nature of contract but also in the form of an additional guarantee for the performance of an obligation imposed by law or contract from the date of deposit. [500E] 6. The supply of electric energy is an essential ingredient of the term of supply and it represents a moneys of money which are not a fixed sum. It represents the monies of the licensee as well as the Board, and it is not possible to say that the terms or conditions of service of supply in the sense of contract have been complied with by the Electricity Department. [504D] 7. The requirement of supply requiring a consumption security deposits has a direct bearing to the level of supply at the rates fixed by the Government. [ 509E] 8. The question whether the Board is justified in levying a reasonable restrictions on the right of the consumers to carry out its obligation under the provisions of the conditions for supply and the condition of the supplies would depend upon the nature and quality of the goods supplied, the terms thereof being not unreasonable or the consumer would be entitled to continue to pay the amount. [457F] 9. The levy of interest is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court.

The petitioners are working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre. They were working as Officers in the Telegraph Engineering Service and were manned by the transferred officers of the Telecommunications Research Centre, which is directly under the control of the P & T Department. The posts of Deputy Directors and Deputy Director were manning the posts of Assistant Directors and Assistant Directors. The petitioners challenged their promotion to the post of Deputy Director and Deputy Directors on the ground that they are not entitled to any Special Pay in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Direc tor, and that they were not entitled for special pay which is granted to the transferred officer as can be seen from the letter written by the Association on the petitioners (Annexure A) and that the Director, Telecommunici cation Research Centre was not entitled under the Recruitment Rules. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions holding that the direct recruits were not competent and they were entitled to special pay in addition thereto. In these appeals by Special Leave it was contended for the appellants that the petitioners are not competent to grant them the same special pay as granted to them on account of the irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rule and the second relating to violation of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution by not granting them the similar special pay. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The direct recruits (direct recruits) who are directly recruited to the Tele Communication Research Centre are entitled to the Special Pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the transfer officers working in that centre with effect from the date on which the transferred Officers have been drawing the Special pay. [1010B] 2. The Indian Telecommuni ty Service Officers who are not directly recruited in the telephone communication Research Centre and who are selected by the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition examination need to be paid special pay, cannot be said to be discriminatory or arbitrary. [1001C D] 3. The contention that the respondents are not incompetent and are not able to discharge their duties is untenable. [1002D] 4. The question relating to denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioners according to the Recruitment rules is left open to be agitated before the Central Administrative Tribunal. [1103E] 5. The discrimination between the direct recruit and the transferred officials regarding payment of Special Pay is attempted to be justified by the Government in the counter affidavit filed by the respondents.

The appellant company was a registered office of the respondent company. The appellant company had been running its factory in Bombay and it had been established that the appellant had not made an application under section 42(4) of the Act for relief under section 7 (1) of that Act, which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed that the order of the Labour court should be set aside on the ground alone. The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4). In appeal by certificate, HELD: (1 ) The scheme of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour Commissioner. [707E] (2) The scheme is that dispute should be referred to the labour court for adjudication. In other words, the scheme of section 7(1) proceedings before a Labour Court in respect of disputes falling under clause (a) of paragraph A of sub section (1), shall be deemed to have arisen if within the period prescribed under the proviso to sub section(4). [708F] (3) The provisions of section 42 are that disputes must be settled by an employer intending to effect any change in respect Of matters covered by section 42. [078A B] (4) The Labour court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by paragraph A. As the scheme is one of the conditions precedent to a dispute falling under section 2(1), it must give notice of such intention in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees. [608C D] (5) The Scheme of the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act, 1966 which was enacted by Parliament in exercise of powers conferred on it by section 7 of the said Act is not a condition requisite for approaching the labour Court and an application to the workmen court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. [700E F] (6) The purpose of section 8(1)(a) is that the disputes should have been settled as soon as possible, and primarily by conciliation and agree ment, it did not stand in the way of conciliation and an order for consequential relief would be made after efforts were made to settlement.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971 and that the appellants had been occupying the premises under a valid lease for 20 years. The appellants ' application was allowed by the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi. The respondents filed an appeal before the Patna High Court against the order of the Judicial Commis sioner, Ranchi, which was dismissed by the judicial Commissioner, but on appeal, the Judicial commissioner, Ranchi held that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable. The Judicial Commissioner confined his decision to deciding the issues between the parties and granting one month ' s time to the respondents for vacating the premises and further held that the appellant would have to make another application under section 13(3) of the Act for evicting the respondents if they did not vacate within the time allowed by court. The respondent filed a revision petition before the Judicial Commission, Ranchi which was rejected by the Patna Bench on the view that in the absence of any month 'S ' notice under Section 12(3), the application could be treated as one under section 17 of the Bihar Act and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The High Court allowed the revision petition holding that the objection petition filed by the appellants before the Munsif was not barred by limitation, and the whole proceeding was liable to be quashed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question is whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the court by an application under Section12 of the . [975F] 1.2 In the instant case, it is the Civil Court, Ranchi who is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or making an application for eviction under section 11 or making such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it and the present case is a most appropriate one for exercise of such power. [976G] 1:3 The question whether a tenant after the expiration of the fixed term tenancy is entitled by an applica tion under section12(1), is not a pure question of law. If it is assumed that an application made under section 10 of the said Act is not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the present ease, in view of the first appellate court in favour of the appellant. [936C] 1 :4 In the present cases it is not possible to decide whether a particular period of lease is available for eviction or not.

The appellant was elected as the Secretary of the Society. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that he had been duly elected as Secretary of a society and that he was not entitled to prosecute or withdraw the suit. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant 's application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable, and that the trial court had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power. The High Court in revision set aside the judgment of the trial Court and restored the decree passed by the trial judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court ought not have interfered with the findings of the Trial Court as the trial Judge had no juris diction to recall the order permitting the withdrawal of suit under section 14 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the court is not barred by any principle or principle of res judicata. [237E] 2. The courts below were, therefore, not right in holding that they had no Jurisdiction to recall their order permitting a withdrawal of a suit under the inherent power and the High Courts have rightly held that the only remedy of the plaintiff was to file a fresh suit. [238G] 3. The Court has jurisdiction to cancel the order allowing the withdrawal from the suit on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside it if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. [239G H] 4. The question whether the appellant invoking the inherent jurisdiction of Court was not barred, must be decided in detail with reference to the evidence adduced by the parties. If a party makes an application before the court for setting aside the decree, he cannot investigate the case in the exercise of its inherent powers and the only relief to the party is to institute a suit. It is open to the Court to examine the matter in the exercising jurisdiction vested in it by law. [240G H; 241A] 5. The Courts below were not right to recall an order permitting withdrawn the suit, on several grounds. The court was clearly wrong in dismissing the appellant"s application as not maintainable. If the case of the party challenging the decree is that he is in fact a party to the compromise petition filed in the case but his consent has been procured by fraud, the Court cannot investigate it. The only remedy to the parties is to file an appeal against the order of the High court. [241A B] 6.

The appellant was a member of the Indian State and was governed by the Indian Independence (Temporary Powers) Act, 1940. The Ordinance was promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the Act. By virtue of the provisions of section 72(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, the period of emergency referred to in section 72 was extended to the territories which were not less than six months from its promulgation. The appellant was prosecuted for offences under sections 161 and 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the ground that he had been convicted by the trial court and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High Court held that the Ordinance was valid and the Ordinance could not be extended to a period of six months after April 1, 1946, when the Act came into force. Held, that the words "for the space of not more than six month from its repeal were omitted from section 72 during the period specified in section 3 of the India and the ordinance having been validly promulgated, the Ordinance ceased to be in operation until it was repealed. The words " for the space ' occurring in section 73(1), which is a saving clause, are not intended to give retrospective effect to the section as it originally stood in regard to Ordinances which had been promulgated between June 27, 1940 and April 1. The Act having continued in force till April 1., 1946, the appellant was rightly convicted by both courts below. Held further, that on the date when the Ordinance came into operation, the words 'for the time being not more or six months before its promulgation were omitted to be given retrospective effect from April 1,. 1946 and the Act having been repealed, the provisions in section 7 of the said Act would apply to the period during which the offence was committed by the appellant and the appellant had rightly convicted.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that they had been awarded to them for murder by a single Judge of the High Court, and that their conviction was based on circumstantial evidence. The High Court confirmed the sentence but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the death sentence should be awarded only in case of murder under section 304 I. P.C.; and (2) the High Courts were justified in confirming the death sentences passed by the trial court, and (3) the sentence of death imposed upon them was excessive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The death sentence to imprisonment for life is not a matter of law but of judicial discretion. [1072C] 2.1 The High Courts have been justified in affirming the death penalty imposed by the High court and the High 's order confirming the sentence passed under section 368(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as it was satisfied that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354(3), Cr. P C., 1973, or "indicative of an improper exercise of discretion". [1073D E] 2:2 The High 'Court has not been justified on the facts and circumstances obtaining in such cases. [ 1074E] 3.1 In the instant case, the death punishment and the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused are constitutionally valid. [1175G] 3:2. The sentence of imprisonment to life is a matter which must be determined by the facts of each case.

The appellant was appointed as a Departmental Promotion Committee. He was promoted to the post of an Income Tax Officer on 30th September, 1953. The appellant challenged his promotion before the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., which was rejected by the Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is entirely a question of fact. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The questions raised by the appellant were not pure questions of fact which should be decided on its own facts. [583 E] (2) The question whether an assessee was given reasonable opportunity of being heard or whether he had been allowed to lead any evidence and if so, what relief could be granted is a matter of fact and it would have affected the final decision. If the exclusion of evidence is of a kind which amounts to denial of natural justice or would have affect the final determination it could not be material. [584 E] The question as to whether the assessee was entitled to be given a further opportunity to produce nine witnesses in defence, all that is suggested is that these witnesses could only state what opinion they had formed about the work, efficiency and integrity of the appellant. If such a point could be raised, there could be no declaration that the departmental proceedings were null and void. [585 E] In the instant case, it was not shown how the witnesses whose production was said to have been disallowed could help the appellant 's case on specific charges. The question of denial of opportunity to the respondent was not considered by the Division Bench. [581 A B] (3) The High Court had not dealt with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently, been forgotten. It was only when an opportunity given to the appellant to produce more evidence in defence that he was given the lesser punishment of demotion and neither dismissed nor removed from service.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The contracts between the appellants and the S.T.C. were inter alia for export of manganese ores from the State to the State Trading Corporation. The contract was entered into by the appellants with their foreign buyers on the basis of a contract entered into in pursuance of which the appellants agreed to sell the goods to their foreign buyer. The appellants contended that they were not the last purchaser but the M.M.T.,C. and the actual exportation of the goods was an independent one between the appellant and its foreign buyers. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the contention and held that there was no privity of contract between the S .T. C. and their foreign sellers. The High Court, however, held that the contracts between them and the M/s. S. T.C., were inter State sales within the meaning of section 2(g) of the , and therefore the appellants were liable to pay tax. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contract between them as well as the contracts entered into between the parties was a composite one between them, and their exportation was an integrated one between two independent and separate transactions in the course of export. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The transactions between the two parties were inter state sales within section 2 (g) and therefore they were liable for tax. [445E] 2. The agreement between the foreign buyers and the appellants was a contract to be considered as integrated contracts in the way of export or they were different. In the course, the contract was one of sale and not a sale. It is the ST.O. which entered into independent contracts with their other foreign buyers for the foreign buyer and the foreign seller would not make the two contracts either inteived or the contract. [444E] 3. The transaction between the appel lants and the appellant was one such transaction. There was no element of contract in the sale of goods within the state of export, because the export sale is an independent and distinct. [442F G] 4. The sales were interstate sales within Section 2(h) of . The Sales tax Act, which provides that the normal presump tion attaching to a contract for export or exportation or export of goods shall be deemed to have been made by the buyer. This Court in Serajuddin 's case (supra) has laid down that the mere mention of F.OB. price or F.o.B. delivery in contract between a merchant and the seller was not sufficient to make the both the contracts either in the form of a separate contract with the foreign sellers on F.0.B., basis. [443F G; 445A] 5. The normal presum bility attached to a transaction is that property in the goods passes only when they are put on board the ship. In such a case, the last buyer within the territory of India is the seller and not the seller. If they are different contracts, as they are in the present case, there was nothing in the contract which would justify the conclusion that the transactions between them were integrated F. O.B./F.C./and the sales tax authorities have no jurisdiction to entertain the contention that the transaction between them was a concluded contract between two parties. [441G H] 6. The true law is laid down by this Court in the Coffee Board case (AIR) and Seraju vs State of Madras, ; , followed.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its head office in Delhi. He was served with a notice of termination on him under section 25B(2) (a) of the . The appellant challenged the said order by a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. The High Court held that where the termination was to be effective by a certain date as set out in the order of appointment it would nonetheless be a retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo), and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25F, termination was held to be invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the termination of service of the respondent was illegal because the termination did not amount to retrenchment within section 2 (oo) and therefore the termination could not be said to have been made in contravention of section 26F; (ii) the order terminating the services of the appel lant was void as it was passed without complying with the requirement of section 24F; and (iii) the respondent had failed to prove that he was a temporary employee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of the service of appellant was abruptly terminated by reason of the fact that he has not rendered continuous service for a period of 240 days within the period of 12 calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date i.e. the date of retrenchment. [532E] 2.1 The termination is illegal because there is no provision in section 25G to treat a workman in continuous service as in continuous employment for a specified period of one year. [525F G] 2:2.2 The termination was illegal and inoperative and a declaration that he continued to be in service with all consequential benefits, namely, back wages in full and other benefits, if any, is not illegal or a lockout or a strike which is not legal or illegal or the lockout of work which is being done on account of sickness or authorised leave or an accident or a dispute arising out of a mine. [500G H] 2 :3. The appellant was not entitled to claim reinstatement in view of section 10(2)(a) (b) of Act, because he had not rendered service for more than 240 days during the period preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, in case of retrenchment the date on which the workman has rendered service, for a further period of six months, he shall be deemed to be In continuous service under an employer for a total period of two calendar months beginning from the date and counting the backwards therefrom. [511B C] 2(a) The termination by the appellant was illegal as it did not comply with the provisions of section 12F of the Act.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated March 17, 1955. He was served with a charge sheet on the appellant and he was dismissed from service. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the ground that the order was not passed without affording him an opportunity to show cause against the order. The High Court held that the appellant was a temporary employee and had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant could not be dismissed or removed from service until he had been given reasonable opportunity of being heard. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order terminating the employment was passed without giving him an adequate opportunity to make his defence and it appears that witnesses in support of the charge and in defence were examined before the Settlement Officer. The enquiry officer did not act in exercise of his authority 's power under section 3(2) of the Act, but he was given an opportunity of showing cause against his order. [717 B C] (ii) The appellant was given no such opportunity to meet the charges and in the defence were also examined before a Settlement Officer for the purpose of ascertaining whether the appellant who was a permanent employee should be continued in service or should be discharged under the terms of his employment, and to "a termination made pursuant to such an enquiry the protection of article 311(2). [718 C D] (iii) The enquiry was made pursuant thereto by the Settlement officer with which it was held that there was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant. It was not necessary for the appellant to show that the enquiry was conducted in exercise thereof. The order of termination was passed after following the procedure prescribed by section 3 of the , and the appellant had been afforded an opportunity before terminating his employment for unsatisfactory work and conduct. [700 E F] Ram Narayan Das vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 816, followed. (iv) The word 'dismissed ' in section 3 (2) has not been used in the sense of punishment. It is only when the order discharging a probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirmed, that is, whether he was found established, to impose punishment and not to an enquiry whether a probationer should be retained or not.

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 under section 133 of the Jammu and Kashmir University Act, 1951, appointing the appellant as Professor of two Lecturers in the colleges. The appellant challenged the promotions of respondents Nos. 1 to 29 on the grounds that the provisions of section 133(2)(b) were not applicable to the case because it was not applicable only to the selection made by the Commission but also to the Selection Committee constituted under section 135 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to take a plea to the contrary and that the Public Service Commission had acted arbitrarily in refusing to give its decision on the suitability of candidates for promotion to the posts of Professors. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government had not taken into consideration the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions from one service to another, and that it was open to the Commission to appoint a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government has in fact placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969, which makes it quite clear that the Government was consulted in regard to the principles for making appointments in question, or on the recommendation of the Committee. [875 D] 2. The Public Service Commis sioner is a member of the State Legislature and he has been appointed by the commission for that purpose. He is not an officer of the Government but of the Chief Minister. It is not necessary to refer to any averment in the writ petition that the Commission was consulted. [887 D] 3. The Commission was also consulted on the question whether the Commission had been consulted in respect of the principles laid down in section 133 (2)(a) of the Constitution.

The petitioner was a member of the Assembly of Bihar. He was elected to the Lok Sabha in 1951 and he was declared elected to Parliament under article 194(1) of the Constitution. The President of India, on May 30, 1957, passed an order under section 3(2) of that Act declaring that the proceedings of the House of Commons were void as it had been contravened by the provisions of article 194 (3). The petitioner challenged the validity of the said order and contended that the impugned order was not ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as it was made subject to the provisions Of the Constitution, and that the President had no power to make any action in respect of the proceedings. Held, that the powers, privileges and immunities of a House of Parliament under Article 194(3) were not saved by article 19 (1)(a). The Act did not authorise the Speaker to take part in the proceedings for the said purpose. The provisions of the impugned Act were not ultra rites or void as they contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(b), (c) and (d) of Part III of the Constitu tion. The petitioner was entitled to succeed on the ground that the House had been declared elected by the Speaker in respect thereof. The proceedings of a Legislative Assembly were illegal and invalid. The Act was not void as the President was not authorised to take any action under article 19(2). The provisions Of article 194, (1) and article 194 were not made subject only to the fundamental right conferred on the House but also to the privileges and privileges of the members and committees thereof. Article 194 (1), which is a part of the constitutional scheme, was not saved from the operation of the provisions contained in article 19. The Constitution did not provide for any procedure or procedure for the exercise of that power. The impugned order could not be challenged on the grounds that it contravened articles 19(3)(a) and 19 (2). Article 194 was not made applicable to the case as it stood prior to its amendment by Act 26 of 1950, but only to those cases which were covered by article 194. The question whether a House has been declared void or not is not directly involved in the present case. The expression "any other law" in article 194 means any law which may be made subject either to the procedure prescribed by the Constitution or by law and no such law can be said to have been made subject merely to the rights conferred on a citizen under article 14 of the constitution. The word "law" is not defined in the Constitution but in the context of the Act itself. The words "any law" are not defined as including any law relating to the conduct of business or profession of the Legislature of a State, and of the member of such Legislature may be subject to those provisions of that Article. The term "law ' is not confined to matters which are specifically mentioned in article 105(3). It does not include any law made by Parliament for the purpose of carrying out its functions under the Constitution; it does not mean a law relating thereto, but includes a law which is not expressly made subject by the law. The fact that the petitioner 's fundamental right is not affected by the impugned orders of the Speaker and the Committee of the Houses of Legislature of the State cannot be said that the provisions in question were ultra vires.

The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971. The college was taken over by the State Government under a resolution dated March 9. 1969. The State Government issued a notification dated March 23, 1971 appointing the teachers in the private colleges to be appointed as Readers. The appellant who had all the requisite qualifications for appointment as Reader and later promoted as Reader filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Government was not competent to appoint ment to take into account the experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the public college since they had all requisite qualifications. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Govern ment had no power to appoint a Reader and that the teaching experience of the Readers in the Government College was completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible for appointment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of draw of Rs.600/ or more on the date of taking over is a serious infirmity. [782B] 2. The condition of draw ing of Rs600/ , does not make any difference to the question of eligibility. The Government has no power under the Government circular of March 23 1971 alone was in controversy in the High court. [777C D] 3. The conditions of draw up of Rs,600/ are not satisfied with the claim of the respondents for appointment on the ground of absence of teaching experience in Government service. For example, if the appellant is less than Rs.30/ , on the basis of the date when taking over, which has been laid down in the said circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment, he would also be simultaneously referred to the Public Service Commission for consideration of their suitability by the Public Services Commission for appointment to the post. [779D E] 4. The fact that the appellant had all necessary qualifications for the appointment as Readers and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over is not a matter entirely for due and proper consideration of the Public service Commission whose recommendations will be considered by the Government in the matter of final absorption. [780E F] 5. The question whether the teaching work of the Lecturers in the Private College is completely irrelevant or irrelevant has to be decided on the facts of each case.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of Chapter IV A of the Act, for plying the passenger vehicles on routes in question. The State Transport Authority granted temporary permits to the appellants for plying their buses on the route. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said orders and the High court allowed the writ petition holding that the scheme had been prepared and published under section 69 C(1 A) of the Chapter IVA of the . The High Court also held that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the State Government were not justified in interfering with the order of the High Courts. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the scheme has been prepared without any application for temporary permit; (ii) the route in question is an inter regional route and therefore an application for a temporary permit cannot be said to have been made under section68 F(l C); and (iii) the State transport Authority alone to the exclusion of others, was entitled to apply for temporary stage carriage permits. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme has not been published in respect of any route or route or part thereof specified in the scheme. [985B] 2. Section 68 F (1 C), C(l A) and (C) are applicable to all temporary permits except those which are specifically mentioned in the Scheme. If the Corporation is willing to operate vehicles to the maximum strength undoubtedly the State Road Transport Authority will have to grant permit to any one else if the Corporation has applied for all the permits. But if the Corpora tion is willing, the Regional Transport Authority or the Regional transport authority as the case may be will have the power to grant temporary permits. [89F G] 3. The High Courts were right in holding that since there was no vacancy and the Corporation applied for a permanent permit, once the Corporation made an application under section 70 C(I) for temporary temporary permits not for the full strength of the scheme and the date of publication of the approved or modified scheme is published, yet if the corporation does not apply for all these vacancies, it would be squarely attracted. [90G H] 4. The Regional Transport Authorities have power under sub section (1 A), to grant permanent permit to persons other than the Corporation to operate the vehicles on the routes for which the scheme is publication till modified or approved scheme is notified. If there are 7 vacancies and the Corporatio ny do not apply, the State Authority or Regional Transport authority as tho case may he will have been granted to any other person willing to be granted permits for the benefit of the large travelling public. But, if the respondent was unable to provide service by obtaining all requisite temporary permits, the appellant could have to obtain temporary permits and ply vehicle because in respect thereof the route under section 67 C(i C) would be covered by the scheme to the extent that even though there are seven vacancies and, the Corporation had made no application for the temporary permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation have made no applica tion for the permanent permit and section 68F(1C) would not be attracted. But when the Corporation does not applied for the regular permits and section 69 F(I C)(C) will be squarely applicable.

The appellant was the son of Sarup, respondent No. 10, who had executed a will in favour of his maternal grandfather 's mother in respect of certain properties which were bequeathed to him by the will dated May 23, 1947. The will was registered on June 30, 1947 and it was recited that the property inherited by the appellant from his maternal grand father was ancestral property. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the property in dispute and obtained a decree for partition. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the properties inherited by respondent No 10 were ancestral property and that the appellant had no right to bring the present suit on the basis of the will. On appeal by certificate, Held: (1) that the High Courts were in error in not following the earlier Full Bench decision of the Punjab High Court in Narotam Chand vs Mst. Ram, A.I.R. 1938 P.C. 905 and Narotham Chand vs Mt. Ram and Ors., A. I. R. , approved. (2) that a Hindu governed by the customary law prevailing in the Punjab is not ancestral property but it is an estate which has been acquired by birth or by birth. The question as to whether property inherited from his paternal grandfather was ancestral or not, is one of fact and must be determined on the evidence adduced before them. (3) that if a Hindu widow acquires jointly with her father an interest in the property, she could not claim any right to alienate the property. (4) that it is open to the son to bring a suit against the other person who inherited the property from his own ancestor in the male line and not from the maternal grandfather and it is governed by custom of the law prevailing at the time when the widow died, that is, the property which came from male collaterals and not on her own volition. (5)that the High court was in error on the ground that the decision of this Court in Smt. Narotnam Chand vs Smt. Ram. A. 1. R., , relied on.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge for offences under section 449 and 449 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut he saw the appellant 's father lying dead with him and when one of them went there, he saw him and while another went there he saw a person lying dead. He also saw the appellants armed with dagger. The appellants were charged under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. for causing injuries to the deceased. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellants under section 448 and 449 I. P.C., but acquitted them. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the charge under section 307 read with s.34 of the Penal Code was not sustainable in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the offence under section 148 and 449 were not sustainable as the offence of house trespass was punishable under section 450 of the I.p.C.; (ii) the charge was bad because the purpose of which the house trespass is committed was not the same as in the two succeeding sections; (iii) the provisions of section 34 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are applicable only to cases where the offence is committed "in order to" the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment. HELD : (i)(a) The offences under s. 449 read withs. 34 I P. C. are not sustainable. The offence under s, 449 readwith section 34 is not sustainable for the reason that a person commits a house trespass with the purpose Of committing an offence punishable under s 302 of the IPC. [447 B] (b) The offence of 'house trespass is prescribed quite inde pendent of the question whether the offence "in Order to" which the House trespass was committed has been actually committed or not. If the purpose in committing the house falls within section 449, it will be proper to say that he has committed the entire criminal act. [49 C] (c) The object of the section is to prevent a person committing an act punishable with death if it is done by a number of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the whole criminal act.[49 E F] (d) The distinction between a person who commits the offence punishable by section 449 read along with section 149 I. p. C., is not permissible in law and must be rejected.
