[50 G H] (e) The charge under s 449 read alongwith section 34, I.I.R. was not maintainable in law as it did not fall within section 448 of the Act.

The appellant was a collateral of the Punjab and Haryana State. He was born in 1947. The respondent filed a suit for declaration of his title to the property as collaterals, but the trial court dismissed it holding that the appellant was not a collateral. On appeal by the appellant the High Court held that the parties were governed by Hindu Law and not by Hindu law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether there is a custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a collaterals are ancestral or self acquired property of her father has been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter who was also a member of the family of the last male holder. [153 D] (ii)The appellant 's right to succeed to the properties in dispute is not a substantive right and cannot be regarded as a collateral to the collaterals even though they were within the fourth degree. The appellant had fully discharged the initial burden that was on him by producing in evidence the Riwaj i am of 1913 and the respondent did not raise any question about the custom which was binding on the parties. [154 D] In the present case, the appellant 'was a collateral and he was a member in the family. The High Court was right in holding that there was no custom in favour of the appellant as the appellant had not pleaded a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral from succession to the self acquired properties of her husband. [155 E] (iii)The question whether the appellant is a collateral or self acquire property of his father has to be decided on the evidence adduced by the parties as to what the custom should be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom recorded in Rattigan 's book so as to shift the onus to the daughter which was not discharged.

The respondent was the Managing Agent of a company which was acting as Managing Agents of several companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Managing Agent was appointed by the appellant as Managing Agent and he was appointed as Managing agent of certain companies. The appellant was appointed to act as Managing Agency in respect of all the three companies. On the question whether the two companies were liable for the assessment year 1955 56, the High Court held that the two firms constituted distinct matters for the purposes of section 5 and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect thereof. Held, that the words "distinct matter" occurring in section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, are wide enough to include all acts which may be done by the donor himself or his representative. The word "distribution" is not used in any sense in a statute. It is only when the instrument is executed by one person that he does not act for the purpose of section 4 and the instrument must be construed as distinct from that of the donor. In the present case, the instrument in question was a single power of attorney and was not a single delegation of power. The words "contribution" in section 3(1) are wide and do not include all matters which can be done under the Act. The expression "disturbance" is used in the context of the general power of Attorney General to act for him in whatever matters he could act, then there is no difference between a single one document of different kinds of instruments such as sale and mortgage, sale and lease or mortgage.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. The assessee claimed deduction under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the depreciation which could have been allowed to him if the Indian income tax Act had been in force and a claim had been made for such allowance. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the words "or which would have been allow" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order were not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that it was not necessary to include the depreciation allowed under section 10(5)(b) of that Act as an allowable deduction under the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, if it had been, in force, and a case had been referred to the High court under section 13(5) (b). The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in para 2 of that paragraph would have no application to the present case. The words used in the last part of the paragraph would be "any laws relating to income tax on profit of business". [230 D] (ii) The expression "or who has not arisen in a particular case in giving effect to the provisions of the Income tax law, is not a word "which would have otherwise been allowed" within the meaning of para 2. In the context of the words used by the Legislature, it is clear that if the intention had not been to include depreciation allowance under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to taxes on profits, of business, which was law of a part of a State before it became included in the Part B States, it was unnecessary to add the words 'or which could be allowed under any law relating thereto. [230 E] (iii) The word "any" used in para. 2 would have given effect to its intention and this part of paragraph would not have been omitted and this would have done so if the Act had in fact been in existence.

The appellant was a contractor. He had to supply the materials for the purpose of construction of the dams in the State of Karnataka. The contract provided that the materials supplied by the appellant were not to be used as raw materials and that the appellant would be liable to pay the price of the materials purchased from the Government. The appellant was also required to furnish a declaration of the value of the material supplied to him. The respondent, however, did not fulfil certain preliminary requirements which under the Notification issued by the State Government had to be fulked out before the forms of tender could be supplied to any intending contractor. The first respondent, who was a Contractor, filed a suit for damages and damages against the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the contract was not vitiated because there was no difference between the requirements in para I and para V. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that it is only para I that stipulates the prequalifying conditions for supply of tender forms. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether there is any difference between clause (c) and para IV of the N.I.T. and the rest of the information were only for assessing the capabilities of the tenderers as well as their eligibility and merely because the appellant in this particular case, the lacuna in furnish ing the information has been set right subsequently by the tenderers before opening of the price documents, the Chief Engineer had come to the conclusion that the firm had fulfilled all the pre quali fied requirements. [236B C] 1.2 The High Courts were justified in holding it not to interfere with their decision. It is true that at least some of the relevant provisions in para IV are intended to verify the fulfilment of the conditions set out in para V, but there are some other requirements in the NI. Ts. which have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply. [237C D] 1:3 The High court was right in holding the appellant guilty of the breach of para I, and that it was only para IV that stipulates that all the documents referred to in para VI are required to be furnished by the applicant. [238D] 1 4. In view of the fact that the lacuna has been put into existence in the relevant documents, it is difficult to accept the view of this Court that it would not be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. [239D] 5. The question as to whether there was any difference in the requirements of para IV and para VI of theNI.t. is a mixed question of fact and of the facts referred to. [240E F] 6. The Court has not been called upon to go into this question. It may be said that the Court may place on the record its own conclusion that it may place the rule in view of para V which sets out the general procedure which the K.P.C. was following in regard to NIl.T., and other details called for vide para 5(c) of the High Courts ' Order, but this is not a case where there has been any difference or difference between para I of the said NIt. The only difference is that the requirement of para VI is that before the tender documents issued by it have been understood and implemented by the KP.T, the first respondent should be stopped from doing so, the Court will decline relief. [241F G] 7. The fact that a party does not strictly comply with para V does not make any difference.

The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property in the State of Punjab. He was appointed an Assistant Deputy Custodian under section 27 of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947. The Custodian General, acting under section 5A of the Act, issued a notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the ground that the order was bad as it had been passed by the Custodian and that the orders were invalid. The High Court held that the application for confirmation was incompetent because the order under appeal was made long before the time when the office of the Custodian General was set up and he was clothed with powers of revision. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of confirmation passed by an Assistant Commissioner in such a case could not be challenged as being administrative or quasi judicial. [1139 C] (ii) The application for confirming the order against which no appeal was filed by any one, and the consequential disturbance of the vested property rights of the appellant was in the nature of perverse exercise of revisional power. The order under section 26(2)(q) of the Punjab Act is a quasi judicial order if not judicial, unless such orders are made in accordance with the provisions of the relevant Acts. [1104 C D] (iii) The words "anything done or any action taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under this Act as if this Act were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action was taken" apply only to purely administrative matters and that his case falls within the scope of the first portion, viz., "the repeal".

The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of steel ingots. The claim for bonus for the relevant years was based on custom and conditions of service. The workmen claimed that they were entitled to bonus for each year. The Tribunal held that the demand relating to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 was not such as would be covered by the Bonus Act, but it did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. The appellant company contended that the claim for payment of bonus was based either as a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees, creating a term of employment for payment to workmen employed in establishments '. The Industrial Tribunal held (i) that the demands relating to practice or practice were not covered by any of the provisions Of Bonus Act; (ii) that there was no provision in the Bonus Rules which required that the bonus should have been at a uniform rate throughout to justify an inference that the payment at such and such a rate had become customary and traditional in the particular concern. The High Court held that it would be subversive of the scheme of bonus and did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i). The Tribunal was called upon by the terms of reference to the dispute relating to bonus. It is clear from the provisions contained in the relevant rules that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of Bonus based on profit to employees employed in establishment '. [603B] (ii)(a) The object of the Act was to provide for the payment of a minimum bonus and confine itself to profit making provision to the payment to employees in establishments. The scheme of the Bonus Scheme shows that the employer is the question of bonus, and the Tribunal has to look into it on its own facts and circumstances. [503C] (b) The Tribunal had to examine the relevant points of dispute and come to a different conclusion from those which were arrived at by the parties. It was not open to the Tribunal to go into the other points raised in the reference. [511D E] (c) The question whether the bonus is payable or not is not correct. The fact that the Bonus Acts are different from those of the Industrial Disputes Act, does not detract from the claim of customary bonus. [55H; 56A] (d) The scheme and the scheme clearly indicate that the parties have to be given their full effect to the provisions in the Act. If the Bonus statute is a complete code and is exhaustive of the subject, then it would have made an express saving provision to that effect as it has done for employees in Coal Mines.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Upper Division Clerks on or after December 31, 1976. The High Court by its judgment dated February 12, 1978 directed that their seniority should be determined by the length of continuous service from the date of confirmation and not according to the rules of rotation. In the meantime, the Governor of Haryana amended Rule 12 by the Haryana First Amendment Rules, 1972 providing that seniority of members of the Service, whether direct recruits or promoted to the Superior Judicial Services shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of Rule 12. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said amendment on the ground that the rules governing seniority were not violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution inasmuch as they had been made by the Governor for a long time after the commencement of the Rules, and that the High Court was not justified in applying the rule of rotation at the time of confirmation. The writ petitions filed by the petitioners challenging the validity and validity of Rule 2(1) were dismissed by this Court.

The respondents Nos. 4 and 5, who were the members of the Andhra Pradesh State Service, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated October 6, 1989 passed by the Andhra pradeshir Board of Revenue, Andhra Pradesh directing the State Government to organise any class or classes of posts in the civil services of the State into different parts of the state to make an order in that regard requiring the State Govern ment to create a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants was illegal, contrary to law and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The creation of separate cadre is a cadre comprising the posts belonging to a category in a Department and located within a specified part of the Government. [573F] 1.2 In exercise of the power under proviso to paragraph 3(1) of the Order, the State Govt. shall have to place necessary material before the President for the purpose of making an order, in that behalf requiring the state Government to create any class, or classes Of posts in a department when more than one cadre in relation to such category exists in each department. [574F] 2.1 It is only for the State Gov ernment to organise a separate cadres in respect to any category or classes thereof in the department that may be created by the State government in accordance with para 3(2) before the expiry of the twelve months from October 20, 1975. No such provision has been made in the proviso to Paragraph 3(i). [574G H] 2:2 The creation is a separate unit for purposes of recruitment, appointment, discharge, seniority, promotion and transfer, and such other matters as may be specified by the Government in respect thereof.

The appellant was the auction purchaser of certain lands in the usual course of management. The mortgagor 's security was to be paid by him as security for the payment of the rent and the amount due from him to the defendants. The mortgagee was entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants, but the mortgagor did not pay the rent within one month of the date of the sale. The appellant contended that he was a subrogated to the position of the Bank and that the mortgage was binding on the mortgagor as the mortgagor had no right to redeem the mortgage. Held, that the mortgagee 's claim was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that it was not binding on him. The question whether the mortgagor in possession having the authority to deal with the property in the ordinary course of administration could be decided by the court of appeal or the High Court under section 66(2) Of the Transfer of Property Act, as amended by the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, was not applicable to the grant of a lease by the mortgagor. The suit for redemption was not barred by the provisions of section 65 A of the Transfer Of Property Act and the crucial test was whether the mortgagee in possession had power to grant a permanent lease in respect of the mortgaged property so as to bind the mortgagee. The words "any other person" in section 66 of the Indian Transfer of property Act, which dealt with the mortgagor ' session in the normal course of action, were not intended to be construed against the mortgagee and that so long as nothing took place,to impair the value or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. The word "may" used in section 65A of the Act was wide enough to include a person who had no power to sell the mortgaged properties and that he could not have any right to redemption under section 65, because, the mortgagor was not entitled to disturb the graves of those who had been doing so before he granted the mortgage, but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption. The fact that the mortgagor dealt with property in a usual course would not affect his rights as a mortgagee and would not alter the character of the transaction by making it a lease. The mere fact that a mortgagor dealt in the property does not affect the value of the mortgagee"s security the mortgagor could not prevail against the plaintiff. The only relevant consideration was whether, in the present case, the appellant had no authority to grant the permanent lease.

The petitioner, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the supply of certain goods to the respondent. The contract was executed by the petitioner on May 27, 1979 but payment was not made. The petitioner filed a suit against the petitioner for damages and damages. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the petitioner had no right to claim any damages. In appeal, the District Judge held that the agreement was void as it did not provide for appointment of an arbitrator and since the petitioner failed to prove his case, he could not approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Act for appointment. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no arbitration clause in the contract providing for appointment or appointment of a sole arbitrator. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contract provided for appointment and appointment of arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause, he is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator, and on its failure it is open to him to approach the court for appropriate relief under section 6 of the . Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Court and the making, after a claim has become statute barred by a submission of it to arbitration. [366B] 2.1 The period of limitation for commencing an arbitration runs from the date on which the cause of action accrued, that is to say, from the dates when the claim accrues. In the case of civil actions the claim is not to be brought after the expiration of a specified number of years from the relevant date. [367C] 2:2 The period for commencing the arbitration runs is from the time on which it should have accrued but for the contract. It is, therefore, open to the parties to plead in the proceedings before him of limitation as a defence. [368D] 3.1 In the instant case, the petitioner did not file any written statement nor filed any written objection. The period prescribed by section 14 of the limitation Act would be applicable to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contracts to the contrary, cause of arbitration for the purpose of limitation shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect of any such matter at the time when it should had accrued but the contract would not be brought about after the expiry of a period of one year from the commencement of the contract unless it is expressly provided that the reference shall be to a person named or designated. [369E F] 2 :3 The provisions contained in the Limitation Acts are similar to those contained in section 14 and they are applicable only to suits in which the claim was not to he brought after expiration of the specified number. [370F G] 4.1 Section 3 of the Indian Limitation Act applies to arbitrations, as it apply to proceedings in the Court within the meaning of section 14. By consent the parties have substituted the arbitrator for a court of law to arbiter their disputes or differences. The procedure prescribed by the Limitation (Amendment) Act, 1976 is not applicable to arbitration proceedings and like interpretation was given to section 14, by consent the party has substituted the Arbitrator for a Court of law for the purposes of limitation. [371F G; 371A] 2(a) The provisions in the Indian Law of Arbitration by Justice Bachawat in Chapter XXXVII at p.549 are similar in terms and they apply only to proceedings under the Act. By agreement, the parties had substituted the arbitration clause for appointment, but it is not open to them to plead that the arbitrator has been appointed or appointed. [372B] (b) The period mentioned in section 3 of Limitation Act is not relevant to the question whether the arbitration takes place after the cause is brought within the period of two years from date when the cause was accrued.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in Bihar. The decree holders sought to proceed against them under section 47 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 on the ground that they had failed to comply with the provisions of the Act and that they were not entitled to execute the mortgage decree. The executing court held that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred by the principles of res judicata and (2) that the bar of section 4(d) of the said Act was not applicable to them. In appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the executing court on two different grounds namely, (1) that it was a case arising under the Bihar Act and (ii) that in construing section 4 (d), it would be necessary to bear in mind the object of the legislation which was merely to provide for the transference to the State of Bihar. In appeals by special leave, HELD: The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to scaling down of debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing the words of section 16, it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the provisions. [912 D E] The object of section 17(d), is to provide a transference between the State and the persons affected by them by notifications issued thereunder. It is true that one of the objects of the statute was to provide that on and from the date of vesting all lands used for agriculture or horticultural purposes which were in khas possession of an intermediary on the date a vesting (including certain classes of land specified in that section) shall be deemed to be settled by the State with such intermediary and he shall be entitled to retain possession thereof and hold them as a raiyat under the State having occupancy rights in respect of such lands, subject to the payment of such fair and equitable rent as may be determined by the Collector in the prescribed manner.

The appellants were allocated to the Indian Police Service Group 'A ' and they were allocated as Additional District Services (Prelimi nary) in 1979. They were allocated from the Indian Administrative Service to the I.P.S. or Central Services, Group 'B ' and who were permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to do so, were allotted to them on the basis of the previous C.S., Group 'C ' or 'I.P., and they had appeared in the next Civil Service Examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS or Central Servi cies, Group B and Group 'D '. The appellants were also allocated to Indian Police Force Group 'E ' and were allocated on the same date as the I P.S, Group D and Group D respectively. They had joined service in the IP.C., and were allotted the same post as the posts of Additional District Service Officers. In the year 1990, they were assigned to the said two different cadres viz., (i) A.I.R. 1989 SC.SC. (ii) A combined seniority list of officers belonging to the same category was prepared in the order of merit and (iii) A common seniority list for the years 1989 and 1989 was prepared on the dates when the I .P. C.T.S was allocated to that cadre. The respondents were also given the benefit of their inter se seniority from the date of their appointment as Additional Distt.S/I.C. or the Central Services Group 'F ', and were not entitled to any benefit of seniority in the service to which they were allotted. In view of this, the appellants were appointed as Additional Sessions Judge on the ground that they had been allocated to I.p.S in the year 1989 and onwards. The said order was challenged by the respondents before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed their writ petitions holding that the appellants are entitled to be given benefit of the seniority from 1.1.1989 to 31.3.1989, but not from the dates of their joining as Additional Session Judge. Aggrieved by the aforesaid decision, the Union of India preferred appeals before this Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the Tribunal is set aside and the respondents are directed to be granted benefit of promotion to the appellants from the respective dates of appointment as Addl. District & Sessions Judge. [534E] 2.1 The appellants have been allocated from I. P.C.; they have been allotted to the Central Service Group B, and they have not been allocated in the earlier years. They have been given benefit thereof. They are entitled for the benefit under the Rules. [540F G] 2:2.2 The respondents are entitled only to be considered for promotion as Additional Chief District & Session Judge, Group C.A. No. 34 of 1990 and they are entitled also to be promoted to the post of Additional Sessions Judges. [541G H] 3.3 The appellants are directed that their seniority should be determined on the date from which they have actually been allocated. [543H] 4.1 It is not open to the respondents to contend that they have already been allocated as Addl District & District & Additional District & Anr., and that they should be given the benefits of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of C.P .C. [542A B] 2.(a) The appellants who have been transferred from the Ip. S.T.,S. to a Central Service, Group A, were allocated in order of seniority as Additional district & Sessions Judges and they could not be given any benefit thereof under Rule 17.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the , by an order dated 25th November, 1986. The grounds on which the ground is raised are not in dispute and the detenu has been denied the assistance of a retired Assistant Collector of Central Excise. The Advisory Board after considering the representation of the appellant, rejected his request for assistance of Sundararajan. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of detention contending that the order was bad as it was passed by the detaining authority without affording any opportunity to the detenu and that the same had been refused. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the grounds on the face of it were not in issue. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Advisory Boards have given its finding in rejecting the appellant 's request for help of Sundararajarajan. It is quite clear from the allegations in the special leave petition and the counter affidavit that the appellant had requested the Board to allow him the assistance to be represented by a retired assistant Collector of Customs, who was also denied the aid of a lawyer. [790B] 1.2 The Advisory Committee has, of course, to be careful in permitting assistance of the detenu, if it is so minded, made a request to the Advisory Board for permission to be represent by a legal practitioner or a legal adviser before the Advisory board. It does not preclude the Board from allowing such assistance to the appellant. [789D] 1:3 The Advisory Advisory Board has, in course, been to be conscious of permitting assistance to a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer, and that he cannot be allowed to represent his case before the Board through a legal practitioners. [788E] 1 :4 In the instant case, the Government merely informed the detenu that he had no statutory right to be represents by a lawyer or legal advisers before the detaining Board. The fact that it was for the Advisory Boards and not for the Government to afford legal assistance to an appellant is not justified.

The appellants were the owners of a certain premises in Calcutta. The appellants were served with notices on them under section 18 of the Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1947, and the appellants filed a suit for possession of the said premises on the ground that they had not been served on them as required by r. 75 A (2) of the Rules framed under the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the notice of requisition was not properly served and therefore there was no acquisition of property within the meaning of section 18. Held, that the service of notices of acquisition was not valid and binding on the appellants. The service of the notice was not a condition precedent to the acquisition of the property. The notice of acquisition did not amount to a requisition for the purpose of the Act and therefore it could not be said that the services of the appellants were validly requisitioned and acquired. Held further, that in view of section 3 of the West Bengal Premises (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1950, the property in the goods passed to the Government of India on September 30, 1946, for the goods were not served on the owners as required under r. 2 of the rules framed under section 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The order of requisition did not affect the validity of the service or the notice and therefore the service was invalid. Held also, that it was not correct to say that the appellants had been served with a notice of the acquisition on them. The notices were valid and they could be served only in accordance with r. 25 A (3) of that Rules.

The assessee company was a private limited company. The assessment year 1963 64 was made on or before the date of assessment. In the assessment year 1964 65, the assessee claimed that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserve and should be included in its capital for purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim holding that it was a Reserve. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section 23A. In further appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue it was contended that since the question referred to the High Court was one relating to the assessment years 1963 64 and 1963 65, it was not open to the assessee to contend that the amount of Rs 4, 50,000 should be treated as a provision. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court had rightly held that the assessee was a ' reserve ' and should have been included in the capital for the purposes of Act. [111D] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal was right in holding it to be a reserve. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve.[111E F] 2:2 The High court was right that the High Courts was right. [112F G] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. In so far as the item in question is concerned it held that it is a reserve, and should not be included. [ 112G] 3.1 The Tribunal was wrong in holding that the claim made by the appellant was not made on nor before the High court. It was also wrong to hold that the provision made by assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision and not a reserve; it did not called a reserve or appropriated. [113E F, 113A] 3:2 In the circumstances of the case, there is no question of holding that any action could have been taken against assessee under section 23A, [114F] Metal box Company of Indian Limited vs Its Workmen, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 871; Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. vs Their workmen, [1964] 65 I.T.R., referred to.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Assistant Engineers on the basis of competitive examinations held by the Public Service Commission. The petitioners challenged the validity of the seniority list prepared by the Union Public Service Commis sioner, pursuant to the decision of this Court in Katyani Dayal 's case (supra). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the classification of persons into those who were appointed on the cadre of Engineers and not on the ground that they had been recruited as Assistant Engineer prior to their permanent absorption into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers, was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. In the appeals by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that the seniority of the officers in a representative capacity across the Union Territory of Delhi should be reckoned from the date of their absorption into Indian Railway service of Engineers Class I as stipulated in their letters of appointment with regard to the time factor, this Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decision taken by the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, this court, HELD: 1. The classification of personnel into those that were recruited on the strength of competitive examination and those who joined service prior to the absorption into that service matters and as held by this Court with regard thereto is not violative of Article 14 and16 of the Constitu tion. [1022C] 2.1 The classification made by the State Government in respect of persons appointed on a particular post is neither discriminatory nor violative of articles 14 and 15 of the constitution. It is well settled that the principle of res judicata is that there should be no discrimination between the direct recruits and promotees. If the Union of India has been made possible and its pace quickened with weightage, it is difficult to find fault with the scheme at this point of time to look for a substitution at the end of the issue of seniority as provided in their appointment matters and the same approved by this court with weightage of half of the length of service subject to a maximum of five years. [1122D E] 2:2 The classification is based on the principle that there are two services, one being challenged as an isolated one, and the other being challenged in a writ petition before this Court which has been decided finally. It would be appropriate to mention that the Union Government is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an independent body across it. [1223D E; 1224F] 3. The principle of constructive res judicata does not apply to the present case because of the bar of re agitation erected by direct Recruit 's cases. [1325G] 4. The distinction between the two services was well settled in the field of law and the doctrine of resjudicata. It has been held that the differentiation is based upon a rational basis which distinguishes persons from those who are appointed on an equal basis. [1424F G] 5. The difference between the one service into the other, and another service to be reckoned on the date when it was called for and its adaptation in order to fill up old issues. It cannot be said that the distinction between two services is well established as a rule of constructive Res judicata. [1525G H; 1326A] 6. The doctrine of constructive estoppel is not applicable to the instant case because the principle laid down by this Courts in Katyanani Dayal vs Union of lndia & Ors., ; , applied.

The appellant was convicted under section 3(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949. The State Government issued a notification under section 5(1), directing certain specified persons to be tried by Special Court and to direct them to try under a special procedure such offences as may be notified by the Government in effect, authorise the State Government to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of this Act. The appellant contended that sections 9 and 11 of the Ordinance were ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as they purported to regulate the procedure for trial of offences and other offences under the Indian Penal Code and section 5 (1) Of the Act was inconsistent with those provisions of article 14 of the Constitution; that the notification issued by the State of West Bengal under section 4(1 ) of the Act did not contravene article 14. Held, that sections 11 and 11 were ultra rites and void as they contravened articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion and the notification which purported to be in conformity with the direction could not be tested with reference to any definite legislative policy or standard. The notification issued under section 6(1)(a) of Act was therefore invalid. Held further, that the notifications were ultra vides of article 19(1). The notification did not infringe article 14 Of the Constitution and as such was void.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of P.W.2 who had seen the occurrence was not in the immediate or direct interest of the deceased; (ii) the prosecution case was that the deceased and his wife were inimical towards the deceased when they entered the house; (iii) the deceased was not known to them as to whether any of the culprits were seen by P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8; (iv) the appellants were in the eastern kotha of the house at the same time and it is not possible to accept their evidence that the appellants had been seen by the deceased or his wife in law when they came near the scene of occurrence; (v) the motive for the murder was not established beyond reasonable doubt; (vi) the High Court erred in rejecting the evidence on the ground that P. Ws. 1 and 7 were interested witnesses; (vii) the fact that the prosecution had not sustained any injury during the occurrence could not be relied upon because they were interested persons; (viii) the circumstances of the case showed that the motive was established beyond doubt; and (ix) the conviction of the accused under section 396 I. P.C., was set aside by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses is not sufficient to sustain the conviction. [519G] 2. The circumstances of a case are such that the High Courts have acted in an unreasonable manner and should be slow to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below. [620A B] 3. The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High court for rejecting the testimony of P,W. 2 and the other circumstances of this case are not convincing. [721B] 4. The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubt. It is not necessary that all the witnesses should be examined in a position to identify them. There was sufficient moon light at the time of occurrence and it was not possible for the prosecution to identify any of them. [700C] 5. The fact that P,Ws.1, 7 & 8 are injured witnesses does not make any difference. It may be that the evidence is corroborated by the evidence in the case.

The appellant Corporation was appointed as a temporary employee on probation for one year. The services of the appellant were terminated by an order dated July 1, 1981. On his reinstatement he filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his service and also the validity of the termination. The High Court held that the termination was bad because it was not a case of retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Corporation that the services of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking were treated as 'retrenchment ' for the purpose of notice, compensation etc. and therefore did not amount to retrenchment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service of a person on the basis of an order of discharge passed by the employer of the service of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. [794C] 2.1 The expression 'ret retrenchment ' is defined in section 2 (oo) and as used in section 25F, it means the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employers for any reason whatsoever. It does not include every termination of the services except those not expressly included in section25F or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the . [795G H] 2:2 The expression "retrenchment" is used in the context of the definition of 'retrench ment ' and it means only the discharge or retrenchment of a workmen. It includes every termination, removal or closure, of an industrial undertaking, whether by way of punishment inflicted by way or otherwise than as a punishment inflicted under any other law. [788G H; 788A] 2 :3 The expression `retrenchment` must include every kind of termination of employment except those specifically included in Section 25F or 25FFF. This expression is used to mean the discharge, discharge or termination of an employee 'for any reason whatever else than as punishment inflicted on him by way Of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workmen, retirement of workman on attaining the age Of superannuation if he is reaching the superannuation of the worker. [789B C] 2(a) The expression in section2(oo), "ret retrenchment" must include all termination of services except by an employer of a probationer for any reasons whatsoever". The words 'ret retrenched ' are not defined in the Act and therefore, did not mean termination of such service except those expressly included therein. [783C] 3:1. In the instant case, the termination is bad because the termination by the appellant was on account of unsuitability and it was a discharge or closure. The expression retrenchment means only an discharge or discharge of the employee for any misconduct or any other reason whatsoever, otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of section 25FF or not specifically provided for under other provisions. [784D] 3.2. In this case, there is no dispute that the appellant Corporation had terminated the services on the ground of unsubservation of surplus Labour or staff and therefore it was liable to be set aside. [781E F] 3 :3. The word "ret retrenched" in section 10(1) of Act means only a discharge of an workman for any cause whatsoever, other than those expressly excluded in section 26F or otherwise provided for in the . The expression is not defined as the expression 'termination of service for any purpose whatsoever ' now covers every kind or termination or closure or closure and it includes all termination or termination by way o.f any other provision of the , such as sections 25FF and 25FF. [779G H, 793A] 4.

The assessee, a dealer in the appellant 's products, was assessed to sales tax under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of the goods did not indicate that the assessee was carrying on business as a dealer. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sale effected by it was a "dealer" within the meaning of the Bengal Taxation (Sales tax) Act and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. The High Court allowed the appeals holding that the sales effected by the appellant were sales under the Act and that the respondent was a 'dealer ' within the definition of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the Appellate Tribunal in each case. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the good came into possession of the appellant and not as a result of any activity of purchase or of manufacture for sale. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It may be engaged in selling scrap and unserviceable material. [781E] 2. The question whether the assessee could be treated as a " dealer" within section 2(c) of the West Bengal Finance Act, 1942, is a 'business ' within section 3(c). It is not an activity that may be described as necessarily ancillary or incidental to its commercial business as carriers of the products. It seems to South Eastern Railway that the activity of such activity was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It was an activity of a dealer for the purpose of the Calcutta and it is engaged in the selling scrap, and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. [782F H] 3. The expression "dealer", as used in section 2 (c) read with C1. (g) of section 2 of the Indian Railways Act, is wide enough to include all kinds of transactions which are incidental or incidental or subsidiary to its trade as carrier or for the purposes of the . [781G H] 4. The word "dealer ' has been defined in the Bengal General Sales Tax Act, 1940. In the other case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and Tyreable material lying with it. It does not mean that the business of so disposed of the articles was adju nated to the Principal activity of carriage of the said goods by a Railway.

The appellant, a Director of the respondent company, was appointed as an agent of the appellant in respect of certain securities. The account books of the company were kept in the name of the Imperial Bank of India and the balance sheet of the Bank was prepared by the Imperial bank at Bombay on September 17, 1954. The accounts of the said Bank were maintained by the respondent and the account books were kept by the appellant for the purpose of the business of the Company. The appellant was appointed an agent in respect thereof. The relevant entries in the account book showed that the appellant had been receiving from the Imperial Banks at Bombay and the amount of Rs. 1,80,00,000 in cash or purchase of securities. In the course of the investigation the appellant made a statement of the account of the Union Agencies with the Bank of Baroda, that the accounts were kept for the year ending September 20, 1954, and that the account was not sufficient to meet the losses. The Income tax Officer held that the amount was received in cash and not through transfers which were not sufficient. On appeal by special leave, Held, that it was not possible to believe that the money was received by the Bank as that represented the true state of affairs and that it had been paid for the Union agencies to meet its losses. It was not necessary to consider whether the amount received in the cash statement was sufficient to satisfy the requirements of section 409(1) of the Indian Penal Code. The fact that the respondent was a Director or an agent, did not make any difference as to what he had done. The mere fact that he did not know that the amounts were received by him for the Bank 's purposes would not justify his inference that he mentioned the amount in the letter of the bank. The receipt of the amounts from the appellant was not a voluntary act and could not be said to have been made out in the present case.

The appellants were appointed to the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Saurashtra and Kutch. By a notification dated November 1, 1956, they were transferred to the Secretariat of the Government of Gujarat. The appellants were promoted as permanent posts in the ministerial cadre of the Secretary to the Government. In the year 1956, the appellants were holding permanent posts under the Secretariat service of that Secretariat. On November 1 1956, their services were transferred from the Secretariat to the State. By an order dated November 2, 1956 the appellants became permanent posts and were absorbed in the Secretariat. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the transfer orders on the ground that they were not entitled to any statutory right under section 115(7) proviso to section 115 (7). The High Court held that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Gujarat State was incompetent as a matter of provisional arrangement to absorb the former Bombay and Kutch States. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transfers were made in connection with the affairs of the new State of Bombay and that the Government had no power to treat them as permanent and that since they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts they will not be deprived of their statutory right. HELD: (1) The transfer of a former Saurashtra was valid and could not be challenged on the basis of any statutory provision. [515 B] (2) The Government of Bombay was competent to transfer and did transfer the appellants to perform service in connection therewith. In view of this rule, according to the High court, it is not open to the officers of theariat to challenge the authority of the government of Gujarat either to transfer officers from the District and to post and assign them duties in the same Secretariat or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the administrative establishment.

The petitioners were dealers in goods manufactured by the first respondent State. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Act on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that it violated articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the constitution. The High Court held that the tax was not leviable at more than one stage, but at different stages in the matter of levy of tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Act is a piece of legislation which seeks to achieve the object of the law and it is not enough for the State to say that a person who is not liable to pay tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund at a later stage. [554 B] (ii) The tax is levied on the first purchaser. If the Central Act makes it mandatory that the levy can be collected only at one stage and that stage, in the case of goods liable to tax, the stage is not reached. [555 E F] (iii) The State Legislature has no power to enact a law which seeks for the enforcement of fundamental rights under article 19(2)(a)(vi). It is not necessary that the State should pay tax at more or less than one point of time. [557 B C] (iv) The levy of sales tax by the last dealer is not a tax on the second purchaser. The tax cannot be said to be a tax which has been imposed under the Act. [553 E F]. (v) The power to levy tax is subject to the provisions of article 19 (1)(f). It does not mean that a tax can be levied only at more one stage. If it is so, it is necessary for the state to say, that a particular tax can he collected only on the sale or purchase of such goods at more then, in its opinion it is open to the State Government to say whether a person has purchased cotton and sells it after the expiry of six months from the close of the year to a registered dealer or in the course of inter state trade or commerce.

The appellant was a mortgagee in the mortgaged property. The mortgage deed provided that the amount payable by him under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition for execution of the decree. The appellant filed an application for execution on the ground that the decree holder had not paid the entire amount due under the mortgage and that the suit was barred by limitation. The District Judge held that the debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the compromise decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 2 to 7 separately. On appeal the District Judge reversed the order of the District judge and held that defendants 2 and 3 had not been able to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court, however, allowed the application for relief under section 47 and directed that in case they did not pay the amount within a period of six months from the date of decree, they would be entitled to avail himself of the benefit of the scaling down of the debt. In appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the mortgage debt was not scaled down under the provisions of the Agriculturists ' Relief Act and the decreeholders were bound by the terms thereof. The decree holders had no right to get their debts scaled out from the mortgaged properties. The judgment debtor was entitled to have his debts sched down under section 46 and he could not be allowed to take advantage of the scheme of the mortgage decree. (ii)The High Court was right in taking the view that the provisions contained in the Agriculturists Relief Act were not applicable to the case. The object of the Act was to protect the creditors from the operation of the provisions relating to the debts and for the rest of them, but there were purchasers of the mortgaged land who were not agriculturists. (iii)The decree holders did not have any right to the benefit under the scaling over the mortgage property even though they had been scaled off in favour of the agriculturist co debtor under the provision of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Ordinance, 1949. The provisions of section 47 were not intended to apply to cases where the debt and the security have been split up, but only those debts which are put down by the decreeholder and that by defendants 3 to 7 separate properties, the debt could be scaled on the assumption that the mortgaged debt and security had been split out. (iv)The provisions of sections 47 and 48 were not attracted in view of the fact that the mortgagor was entitled under the Act to get the benefit thereof, but the question arose whether a purchaser could get the benefits of the said decree which has been sched off by the Court.

The appellants were the tenants of a premises in question. The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground that they had been inducted into the premises by the first plaintiff and were entitled to protection under the Act, and that the second and third plaintiffs were not entitled to any relief claimed by them. The City Civil Court held that the suit was maintainable as it was barred by section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. XLIII of 1947). The City civil court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the grounds that there had been no lawful subletting by the second plaintiff of the premises to the second defendant. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the City Civil Judge and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The suit was not one between a landlord and tenant because the defendants were tenants of the property within the meaning of the Act. [374 B] The City of Bombay vs N. D. M. Desai, ; , referred to. (i) The City Court had jurisdiction under section 28 to entertain and try such a suit as it thought fit in the circumstances of the case. The suit of the plaintiffs was not a suit between the landlord and the tenant because they were tenants within the definition of the expression "tenant" in section 28 and no other. Eviction of the tenant and those to whom he had sublet the premises was sought on the basis that the latter were tenants. [375 B] (ii) The Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1946, did not apply to the suit of a landlord for eviction of the appellants from the premises in dispute. The Act did not contemplate the filing of any suit relating to possession of the suit premises. It was only when the plaintiff was in the nature of a title to the premises that was to say that none of the defendants to that suit were protected from eviction by any of its provisions. [373 E] (iii) The suit filed by the appellants was not within the mischief of section 28 because they had no right to continue in possession. The Bombay Act did apply to suits for ejectment of tenants and those who were tenants under the Bombay Act would be governed by that Act. The suits were therefore governed by the Bombay Rent Control Act. There could be no doubt that the City civil Court was one relating to the possession of a tenant to which any of the provisions of Part 11 of the Constitution applied and in that suit claims and questions arising out of the said Act or any of them had to be dealt with.

The respondent was a private company. The managing director of the company, who was incorporated under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., had been appointed as managing director in his place. He was appointed as the managing director on July 7, 1955. On July 7 1955, the appellant was appointed by the company to take over the management of the business. The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that he was not entitled to any share in the profits of the firm and for an injunction restraining the respondent from assigning his office or appointing him as managing directors. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court, on appeal, held that the appointment by the appellant did not amount to an assignment of his office by him and therefore the appointment was void under section 312 of the Indian Companies Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the word "assignment" in the section included "appointment", and so, the word 'assign ' must be construed as meaning a transfer of office. Held, that the words "any person who is appointed to the office which he previously held but did not hold any office by himself, do not constitute an assignment. The word "asign" in section 312 meant a transfer or appointment of a director and does not include "appointment". It was not intended that the term "assign" must be given the meaning of the word. The words "assigned" in s.3(2) were wide enough to cover all kinds of appointments including appointment, but they did not exclude the word, "assired", nor did it mean that the expression "any other person" was intended to include "appoint". It would be wrong to say that the use of the words 'any person ' in section 3(2), meant a mere transfer of an office by a director who is not an assignment or appointment. The rule of construction on which the High Courts relied on in arriving at the conclusion that it did, was put in these words: "appointment" would include an appointment of an alternate director by him for the old Act contained in section 83B.

The appellants were the partners of a partnership firm. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellant firm on the ground that they were unlawful sub tenants and that they had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to them. The Rent Controller dismissed the eviction petition holding that the appellants had unlawfully, and without their consent, sublet the premises to the said firm. On appeal by the tenant, the Appellate Authority held that the appellant had unlawfully sub letting the shop to M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart without joining any of the partners as sub tenants. The High Court also dismissed the revision petition holding inter alia that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable because it was filed against the appellants firm and one other partnership firm, and that the tenancy petition was not tenable at all. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction Petition was filed in the High Court only after the respondent had filed a fresh suit for eviction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the appellants were sub tenants or not is one which would have been fatal to the eviction application. [420C] 2. It is not open to the appellants to raise this contention at all before the High court that the case was filed by the respondent landlord against the firm and another partnership firm in the premises even for some time during which the appellants ' firm had ceased to carry on business. The fact that a notice was given by the sub tenant to the appellant and M/S Adeshwar glass Mart, would justify the finding of subletting. [421D E] 3. In the instant case, there is evidence to show that M/ s. Adeshwar Excise Mart was carried on business at the said premises even in some time after which the appellant Firm had ceased lo carry on the business there. The tenancy petition filed by M/ S. Aday Glass Mart was not therefore maintainable. [416E] 4. In view of the fact that the notice was issued by the Respondent to the appel lants and M.S.

The Andhra Pradesh Act, 1961 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land situate in urban agglomeration and since the definition of 'family unit ' in section 2(n)(A) of the Act was not applicable to the lands situated in urban areas, the Act would apply in relation to land situate within such area. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature passed the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1975 which came into force on 1st January 1975 and it was with reference to this date the definition was amended by the Andhra Act. In the meantime, the Andhra Area of Andhra Pradesh became a 'urban agglomeration ' under section 2 (n)(B) of that Act. The appellant State filed writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore violative of Article 19(1)(A)(ii). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the definition in section 3(f) of Central Act was an inclusive one and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified as an urban agglomerations. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that (i) the definition given in section 1(1) of Act was a comprehensive one and therefore the definition should be construed in relation thereto; (ii) the expression 'urban land ' in the definition is not defined in the Act and hence the definition would apply to lands situate within the urban agglogenations referred to in section I(2)(A). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of `family unit" in section 4(n) of Andhra Act is an inclusive definition and any other area with a population of less than one thousand acres can be notified to be an urban land. [419C] 2.1 The definition given by the definition under section 3 (f) is not exhaustive but only inclusive. It is only in respect of land situate outside the urban areas that the Central Act would have no application. [420D E] 2:2 In the instant case, the definition has been given a broad and comprehensive meaning and it cannot be said that merely because an area may possibly in the future be notified under section 1 (1) the Central Legislature would cease to have competence to legislate with respect to land situated within such areas. [416D E; 417A] 2 :3 The definition in Section 3(j)(A), is a comprehensive and inclusive one, and it is only where the area in question is notified as a urban agglarily or future life, that would be included in the family unit and by reason of section 4 his land whether self acquired or obtained on partition would be liable to be clubbed with the land held by other members of the family units not because the partition is invalid but because the land hold by him whatever acquired is liable to he clubbed together with the lands of others for the purpose of applying the ceiling area to the family Unit.

The appellant company was a permanent employee of the Company and was employed in the Company. The workmen were dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that they had not been given any opportunity to explain their conduct. The appellant contended that the workmen did not join the service as of right without notice and therefore they were not entitled to be taken back as of rights under the Standing Orders. Held, that the company having held a regular and proper enquiry in which it was found that the respondent workmen had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence and that was the reason why they were dismissed from service. The Industrial Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant had not discharged its duties as required by the Standing Order. The Tribunal was justified in refusing leave to appeal. The company having been dismissed on the grounds, it could not be said that the respondents did not discharge them. The fact that the workers were employed in a regular employment does not make any difference. The case of the appellant was that the work of the respondent was very much terminated by the company and the notice terminating the services was given to the workmen. The termination of service was justified on the basis of the evidence adduced before the Tribunal. The circumstances showed that the employees were in charge of a regular, and there was no justification for holding that they did not participate in the enquiry. Held further, that though the appellant 's case had been referred to the Industrial Tribu nal for adjudication, it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Tribunal should have interfered with the decision of the company unless it found that there was any evidence of its absence or victimisation. The Labour Appellate Tribunal was not justified in interfering with the order of the Tribunal unless it finds that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany and such other posts. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5(1) of the Urea Kant was constituted for selection of candidates for the said post. The appellant, a candidate in the Department of Botsang, was selected by the Selection Committee on the ground that he had been appointed as Professor in Bothis in the University of Rajasthan. He challenged the appointment of Dr. UreaK. Jain and also the validity of the selection made by the selection committee. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Selection Commit tee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joined the post, he would be eligible for appointment if any vacancy is caused during the validity period of the reserve list. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once the selected candidate joined the said service, he must be deemed to have been appointed in accordance therewith and that once such a selected candidate joins that post, the reserve lists exhausted itself. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Selection Commis sioner is not a person selected for appointment unless it is shown that he has joined that post or has joined the service. [422B] 1.2 In the instant case, the Selection Board constituted under Section 5(2) of Urea K. Jain (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1974 framed by the University was constituted in exercise of powers conferred on it under section 6(4). The Selection Board in its resolution dated 10th July, 1978 had resolved that the reserve List be prepared for selection by the Committee. [420C D] 1:3. In the present case, there is no question of any violation of the provisions of Section 5 (1) and (2) as no fault can be found against the appellant. The very purpose of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High Court is accepted that once an person selected by selection committee has joined his post then selection made in order of merit and shall further prepare a reserve select list to the extent of 50% of the vacancies and persons kept in the reserve register will be considered as having been selected for the concerned post and shall be entitled for appointment. [416D E] 1 :4. The selection committee constituted under sub section (1 ) of Section 6 is not required to be made by a Selection Committee which is constituted for selecting a candidate on a vacant post caused during its validity period. It is not necessary that the person selected should have been selected in order to fill up the vacancy and shall also prepare a reserved list to that extent of 25% of vacancies and candidates kept in reserve list will be eligible to appointment if some vacancies are caused during such period of one year. [414E F] 1 5. The fact that the appellant was appointed by the State Government on the basis of the Selection committee constituted for the selection of a teacher in the university is not relevant for determining whether he should have joined the posts or not. If it is found that the appointment has been made in contravention of sub clause (i) to (v) of Section 4, then the reserve select lists are of no avail and becomes extinct. [413F G] 1 6. The procedure prescribed by section 5 (2), therefore, clearly provides for the preparation of a reserve List. [411G] 7. The Committee constituted for Selection of a candidate is required to make a selection list to be prepared in order that the reserved list may be made available to the candidates on a suitable post and the reserve panel is of no relevance. There was no scope for making the reservation in the reserved lists by the Board. [409F] 8. The State Government has not been able to show that the vacancy had been filled up by selection by selection Committee.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands in the State of West Bengal. The petitioners challenged the validity of section 4 and 11(3) of the Act on the ground that they had been deprived of their right to hold property under a notification issued under section 10 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The High Court held that the local authority could not have delayed the acquisition of any land designated for public purposes under section 7 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the local authorities could not be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision; (ii) the notification issued by the State Government under section 17 of the , was invalid as it had been made in contravention of section 9 of the ; and (iii) the provisions of sections 4 to 16 were violative of article 14 of the Constitution. HELD : The local authority can validly take action for acquisition of land designated as a public purpose under section 3(1) of Act, at least once within the fixed limits of time, he ceases to be bound by the designation of his land as given in the development plan. [284 E] (i)(a) The provisions of the two sections are not intended to operate retrospectively and they have no application to the acquisition proceedings under section 4 of the Central Act. The local authorities can validly make a declaration of its intention to prepare a development plan for any area or class of land within the limits of the said area after the date on which a declaration is made. [285 E] In the present case, the local authori ty could not possibly delay the acquisition and resort was not proper for the local body acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the ' Act. [286 G H] (b) The local author ity could not take advantage of the provisions contained in sections 4 and 16 of the impugned Act. If the provisions are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was no reason for the Local authority acting arbitrarily.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain villages in the State of Kutch, claimed that they had been granted a lease of land to them for a period of five years from 1st April 1948. The Land Acquisition Officer rejected their claim on the ground that the lands were not 'land ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of the , and that the appellants had no right to grant leases in respect of the lands. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the land was a part of India and had been so long as the dispute was settled by arbitration, (i) the dispute between the parties was not a matter of law; (ii) the award did not purport to be made in accordance with the provisions of section 3(1)(d) of Act No. 1 of 1948; (iii) the appellants were entitled to the grant of leases for a specified period and (iv) the claim of the Government of India to the Rann of Kutch was barred by limitation. HELD: The award did no more than define on the surface of the earth, that the area in which the Ran was situate was within the competence of the Executive wing of the State Government and no constitutional amendment is necessary. [319 D] (i)(a) The dispute between parties was a matter relating to the interpretation of the relevant provisions of the Act and the decision to implement the Award by exchange of letters, treating the award as an operative instrument after the boundary had been marked in this area. [328 E F] (b) The question whether the land is a part or parcel of India is irrelevant for determining the scope of the reference under section 3 (1)(a). If the dispute is one relating to a matter which is referred to arbitration, the decision would be final and binding on the Executive. [330 G H] (c) The award does not purport either to refer to the surface or to refer it to the arbitrator. Nor can it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cedease the land in question. [332 B C] (d) The claim of Government of Gujarat to the State for the grant was not made in conformity with the requirements of section 4(1) (d). [330 E F; 331 A] (2) The High Courts were right in holding that the award was not hit by article 19(1), because, it did not deal with the question whether it was a case relating to land which was covered by the Act. [333 B C]. (3) The reference made by the Tribunal under section 1(1 ) of the Land Acquisition Act to the Tribunal was valid and must be upheld. [320 G] (4) The contention that the Government had no power to make laws cannot be accepted without the authority of an amendment is not correct.

The appellant was the proprietor of a five annas share in Mauza Bahaldih. The mortgagor had leased out his interest to one M and the latter had executed a mortgage deed on June 14, 1946, in favour of the appellant. The mortgagee did not execute the mortgage deed within twelve years from the date of dispossession. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due by the mortgagor on April 7, 1937, as arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that M was entitled to recover the amount claimed by him under the two deeds dated June 14 and August 27, 1922, and that the suit was barred by limitation. On appeal the High Court held that the claim was within time and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the mortgage in respect of the first mortgage was not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 1, 1937 by the auction purchaser who purchased the mortgagor 's rights in Mauza Bakhshur lands at the time of the suit, he had lost all his interest in the mortgaged property. HELD: (i) The mortgage deed dated June 18, 1946 was a usufructuary mortgage and even if it be assumed that the mortgagee was entitled under the mortgage to recover it from M, the mortgagor had lost his interest therein. [699 D] (ii) The suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell was barred under article 120 of the Limitation Act from the dates of dispossession in 1937. The period of limitation for a suit to enforce the mortgage is one for compensation and the period of time for a claim to recover possession of the mortgaged properties is governed by article 120. [641 C] (iii) The right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the mortgage security or disturbance of his possession by the creditors of the mortgagor, dispossession having taken place in 1937, the suit filed on July 12, 1946 could not be said to have been barred by law of time because the mortgagee had lost the interest in Mauzas Bansjora and that he was entitled only to her costs in respect thereof.

The appellants were transport vehicles owned by the respondent company. The appellants were carrying passengers on a public service vehicle and were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for transport services. The tax was levied on the appellants under section 3(1) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958. The contention of the appellants that they had not levied any charge at all for the transport facilities granted to them was rejected by the authorities and the High Court.
