In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the tax could be levied only on passengers who were carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public services vehicle, and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that very wide meaning has been given to it. [361 E] 2. The word `public service vehicles ' has been defined in section 2(7) of Bombay Motor Vehicle (Taxationon Passengers)Act, 1958 as meaning a motor vehicle which could not be termed as public service vehicles. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [362 E] 3. The words 'public services vehicle ' have been defined separately in section 3 (1) and therefore, they must be construed strictly in their widest sense. [364 F G] 4. The expression `public services vehicles ' is not defined either under the Act nor by the rules but that is only a general term which includes the employees or persons of the private company. It can by any processes of reasoning and stretch of thought be deemed not include employees, of a Private Company who are giving facilities not on a special category but as held by this Court in State of Bombay vs M/s. J. K. Jain & Co., ; , referred to.

The appellants, who had obtained a licence for a cinema house in the city of Jabalpur, applied to the State Government under section 5(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1951 for a licence to establish a cinema theatre. The State Government granted a licence on the same terms and conditions as well as the licence. The appellants filed an application before the High Court under section 795 of the Act for a writ of mandamus directing the State Govt. to grant a licence in an appeal against the order granting a licence. A Single Judge of the High court dismissed the petition holding that the licence was not vitiated by any legal infirmity and, therefore, it was not a fit case for interference with the decision of the Single Judge. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the grant of a licence and also the order of the State government refusing to grant the licence in a revision application against that order. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there was no impediment to the grant or renewal of a cinema licence, and therefore it was a fit one for the purpose of granting a license. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the appellants who had objected to the renewal of the licence were not entitled to be heard; (ii) the High Courts erred in holding that since the licensing authority was not influenced by any extraneous consideration, the order passed by the State Govern ment could not be interfered with. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 5 of the , do not confer any right on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing authorities against the grant, but whose objection had been over ruled, can subsequently oppose the grant. [897G] 2.1 The High Courts were in error in holding the application of the appellant to be incompetent for granting a writ under Article 227 of the Constitu tion. [798B] 2:2 The provisions contained in section 5 are not intended to confer any rights on a licensee who might raise objections before him against the granting of a license, but they cannot now be permitted to urge a right to oppose the application or to file objections and nor were they entitled to have an opportunity to defend the grant by the licensing authori ty. [998C] 2 :3 The provisions in section 6 of the are not exhaustive and do not contain any provision for the grant and their effect is that the licensing Authority may refuse to grant such a licence if it considers necessary so to do. [1099E F] 3:1. The power conferred on the State Legislature by section 5 is subject to the limitations imposed by the statute. It is not open to the legislature to make any provision in the Act which confers any right of appeal on a party aggrieved by the decision or order of a court. [1012D E] 2(a) The provisions relating to grant of licence are not inconsistent with the principles of natural justice. The Act does not confer an absolute right on the licensee who has raised objections to the granting or refusing a licence, but it is the stage of renewal of an existing licence subsequent to the stage where the grant was under consideration. [1003E] 2.(b) The High court erred in taking into account the provisions of the statute and the rules framed thereunder relating to the issue of a writ for granting licence. [1000F] 3.2. The scheme of the Rules shows that the grant is not the stage for grant of an "no objection" certificate, but only the stage at which the grant has been made. It does not contain anything more than what is required by the rules to be framed under the Act. [1001G H] 3(a).

The appellant, a lessee of a mining lease in respect of certain areas of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and claimed to be the owner of the mining lease. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no concluded contract as alleged in the plaint. Held: (i) The plaint did not contain any concluded contract, and the respondent was entitled to remain in possession of the lease. [584 E] (ii) The suit for specific performance must be based on an oral agreement between the parties. The plaint in a suit for Specific performance should allege a concluded contract. In the present case, the plaint was not an acceptance of the offer but it was communicated to the respondent before his withdrawal. There was no contract unless the offer had been withdrawn before the filing of the suit. [585 E] The plaint was filed on November 5, 1957 and the appellant was at liberty to revoke the offer at any time before its withdrawal. [585 F G] (iii) The plea that by the letter dated September 2, 1957 the defendant agreed to assign the mining leases was not accepted, was not a case of acceptance. The letter was not in writing nor was it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the Court. [583 F G]. (iv) The High Court was right in holding that there had been no concluded contracts between the appellant and the defendant.

The appellants were sugar factories in the State of Bihar. They were also sugar factories. The sugar factory was taken over by the Central Government under section 3(1) of the Essential Commodities Act, 1950. The Central Government issued a notification on 27th August 1955 under section 4(2)(b) of that Act declaring that the sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed was to be deemed to have been converted into sugar and that the sugar factory had not been taken over for the purpose of the sugar factories and therefore the sugar mill was not liable to pay to the sellers. The appellants contended that they were not entitled to any compensation under section 7 of the Act. The High Court held that the Central Govern ment could not take up the investigation of the offence alleged against them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State Government had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, and therefore, the police could not have taken up the Investigation of that complaint. HELD: The Central Act does not make any difference in the case of sugar factories where the sugar industry is being carried on by the State. The State Government was well within its powers in legislating in regard to sugarcane and the Central Legislature was well outside its powers. [677 E] The power conferred on the Government under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution is subject to the legislative competence of Parliament to enact the Act and hence the police can not have any jurisdiction to investigate the same.

The appellants, who were the owners of a public sector undertaking, had been granted licences for the manufacture of certain types of misuse and the earlier orders issued by the Government of Karnataka in exercise of its powers under section 8A of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court on the ground that it was not open to them to contend that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the State Government that the concession granted under the earlier order dated 12th January, 1977 was not a valid one. The High Court held that the said concession could be given only if it was shown that the concessions were in fact misused and the later orders had been issued to the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the principle of Prom promissory estoppel was not attracted in the case because the doctrine was not applied in the instant case since it was held by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the benefit granted under section 7A of Karnataka Sales tax Act,1957 was a valid exemption and the order of 30th June 1969 was ultra vires and bad in law. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is not applicable to the present cases because it is found by Government of India that the grant of concession under the said Order dated 12.1.1977 was made subject to the condition that the grantee would be entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order dated 13th January 1977, was ultra rites and void. [950G H] 2. The principle of promissory estoppel is not attracted because it has been found by this Court in State of Bihar & Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., ; , that the decision of this Court on 12th Jan. 1977 was rendered binding on the appellants as well as the High Courts. [951A B] 3. The plea of promissory Estoppel is a pure question of law and cannot be allowed to be raised in this case because such a plea has been negatived by this court in State vs Usha martin Industries, ; , [1987] 65 STC 430; State of Kerala & Anr., vs M/s. Usha Marin Industries Ltd. & Ors., ; ; and State of Orissa vs U.P. & Anr.; , ; , relied on. 4. The State Government had no authority to provide for the grant or concession in the said orders. [953B] 5. The fact that the order was passed by the High court on 12. January,1977 would not make any difference because such an order could be made only if the concession was granted in the nature of exemption from the payment of sales tax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the order.

The appellants were charged under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. for having committed the murder of one of the persons belonging to the group of A 1 and A 2. The Trial Court acquitted A 3 of all the charges but convicted them under section 302 readwith section 34 I. P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the identity of A 3 in the unlawful assembly consisting of A 2 and A 3 was not established; (ii) the common object of the unlawful unlawful assembly was to kill the deceased, and (iii) the appellants being three in number could not have formed an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.p.C.; (iv) the evidence of P.W.3 in so far as the presence and partic ipation of the accused in the attack on the deceased was concerned; (v) the participation of A1 to A 2 in the assault on the appellant was not proved beyond doubt, and that the appellants were acquitted under section 148 and on applying 149 I P. C. they were convicted under Section 302 read With section 34 IPC. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution case is that A 1 to A 3 had been acquitted by the courts below. There was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful unlawful com panyment within the meaning of Section 149. [8A B] 2. It is in evidence that all the accused persons formed the unlawful object of unlawful assembly and there was a long standing enmity between the parties. The common intention of A I to commit the offence was to murder the deceased. There were no circumstances which justify the conclusion that the common intention was to cause one or the other unidentified persons. [88B] 3. It would be in evidence if the evidence disclosed commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intent of them all. The non applicability of Section i49 I.e. the common purpose of the assembly was not to kill A 1. There is no question that A 2 committed any unlawful assembly with the common knowledge of A l to A 1 or A 3. [89C] 4. It may be in a case where there are several number of injuries on the person of the deceased and the accused were acquitted by applying 149, but the High Courts have not taken into consideration the evidence adduced by the prosecution. The fact that the deceased had been convicted under section 147 I.PC does not make any difference to the facts of the case. [90D] 5. It was in evidence on record that all these accused formed an assembly with a common intention to kill and that there was no unlawful assembly at all. There could be no doubt that A l and A 1 were members of the same unlawful assembly. The High Court rightly held that the appellant could not be convicted under Sections 148 and 149 I .P. C., because they formed an offence within the defined meaning of section 141 I P C. [91E F] 6. It cannot be said that the accused had committed any offence under Section 147, read with 34 I P .C. or if the prosecution case disclosed commission thereof all the offences.

The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to wealth tax on the ground that the transfer of property in the family was effected by him with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains. The Wealth Tax officer assessed the said sum as income from undisclosed sources and also imposed penalty under section 52(2) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In an appeal before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the assessee was not entitled to any relief on account of the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of the transferred exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assessee by an amount of not less than 15% of the value so declared, which was indisputably the position in the present case. The Tribunal held that the transaction was a sale and that it was sufficient to attract section 52 (2) and accordingly imposed penalty on the assessee. On further appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true test for determining whether a transfer is effected or disclosed by the person who is not disclosed and in most of the cases, if not all, it would be possible for the Income tax officer to determine precisely what is actual consideration received by the assesee or in other words how much m ore consideration is received by him. [642E] 1.2 The true meaning of section 52 is that where an assessee transfers a capital asset and in respect of the sale of the goods, the value of such asset as on that date exceeds the full valuation of the consideration declared in respect thereof, the difference between the market value and the full price so declared by him, sub section (1) provides that the fair price of the asset as at the date when the transfer is made shall be taken to be the full market value. But if a capital value of a capital assets is not shown or disclosed, it will have no application in case of a bona fide transaction where the value is not stated and the consideration has been under stated and in many cases, the price declared by an assessee is more than what is declared in the instrument of transfer and the assessee shall be taxed on capital gain. [643E F] 1:3 The true position of section 53(2), as it stood at the relevant time, is that if a person transfers a property and in other terms, the consideration actually received by an assesses is more or less than what was declared by such assessee, then the difference would be liable to be added as part of capital gains taxable under the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. [641A B] 1 :4 In the instant case, the transaction in question was not a sale but a sale of property and therefore it could not be said that the value declared by it was more than the market price declared in its entirety. [651C] 2:1 The High Court was right in holding that the transactions were not sales within the meaning of Section 52(1) of Income Tax, 1961 and that the true market value was not liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated food. The prosecution case was that he had purchased the same from the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption, and thereby committed an offence under section 7(i)(f) read with section 7 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1955. The trial court convicted him but acquitted him on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human use and not for human food. HELD: (i) It is well settled that in order to judge whether a particular offence is ordinarily used for human purpose, it must be proved that the accused has committed an act which is punishable with imprisonment when reasonable doubts arise. The burden would have shifted on the prosecution to prove that what he had stored was not really food meant for consumption but an article kept for human purposes. [334E] (ii) It was a matter of common knowledge that black Tils were used for pooja and not as human food, and therefore it could be said that this case had been done by the Food Inspectors in contravention of section 2(1)(f). [330F G] (iii) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses did not corroborate the version of the Food inspector. It was also not correct to say that the entire object for which the Til seed was kept in the accused 's shop was neither "fruit" nor meant to be so used as food. [330G H] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge of adulteration against the appellant. [328H; 330A] (v) It may be true that the evidence of a Food Inspector who said that he could be used as 'food ' but it is not correct, because it is a matter which is common knowledge and not that of the accused. The fact that the signatures of Tambe was absent on all those documents on which they would have been present if section 10(7) of Act had been strictly complied with. [ 330B] (vi) It cannot be said from the nature of the article itself or the circumstances and manner of offering it for sale. Further, the prosecution has failed to establish that the article which is the subject matter of an offence was ordinarily used by the accused for human health as food when reasonable doubt arises. [332C D] (vii) The prosecution had not been able to prove this case. It could have been kept for the purpose of being sold in a shop. But it was not possible to say from the evidence that the prosecuting Food Inspector, who said to have purchased the Til oil meant for poojas, was not there at all to witness the occurrence. [333D] (viii) The fact of the presence of Tam be was absent from all those papers on which he would have actually been present when section 10 (7) was strictly complied.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th of January, 1966. He filed an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966, but the same was dismissed in limine. The respondent 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. The appellant 's appeal against the said decree was dismissed by the District Judge. In second appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to file the appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed. [54H] 1.2 In the first two cases where the order was passed by the lower authority and an order passed by another officer next higher in rank dismissing an appeal therefrom and an appellate order being after the Constitution came into force, the writ petition would be maintainable. The High Court could not exercise its jurisdiction or was it one pending at the commencement of the Constitution and the revisional order being subsequent to the Constitution. [55H] 2.1 In the second two cases, where the orders of the lower authorities are either reversed or modified it is the order passed in appeal therefrom. [56A B] 2:2 The cause for action shall first accrue and where such order is not made on the expiry of six months from the dates when the appeal was filed or representation was made, the right to sue shall first accrued and where no such order was made on that date, the rights to sue would first accrue. [57B] 2 :3 The cause or action shall once accrue and if such order be not made, on the expiration of six month from the said date when it was filed, the claim to have been made to have first arisen. [58C D] 2 4. In the instant case, the order dated 31st March, 1966 was passed in favour of the appellant and the order dismissing the appeal therefrom by a yet higher court, and therefore, as far as Government servant is concerned, Article 58 may not be misplaced in view of the special limitation.

The appellant, a displaced person, filed a suit against the respondent for partition of his property in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decision of the trial court was not final and the decree passed by the trial Court was not a decree of affirmance and this position would not be affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation was made in favour of the intending appellant. [494 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the appellate decree which confirmed the decision of trial court did not affect the character of the appellate order. [595 E F] (iii) The finding of the lower court that the respondent had not paid the price was a part of the dispute between the parties, and in that sense, it could be implied from the nature of the decree which was proposed to be brought to this court under appeal. [696 G H] (iv) The question whether the variation is made in respect of the subject matter of the suit or not must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. If there is a variation made by the appellate court, it is not a judgment of affirmation and this is not affected either under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [643 B] (v) The words "decision" in article 133(1) should be construed as meaning the decision on any matter which is directly or indirectly connected with the subject covered by the decree. In construing the word "decision", it must be held that the judgment of the High court must be read as a whole and not as a judgment. [641 C] (vi) The expression "decision ' in article 134(1), means the decision which is final or not. It does not mean the final decision. If the appellate Court makes a variation in the decision, it will be open to the appellate authority to consider whether the difference is made between the original and the original decree.

The appellant, a resident of Uttar Pradesh, was allotted certain agricultural lands in the State of U.P. The respondent filed an application under section 115 Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the order passed by the District Court on the ground that he was not entitled to get the benefit of the provisions of section 115, Code of civil Procedure. The District Court held that the High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act and directed the District Judge to decide the revision petition afresh in accordance with law. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the revisional power conferred by section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not exhausted as the High court has no jurisdiction under Section 115, C.P.,C. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction to decide a revision petition under section 5, Provincial Civil Procedure Code over a revisional order made by the district court under that section. [38B] 2. The power of the District Courts under section 50 is not confined to cases decided by a District Court. It is a point for consideration in this case whether the High Courts possess revisional jurisdiction under s 115, code of Civil procedure. [39C D] 3. Section 115 of Code of C. P.C.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands in Jaipur and wanted to challenge the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Trust Act, 1959. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity and legality of the said notification dated February 8 , 1984 issued by it under section 51(2) of that Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned notification was not in accordance with law and was sufficient to invest the Calcutta High Court with jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the notification. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government by its order dated March 13 , 1984 had issued a rule nisi on the basis of such petition from which the writ in the nature of mandamus should be issued. [605D] 2. The power and authority of the State Govern ment to acquire the notified land under section 53(1 ) of the Act or the legality and propriety of the notice issued by him under section 54 (1) is a flagrant abuse of the process of the Court. [613E F] 3. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under Section 52(2), for the purpose of implementing a development scheme at public expense, namely, for the implementation of a development Scheme at public expenses, viz., the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, the said scheme being a complete code and the same would be governed by the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. [625E F; 602A] 4. The whole cause of the action culminating into the acquisition is a pure question of law and fact and the jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 of Constitution to quash the notification dated March13, 1984 issued under section52(1), or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section 55 (1). [606F] 5. The proceedings before the Calcutta Court are quasi judicial in nature and the High court has no power to issue a writ in respect of any particular land which is not covered by the Act. It is not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer, nor can they be shown to have been served upon them by a proper notice under section 50(1). The High Courts have no power or authority to issue writ in regard to any particular area which is covered by a statute. [600F H] 6. The impugned notification dated April 9, 1976 issued under Section 51(1)(a) of Act is not in conformity with law.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. The landlord filed an application under section 25 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of the appellant from the premises on the ground that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the building in question had been constructed in 1968 and that it would be covered by section 39(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the landlord that the Act did not apply to a building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed, and therefore the new rent could not be said to have been completed on 1st October, 1971. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that by seeking the benefit of section 39 of the new Act there was a change in the cause of action. [334E] In the instant case, the building was subject to assessment therefore it would not be open to the appellant to get any protection of the old Rent Act and the appellant cannot get any relief of the same kind. The question whether the building is within ten years old on the date of the suit and was exempted from the operation of the amended Rent Act can be governed by it if ten years expired during the pendency of the litigation. [340G H] In view of the fact that the landlord had been in occupation of the building for more than ten years, the appellant would be entitled to get the benefit under section 39 as the building had not become ten years after the date when the revision came into being by the High Court and, therefore, there was no question of giving the benefit to the tenant.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in 1942. The appellant entered into two contracts for construction of aerodrome and the second contract was to be executed on behalf of the appellant. The first contract provided that the appellant would execute the agreement in favour of the respondent. The second contract provided for arbitration of disputes arising out of the contract. The parties entered into three contracts with the appellant, one for the execution of the work and the other for the construction of the works. The contract was executed on November 5, 1942. On the first of them being signed by the appellant as well as by the second respondent, the appellant filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bihar, praying that the agreement be made in terms thereof. The Subordinate judge held that the contract was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and that the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that therefore it fell within item 12 of the first contract. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that it was a nullity and that no decree could be passed in terms of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date. The question for decision was whether the award made by the Subordinate judge was a valid reference to arbitration under section 175 (3). Held, that the award was not invalid because it was not a certified copy of an instrument relating to the execution and was not properly stamped. It was not open to the appellant to contend that the document in question was not an original one relating thereto and that it fell outside item 12. The agreement actually before the court was, what it purports to be, "a certified copy" and that under section 35 of the Stamp Act there can be no doubt that the original and not a copy of the award.

The appellant, a government servant in the State of Punjab, was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the Government of Punjab. He was posted as Executive Engineers in the Public Works De partment Department in Punjab. The appellant was working in the Department in a department in the Punjab and Haryana. On his return from the Department he was transferred to the Punjab Public Works Branch in the year 1979. In the year 1980, he was promoted as Executive Engi neer in the department of the State Government. He filed a complaint against him under section 161 IPC for having committed offences punishable under sections 409/109/109 IPC and section 5(2) read with Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Trial Court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been convicted by the trial court. On appeal, the High Court set aside the acquittal and convicted him under Section 161 IPC and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Courts were wrong in taking the view that the said rule cannot be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general prohibition on prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied; and (ii) the words "in any case" occurring in clause (b) with regard to pension of such a Government servant are not to be found in the main rule 2.2. The High Court was, therefore, right in taking into consideration the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 2.3. The contention that the third proviso to clause (a) of Rule 1 is in the nature of beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the rule has been framed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso to Clause (b), of Rule I, as it stood at the relevant time, is not to place an embargo on prosecution. It is only when a government employee is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause of action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause(b) of rule 2, [919B C] 1.2 The second Proviso to clause(a) is in two parts: (i). The third proviso is in respect to a Government employee who has been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment in judicial proceeding in respect thereof. The second part provides that the period for initiating prosecution shall not be less than four months before such commencement of the Act or event mentioned therein. [920C D] 1:3. In view of what has been said above, the third Proviso to Rule 2(2), cannot be invoked by the respondents in support of their interpretation of the third sub rule. [936D] 1.(a) The second Explanation to clause 2(1) is not applicable to a government Servant on whom the conditions have been framed and who had been framed for a different purpose namely to provide an exception to the power of the Government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing etc.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The authorised capital of the company was Rs. 1,000 ordinary shares and Rs. 2,000 preference shares of Rs. 3,000 each. The respondent company paid up its share capital to the respondent company on the basis that it had been receiving dividend from the shareholders as dividends by way of dividend. The Income tax Officer held that the respondent was one in which the public were substantially interested and there fore the income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23 A of the Act for any of the three years and on that footing answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression "reserve" in section 23A is wide enough to include a company in which public are substantially interested. It does not mean that the company is one in whom the public are substantial. [321 B] (ii) Section 23 A is a provision which defines what a company, in which it is substantially interested, is. The expression 'reserve ' has been defined in section 2(g) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 as meaning "any company in Which the public have substantially interested". But the Legislature by the Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of the Company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group. The Legislature by its Explanation has taken a conclusive evidence in those matters where shares are not substantially interested but are held jointly by the public. [421 B C] (iii) Section 3A is in reality a clause which defines "reserves" and not to include "any person who have been substantially interested" as would be regarded as one in Which it is not substantially interest. The legislature by the explanation has raised an conclusive presumption that the shares of a company carrying not more than twenty per cent or more of the vote are held, by personsother than the control group. [427 B C]. (iv) Section 22A does not say that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23 is in itself a clause. The Explanation has no application where shares have been fully interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company was held by the parent company or by the nominees thereof.

The appellants were carrying on business of manufacturing and selling cotton. The goods were delivered to the appellants at Dharsi Moolji for delivery in the same truck. The appellants were prosecuted under section 120 B read with section 34 I.P.C. for having committed breach of contract by them. The trial court acquitted the appellants but convicted them under section 409 I. P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the delivery of the goods by the appellants to Dharsi was not a mere physical delivery but an actual delivery of goods; (2) the sale was not in the course of trade or commerce, and (3) the High Courts were wrong in holding that the delivery was not made as required by section 34(1). HELD : (i) The delivery of possession of the cotton had passed and when Dharsi did not comply with the requirements of the form because the form required information regarding physical delivery to the quota holder or his agent, the same was not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but means what it says, namely, that the person to whom physical delivery was made whoever he may be. [830 B] (ii) The fact that the goods were in the physical possession of a person does not make any difference because they say, namely the person who is to whom the physical delivery of a goods has been made whosoever may be; and the mere fact that it is not the actual delivery would not make the goods liable for loss. [930 B C] (iii) The High Court was wrong in treating the delivery as having been made by the agent of the Mills. It was not correct to say that the sale took place when Dharendra paid the price and the delivery could be taken back to the Mills 's premises, because they were in physical possession.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "obtains" in clause (d) of section 6 of the Corruption Act mean a person who is an officer in the service or pay of the Government or was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty; and (ii) the use of the word "obtained" in cl. (d), of section 5 of the Act, as it stood at the material time was as follows: "The expression "obtain" means a person in the serv ice or pay or commission of a Government or an agent for the purpose of any Public servant". The expression "exempt" is defined in section 2(g) of that Act to mean a public servants. " The word "exaction" has been defined in the Act to include a public officer who is not a public Servant. The definition of "public servant" in section 5, as amended by the Prevention Of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1969, shows that the expression "public servants" means any person who was an officer or servant in the employ of the government or was employed for the purposes of any business or profession. The word 'obtains ' has been used in the context of the definition of public servant. In the present case, the appellant was not a Public servant when he was acting as an examiner. He had no connection with his being a public employee. The prosecution was therefore not barred by section 5. (i). The High court proceeded on the basis that for the offence of bribery under section 6(1) read along with section 7(1), the appellant must be held to be a public person within the definition. In this appeal it was urged on behalf Of the State that (a) the expression 'obtained ' in cl.(d) is wide enough to include the word 'public servant ' and therefore, the use by the public servant of the public servants for the discharge of his own duty and thereby obtain valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. HELD: The definition in section 3(1 ) of the Indian Penal code has to be read as a whole and not merely a mere element of effort on the part of the receivers. [723 B] (b) The expression 'exempt ' is used in cl (d). It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (a), a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of sub section (1) of s.5(1). [724 C D] (c) The use of words "exercising" in el. (e) of cl.

The petitioners were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10,140 to 16 years in the construction Department of Signal Unit in the Northern Railway. The petitioners were granted temporary status on completion of 180 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement. They challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition before the High Court contending that since they had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration should be treated as temporary servants and have applied different criteria for regularisation of their services. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to the same pay as is 1/3rd of the period which was their previous requirement and that they should be given temporary status. The respondents filed a writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity and legality of the order of the High Courts. The main contention raised by the petitioners was that since the petitioners had put into continuous service, they were entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Railway Board. It was further contended that the respondents should be granted temporary appointment on completion Of 180 days or not. The learned Single Judge of the Court allowed the writ petition holding that since there were break in such continuity of service, the casual labourers are entitled to be treated at par with regular employees and they are therefore entitled to full pay for similar work and that the Railway administration is bound to take prompt steps to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. The Division Bench allowed the Writ Petitions holding that there was break in the continuity of services as against 240 days which were the previous requirements. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since no pensionary benefits are admissible to either category of employees, they should not be treated differently and that their claim for equal pay is not admissible to both categories of employees. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The benefit of Discipline and Appeal Rules is also applicable to casual labour with temporary status as laid down in Chapter XXIII of the Indian Railway Establishment Manual. [144C] 2.1 The petitioners should be entitled to similar benefits even to temporary servants who have been appointed on regular basis. [145D] 22 In the instant case, the petitioners should not have been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievance has been very much reduced. [146E] 2:3 The petitioners shall be entitled for the same salary as is the 1/ 3rd of their period in the project. [147F] 2 :4 In the absence of any specific direction by the Railways and the Northern railway authorities and the Railway Headquarters were placed before this Court to show that the Administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. [148G] 2(a) The petitioners are entitled for equal wages as is one of the conditions of service. They should be paid the same scale of pay, increments etc., and they should also be given such pay as was 1/4th of the periods which were their previous requirements and not with those who have already been tested.

The Forward Markets Commission was constituted under the Forward Markets Act, 1946. Under section 12(1) of the Act, the Central Government had power to make bye laws for the purpose of carrying on any business in such matters as are referred to it by the Central Govern ment. The Forward Markets Commis sioner issued a notification under section 12 (1) declaring that the Forward markets Commission could not, after considering the objections, be constituted under section 11(2), impose a bye law with retrospective effect and that the provisions of the Forward Market Act were not inconsistent with the provisions contained in the Act. The appellant who was an association of traders filed a petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification on the ground that it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the bye laws were ultra vires and that section 12 of the , did not offend article 14 of the Constitution, Held, that the Act was valid and the provisions in the Forward market Act were void. The power to frame bye law under section 4(f) of Act No. 1 was a legislative power within the meaning of article 19(1)(a) of that Article and it could not be said that the Central Legislature had no power under section 2 (f). The Act did not confer any such power on the Central Govt. to make a bye laws with retrospective operation and therefore, the provisions Of section 12 were void as they contravened article 19 (1)(b) of Constitution.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled as the Ukhara Estate Zamindaries Ltd. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ were taxable as dividend income and not dividend income. The Income tax Officer held that the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was liable to be grossed up. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term leases after the 31st March 1948 was a receipt of income in his hands and not income of the asses see from other sources. The High Court further observed that the distribution to assessee of Rs. 1367/ was not taxable as dividends, but as income of assessee from other source. In the appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the distributable dividend out of capital gains was taxable as a dividend income under section 2 (6A), and that the amount distributed as dividend for each of the three years in question was income assessable as dividend. HELD: The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain or not. [738 D] In the instant case, the distribution of dividend out from capital gains is a capital asset and not a dividend. It is only a portion of it which is statutorily payable on compensation is income and is not capital gain. The question of distribution to be made by the assessee does not arise in this case.

The appellant was a forest produce within the meaning of section 2(f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1963. The timber was notwood oil as defined in section 2 (f) of that Act. The appellant was granted a permit for felling and cutting of trees on the ground that it was not wood oil as understood in trade parlance. The forest produce whether found in or 'brought from a forest or not is a forest Produce which includes wood oil. The Forest Department, however, issued a notification under section 2 of the Act exempting the timber from payment of tax. The respondent challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court contending that Sandalwood oil was not 'wood oil ' as defined under section2(f)(1) (i) of Act. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that Sandals, which were admittedly forest produce, were not wood oils and therefore it was a 'wood Oil ' within the definition of 'agricultural produce '. The High Court held that sandalwood was not timber oil as contemplated under section 3(f). Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'wood ' is defined in the Act to mean any person who has a right to cut from a forests or not. [164G] 1.2 The expression 'wood" used in the definition is not meant to prevent the word ' wood oil ' but to enable the word as used in it, when there is nothing in the context or the subject matter of the statute. [165H; 165A] 1:3. The word `wood ' has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be restricted in such a way so as to defeat the purpose and purpose of the legislation. [166B] 1.(4) The word "wood oil" used by the legislature is not static vehicle of ideas and concepts and as ideas and expressions are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the statutory provision undergo a change. [167D] 1(5) The expression "wood" has to receive its colour from its context and connotation. The dictionary meaning of the word is not defined in its ordinary sense but as understood by the people in general parlance. It must be construed according to its popular sense, but in the wider sense it cannot include wood oil which is used in commercial parlance. [168E] 1 (6) The use of the words "wood ' and "wood Oil" in the statute will require literal interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning would have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. In the instant case, the word ` wood oil" has been defined in Section 2(g) of Kerala and Tamil Nadu Act, 1962. [169F G] 1 :4. The use being technical and being part of an inclusive definition has to he construed in the popular sense in which it is being understood in commercial sense but not in a narrow manner. [170G H] 1 5. The expression `wood oil used in section 3 (f)(i) (ii) of Tamil Nadu Forest Act 1963 is wide enough to include wood oils. [171F G; 169A] In the present case, it was interpreted by this Court that sands were wood oil within the ambit of the term 'wood. The meaning and scope of the expression 'greenwood oil in the Kerala Act will require liberal construction.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code but acquitted him. The High Court, in appeal, reversed the judgment of acquittal and convicted him under section 304 Part I.P.C. and sentenced him to transportation for life. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the conviction of the appellant was not sustainable as it was based on circumstantial evidence and the High Court had rightly set aside the conviction. The circumstances in which the judgment was passed were not such as to justify interference with the findings of the trial court. The Sessions Judge was of opinion that the evidence of the doctor was extremely unsatisfactory and that his statement was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon, and therefore it could not be said that there was no compelling reasons for setting aside the judgment. The appellant had been given a chance to explain the circumstances against him which he had relied upon. Held, further, that there were no compelling reason for setting the conviction and the acquittal of the accused. The evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the respondent could properly be drawn. The judgment of the High court was not correct. The fact that the doctor who was present on the spot by using the statement of another man who was in all probability not there was any compelling reason to set aside his conviction, would not make it a fit case for interference under article 136 of the Constitution.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1947. The workmen of the appellant company were also employed by the appellant 's factory at Ranchi and their workmen represented by their union. The dispute between the appellant and its workmen was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the reference was valid and directed the appellant to pay Rs. 1,000/ as bonus to the workmen of its factory at Patna and also the said amount of bonus to workmen of other establishments. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the company that the dispute raised by the union was in respect of the employees of the Company where they may be stationed. The appellant company had no concern with the affairs of the respondent company and its employees represented by its union. It was also contended that the said reference was made in October 1963 and the said statement was made before the Tribunal. HELD: (i) The dispute referred to it was not a dispute between it and its employer. The award was operative only from January 6, 1963 or 21, 1963. [553G] (ii) The reference was not justified in directing the appellant Company to grant special leave to attend the meetings of the union and the Tribunal 's extension of that award to workmen in the company 's other establishments was clearly without jurisdiction. [554H] (iii) The award is operative only when it is made clear that the disputes referred to a Tribunal were not capable of being adjudicated by the Tribunal, but it could be decided by the tribunal on the considerations mentioned therein and the award would cover them also. [555A B] (iv) The Tribunal 'rejected the rest of the claim as unjustified and cannot be sustained. The Award is operative in respect to the employees in the appellant. [556B C] (v) The question whether the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6 or 21 1963 or that it was necessary for the union to grant Special leave to the union should be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties and the evidence led before the tribunal.

The assessee firm was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business, inter alia, in timber business. The assessee claimed that the firm had been dissolved on March 31, 1939 and that the business of the firm was taken over by two partners of the partnership firm. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was carrying on business at the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, and that it was not entitled to relief under section 25(4). On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was carrying out business at a commencement of Indian Income Tax (Amendment), Act 7 Of 1939, when the assessee 's firm was dissolved and on that account the business was taken by the assessee. [657 B] The assessee was not carrying on any business at all at the time of dissolution of the assessee firm. It was therefore, not entitled under section 26(4) to claim the benefit of section 25 (4). [658 C D] The High court was right that the respondent was carrying from the timber business in timber which was carried on by the firm and that its business at Abdullapur was taken away by the partnership deed. [641 B] In the absence of other evidence, it may be held that there was a change in the constitution of the partners. But the assessee could not carry on the timber trade during the relevant period. The fact that the accounts were settled upto March 31 1939 and the business at Mollapur in the name of the Firm Hakam Mal Tani Mal would not do business after March 31.3. 1939, was not set out in the instrument, and there is no other evidence in that behalf.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal against the order of the State Government granting the permit to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the Secretary to the Regional Transport Authority, Shimoga, had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Act, 1963 (briefly the Rules) after a lapse of such a long time from the date of grant of the permit. The State Transport Tribunal held that there was no period of limitation under Rule 119 and therefore the appellant could not be granted a permit. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdic tion to issue the permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional transport Authority granting the permits. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The appeals must be allowed and the order granting the renewal of the permits is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of a permit.[189 E] In the instant case, there was nothing on record to show that section 64 of the Act was the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant. [189 G] The State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal had no Jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order passed by the Regional Authority granting a permit in pursuant to an earlier decision of the Tribunal granting the same. [ 189 E] The appeals before the High court were therefore not competent under section 64(11) of the .

The appellant was a candidate for election to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in the year 1967. He was declared elected by the Election Commission of India and his supporters entered the office of the Republican Party on 7th February, 1967. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the appellant had been denied the opportunity of meeting that case. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 2 1967 and there was no evidence to show that the respondent was guilty of corrupt practice. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in not considering the evidence of the witnesses who were examined as a witness to prove the charge against the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The evidence on record is not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellant on the basis of the oral evidence of P.W. 18. [895 B] (2) The High court rightly came to the conclusion that no election meeting was conducted at Hapur and there were no witnesses to prove that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri had chased the appellant or threatened his workers. The evidence in support of the case is not enough to sustain a conviction on the sole ground that he was denied the right of voting by the respondent. [8895 B C] (3) The appellant 's case was that the election meeting which was held was at Hapur, was an election petition and there could be no attack on the office or the supporters of respondent Prakash. The allegation in the petition was that respondent Gupta had assaulted the appellant and threatened his worker with dire consequences.

The appellant purchased the property in a suit for delivery of possession of the property. The sale was confirmed by the District Judge, Jaipur City, Jaipur, holding that in view of Article 134 of the Limitation Act, the application for setting aside the sale was maintainable and not barred by limitation. The District Judge held that in spite of the settlement of the sale on July 17, 1979, the decree holder had no right to set aside the said sale. On appeal, the District judge upheld the order of the District Court. In second appeal, it was contended for the appellant that since the application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable and the period of limitation prescribed by Article 134 was not computed from the date of the decree irrespective of the date on which the sale took place. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the application filed by the appellant under Order 21 Rule 95 was barred by time, and that as the application was quite within the period prescribed by article 134 of Limitation Act the order for setting it aside the order passed by the Executing Court was not sustainable. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 134 will apply to an application under O. XXI r. 95 of Civil procedure Code. The provision in O.XXI of the Civil Procedure Code is applicable only where there is a specific provision for setting up a period of time and not in the manner prescribed by that Article. [368C] 2. In view of the provisions of Rule 89, 90 and 91 of Order XXI of the C.P.C., an application for set aside sale can also be made within a period Of 12 years from the commencement of the Act. The order passed under OXXI, r. 92 of the code will be governed by Article 136 of the . [368D] 3. In the instant case, there is no merit in the contention that the sale becomes absolute only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 92 and not Article 134. [369E] 4. The application for delivery was quite clearly within the time prescribed by the Article 134 and therefore, the period during which the order disallowing the application to set it aside was within a reasonable period of 12 years. [370F] 5. In any event, an application filed under O., XXI r., 95 of C. P.C. is not maintainable. [371G] 6. The period of Limitation prescribed by Rule 89 of the CPC is not attracted.

The appellant was the owner of a house in the town. He had been residing at the time of election and had gone to his residence. The appellant 's father was also residing with him. In the election petition he alleged that the wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance of the appellant. The respondent filed an Election Petition challenging the validity of the election of the first respondent to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattan Constituency No. P 14 and P 15, the appellant ' s election agent. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that exhibit P 1 was not proved by any evidence and that exhibit PW 1 was a clear and specific case of the second respondent that exhibit A 1 was signed by him as the murderer of the four victims, and that the first Respondent had made it clear that he was going to examine witnesses only in connection with the pasting of the poster. The Election Petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that exhibit D 1 was inadmissible in evidence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that exhibit R 1 was admissible under section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that it was an admitted fact that the second Respondent had not seen the wall posters at the behest of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The contents of the wall pamphlet directly named the first appellant as the leader of the two victims, are known to be the leader in the locality. It is true that the contents of this wall poster directly named a leader of a particular locality are not conclusive evidence and it is only when it is proved that the said poster was affixed prior to the election by the workers of the appel lant with his knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (4) Of the Act. [776C D] (2) The evidence of the contents in exhibit P1 is not conclusive but only a direct reference to the first and second respondent. It cannot be said that the copy of exhibit PI was not admissible under Section 123(3). [775G H; 767A B] (3) The High Courts have recorded findings on the question whether exhibit P I was admissible in evidence under section 116A of the Act, and if it is found that exhibit p 1 was affixed before the election. [76776B C] (4)(a) The appellant had made a statement to the effect that he had not taken the photographs in question on the said day and that he himself had seen the incident. He has also deposed to the fact that he has not seen any of the witnesses who have stated that they had taken the photograph in question, has gone further and stated that all the wall writings and wall posters were not mentioned in the notice issued by him. [7776C] (b) The first respondent 's evidence is not admissible in law under section 117 of the Evidence Act. It may be necessary to prove that the words complained of are reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the candidate 's election. But it is not necessary to do so because the first part of the notice is not only vague but also contains a clear statement that he did not take the photographs even on 25th and 26th March, 1987 but also in the Court. [75776G H] (c) The second respondent has made it abundantly clear that the publication was intended to create an impression that the incident of murders had taken place a day prior to election. It would be difficult to understand as to how this witness could have seen the walls and posters. [765C D; 767D] (d) The fact that in the first instance, the first respond ent 's witnesses were not examined by the appellant with his consent cannot be accepted.

The respondent No. 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner of Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay, and directed the appellant to grant sanction for construction of a five star hotel on the said land. The respondent No 2 filed an application before the Municipal Corporation for permission to construct a five Star Hotel. The Municipal Corporation rejected the same on the ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order granting sanction of the plan. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the property was not a public purpose and that it had no application to the facts of the case. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in rejecting the application for approval of the scheme submitted by respondent No 1. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The ground for rejecting the plan submitted by the respondent No, 2 is no longer tenable. [924D] In the instant case, the Municipal Commissioner rejected the plan and did not challenge the order passed by the Corporation on the grounds that there was a proposal for revision of its plan. It was also not disputed that the draft revised development plan had been published and the plan was submitted by Respondent No. 1. The plan submitted on April 30, 1984 was approved by the Municipal Commis sioner. [936E] In view of the clear provisions of sections 46 and 31(6) of the Act and having regard to the position that in the sanctioned plan the said lands were included in the residential zone and no proposal for the preparation of a draft revised plan had already been published, the respondent NO. 2 directed sanction of it to be made by the appellant. [951F] The High court was right in rejecting this contention.

The appellant employer, a domestic undertaking, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling textiles. The workmen were charged with an offence under section 28 read with sections 2(1)(b) and 4(a) of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 (`the Act ' for short). The Industrial Court held that the employers had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the employer had not been closed or at any rate has resumed working in full and that the old workmen were being re employed in full, and that since the new workmen were not being re employcd and new hands are being recruited, they could not be treated as a lockout. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The employer has imposed a lock up or has closed down the industrial activity. It is to be determined with reference to the circumstances of each case. [678C] 2. In order to be assured that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit it is necessary to find out what was the intention of the employer at the time when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down, the industrial establishment must be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. [688D] 3. The closure of the industrial undertaking is not an unfair Labour practice. It may be possible to say that the closure has been stopped by reason of the closure of industrial activity, the Industrial Court in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practices must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employers. [698E] 4. The question whether the employers have imposed a ban on lock out, or has stopped working in an industrial establishment, depends upon the circumstances and circumstances of the case. If the employer has resorted to closure of an industry, the appropriate authority is not required to approach the matter from this angle that the close of the industry will be completely closed. [708E F] 5.

The appellant company was incorporated on July 29, 1924. The assessee company was a registered firm and its objects were to be carried on by the company in accordance with the provisions of section 66(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee company had a right to deal in investments but the case of the company was not one of the Memorandum of Association giving the power to the company to deal with investments but it was only an investor and not an investor. On appeal by certificate the High Court held that in the case where the assessee Company did not merely the memorandum of association but also the memorandum or the memorandum, that it was a dealer in shares, securities and properties and not merely an investor, had relied on two basic facts, namely, (1) that the objects set out in the Memorandum were to carry on business in shares and investments; (2) that since the assessee 's company was registered as an investment company, the object of which was to carry out the activities of the assessee was of dealing in shares or securities and (3) that because of its assertion made by the assessee it could not be held to be an investor; and (4) that as a result of the memorandum the essential characteristics of the business of dealing with shares or that of an investor were, therefore, not excluded from consideration. HELD: The question whether the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares or any investment in securities and immovable properties of the asses see are matters of fact and law is one of fact. [655 B] In the instant case, the assessee had a clear connection with the business carried on in shares. It was not necessary to decide whether the profit and losses arose out of the sale. The question as to what were the characteristics of business in share or that the income from securities and movable properties of assessee company can be taxed as business profits.

The appellant was appointed as Subordinate Judge in 1935, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate judge of Masulipatnam. On June 19. 1954, the Government issued a notice to the appellant under Rule 4(1)(a) of the Madras Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The appellant filed a petition in the High Court for a writ quashing the order of suspension and also for a direction that he should be reinstated with effect from October 1, 1953. The High Court held that the enquiry was bad as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 4 of the Andhra Civil Services Rules, 1954, which came into operation from October, 1953 was not ultra vires and void. [421 B] (ii) The order passed by the High court on January 28, 1954 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311. But under Rule 13 of the Tamil Civil Services(Disciplinary proceedings) Rules 1953, it is the duty of the Government to hold a fresh enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e). [422 C] (iii) The appellant was not entitled to have his case referred to the Tribunal for adjudication and it was open to him to make an order in accordance with Rule 4 (1)(b) of that Rules. [420 D E] (iv) The Government had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally, that the findings given by the enquiry officer were bad. [416 G H] (v) The report was then sent to the Government for action and it is not open to the State Government to make a fresh inquiry into grave charge under Rule 17(a). [420 E F] (vi) The High Courts of Judicature at Madras, in exercise of their powers under article 311, have jurisdiction to deal with the question whether the charges were well founded. The order of dismissal passed by them was merely an one of suspended pending final order by the State Govern ment. It is not necessary that the Government should hold a further enquiry into the conduct of a judicial officer.

The appellant was a registered holder of 2674 shares of the appellant. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 23(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to the appellant for the assessment year 1952 53 and the appellant filed an application before the Income tax officer claiming that the income from the estate of the respondent had been assessed as income of the assessee in the hands of his legal representative when the order of the Income Tax Officer pursuant to which the income was to be deemed to be distributed was made after the death of the shareholder. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the application and held that the appellant was not liable to pay tax on the dividend so deemed to have been received by him or his legal representatives after the expiry of the account year in which such person died, and therefore he was not entitled to any relief under section 24B. On appeal the High Court set aside the order passed by the Income. Tax Officer and held against the appellant but the High court restored that of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue: (1) that the expression "assessee" in section 2(2) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1961, is wide enough to include a person by whom income tax or any other person has been received and therefore they are not liable for taxation as income. HELD : (i) The expression "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" cannot be deemed by fiction to have beer received by the dead person and therefore it is not liable under section 2 (2). [312 D] (ii) Section 24B of the Act provides that where a person dies, his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall be liable to tax as if he was a member of the family. The expression 'assessee ' in section 24 B means a person who is entitled to receive income tax on any income from any estate of a deceased person in the assessment of which such assessee has been paid. [313 D] In the present case, the assessee had not made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the estate and therefore the expression 'any tax ' in s 2(1) of that Act was wide enough. [313 E] (iii) The word "assessee", in section 25B as substituted by the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a 'person by whom the income tax is payable ' and not a person under whom it has been made. [311 G H] (iv) The words "any amount which would be payable by such person" in s.2(1), are wide enough for the purpose of assessment of the income received by a legal representative who would, but for the death or the amount of refund due to him, have been receive by such legal representatives. [310 G H; 312 A] (v) The term "assessee ' is not defined in section 3(2). It means a firm or a Hindu undivided family which is a person and by whom it is made liable to income tax. [309 B C] (vi) The definition of the expression in s, 2(3) as substituted for the Indian income tax (Amendment), Act 25 of 1954 with effect on April 1. 1952, meant a person, by whom any income tax was payable, and not by whom he had received the income. [308 E F] (vii) The Legislature has not made an express provision generally to assess tax on such receipts on the footing that it is the personal income of a legal repre sentation which would, though for the life time, have become taxable under the Act if the person earning income tax and this Act had been taken for the first time before the expiry thereof.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a Ruler of an Indian State and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owners of the lands specified in Schedule A and C of his Petition under articles 227 and 227 Of the Constitution, and that as he was not a 'Ruler ' within the meaning of article 366(22) of the constitution he did not come within the expression "maufidar" in section 2(m) of Act. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler and as he had no right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages, he could not conceivably be a maufidar. The High Court rightly held that the respondent was an Ex Ruler and that his status as a Ruler was not confined to a grantee from a State or Ruler of a State.
