Held further, that in view of the definition of 'proprietor ' in section2(m), the appellant could not be regarded as an ex ruler and as such he could claim protection under article 366 (22) Of the constitution. The word "maafidar" is defined in section 3(m). The expression "amaufidar ' is defined by section 2 (m) to mean a person who has a right to obtain possession of land in any village or part thereof. The definition of "proprietor" in the Act does not make him a Ruler for purposes other than the Constitution and for the purposes of the privy purse guaranteed, he is a Ruler as defined in article 366.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. He was transferred to Pouri (now in the Central Administrative Tribunal). The order of transfer was challenged before the High Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of his transfer on the following reasoning: (i) That the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer; (ii) That there was no reason why the transfer should be cancelled; (iii) that the guidelines are applicable to the case of the respondent, and (iv) that he should be transferred anywhere in India. The Division Bench allowed the appeal by a common judgment dated 3rd April, 1986. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines do not require the two spouses to be posted at different places. [440E] 1.2 In the case where all India services, the parties are posted at one station, they have to bear in mind that the spouses thereby would be posted in another station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [ 432A B] 1:3 The guidelines say that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted on different places, the couple have to pay at one place, i.e., at one stations, 'they cannot as of right claim to be relieved of the ordinary incidents of all India service and avoid transfer to a different place on the ground that the spouse thereby would he posted at another station. [42E] 2.1 In the instant case, the guidelines say, that as regards possible husband & wife must he posted in one station if they are posted there is no question of any inconvenience or hardship to that reason. The guidelines says that as soon as possible, husband and husband should be posted there should be a transfer at another place if it was possible without some detriment to administrative needs. [41E] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta ; , referred to. 2.2 The guidelines are not followed in the instant cases. [44G] 3.1 It is not the case that the respondent has been transferred from one station to another station, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of rights if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authority should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two parties to live together at one Station if it be possible withoutany detriment to its administrative needs, and the claims of other employee. [40G H] Bank Of India vs State of Bihar & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. for causing the death of one Jawahar and three others by shooting on the deceased. The Trial Court convicted them under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the participation of the appellant in the occurrence which resulted in the death was proved beyond doubt; (ii) the presence of the accused in the crime which resulted from the death by shooting was not sufficient, in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and (iii) the conviction of the appel lants under Section 326 read with 34 I P.c. should be maintained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the deceased was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of section 325, I P C. [634C] 2. The participation of appellants in the commission of the crime is proved beyond reasonable doubt. [735E] 3. The object of the Act is to cause simple hurt and not a murder. It is also provided that the offence should be committed by the accused person who has been convicted for the offence under section 302 readwith Section 34 I, I., P. C. and was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. [700H] 4. The conviction of appellants under Section 323 read with 149 I.p.C is set aside. [750B] 5. The prosecution evidence shows that the participation in the offence which resulted into death of Jawahar has been proved beyond any doubt. It also imposes a sentence of fine on the appe lants. [751D] 6. The appellants shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial Court within four months from today. In the event of non payment of fine the appellants shall undergo rigorous imprison ment for five year.

The appellant Bank was incorporated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Banking Companies Act, 1949, was enacted to provide for the establishment of a corporation by the Central Government and before the words `special Indian law ' were inserted in section 4(e) of the Act. Section 4(a) of that Act provided for the constitution of a Corporation under the Act and not by the State Government. The appellant Bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said provisions of the said Act as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1976 was a special law enacted by the Indian Parliament and not in pursuance of such a law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that since the words 'in pursuance of ' in section 3(e), were `special ' in Section 4 (e) and related to a special Indian Law, the Banking Company Act is a special Act and the provisions of section 4 (a) are not applicable to the appellant bank. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words `in pursuance to ' in s.4(e)(i) of Act, are wide enough to include a law enacted for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions contained in the Act or the Act itself. [968C] 2.1 The expression `special" is used in section 2(g) of this Act and it is not a corporation within the meaning of section 3 (e). It is not an ordinary Indian law but by or under a special statute. It is a general law enacted to protect the citizens against exploitation of corporations created by the Government of India Act, 1935. [936D] 2:2 The words 'any special Indian law" in s 4(c) are wide and comprehensive enough to cover all laws which have been made by the British Parliament or Legislature. It would be highly unreasonable and inequitable to think that as a corporation has been formed by or through an ordinary law, it will not come within the purview of section4(a). [967D] Krishna Murthy vs State of Mysore, ; , referred to. 2.3 The words "any special I law" occurring in s 3 (a), are wide in scope and include a statute enacted by Parliament or legislature. It does not mean that a corporation is created under the general law. It cannot be said that it has been created under a Special Indian Law. [951E] 2 :4 The words, 'any Special Indian law " have been defined in section 1(e). The words used are `in pursuant to ' and 'in pursuant thereto '. The word `in furtherance of ' is not defined in the General Clauses Act. It means a corporation which is a corporation established by orunder a special enactment. [948E] 3:1. In view of the language of section 2 (e), it cannot be held that it was created under an ordinary statute, for an ordinance is as much a law as an enactment of Parliament or State Legislature. [947F G] 2(a)(i). The word 'in furtherance ' in the section means a law made by a State Legislature and not a law which is an Act of Parliament. It will be highly inappropriate to think, that as the words "in pursuance thereof" are `special I law ', it would be more appropriate to refer to any law made under the Constitution and not to the law itself in order to come within purview of the section. [946F G; 969A] 2.(b) The expression 'any ' in clause (e)(ii) of section 1 is used as a word 'under ' in that clause.

The petitioners who were manufacturers of sugar in Punjab and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the notification dated July 30, 1958 issued under section 3 of the Act on the ground that it was violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned notification was beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government by section 3 Of the Act and cl. 5 of the Order did not authorise the Central Govern ment to fix ex factory prices and that the notification violated articles 14, 19(i)(g), 31(1) (g) and 31(2). The petitioners contended that the notifications were invalid because they infringed article 19 (1)(f) and (g). Held, that the object of the impugned Act was to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of sugar. The object of section 3 is to ensure fair prices for the consumer at a fair price and not to prevent abuse of power and no provision for a check by way of appeal or otherwise; it is only when fair prices are fixed that there is no reason why the Government should go on also to fix the wholesale or retail prices. The impugned notification merely fixes ex factory price and is bad as it does not follow from this that the Government was competent to fix prices at what they were either in the week before June 27, 1958 or in the last week of May, or in any other manner. The fact that the prices fixed for factories only in Punjab are controlled by the Central Govt. cannot be said to be unreasonable and therefore the impugned notifications are invalid.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of tea and its employees. The workmen were employed in the appellant 's factory at Calcutta, and their services were terminated by the appellant on the ground that they had not been paid any wages for all the relevant years. The Company contended that the workmen were entitled to be paid only 75 per cent of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise in the cost of living index. The company also contended that there was no dispute between the appellant and its workmen as to what should be the minimum wages for the working class menials and their employees, and that the Tribunal had not considered the evidence adduced by the Company before it and dismissed the reference. The appellant contended that in view of the fact that the company had made a profit making provision for the payment of dearness allowance, the Tribunal was justified in holding that full neutralisation of the deficiency as a result of rise in cost of production could not be allowed and therefore the reference was bad in law. Held: (i) The Tribunal rightly relied on the evidence of the Company which was really one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working classes of workmen and the question of bonus to which it would have been entitled had been raised, was a substantial difference between the basic wage and dearness allowance. (ii)The Tribunal wrongly relied upon the evidence given by the State Government on the assumption that full dearness allowance could not he allowed and that there were no material to show that the appellant had made any profit making provisions for the living index in the year 1957. The Tribunal was right in holding the workmen entitled to the benefit of the award. (iii)The question whether the Tribunal should have taken into account the working Class cost of the living Index was a matter of fact and not one of fact. The award was bad because it had no material before it to show how it could be said that there had been substantial change of the working standard of living in the years 1957 and 1957. (iv)The appellant 'rejected its claim for bonus on the grounds that the award was invalid as it did not contain any material to support the finding of fact given by it from different angle. The High Court was right, in holding: (1) that the reference made by the Tribunal under section 10(2) of the Act was binding between the parties and therefore, the reference could not have been validly made; (ii). The award did not show that there Was any substantial change on the working category of workmen. (3)The award was not invalid because it was based on a material which showed that the Company had made profit making available to the workmen for the purpose of living and that it was not possible to say that the amount of bonus could be allowed only 75% of the increased dearness allowance; (4) The award made by it was binding on the parties as well as the Tribunal.

The appellant was the Matadbandha of Sri Gavi Mutt. He was appointed under the Madras Act 11 of 1927 as a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The said management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under section 63 of the Act for the proper administration of the Mutt, was not challenged by him in any court. The appellant contended that the scheme having been framed as early as 1939, it must be deemed to have been settled or modified under the provisions of the earlier Act. Held, that the schemes were validly framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early and the question whether the scheme was consistent with the appropriate and relevant provisions of this latter Act did not arise because the scheme had been framed in 1952 and the executive officer could not take over the actual administration of Mutt and its properties. The scheme was a piece of legislation which was valid under the earlier law. The object of the impugned scheme was to provide for the better administration of that Mutt and the endowments of the community, and it was open to the challenge that it is invalid on the ground that it contravened the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) and (g). The scheme had not been fully implemented till 1952. The Act did no more than provide for a scheme which was framed under the Act. The provisions of section 103(d) were not retrospective in operation, but were intended to be retrospective in effect.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in the Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Committee was made available. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointment and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. The appellant continued to be serving as Hindi teacher in the appellant 's school on ad hoc basis. The management terminated his services on the ground that he had been appointed regularly by the Managing Committee without any break or break or with a break or breaks in one or more aided schools or Colleges and who were continuing as such teachers or lecturers for a further period of at least one year without any interruption or break. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State of Orissa will do well to consider the cases of all those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December 31, 1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services. [995B] 1.2 The High court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the basis that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. The State Government has not been able to show that the initial appointment was made otherwise than in accordance with procedure laid down in the Education Act and the Rules and Regulations framed thereunder. [996C] 1:3. The order of the High Court is set aside and the respondents are directed to treat the appellant as regularly appointed Hindi teacher with effect from July 12, 1982. [997E F] 1.(4) The State has been enacted by the Orissa Legislature with the obvious object of granting relief to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping them in short spell appointments like 89 day appointments as here with one day gap and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other service benefits. [991D] 1(5) The High Courts erred in deny the benefit to the appellants on the grounds that his appointment was conditioned under the stipulation of the agreement that he will continue until replacement by a person from the selected list. [999E F; 997A] 2. The Court read into the Act what was not there. In response to the notice issued in the Special Leave Petition the managing committee through its Secretary cum Head Master has stated that the appel lant is still continuing to serve as Hindi teachers and he will have been entitled to the benefits of summer vacations and other breaks which must be taken as non est, from the date of his regular appointment i.e. July 12 1982. The respondent is directed to pay the arrears of salary and allowances and other emoluments due to him as a result of his regularisation within a period not exceeding three months from today.

The appellant was elected to the Panchayat Samiti and the appellant was declared elected. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the election on the ground that he had been disqualified from being a candidate for the purpose of holding an office of profit under the Punjab Panchayat Samiti, 1961. The High Court held that the allowance paid by him was in excess of his salary and that the appellant could not be said to have been disqualified for being a member of the Panchayat Samithis. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the payment of travelling allowance under r. 3 to 7 of the Rules did not convert the office of Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti into an office or profit and therefore, the amount of travelling allowances could not have been claimed by him as a member for the purposes of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. HELD: (i) The High court was right in arriving at the conclusion that this allowance of Rs. 100/ was clearly meant only to cover additional expenditure and out of pocket expenses of the Chairman and Members of Panchayat Samits, non official members of a panchayat Samiti, and, therefore, it must be held that he was not entitled to any mileage allowance. [419 D] (ii) The appellant had failed to establish that the allowances paid under r 3 to7 were in addition to the payment to him of daily allowance. The payment of Rs 10/ as a consolidated amount in lieu of the travelling allowance, daily allowance or any other allowances to which he might have been entitled in order of remuneration is in excess thereof.

The appellant was the tenant of a permanent plot in which he had been running a Dal and Oil Mill. The appellant was inducted into the shop by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords. The landlord filed an application for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the tin shed shown by letters ABH, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, and B were constructed by him with the permission of the landlord. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate court held that the respondent was not entitled to recover possession of the premises without obtaining permission of District Magistrate but if the tenant had not obtained permission of his land lord he could not get the permission from the District Magistrate. In second appeal, the High Court reversed the findings of the trial court and decreed the appellant 's suit for eviction. The High Court also held that since two sides of the tin sheds were resting on the pucca wall it was open to the landlord to file a suit for ejectment of a tenant without obtaining leave of the District Judge but if he had not the landlords permission made or permitted to make construction which in the opinion of the court has materially altered the accommodation or is likely to diminish its value, the landlord is free to file suit for possession. The respondent filed an appeal against the High 's judgment and decree. The appellate Court held that a mere fact that a construc tion was permanent or temporary in nature did not affect the question as to whether the constructions were sub stantial in nature and they did not constitute material alterations as the same were temporary in character which could be removed at any time without causing any damage to the accommodation. The first appellate Court also observed that the finding of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether the tin roof was permanent in nature, did not give rise to a substantial change in the front and structure of the accommodation, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out to the tenant. In the second appeal the High court held the appellant tenant 's case that the disputed construction was permanent and temporary in terms of the agreement between the parties and that the mere fact of creation of a partition wall did not make any sub stances as the constructions had been constructed on the open land adjoining the accommodation and it was enclosed by Bamboo structure, and therefore the tin shop was not a material alteration. The second appeal filed by the respondent tenant was allowed by the High. In this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts erred in interfering with the findings recorded by both courts below on the questions of fact. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether a construction is permanent or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [975E] 1.2 In deciding this question the Court has to consider whether the construction has been made with the written consent of a landlord and if so, whether those constructions are permanent or permanent, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alteration '. The nature of the constructions, whether they are permanent, or temporary, is not a relevant factor in determining whether the building materially alter the accommodation is permanent. [936E] 2.1 In deciding the question, the Court must consider whether there was substantial change of the user or not. If the construction is found to be permanent or irregular it would have to be considered as material alteration as the construction may be necessary for the purpose of determining the questions in controversy. The question of material alteration is a mixed question of fact and law.

The appellant company had filed a suit against the appellant company for setting aside an ex parte decree. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that summons was not properly served on it, and that the summons had been duly served by post to the company. The High Court allowed the revision petition of the appellant against the order of dismissal of the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the service of summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it could not be said that there was no service of any summons on the appellant Company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of rule 2 would mean managing agent and it can under this rule be on a juristic person. [1032C] 2. The meaning of clause(b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in order 5, which is meant for issue and service of summon on the principal. It is not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Case that the appellant under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. was not an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on the Company in the sense as to what is meant by service of notice on the Secretary, Director or Principal Officer in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. and another vs The Union of India and others, ; , referred to. 3. The word "Principal officer" in cl. (b), has got a wide connotation and includes managing agents, it can be understood as having been employed by the company in the context of the provision of the code in order to give effect to the intention of the legislature. [1132D] 4. The expression "Principal Officers" in section 2(a) is not an inclusive provision providing that all modes or methods of service must be followed by the Company itself. In the instant case, the service was duly served and it was left at the registered office of the company to ascertain as to how the ex parte judgment was passed. [1103E] 5. The appellant under the orders of the Court had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. The respondent had no knowledge of the exter ments. The service of the summons as contemplated in the first para (b). [1133G] 6. The fact that the company had no know of the decree was not sufficient to make it a ground for setting it aside the ex exparte decree, even otherwise before 29 71975.

The respondents were tried for offences under sections 145, 146 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate passed a preliminary order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. The respondents filed an application before the Magistrate under section 145 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition holding that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace, it was not necessary to record a finding on this aspect of the matter also but in the circumstances, it could be safely presumed that the apprehension of the breach of the peace existed at the time the order was passed. The appellant filed a revision petition before the High Court which allowed the same and remitted the case to the Magistrate for fresh disposal. In the appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the final orders were bad as contemplated under section 146(5) Cr.P.C., and therefore the preliminary order was bad and the High court erred in holding that the preliminary orders were vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of law had been committed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The preliminary order passed by the High Courts is limited to the question whether there was a breach of a peace or not. If the Magistrate has given a finding thereon he has given the finding on that aspect of matter also, but in his opinion it can be safely inferred that apprehension of a breach was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court. [94C D] 2. The order of acquittal passed by a Magistrate is limited only to the extent to which he has jurisdiction to take proceedings under section145 Cr. It is not necessary that at the date of passing the final Order, the apprehension should be recorded in the preliminary Order itself. Once a preliminary Order drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a breach or breach of any peace existed, it cannot be said that there has been a breach on the basis of which the satisfaction of the magistrate is based. [95E F] 3. The power to issue a preliminary orders under section 144 Cr. was limited to those questions to who were in actual possession on the date when the preliminary decree was passed or the date on which the preliminary adjudication was made. But once he is satisfied on these two conditions the section requires him to pass a preliminary decree under sub section (1) and thereafter to make an enquiry under sub s.(4). [95F G] 4. The object of the Code is to prevent abuse of the process of law by any person or persons who have the full benefit of the law.

The appellant was a non resident of the State of Madras. He sold its goods to the appellant and delivered them to the latter in Bombay. The appellant sold the goods to him on the basis that they were liable to pay sales tax under section 42(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions between the parties showed that the intermediaries firms and companies were benamidars for the appellant. He also held that it was not liable as it had not been treated as profits by the assessee and that the decision of the Tribunal was final. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of the Commissioner was correct and must be set aside. The finding on the question whether the transactions were genuine or not is open to challenge in a reference under section 66(1). [710 D] (ii)The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal is final and conclusive. It is only when it is an inference from facts that the finding is one of pure fact or mixed question of law and fact. The findings of the Income tax authorities are not open to attack on any of the grounds on which such a finding could be assailed in a Reference under section 67(1), but they cannot be questioned as evidence or if it is unreasonable and perverse, or even on the ground that it is not supported by any evidence or evidence. [711 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., ; , followed. (iii)The question whether a finding of facts is open for review under section 35(1)(c) must be decided in the light of the principles laid down by this Court in Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay vs Ahmedabhai Umarbhai & Co., [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869 and Commissioner of Excess Profits Pax Ltd. vs Ahmed Umarbhai, ; , referred to. (iv)The High Court was right in holding that the findings of fact were not open for interference under section 11(1); it was only after a finding is recorded by it that the Tribunal had reached its decision as to the legal effect of those findings and that it had no jurisdiction to interfere with such findings. [611 D E] Commissioner, Bombay City vs Ahmedji Umarbhaiwala & Co. , followed, (v)The Commissioner of income tax, Bombay, vs Ahmedjibhai Umarbhai Umarabhai & Co, ; and Commissioner for Income tax, Gujarat vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai Manibhai and Co.

The assessee was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager, Shri J.P. Vaish, who had been allowed by the Income Tax Officer in computing his remuneration for the assessment years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim on the ground that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish, the General manager had no power to make any order from the account of which he could be allowed by him. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the amount of Rs 75,467 paid to him was not real or that it was not incurred by the appellant in the character of a trader or it was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is well settled that where a person who worked in the mill at the initial stage and does not make profit of even a lakh of rupees in the past and that the rate of 25% was fixed for him, he cannot be said to have been paid wholly or exclusively for his purpose of business. [526 B] (ii) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the respondent the entire amount of RS. 75465 paid to Shri Vaish was an sum laid out or expended wholly and solely for the purposes of the assessee 's business. It is not the function of the Tribunal to determine the remuneration which in their view should be paid to an employee of the appellant. [525 B C] (iii) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out, or expended partly or exclusively within the meaning of section 10(2)(Xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922 has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each particular case. [500 E F] (iv) The principles of this Court apply to the instant case and the question as regards whether an expenditure is wholly and undoubtedly laid out for the business or it is not laid out entirely and exclusively within its ambit.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. The appellant filed an application for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of dismissal on the ground that the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for a direction to the Tribunal not to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 's case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the dispute was not properly referred by the Tribunal and that the tribunal had rejected the prayer for representation by a person of his own choice instead of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and thereafter in making an award on the basis of the reference. Held, that the appellant was entitled to be heard independently of the union and the Secretary was bound to act according to law. The Tribunal committed no error in refusing to record a compromise in regard to the dispute between the parties. It is not unreasonable to think that section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act recognises this position by providing that the workman who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled to an order giving him proper relief on the question of representation as well as regarding the award that had been made. The provisions of section 36 are wide enough to cover disputes between an employer and a single employee, but it has not been expressly stated in the Act that the workmen who is not a party thereto can claim an order given by a particular workman under the Industrial Dispute Act unless it is taken up by a Union of the workmen or by a considerable number of workmen. The only exception to this is that the individual workman is at no stage a party, not independently of any union which has espoused his cause.

The appellants were the tenants of a joint Hindu family. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the appeal filed by the surviving appellants against the decree was dismissed in limine. The appellants then filed an appeal to the High Court which was allowed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is not proved that Kedar Nath died leaving behind his widow and the other appellants constituted a joint family. [553 B] (ii) The suit for ejectment against the surviving plaintiffs could be decreed only after the death of Kedar Nath. The decree was passed in favour of all the defendants. The appeal filed in the High court was not filed by any one or more of them as an appeal against the whole decree in view of the provisions of O. XLI, r. 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [554 C] (iii) The appellants could continue the appeal even after the deceased appellants died and the abatement of the appeal so far as they were concerned was concerned under O.XXII, r, 33. [555 E] (iv) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving respondents when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated. [556 G H] (v) The provisions of 0. XLI r.33 of the Civil Procedure Code apply to the stage when an appeal is filed and empowered one of the plaintiffs or defendants as they desire the reversal or modification of the decree in favour thereof as well. [558 E] In the instant case, the suit was not instituted by any of the appellants or even some of them, as an appellant or defendants, as he wanted the reversal of the judgment of the High Courts. The High court could not, therefore, have heard appeal against that order.

The appellant landlord sought to break through the medium of a suit for ejectment against him on the ground that he had failed to comply with the terms of the lease. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in appeal confirmed the decree. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the lease having expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, the lease had lapsed and the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms thereof by the deed of demise could not be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g) because the document was not a rule of justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The statutory law as it now stands, however, applied to the present case. [920 B] 2.1 The statutory provision in section 111 of the Registration Act is applicable only where there is no specific provision in the Transfer Act or by forfeiture following the breach by the tenant of the express condition regarding sub letting in terms of a special statute. It does not require that the provisions of the Act apply to the lease of 1952. [936 B] 1.2 The statutory requirement of a written notice under section 106 and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience are the same as those contained in section III(g). [921 C D] 2:3 The statutory right of the tenant to terminate the tenancy is not based on any well established principle of law. It is a cardinal rule of construction that where a statute creates a legal fiction by necessary implication, it must be construed strictly and in consonance with the principles laid down in section 11(g), it is not possible to read into the statutory provision a mere technical rules of equity and bad faith. [951 D] 1:4. The requirement of written notice in writing to the lessee of an intention to determine the lease, by giving notice in that behalf, is not merely directory but also mandatory. It must be complied with in accordance with the provisions contained in the statute. [952 C] 2 :4. In the instant case, no notice whatsoever was sent to the tenant for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds of default. The appellant had accepted the application, not of the kind referred to in section II(g); but of the rules of justice equity and well conscience; it is a fitting finale to this part of the rule of equity, justice and good faith. It cannot be said that the statutory law has been violated by reason of non compliance with the requirements of a statutory provision. [942 D] 3:1. The High Court was right in holding that the notice under the lease was not based upon any principle of justice and bad no application to the facts of this case. The provisions of section 111, (g), (g and (h) (ii) of section III of the Indian Registration Act are applicable only when there is a specific provision of law which provides for termination of tenancy in the present ease. [943 D] In the present cases, no written notice was sent by the appellant to the appellant on the basis of the terms and conditions of the deed. The notice was not issued to the respondent tenant of an application for eviction under section 112(g)(a) of Transfer of property Act. The respondent tenant had failed in his attempt to break the tenancy in terms thereof.

The appellant was a member of the Assam Legislative Assembly. He was removed from service by an order dated June 10, 1965. The Governor passed an order under section 3(2) of the Act directing that he should be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank until he had been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed by a Single Judge. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the impugned order was not passed as it was passed without giving an opportunity of being heard; and (ii) the order was passed in violation of article 311(2). HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the impugned orders were bad. [488 B] (a) The power to dismiss or remove a person from service is conferred on the Government by section 3 (2) and the power to suspend a member is not an absolute power but only a limited power to impose a penalty. It is not expedient to give the Government servant an opportunity to show cause against action proposed in regard thereto. [486 C] (b) The order of dismissal or removal was passed on June 10 63, 1965 and the appellant was removed or retained in rank without any reasonable opportunity. [487 E F] (c) The impugned order is bad because it was made after the amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act 1963. It was not expedient for giving the Government a notice of show cause to the appellant as required by section 5(2), that the Governor had to arrive at his conclusion on the merits of the case and that he was not entitled to any opportunity of making representation against the proposed action proposed. [485 G H] (d) The word "may" in article 311 means "shall be deemed always to have been used for the purpose of giving an adequate opportunity of explaining cause against such action proposed". The words "may", in the context, mean "shall" and not "may". The expression "may ' is not defined in the Act. [484 G H; 484 A] (e) The words 'may ' and 'shall ' are used in the widest sense. The word 'may" has been used in a wide sense. It may be used to convey an idea of the meaning of the word 'shall".

The petitioners and the Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, were members of a society known as Shia Wakfs. They challenged the validity of the Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board of Waqfs (Amendment) Act, 1954 on the ground that they had been registered as Shiasis in accordance with the provisions of the Act and were not registered as a Shia Wakf. The petitioners contended that the impugned Notification dated 27th February 1944 issued by the Shiasies under section 4(1)(c) of 1936 Act was ultra vires the State Legislature, that the notification dated 26st February,1944 issued under Section 5(2) of Act was invalid and that the Notification was not valid as it was based on considerations of high public policy to achieve two objectives, namely, (a) that there must be a finality to litigation and (b) that the petitioners and their family to perform their religious ceremonies and functions in accordance therewith. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondents had failed to prove that they were not entitled to customary rights to the customary rights of the Shiadars to perform the religious ceremonies, and (c) that no notice was issued by any authority under section 144 Cr. P.C., and that no opportunity was given to them to show cause why they should not be dismissed from service. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity and legality of the notification. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petitions holding that it was a clear case of an existing or established entitlement to customary right to perform its religious ceremonies; that the order dated 26.2.1944 issued by Shia Waqfs for performing their religious rites and functions was invalid as being violative of Articles 14, 19(1), 21 and 22 of the Constitution; that no such opportunity was afforded to the Shibars to showcause against the action taken by them; that they could not be allowed to raise the plea of estoppel or the bar based on the principle analogous to res judicata. The Division Bench dismissed the Writ Petition holding that there was no adjudication or decision on the rights of parties and hence the writ application filed by the respondents was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Notification issued under s.5(1 ) of 1936 was invalid because it was founded on considerations extraneous to the object of the impugned notification; (ii) the notification did not contain any provision for the determination of the question of customary rights and the decision of this Court in Mohammado vs State of U.P., ; , that the appellants and their families were governed by the provisions contained in the Notification and therefore they could be relegated to a civil suit on the assumption that the Notifications issued by them were valid; (iii) the impugned notifications were invalid as it purported to have been passed without jurisdiction and, therefore, the notification was bad. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Notification dated 25th February,, 1944 issued in exercise of its powers under section 6(1). [226B] 2. The notification dated 27.2 1944 issued thereunder is valid and not invalid. It is only when it is found that the notifications issued by this Court are invalid or illegal, that is, that there is no adjudication of any right or interest on merits as a result of the final order passed by this court in the appeal. [226C] 3. The impugned Notification was therefore valid and must be struck down. [227D] 4. The appellants and through them the petitioners are not entitled for customary rights under the aforesaid notification. They are entitled to the benefit of the customary right of the parties on merits. [228E] 5. The object of this Notification is to ensure that the persons who are in possession of the property should be given their right to enjoy the customary privileges and privileges which they enjoyed by them.

The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business in manufacturing and selling textile goods, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1965 66. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act against the said amount. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal of the assessee holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim for set off could not be allowed to be allowed as a deduction under section 24(1)(a). The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that there had been no genuine losses. In the reference under Section 256(1) of Income Tax Act, 1961, the High Court held that the assessee was entitled to set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and any subsequent assessment year which is car ried forward in accordance with the provisions of sub section (2B) of Section 24, the income tax Officer had not computed the loss or passed an adverse order. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that there were genuine loss and it was merely notional in character and that no loss could be set off against income under any head in accordance to sub section(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the claims of setoff were admissible in the computation of income as capital gains. [1166D] 2. Section 80 of the 1961 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 statute and notwithstanding anything contained in sub section 2B) or sub clause (ii) of clause (a) of that sub section, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following year and set off in accordance therewith. [1266D E] 3. The provisions of Section 74(1), 80(2)(a) and (b) of 1961 Act, continued to remain in force till the assessment for which the loss was first computed under the Act or as the case may be. [1366E F] 4. The provision of section 74(i)(b) and section 80(3A) are not attracted in this case. [1466F] 5. Section 74 (1)(b), read with Section 80(1 ) of the latter Act, is applicable to a situation where the loss sustained is a loss falling under the head 'capital gains '.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) and Production, ( Air) and Engineering (Mechanical). He was promoted to the post of Assistant Director of Technical Education and Production. The Respondent was appointed as a Junior Scientific Officer in the Ministry of Defence on October 13, 1966. He joined the Department of Technical development and Production after he had completed three years of service. He continued in service till his retirement from service. On his re instatement he was promoted as Assistant Director on October 11, 1966 and was posted at the Directorate. The respondent challenged the order of promotion before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years. The Tribunal held that the respondent was entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Union of India that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units and merely because the superannuation of the members of the service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these Rules, shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect thereof. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid. [102C] 2.1 The question involved in the present case is whether the respondent who belonged to another unit viz. DAQAS and was entitled tO the benefit of the enhanced superannuation age to the members thereof. [113D] 2:2. In view of the decision of this Court in Union of india & Ors. vs Union of lndia & Anr., ; , the denial of the benefit by the enhanced superannu tion age to members of one 24 unit while the same is granted to the member of other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [1103D E] 2 :3. The question whether the Government has such power depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not necessary that the Govern ment had such power.

The appellant was elected to the Maharashtra State Legislative Assembly from a constituency in the State of Maharashtra. The appellant challenged the election on various grounds, inter alia, that the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in allowing him to be called as court witnesses and this vitiated the whole trial and therefore the High Court was not right in refusing to quash the order of the trial Judge based on the evidence of these two witnesses. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that having rejected the application of the election petitioner on the ground that there was no fair trial of the petition to the prejudice of the appellant, the High court should have set right by quashing the order. HELD : (i) It is well settled that a party who has been guilty of an offence under section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1965 must be given an opportunity to explain his conduct and make a proper representation in support of his case. The first question whether there was any evidence on which the Judge could have come to the conclusion is one of fact and if not impossible for the Judge to have come into the conclusion he did and found him guilty of corrupt practice. [975 D E] (ii) It cannot be said that there is no evidence on record to show that the witnesses were examined as court witness and this was a serious irregularity which the High Courts should have gone into the matter and found out why there were two publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21(1). [976 D] (iii) The trial Judge had not come to his own conclusion as to the period during which he could have came to the finding that the appellant had been personally responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as such found him liable to be dismissed.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, its registered office being at Kanpur in the State of Uttar Pradesh, was assessed to sales tax on the sale proceeds of jute. The Sales Tax Officer (1) assessed the petitioner to sales Tax in accordance with the notification dated March 31, 1956, but the Sales Tax officer (2) assessed him to salestax in accordance therewith. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that there was no power under the State Legislature to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31 1956 as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956 and that it was not a law which the State legislature was competent to enact and it was therefore a nullity. Held, that the Validation Act is ultra vires the powers of the legislature under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The Validation Act was valid as it stood on March 1, 1957, and the impugned Notification dated March 30, 1956 was not saved by the new Act. The validation Act was therefore void. The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , followed. Held further, that in view of the decision of this Court in Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officers (1), the Validation Ordinance was valid and the Validation Acts were valid. The impugned notification dated April 1. 1956, which imposed a tax on jute goods as defined by section 3A of the Act, was not ultra vires. Firm Bangur Mal vs State of Bihar, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 4 years R.I. for having committed rape on his cousin 's wife, while the first information report was lodged and a charge sheet was submitted against him. The Sessions Judge acquitted him but convicted him under section 5 years R, I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, the High Court affirmed the conviction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The sentence of imprisonment a few directives to ensure that the carceral period reforms the convict is not excessive. [855E] 2.2.The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, inhuman and brutal treatment which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and tenderable. The victim of rape is a serious offence. It may be marginally extenuatory to mention that modern Indian conditions are drifts. [955G H] 2:3. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation, apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of the pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [936B C] 2 :4. In Sunil Batra 's case, this Court has held that the sentence of death is not unreasonable. The current efforts of Governments, Central and State, to reform jail regimen, and rehabilitatively small and the State has, as yet, no convincing national policy on female flesh and sex sanity. [981B] 2(5) In Sunilier 's cases, this court has held, in Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration, that the accused may procure such condonation from unwilling victim, sex explosion in celluloid and book stalls and corrupt morals reaching a new 'high ' in high places. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term.

The respondent assessee, a limited company dealing in land, filed an application before the Arbitrator claiming compensation for the said land. The Arbitrator awarded a sum of Rs.724,97,249 as compensation payable to the appellant. The arbitrator awarded a total amount of Rs,724.97,250 as compensation. The High Court allowed the appeal and held that the amount of compensation received by the assessee was not a receipt of revenue nature. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had wrongly decided the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that the compensation received under the Land Acquisition Act in Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladin & Sons. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, ; , not applicable to the case. [395G] 1.2 In the instant case, though the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount, it is only that amount which had accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact paid or not. As has been stated earlier, a mere claim by the appellant after taking of possession of the land, at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation. [397C D] 1:3 The High Courts were right in the view taken by it and the High Courts. [398D] 1 :4 In the present case, although the award made by an Arbitrator on June 29, 1956 enhancing the said amount of compensa tion was not compensation but a question of merely quantifying the amount to be received, and cases where the right to receive payment is admitted and the quantification only of the amount payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles.

The appellants filed a suit against the appellants for eviction of the appellants on the ground that they had withdrawn all their defence to the application filed by them under section 12(1) (f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1947. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the compromise was not binding on the parties and decreed the suit. In appeal the High Court reversed the decree and held that the appellants were entitled to possession on one or more of the statutory grounds mentioned in section 12. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise" the court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith. The protection under section 13(1)(f) is inherent. [512C D] (2) The provisions of Order 22, Rule3, Code of Civil Procedure are mandatory and must be complied with by the Court. If on the other hand, the court is satisfied on consideration of the terms of the compromise that a ground for passing such a decree is not made out, it will be presumed that the Court was so satisfied that the court was so satisfaction and the decree for eviction would be passed only if it is satisfied that a case for passing a decree has been established. [511D E] (3) The object of section 12 is to protect a tenant against eviction by a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act. The purpose of the Act is to provide that no suit shall be filed in any Civil Court against a tenant for his eviction from any accommodation except on one of the grounds mentioned therein only, namely, (1 ) that he has been permitted to occupy the premises for more than three years; and (2). If the agreement or the compromise for the eviction of a tenant is found, on the facts of a particular case, to be in violation of a specific provision contained in section 13, it would be presumed, that the landlord was entitled to have such a suit under the law. [550G H] Nagindas Ramdas vs Dalpatram and Ors., ; , followed. (4) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for ejectment because the landlord, in the circumstances of this case, was entitled under section 11(1), to have the decree passed by the Civil Court in accordance with the requirements of the statute. [552G H; 552A] (5) The language of section 13 clearly shows that it is clear and definite especially in the context of the pleadings of the parties that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit, so in an eviction suit the court has no jurisdiction to pass a judgment or order for eviction. [553B C] Naginda Prasad vs Dalichand, ; , referred to. (6) The provision of section 11 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is mandatory and not directory.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling agents. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that in view of the capital loss the loss could not be taken into account for determining the taxable income, if it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company. HELD: The High Court was right in holding on facts and circumstances that the assessee had suffered a capital gain of Rs. 12,00,000/ . [861 C] The question whether the value of the shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors were justified in not declaring dividends in respect of those years in view Of the capital losses incurred by them. [862 D] In the instant case, there can be hardly any doubt that the appellant had suffered capital loss of Rs 12,000 and it was not possible to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect thereof. The question is not whether the shares are justified in refusing to declare dividends in view or not. [873 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs M/s. Texecon India Ltd., ; , referred to. In the present case, the Tribunal was considering a reference made by the High Court under section 66(1) and levied additional super tax at Rs. 4,00.000 on the surplus of Rs, 12,30,000. The High court was not justified in holding otherwise.

The appellant, a displaced person, filed an application under section 12(4) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, for setting aside the award on the ground that it was not maintainable as the provisions of section 15 of the Act were not applicable to arbitration proceedings under the Act. The Civil Judge held that the Civil Judge was not justified in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding and dismissed the application. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) Section 37 of the is a self contained provision which provides for appeals against an award made under section 16 of the . It does not provide for appeals to the Civil Court from orders passed under the Consolidation of holdings Act. [935 B] (ii) The effect of section 46 and section 47 of the , is that all the provisions in the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the consolidation of Holdings. In the present case, the Civil judge had not applied his award on May 14, 1956, but on the merits he held that it could not be said that the provisions Of section 15 were applicable because the appellants had apparently applied under section 15. [936 B] The High Court was right in holding that the decision of the Civil court modifying the Award was appealable under section 39 of the ; and the award announced by Shri Bhagwan Singh, was accepted. [951 F G] (iii) Section 12(6) does not apply to arbitration under section 37 of Act.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. The petitioner was promoted to the said post on that date. He challenged the promotion order by a writ petition in the High Court, which was dismissed by the High court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended for the petitioner that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post as Superintending Engineer since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [252E] 2.1 The rules provide that graduates should be eligible to such promotion in the exclusion of Diploma holders do not violate articles 14 and16 of the Constitu tion. It is now well settled that for the purposes of promotion, a valid classification can made among members holding the same post on the ground of educational qualification. [253G] 2:2 The rule provides that graduates will be eligible only if they are Degree holders or Diploma holders. The rules providing that graduate Engineers shall be considered for promotion to any particular post on a basis other than that in the case before them the classified for purpose of promo tion on a particular post. It may be observed that it is not a case where the classification was already made which was challenged before the Court. [254G H] 2 :3 The rule provided that graduates who are Degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holders should be considered to be eligible under the rules. The Rule providing that degree holders shall be qualified for such promo tion to the exclusion, of diploma holder does not contravene Articles 14 or 16 of Constitution. The Rules provide that graduate engineers shall be entitled to such promotions as may be prescribed on a rational basis other wise than that they were drawn from different sources. [255A B] 2(4) The rule is in consonance with the practice followed till 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. It was not a matter where the rules and regulations are silent. The principle of classification is based on the nature of work and bear the same responsibility whatever their qualification, whether they are degree holders or diploma holder. [256B] 2.(5) The Rules providing that Graduate Engineers shall he eligible for promotion in exclusion of Degree holders does no more than by carving out two classes in the same category of Junior Engineers o the basis only of their qualification which is not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the said category on the strength of merit and on seniority is well known and permissible. [257C] 2 (6) The rules provided that graduate Engineer shall be deemed to have been eligible for promo tion from any particular cadre to any other post on such basis as may he prescribed by the Government from time to time. The Junior Engineers do the similar kind of work, but they are not a class in the category of junior engineers.

The petitioner, a member of the Indian Administrative Service, was appointed as an Additional District Judge in the State of West Bengal. He was appointed to officiate as Additional District Judges on deputation basis. The petitioner challenged his appointment by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In the meantime, the Chief Justice of India had been extended from time to time and the petitioner was placed under suspension pending disposal of the writ petition. The High Court held that the Chief justice of India should be given an opportunity to represent his case before the Chief Minister for being heard. The Chief Justice was directed to hold a meeting of the Chief Justices of the High Courts in the matter of appointment of Additional District judges and other Judges. The matter was referred to the Chief Secretary, who was also appointed as Additional Sessions Judge on deputation. On receipt of the said report, the petitioner filed a writ Petition before the Supreme Court challenging the validity of his appointment. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that the constitutional obligation of the Union of India to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the failure to consider the question of suitability of the petitioner for appointment was not justiciable. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Chief justice is the only authority which can be said to have been constituted by the Central Government. [439C] 1.2 The Chief Justices are the only persons who are members of the Bar and not those who are not members of a Bar. They are also members of Bar and are not Members of the bar. [441D] 1:3. The constitutional obligation to provide for the sanction of the President is not justiciable but it is implicit in the Constitution that the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govern ment. [442E] 1 :4. The executive power of the State is vested in the Supreme court under Article 124(1) of the Constitution. It is a well settled principle of law that the executive power must be exercised reasonably and fairly, justly and reasonably. [443F] 1.(a) The executive function of the Government is not to be judged by a larger bench of this Court. The judiciary is not expected to act judicially in a manner which is fair and just. It has been held by this Court that the decision of the majority in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Courts is not open to challenge on any ground whatsoever.

The respondent was appointed as an Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Engineer, on a report made by him. The Enquiry Officer submitted his report to the Chief Execu tive Officer, who recommended his retirement from service. The respondent challenged the order of punishment before the High Court which quashed the impugned order of dismissal and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that such an enquiry was incompetent and without jurisdiction and that the order imposing punishment was bad in law. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court ought not have permitted the respondent to question the competence or jurisdiction of the Chief Engineer to impose any penalty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Courts is set aside and the order passed by the Single Judge is restored. [199B] 2.1 The High Courts were right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment but it should not have ordered payment of all consequential benefit to which the respondent would be entitled on superannuation. [200C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent succeeded in getting the order dated January 9, 1988 passed by him and if the order imposed was quashed he would ordinarily have to be paid his wages etc., upto the date of his retirement. The fact that the impugned Order was without jurisdiction or competence, there is nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm it.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation, was formed under the Delhi Development Act, 1957. The appellant applied for sanction to the plan and the sanction was granted by the Government on May 10, 1967. The sanction was refused by the Commissioner of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of rejection of his application. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the permission granted was legal and was justified by the provisions of section 336 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction given by the respondent was legal, and (ii) the proposed user mentioned by him in the plan was not in contravention of the Master Plan; (iii) the permission was legal because the land had been acquired for a public purpose and therefore the proposed use was not permissible under section 14 of the Development Act. HELD: The High court was right in holding that it was not the scheme of the development Act that the appellant should have established, as it seeks to, that the proposed building or the execution of a work, unless such a building or work would contravene any of the provisions, of sub section (2) of section 337. [167 D] The High Courts were right in rejecting the contention of the respondents that the sanction granted was valid and not legal. [168 E F] In the absence of any indication in the Master plan, in this case that any part of the land of the Respondents will be covered by a road, or portion of a road it is not possible to accept the contention that there would be any violation of section 14. [169 G H] The appellant 's application for sanction was legal as it had been made available by the Delhi Municipal Corporation under section 3 of the Delhi Act. The respondents ' lands were not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part thereof.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2, the Minister in charge of the Department of Industries, and the Chief Minister of the Industries and State Government. The appellant No 1 was a Minister of industries and the Minister was present at the time when the raid was organised and was carried on by the appellant Nos. 1 and 2. On the day following the raid the appellant was found carrying currency notes from his house and a sum of Rs. 50,000 was recovered from him. The currency notes were seized from him and he was prosecuted under section 161 Indian Penal Code for having committed the offence of taking away currency notes. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 165 I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the evidence of these witnesses was not admissible in evidence as it had been corroborated by the statements made by the accused No. 2 to the effect that he had brought those moneys from his home to the police station and that the appellant had not produced them before the Magistrate. Held, that the statement made by a witness to the search of the house was inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. It is true that the statements of the witnesses were not admissible under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but they were only statements made to the Police authorities and given to Nagindas and Pannalal on the other hand and the police witnesses as well as the police officers as well. The statement made to them by the police authorities and the statements recorded at that time was enough to establish the falsity of the allegation made by them.

The respondent was serving as a constable in the State Police as a Constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971. The charge against him was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh, who was also charged with offences under section 325 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and several other sections. He was acquitted by the trial court. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of dismissal on the ground that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. The State filed an appeal against the said decision which was dismissed by the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the first appellate court and the suit is accordingly dismissed. [826E] 1.2 In the instant case, the trial Court has rightly held that the impugned judgment was void on the grounds of arbitrariness and, there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. It is also observed that this decision would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment if the other police officials convicted with him were not satisfied with the allegations of misconduct or otherwise. [825E F] 1:3 The question raised in the appeal should not be lightly brushed out by the Court on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and not denied by the respondent that the said adverse finding was vitiated by arbitrariness and there fore the bar under section 34 would not be ignored on the plea that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [827F G] 1 :4 The question whether the suit was barred by limitation is a matter to be decided by the appellate court. It has been stated on oath before this Court and not controverted by the appellant that the aforesaid decision had been taken in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [828F G; 828A] 2:1 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the question involved is a question of law of limitation. The question involves a question as to whether the plaintiff was entitled to be heard by the court in certain conditions, and the direction regarding payment of salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned Single Judge allowed the second appeal in limine. [829F G H] 2.2 The question is not raised before this court in the instant appeal. It will be open to the appellants to file an application for admitting additional evidence in regard t he further orders passed against Kahan Singh subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour, and to argue before the High Courts, that the case was distinguishable.

The appellant assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden and selling tea. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were not speculative and therefore the loss should be treated as business loss. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transaction involved mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of goods. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the sales in question were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Act. [183F] In the instant case, the assessee had taken actual delivery and not actually delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was no actual delivery, the transaction would be a speculative transaction within the definition of Explanation 2 to Section 24( 1). [184G H] Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; , followed. The High Courts were right in treating the transactions entered into by the respondent as mere sales of delivery orders or sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 24 (1) and not under section 6 of the Indian Income Tax Act. The view taken by the High Court that the sale was a speculative transactions is correct. [184H; 184A] Raghunath Prashad vs Commissioner, of Income Tax, Calcutta , followed in D.S. Nakara & Ors.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, challenged the validity of the election on the ground that the nomination paper was not signed by him and that he had not been subscribed.
