The Election Tribunal held that the signature of the proposer was not genuine but it was admitted that the Returning Officer had not signed the nomination papers and as such the rejection of the nomination was illegal. On appeal, the High Court set aside the election. Held, that the word "sign" in section 33(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, must be read as a whole and not to " signing". The words " signing" are used in the same sense in the Act because a special meaning has been given to the word 'sign ' and not the word. The word " signing", is not defined but it is used in a narrower sense than the word of the word, it may sometimes be used in different senses, then it must be understood in its ordinary sense as a word, and not in a narrow sense. It is well settled that the words " sign" are not defined in the General Clauses Act, but they are intended to convey them in their ordinary sense. The words ' signing ' have been used in section 35(1), and not by any other provision of law. The use of the words 'sign" is not a word of substantial character but it must mean something more than the writing. In the present case, the Returning officer had omitted the attestation because of some slip on his part and as their marks were not attested, he could not be held guilty of any corrupt practice under section 33 (1) (a).

The appellants, a company registered under the Companies Act, were employed by the appellant company in the Company. The Company sent separate letters to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972. On September 21, 1972, the Company sent a letter to the Company stating that its letter dated September 7, 1972 had reached them only on September 20, 1972 and did not do so. The company sent a reply to the said letter dated October 22, 1972 requesting the Company to report the matter to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication of the dispute. On October 2, 1972 the appellants wrote to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of their services by the Company and failing which they were dismissed from service. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the action taken by the appellants on the ground that the action of the company in removing them from service was illegal and arbitrary, that the appellants had not abandoned the service of the Company; that the termination of services could only be in terms of the appellant 's standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, their names had been struck off from the rolls of the respondent company. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the dismissal of the appellants was illegal, arbitrary and unjustified and that the order of termination of the services could be sustained only if the complaints were made against them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the letter dated Sept. 7,1972 addressed by the company to the workmen did not refute the plea of abandonment of service of 25 workmen (including the appellants) and that they had not voluntarily abandoned their service; that even if the termination was illegal the termination could only mean that the employer had abandoned the services of the workmen in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the company 's action was manifestly illegal and invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High court is set aside and the appellants are directed to reinstate the appellants in the aforesaid circumstances. [629B] 2.1 The termination of service could only by way of punishment or punishment for misconduct. But it cannot be said that the company had voluntarily abandoned the employment of the appel lant. It was not open to the company, therefore, to contend that the appellant had voluntarily abandoning the service and that it had not terminated the services. [625E] 2:2 The termination order of removal could only have been passed by way or punishment or in accordance with law. [613F] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellants were no provision in the certified standing orders by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the service. There was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the parties indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knotor tively. [529G] 3:2. The fact that the workmen concerned have been employed elsewhere during this period, still does not make any difference in the circumstances of the instant cases.

The appellant mortgaged a house belonging to the trust to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000 and an action was taken against him under section 36(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1913 for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage by monthly instalments of Rs, 1,910. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under a decree. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge for recovery and mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the expression 'sale ' in section 36 (a) includes a sale of the property of a public trust; (ii) the words 'sale of immovable property in execution of a decree ' which expression includes execution of decrees for sale of mortgaged property, and (iii) the word 'sale in section 37(a), means a sale in execution. HELD : (i)(a) The expression 'Sale ' in s 36(b) includes execution by a person who is not a party to the suit. [446 B] (ii)(a). In the present case, the appellant having agreed to, abandon the execution proceeding and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustees, abandonment of the execution proceedings was in law equivalent to payment to the decree holder of the money. The High Court was not right in holding that a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of the High court after due consideration of the points before it is liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Bench. [465 C D] (b) The word 'Sale" in section 35(a)(1) includes sale of property in a suit for recovery by a decree for sale, and on that account a sale is set aside. [467 E F] (c) The words 'Sale of immovable properties ' in the section are not complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set aside the sale held in execution proceedings. [468 G H] (d) The High Courts were right in taking the view that the earlier decisions of the Division Bench of a High Court after due consid eration of the point before it was liable to have been regarded as relevant and binding on the appellant. [470 E F]. (e) The judgment of the Allahabad High Court is binding upon Raju J., if the Full bench of the same High Court had no Power to refer a case to a Full bench for decision, it would be impossible to hold that a Judgment delivered by the Full Court was binding upon the appellant because the Full Benches of the Court were not complied. [471 G H; 471 A] (f) The Division Bench was bound to follow that precedent. [473 E F; 475 C D].

The appellant joined the Post and Telegraph Department as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was promoted to the post of Telegraph Department in 1962. The Government of India issued instructions dated July 11, 1955 under which he was entitled to retire from service at any time after he had attained the age of 55 years. The appellant challenged the validity of Rule 2(2) of Pension Rules on the ground that it violated Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The High Court held that Rule 2 (2) was ultra vires Articles 14 and16 of the Constitu tion and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that Rule 2046 of the Pension Rules is ultra vires articles 14 and 15 of the constitution of India and as such cannot be statutory. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The instructions being supplementary to the Rule 2, are executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) of the Consti tution. [899C] 2. Rule 2 of Pension Rule is a statutory rule and has the effect of amending Rule 2. The rules do not confer arbitrary power on the Government to retire a Government servant at any stage after he has attained the prescribed age of superannuation. It is well settled that the executive instructions are statutory and have the effect, of amending Rules 2(1), 3(2), 4(3) and 5(4). [898E F] 3. Rule 20 46 of the Railway Pension Rules cannot be construed as laying down any guidelines or a rule framed under Article 309 of the Con stitution. The executive instructions do not have the same effect as they are statutory rules. They are statutory ones. They have the power to retire under para 6(2). [800F] 4. Rule 22 of the pension Rules is a Statutory provision and has no application to the instant case. [800G] 5. The memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2 which lays down that retirement under para 620 of the railway Pension Rules can only be exercised to weed out unsuitable employees after they have attained the minimum age of 60 years. [799F G] 6. The Memorandum is in no way inconsistent with it. Para 620 of Railway Pension Manual is executive instructions and has been issued by the Union Government in exer cise of its executive instructions. [ 800A B] 7. Rule 1046 of Pension rules is a mandatory provision. It does not confer any arbitrary power to relax the statutory provisions or to relax any statutory provision. The said rule cannot be struck down as ultra vires Article 14. [900G H; 900A] 8. The circular is in nature of administrative instructions and it has the force of law.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period ending 31st March, 1944 to 31st December, 1943 was the same as the previous year ending 31th March, 1942. In the assessment year 1943 to 31.3. 1943 the assessee claimed that the loss in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending 31.03.1944 and 31.12.1943 to 31th April, 1944 was not liable to be set off under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. The Assistant Commissioner rejected this claim on the ground that there was no profit attributable to the manufacturing activity between 28th October, 1940 to 31rd March, 1943 and 31st August, 1942 and as such there could be no deficiency of profits. In appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable assessment period ending on 31st day of March, 1941 was not attributable to manufacturing activity during the chargeable year ending on 1st April, 1943 which consisted of the periods 1st September, 1940 41 to 31 st March, 1946 and 31th November, 1942 to 31St March, 1945. The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner held that there were no profits and losses during the relevant accounting period, namely, 1st October, 1941 to 31nd March, 1949 and as a result of the said assessment year ending 30th March 1944, it could not be said that there had been any deficiency of profit during those periods. The High Court, however, held that since the chargeable account ing periods ending on31st March 1943 and 1st March 1942 were occupied with manufacturing activity alone and there was nothing in the Act which would justify the conclusion that because the chargeable accounts for the relevant assessment year ended on 31th December, 1941, and 31 st April, 1942, had to be taken into account while computing the excess profits for that period should be computed at the excess profit for the previous years ending 31 st day of 3, 1944 and 31rd August, 1943. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that the excess of profits during the assessment period was not assessable to excess profits tax under the third proviso to section 5 of the Income Tax Act. [606C] 1.2 In the instant case, the assessee had claimed that there could not have been any loss during those years. The assessee had also claimed that it could be said to have suffered any deficiency in the profits during those assessment years. [613E F] 1:3. The method of computation under section 7 of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1944, was not applicable to the case. The question whether the assessee could be held to have escaped assessment for the year ending March 31, 1943 must also be determined on that basis and after set off carried forward to be computed in computing the Excess Profits Tax. [625E F; G] 1 :4. In view of the fact that a loss has been made in any charge able accounting period during the previous chargeable accounting year ending December 31st, 1942 or before the 31st of March 1941, it cannot be said, that there is no deficiency in profit during that period.

The Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch) was constituted by the Kerala State Government under the Kerala University Act, 1961. The petitioners were appointed as Civil Engineering graduates in the Kerala Medical Colleges in Kerala on a competitive examination held by it. They challenged the validity of the Kerala Engineering Service (Special Branch). The High Court dismissed their writ petitions and directed the Government to prepare two separate list for the posts of Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering. The appellants filed appeals before this Court against the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court dismissing the Writ Petitions. The learned Single Judge allowed the appeals and directed that the State Government and the Public Service Commission should prepare two different rank lists, one for the Civil Engineering degree and the other for the Mechanical Branch. The writ petitions were dismissed by a common order dated 23rd April, 1980. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the applicants who had qualified in Civil Engineering examination and who had obtained the diploma in Engineering and the question of passing the test were not open to challenge. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Kerala Government or the Public Services Commission is directed either by the Single Judge or by the Division bench of the State High Court. [775G] 2. The State Government or a Division Bench cannot be said to have decided to prepare separate lists. It has also been stated that the petitioners will be entitled to exercise their option and then take his turn according to their rank in the common list prepared by the Public service Commission. [761A B] 3. The High Courts were right in dismissing the writ petitions. [771B C] 4. The Division Bench was right in holding that there were directions given by the learned Single judge or by Division Bench. [752C] 5. The expression "the common list" is not intended to be used as a whole but only meant a common list though no common list was directed to be prepared or was prepared by a single Judge or Division Bench or by a Division bench. [754G H] 6. The word "the Common List" in the Act does not mean that the common name is not directed to prepare or was preparing by the single judge or Division Benches of the Public services Commission. It may be mentioned that preparation of no common lists is directed to comply with the directions given in the judgment. [752B] 7. The Court has also held that the expression "in accordance with the judgment" in its order dated 28th April, 1981 and that these two rank lirts are not directed against the Judgment of the Single judge.

The respondent plaintiff respondent No. 1 filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm on the ground that he was a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers and defendants Nos. 1 and 2. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove any decision to the contrary, and that the valuation given by the plaintiff was grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The High Court dismissed the appeal preferred by the respondent No 1. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the correct value of the suit is beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The valuation of the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. [512C] 1.2 In a suit under section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, the High Court has held that when the valuation put by the appellant on the relief claimed in the suit was arbitrary and unacceptable, it would be open to the trial court to take into consideration the statement in the plaint that the defendant had been ousted from the partnership business. [511D] 1:3 The plaintiff 's objection to the valuation was rejected by the trial Court. In such a case it is not only open to him but its duty to reject such a valuation. [506F G] 2.1 It is true that in a suit of accounts the plaintiff has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under estimates the relief he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. [ 509F] 2:2 In the instant case, the valuation of suit was not governed by section 7 (iv)(b) of The Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1908, as also by the Allahabad Court. [ 510A B] 3.1 In a case for accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is neither possible to give an accurate valuation of that claim at the inception of the plaint. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of a suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [ 512B C] 2 :3 The case of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be correctly decided. [ 511C D] In the present case, there is no dispute that the respondent 's claim was not obliged by the defendant to state his exact amount as he had been allotted to him. He has not disclosed any decision in the instant suit that the appellant had been ousting from the firm. The valuation put forward by the appel lant before the High court was arbitrary, and unacceptable. [H] 2 4. In a trial for accounts, the plaintiff cannot be expected to state a correct valuation of his claim at a inception of a plaint. It is not open to it to the Court but its duties to reject the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. The case is not one of the nature of the relief which has been claimed in a civil suit for accounts. [500C D; 501A] 5. In the absence of any decision on the question of valuation put, the court cannot take into account the statement made by the parties before it.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of certain products in the State of Madhya Pradesh, was manufacturing and selling products. The State Government exempted the class of dealers specified in column (3) of the Schedule to the notification. In respect of the said goods, the State Government issued an order dated 1st April, 1981 exempting the class or dealers specified therein from payment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in Column (2), subject to the restrictions and conditions specified in the said notification. The respondent assessee filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order on the ground that the industries run by them were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Industries Depu tive industries were excluded from the exemption under the notification and that the State was entitled to claim exemption only in respect of those industries mentioned in column(2) of Schedule to it. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the notification did not set out the conditions on which exemption had been granted, it could not be said that the industry run by the appellants were "suitable industries" and that they were eligible for the exemption. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect to the industries mentioned by it is clear from the Notification itself and all that the Director of Industries had to do is to satisfy himself that those condi tions are fulfilled. [610C] 2.1 The exemption conferred by the 1982 notification in regard to industries mentioned under column (2) is not available to traditional industries because of rule 14 above, the same should be the position in regard t he exemption provision also. [613D E] 2:2 In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding the exemption granted to the respondent assessee. The benefit of the exemption cannot be denied to them on the basis that the industrial units run by it are "tractive industries" within the meaning of section 12(1)(i) of Act.

The petitioners were appointed to the Delhi Judicial Service in the year 1980. They were promoted as Additional District & Sessions Judge on the basis of a competitive examination held by the High Court. The petitioners challenged their appointment before the High Courts and contended that they had been appointed regularly in accordance with the Rules and that the appointments were made without any statutory rules, and that they were not entitled to be confirmed in their substantive posts as Additional district & Sessions Judges. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not appointed on the dates of appointment but on the date of appointment. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Rules did not provide for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits and promotees, and as such they could not be promoted to the post of Additional District and Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The rules are made in accordance therewith by the Government from time to time. [395C] 2.1 The Rules do not provide that a quota is to be filled up by direct recruitment on the recommendation of the High court. It is true that under Rule 7(a) the promotees are appointed to temporary posts in the service, but they are appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the Service. [397D] 2:2 The rules do not prescribe any quota for direct recruit ment. They are made by direct recruits on the recommendations of the Delhi High Court under Rule 5(1) and the promotees who are appointed after a member of the Central Civil Service, are appointed on a temporary basis. [399E F] 3. The Rules provide for recruitment to the service in the State of Punjab and the Union Territory of Delhi. The quota rule provides for recruitment by direct appointment from amongst members of the Haryana Judicial Service. Rule 7 provides that temporary posts shall be filled in by promotion from members of Delhi Judicial Services, and Rule 8(2) provides for appointment to the posts of Additional district and Sessions Judges on the advice of the Punjab High Court as enjoined by Rule 7 (a). [399F G] 4. The rule is not intended to provide for direct recruitment to a temporary post in the cadre. It does not contemplate that the rules do so. The only way of recruitment is to fill up the vacancies by promotion on the principle of selection from members, of Delhi judicial Service, who have completed not less than ten years of service in Delhi Judicial service as required under Rule 16(2). [398F G; 399A] 5. The appointments are made on the one hand and the members of a Delhi Judicial Department are appointed by direct recruit ing the posts to which they belong. [398C D] 6.

The appellant was a member of the Hindu Undivided Family. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the appellant in respect of the assessment year 1966 67, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment on the ground that the income from the business was not liable to be brought to tax on that footing. The High Court held that the assessee was a stranger to the assessment proceedings and the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to direct after setting aside the orders of assessment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the Income tax officer could give directions in the case of Ambala Flour Mills to the effect that the business of the assessee be set aside on the grounds that the case was remanded to the Income Tax Officer to assess the income as "the income of a family of individuals" and not "an order of reassessment". The High court held that there was no question of any direction in the matter of remand. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The power of the Appellate Commissioner to make the impugned direction was not conferred on the Tribunal by section 66(2)(a) of the Income. tax Act. [392 B] (2) The word "person" used in section 33A includes a person who is a member. It means a person whose name has been included as a member and who has been excluded from the assessment. If the assessment had to be made on the assessee or any person 's name he must have been included in the assessment of the income. [391 C] (3) The Income Tax officer was of the view that the appellant was not entitled to make an order under section 33B, and that the appeal should be remanded to him for fresh disposal. [390 G H] Commissioner of Income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndicate Ltd., ; , followed.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his claim for partition and separate possession of the property. The appellant contended that the valuation was in order to be adopted by the appellant as the value of his share was not taken into account in computing the court fees payable under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The suit was not barred by section 7 (iv)(a) of Act 1 of 1939 and it could not be reopened at this stage. The valuation for purposes of jurisdiction on the basis of a plaint is final under the provisions of section 7 of the Madras High Court Act. The question whether the court fee has to be determined in respect of suits falling under sub section (iv) or section 7 is a matter which is directly within the scope of section 17 B of the Indian Limitation Act and it cannot be reopened on this ground. The decision of the Division Bench of the High Court that the memorandum of appeal should be taxed for the purposes of court fees was not correct. The judgment of the division bench of the Calcutta High Court in the present case fell under section 8(iv) (b) and therefore, the proper court fee to be paid was the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction and it was on this valuation alone that the appellant could be properly called upon to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the memorandum Of appeal. The order of the single judge of the Bombay High Court was not in error in holding that the court Fees were not payable under the Act as the valuation had been made by the plaintiff for the pur pose of court fee.

The respondent No. 1, a private limited company, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1989 and also the order of the High court dated 28.4.1989 rejecting the claim of the appellant for compensation on the ground that it was not permissible to impugn the decision of this Court in the case of the respondent No 1. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the construction of the "Refuge Areas" is covered by Bye law 16.4,8.1 and 16. 4.8. 1. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the policy to implement the Master Plan for the purpose of constructing a house in the ratio of one sq. metre per person on each floor was not considered by the Chief Fire Officer as a better and more reliable fire safety measures than those envisaged by the bye laws and the Chief fire Officer preferred to accept them; (ii) that the policy of the Government was not inflexible, and therefore the policy could not be withdrawn; and (iii) that there was no justification for the High Courts to interfere with the decision. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy of "Refancy" is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the legislature to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety in a measure better than those contemplated by the Bye law. [608C] 1.2 In appropriate cases where the plan and designs incorporate fire safety measure which, in judgment of the Council are considered to be a better or more reliable Fire safety measures as well as the policy, the construction would be rendered possible. The policy is an extra ordinary and equitable method and not an inflexible one. [613D] 1:3. In appropriate case where the plans and designs incorporated in the Bye laws have been considered to provide for the safety in the building and, pro vided further, that they are located on external walls, by the Municipal Corporation, within the meaning of Bye law 17.4 8.1 or that the plan was not a valid one. The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal development requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and proba tions inherent in the insistence upon construction of such buildings are to be decided on the basis of the policy taken by the Corporation. [625E F] 1 :4. In order to avoid any conflict between a statute and the statutory provisions, the Court must take into account all relevant factors including the policy which it seeks to achieve. The scheme of the Act is not inflexible and that in appropriate cases, where the policy is considered to have been adopted by the authority concerned, the respondent 1 and 2 would undertake to put up such a pedestrian walk way and Podium. [600E F; 600A] 1.(5) In appropriate situations, where, the plans or designs incorporate the fire safety standards which in judgment are considered as adequate, the building plan providing for adequate Fire safety is conclusive and binding on the NDMC. The construction of these buildings is not an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on such a profession or trade. [599F] 1(6) In the instant case, the policy was not uniform and that the requirements of Bye laws 16.04 were not inflexible. [596G] 2.1 It is well settled that in order to meet the exigencies of the situation, where a plan to implement a Zonal Developmental requirements in the matter of construction of a building is considered as a proper and reasonable one for the purposes of the statute, it would be unreasonable and inequitable to allow the authorities to take such steps as they may think fit. [508C D] 2:2 The policy to provide an additional accommodation to the residents of the city is not only in conformity with Bye law but also with the policy.

The plaintiff was the owner of a motor business in the State of Bombay. He had a right to ask for accounts of his business and that he had a power to ask him for accounts. The plaintiff claimed that the suit was barred by res judicata or by Order II, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the compromise was made after due deliberation and that the parties agreed to provide for the payment of money as well as the agreement between them, and the plaintiff was under a misapprehension about his legal right inasmuch as he thought that when the accounts were to be taken up to March 31, 1946, he was under an impression that the business had been taken up before March 31. The High Court held that the cause of action in the first suit was different from the cause. Held, that the plaintiff could not be said to have committed a breach of contract by reason of his conduct or acquiescence and that it was not necessary for him to prove that he was guilty of any misconduct or negligence. The mere fact that the agreement was made before March 1, 1946 did not affect the validity of the compromise. The cause of suit in the second suit was the same as the cause for action in a suit for partition. The present case was one where the plaintiff had abandoned his claim to account up to the date of the final decree and the defendant was bound by the terms of the agreement.

The appellant was carrying on the business of manufacturing salt. The appellant was prosecuted under section 92 of the Indian Penal Code for having manufactured salt in contravention of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The prosecution alleged that the salt works were being carried on in the "exhibitory sheds" within the meaning of the definition of "manufacturing process " in cl. (k) of section 2 of the Bombay Salt Act, 1948, and that the appellant had been using the salt for manufacturing salt in the salt factory without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the said Act read with r. 7 of the Rules. The trial court held that the Salt Works would come within the definition Of "manufactured process" in cl.(k) and that it was not necessary to show that the expression "manufacturer" in el. (p) of s 2 of Bombay Salt act, 1948 was used for the regulation of employment of children in factories and provided that the Act would be construed together with the previous Acts as one Act. The High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show the existence of the salt Works in question and that therefore the salt work did not come within section 2(k) Of the Act. Held, that the word " factory" in cls. (a) and (b) of r.7 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, must be construed as including the expression 'manufacturing processes ' in cl., (k), and therefore the appellant was rightly convicted of the offence of working the salt.

The respondent was appointed as Lecturer in the appellant 's College in 1935. He joined the post of Director of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that he should be absorbed in the Department of Technical education with effect on November 28. 1949. On November 28., 1949, the respondent was informed by a communication dated February 19, 1960 that he would be absorbed as Tailoring Instructor from the date of his appointment as such. The appellant challenged the order of the Government by a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition and directed the absorption of the respondent in the department of Technical Educational with effectfrom November 28 1949. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government had evolved a principle that if a person was deputed to the Department, he should also be absorbed permanently in the service of that Department. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent 's services were not similarly situated because there was a break in the respondent service with the Department. [262C] (2) In the present case, seven employees had come on deputation from other Departments to the Polytechnics and all of them, except the respondent, were absorbed permanently. The Government by order dated February 2, 1960 directed that the promotions of the respondents therein should be given effect from the dates on which they came on deputation. [263D] (3) In view of the above, the State Govern ment had evolved the principle that whenever a person is deputed to an Department of technical Education from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he was initially sent.

The petitioner, a foreign parent, filed an application for being appointed guardian of the child in the Court of the Special Judge, Delhi and Gujarat. The Court granted the custody of the minor child to the petitioner on the ground that the child study report was not satisfactory and that it would be for the welfare of the children to be allowed to be adopted by the foreign parents and if on a consideration of these reports and material, the court came to the conclusion that it will be for them to take the child to his own country with a view to its eventual adoption. The petitioner filed an affidavit in this Court stating that the petitioner was not willing to adopt the child as he had no children to stay in the courts at Bombay, Delhi, Delhi or Gujarat and that the court should make an order appointing the foreign parent as guardian of a child in adoption. On behalf of the petitioner it was contended that the Court has no jurisdiction to appoint a foreigner as guardian unless it is satisfied that the application of the foreigner for adoption through a recognised social or child welfare agency in India through which the application for guardianship is processed, so that one copy can be filed in court and the other can be made available to the foreign parties. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The court has no power to appoint an Indian citizen as guardian in India, if he desires such a child to be given in inter country adoption. [804C] 2. In order that an application of a foreigner for appointment under section 9(1) may be made by the recognised social and child welfare agencies, it is necessary to provide for the custody and control of the foreign or child careless child welfare and whether it will he in the interest of the applicant. The Indian law has been enacted with a purpose to protect the interests of the person who is not able to live in India and to get the child admitted in adoption and in case they do not have the child education, the Court may direct that the foreign child study reports be submitted to the court so that the courts may be able to satisfy itself whether the principles and norms as also the procedure laid down by this Court in this judgment have been observed and followed. [8805C D] 3. The recognised social/ child welfare legislation is a welfare legislation which has a constitutional or other constitutional obligation to provide a just and fair treatment for the persons who are able to get their children, if they are not able, to get them at all through the court. The courts have no power in this regard to grant or refuse relief to the person aggrieved by the order of the Court. [8905D] 4. In the instant case, the petitioner has not been able to establish that he is a child under the Act and that he has not established any other social or economic obligation to make an application under section 10(1)(d) of the Act for guardianship of the respondent. The foreign parents who have taken a child on adoption are also entitled to get a child as guardian. [90G] 5.

The appellant company was a registered firm. The Central Government by its order dated June 23, 1967 referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the allocable surplus of the workmen was not properly made in accordance with the Act and that the claim of the Company was not justified. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the computation of allocable available surplus by the company has not been properly made, and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back as allocable return for arriving at the actual gross profits. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was justified in disallowing deduction of certain items from the gross profits under the Act. [21D] (ii) The claim of a company that it has not to pay bonus is not an item which could be deducted from the net profits under section 6, but not the bonus payable to the employees. [22F] (iii) The appellant company had not accepted this contention of the Unions on the ground that the amount of Rs. 65,764 has not actually been declared for the year 1964 65 and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. The claim for deduction of some items from gross profits is not made by the appellant. [23F] In the instant case, the Tribunal had rightly rejected this claim of Rs, 65,774 on the basis that the principle adopted by the Tribunal in respect of direct tax is found to be erroneous by this Court. [24G] (iv) The question of calculation of direct taxes under the , is not a matter which could have been referred for adjudication. It is clear from the evidence that bon is at least Rs. 66,743. The appellant had not paid any bonus to make up the 14.02% as allocability of the available surplus and the rate at which the bonus was granted can subject to scrutiny.

The appellant was working as a Commercial Tax officer in the Madras Commercial Taxes Department. He was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Tamil Nadu. The appellant was posted at the Commercial Tax Office in 1966 and later on as an Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1972. In 1969 he was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of the Commercial Taxes. On promotion as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial Tax Officer, the appellant was promoted to the post of Joint Commercial Tax officers in 1957. The order of promotion was challenged by the appellant before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Government is entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion. [812 D] 2. The word 'regular ' in section 3(1) of the Act means a regular post. There is no provision in the Act for any time being in force. It is only when there is some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past read they all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But, with nothing of the sort, it is difficult to sustain the order of the Government retiring the appellant from service. [912 F G] 3. The effect of the order was that the said charges may be dropped. There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of the appel lant in 1969. The basis of the entry was blotted out by the promotion of the Appellant as Deputy commissioner of Commercial taxes and posted as member, Sales Tax Officer. [936 G H] 4.

The appellants were owners of certain transport vehicles. The State Transport Undertaking was formed by the Corporation under the provisions of the , and the Corporation was constituted under the Act. The Corporation made an application to the Government for a permit on the route in question. The appellants filed applications before the Government under section 68 C of the Act, claiming that they were entitled to be granted permits under Ch. IV A of the . The State Government rejected the applications. The High Court held that the scheme was vitiated by non compliance with the requirements of section 68C and the Rules made thereunder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the schemes were invalid as they had not been complied with in accordance with the provisions Of section 68 D, and that the Scheme was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The scheme is vitiated by noncompliance with the requirement of section 69 C. [368 E] (ii) The procedure prescribed under section 69C is to have effect notwithstanding anything in Ch. No. 883 of the Corporation Act or any other law made thereunder, the provisions contained in Ch, No. 68 D shall not apply to a permit by reason of section 70 C. It is only when the Regional Transport Authority of that area cannot grant permits under the said Chapter or make an order under Ch, IV A. [369 E] The scheme framed and approved by the State Government was valid. [370 G H] (iii) The Scheme was not vitiated by any non compliance of section68C. [371 D] (iv) The schemes were not vitiated because they were not complied with by the Regional transport authorities. They had to be quashed as not warranted by law. [372 E F] (v) The provisions of Ch. V, C. P. and Berar Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, are not violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the constitution. [373 G H; 370 A B] (vi) The object of section 67 C is to provide for the nationalisation of transport in certain specified areas and to provide that no permit shall be issued by reason only of the scheme framed under Ch., IV A or any rule made thereunder and that such a scheme may be modified by the Government.

The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellant was assessed to sales tax for the assessment year 1941 49 and 1949 50 on the ground that he had not furnished the declaration forms prescribed by the purchasing dealers in respect of the said sales made to him. The assessing authority rejected the claim of the appellant on the grounds that the declaration form was a condition for claiming exemption under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act, and that the appellant was entitled to exemption thereunder. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but the Tribunal held that the said declaration forms were not in accordance with law. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The expression "any other relevant evidence" in section 5 (2)(b)(ii), means any document which is produced or produced for inspection and certified by the registering authority. In the present case, the appellant had not filed the declaration Form prescribed by it before the purchasing dealer but only filed a return showing the particulars of the goods purchased by him. It was not open to the appropriate sales tax authorities to make an assessment under section 21A of the Orissa Sales Tax and to avoid that conflict it would lead to the position that if the declaration formed part of the declaration, well and good, but if not furnished, other evidence can be produced. The object of section 5 is to prevent fraud and promote administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. (ii)The appellant had no right to claim exemption thereunder under section 6(2) (a)(iii). The appellant had failed to produce the necessary documents for inspection of the dealers and the appellant did not file any such declaration forms.

The petitioners were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed their petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the provisions of section 167(2) and (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not complied with; (ii) the State should furnish to this court the dates on which these under trial prisoners were remanded to judicial custody from time to time by the Magistrates, so that they could satisfy itself in regard to compliance with the proviso to section 167 (2); and (iii) the petitioners had been deprived of their fundamental right to apply for bail and help them to secure release on bail. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The State should be directed to furnish to the Court within three weeks from today particulars as to the location of the courts of Sessions in each sub division of the State as on 31st December, 1978 giving year wise breakup of such pending cases and also explaining why it has not been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been pending for more than six months. [538C D] 2. The petitioners are under a constitutional obligation to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. [540D] 3. The Court should not ordinarily interfere with an order of detention unless it is shown that there has been such delay in the investigation or the delay has occurred in the course of investigation. [541E] 4. The power of the High Court under section 167 of the Criminal Procedure Code to direct the State of Bihar to furnish a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail, provided that no objection is raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for release is made, the Magistrates or the Sessions Courts, as the case may be should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad outlines set out by us in our judgment dated 12th February, 1979. [544E F] 5. The provisions of sections 167(1) and 167(3) are not complied within three months from today.

The appellant was the landlord of a protected tenant. The respondent filed an application under section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar held that the tenancy had been terminated by notice dated December 31, 1951, under section 34(1) of that Act. On appeal the Collector held that as the tenancy was not terminated, the appellant was entitled to terminate the tenancy. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 34 (2 A) were applicable to the present case and the notice having been given before the Amending Act came into force, the notice under section 35(1), must be taken into consideration in determining the right of the landlord in the matter of termination of tenancy. Held, that the notice was not a valid one as it had been issued after the amendment in the present ease. The notice under s 34(2 A), which came into operation before the tenancy stood terminated by the notice, did not affect the date on which the right to terminate tenancy was extinguished, namely, the day on which, the tenancy actually terminates in consequence of the notice given to terminate, it. The period of notice is the same before and after the Amendment Act came to force. The words "the tenant of the intention of the landlords" occurring in section 34 are wide enough to cover cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy has not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Acts, it would be a law existing on the date of notice and therefore the court had to see whether the termination is in accordance with the restrictions imposed by subs. (2A) on the landlord 's right to terminating the tenancy, the crucial date is not the date when the right is given. The provisions of the amending Act which came to be effective before the tenant could be applied to all cases where notice had been given, the law to be applied in case of notices were given after the coming in force of that section and therefore it was open to the landlord not to carry out his intention.

The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan. They filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notification issued by the Custodian on January 10, 1952, under section 7 of the Act and their properties being evacuee property. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses and that they were not entitled to them. Held, that the order was without jurisdiction as it was passed without jurisdiction so far as the petitioners were concerned. The orders of January 10 1952 were without jurisdiction. The order of January 1, 1952 was without any jurisdiction so long as the notification was issued under section 8 of the , and he had no longer any claim to them, and was not therefore invalid. The Act did not affect the rights of an evacuee which the petitioners could not be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 6 of the . Held, further, that in view of the provisions of section 12 of the Central Act, the order being a quasi judicial decision, no appeal by him against that order lay or was necessary. The acts of the Custodian in so faras they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. The proceedings of the evacuee in so much as they deprived the petitioners from their rights under the will, if any, and say nothing about them. The act of the custodian in so longas not vested in the Custodian was not a quasi administrative decision. The action of the officer in so many cases could not have been challenged by him.

The assessee company was a manufacturer of yarn from raw and waste wool and claimed deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by it in its business. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that the agreement dated October 20, 1955 contained an arbitration clause which provided for payment of 50 per cent of the losses incurred by the assessee company from raw materials and the losses would be deemed to have been incurred by them in order to earn profits and would therefore fall within the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act. The Tribunal held that the agreements were not legally deductible under section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax, 1922, as it was not incurred for the purpose of business or for earning profits. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the Revenue: (1) The agreement dated November 20, 1956 amounted to a joint venture for distribution of profit and therefore the amount paid to the agents could not be claimed by the appellant company as a deduction under section10(2) (xv) Of the Income Tax Act, 1922. (2) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that the payment made to the selling agents would be treated as an expenditure incurred by a company as laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business of the assessee and to disallow it. HELD: (i) The finding of the Tribunal that the payments were not properly deductible under s 10(1)(xv), was correct. [192F] (ii) The High Court was wrong on the view that the mere fact that the agents agreed to share the losses to the extent of 50%, which were to be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agent would not take the case of the appellant Company as a deductible under sec. 10(3)(xv). [192G] (iii) The question whether the agreement amounted to joint venture or was one for distribution must depend on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. In the instant case, the agreement did not amount to a separate contract but it was clearly proved that the transaction amounted to an agreement entered into by the parties with the selling agent.

The assessee company was a non applicant for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 18,950 constituted accumulated profits for the purpose of section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal held that the accumulated profit will not include current profits and therefore the accumulated profits could not be included within the accumulated income of the company. On appeal by certificate, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) is used in the widest sense and includes profits which have accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting years in a recent case. [950 F] 2. The words "accuumulated profit" in that clause must mean profits which had accumulated prior before the accounting period of which income profits or gains were to be assessed, though current profit will mean the profit of the year in which the Income Tax officer has made his assessment. If the application is rejected by the Appellate Tribunal the applicant is entitled to apply to the High court again within a prescribed period of limitation and the High Courts may, if it is not satisfied of the correctness of the decision of the Appellate tribunal, require the Appellate Tribu nal to state the case and refer it. [951 F G] 3. The question whether the provision of Rs 6,900 for dividend can be taken into account when determining the accumulated losses as on March 31, 1958 is not related to the question whether accumulated profits can take in current profits. If an application is made by the aggrieved party it is open to that party to file a reference under section 254. [952 A B] 4. The form of reference application prescribed by rule 48 of the Income tax Rules, 1962 specifically requires the applicant to state all the questions of law which he desires to be referred to the Court. If he does not apply for a reference of those questions of Law which he wants to be refer, he is entitled under section 256(1) to apply for that purpose.

The respondents were the owners of certain lands in a village known as 'Mouza Nala '. The defendants claimed that they had been granted in permanent Mokarrari grant of those lands by the Maharaja of Burdwan to their predecessors in title long before the permanent settlement, and that they did not form part of the zamindari of Burdwan. The respondents contended that the lands were not Mal lands within the Zamindari of Burdwan but had been given as 'Mal lands ' under a "Mouza" and that the suit lands were in fact settled by the Raja of Burdwan and were therefore entitled to assessment of fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their possession. Held, that the respondents were entitled to assess the fair and reasonable rent on account of the lands for a long time without payment of rent, that they were not entitled to claim any right to them under the Estates of Burdwan or under a permanent settlement. The suit properties formed part of a village within the zamindari and were not liable to pay rent. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 3(1) of the Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1950, the respondents could be said to have asserted a hostile title to them and that as they had not been in possession of the land for a considerable period of time under an assertion of title without challenge, Courts in England were inclined to ascribe a legal origin to such possession. The mere fact that the defendants claimed to hold under a Zamindari ofpore did not make any difference between the case of the respondents and their claim was not barred by reason of article 131 of the Limitation Act.

The appellant was the tenant of a land in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of contract on 15th December 1965 for sale of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas, which was agreed to be sold by the respondent No. 1 to the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was an agriculturist and therefore ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Tenancy Act. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal. In second appeal the High Court held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question which arose under the Tenancy act was a civil suit and that the trial court was not competent to entertain the suit. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of civil court to settle the dispute in a properly constituted civil suit is ousted. [592F] 2.1 The jurisdiction conferred on the Civil Courts under the Bombay Tenancy Act is a special jurisdiction and it has no answer to the provisions contained in section 63. [593G] 22.2 The jurisdiction to settle or deal With any question arising under the tenancy Act, is not only ousted but also the civil court is under a statutory obligation to refer the issue to the competent authority under the Act. [591A B] 3.3 The jurisdiction under the Civil Procedure Code to settle and decide or dealt with any matter which is required to be settled, decided or dealt With by a competent authority is ousted.[592C D] 4.1 In a suit properly constituted and cognizable by the civil Court, it would have no answer from the conclusion that where in a suit property properly constituted, civil court has jurisdiction to decide or dealing with such issue under this Act, it will have to be referred to the Competent Authority under the provisions of the tenancy law. [589F] 3:4.2.3 A question arises in a civil Court whether a person is an agriculturist within the meaning of the Bombay Rent Act and which is require to be determined by competent authority. If there is an issue which has to be decided or dealwith by a Competent Authority, under the Maharashtra Tenancy Act, the jurisdiction to adjudicate upon such issue would not be ousted because the issue is not required to he decided or dealing in any matter under the Land Revenue Code.

The two industrial undertakings owned by the assessee company were formed by reconstruction of the business in the appellant company. The two industrial units were amalgamated with the respondent company. In the assessment year 1958 59, the two industrial undertaking was merged into the new industrial undertaking and the two new industrial undertakings were formed on the same date. The three industrial undertakings which were owned by it were transferred to the new Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the two Industrial Undertakings were not entitled to exemption under section 15C of the Act. In appeal, the Tribunal held: (1) that the jute mill was an industrial undertaking to which section 15 C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 applied and that the assessee was not entitled (2) that it could not be said that the three industrial undertaking had been formed out of the reconstruction of its business already in existence. The High Court held that there was no bar to an assessee carrying on a particular business to set up a new industrial unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The two new undertakings are independent and distinct from the original business of the assessee. [776C] (ii) The Tribunal was right in holding that the four industrial units could be said to be not formed out Of the reconstruction. [765D] (iii) The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new Industrial undertaking expands his existing business, which he certainly does, would not, on that score deprive him of the benefit under section15C merely because it goes to expand the general business of heavy engineering will not prevent him from setting up new industrial units and from claiming benefit under s 15C.

The inamdars were granted to the inamdars as remuneration for services rendered by them. The inamdars filed a suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Madurai for recovery of arrears of rent and mesne profits from the inamdar on the ground that they had been granted in favour of the inamholders. The trial court held that the inams were not adverse to the Government under section 44 B(2)(a) (i). On appeal by the State, the High Court reversed this finding and held that there was no limitation for the grant of exemption from payment of rent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the inam holders were entitled to the kudiwaram rights in the inam lands against the Government and thereby defeat the latter 's right to resume the inam land. HELD: (i) The inams were granted by the inam authorities under the Inamdars ' Act, 1920, to the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. They were inams granted to office holders as remuneration or service in respect of the lands under the inam estates. [557 B] (ii) Section 44 B (2)(b)(i) is attracted if the holder of the Inam land has made an exchange, gift, sale or mortgage of the land or has granted a lease of it for a term exceeding five years. The grant of a permanent lease and the inams are not adverse against the inamers. [544 C] (iii) Section 45 B(1)(a)(i). does not authorise resumption of the inams on the grounds of any alienation thereof made before 1934. [541 D] (iv) The grant was not adverse in character but only adverse to a person who had been an alienation of the properties. [543 G H] (v) Section 43 B(3)(a), which is attracted when the holder or inamdar has made a gift, mortgage or mortgage, of the same kind, does not affect the right of resumption of inam lands in the Inam villages. The rights of the holders are thus adverse to them. [540 G H; 541 A] (vi) Section 46 B(4)(i), which provides that no person shall be entitled to resume an inam land except under a lease granted by him for a period exceeding five year.

The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The respondent Municipality was assessed to tax on the basis of gross annual letting value at 7% of its gross annual rent and the appellant was assessed as a 'annual letting value ' under section 2(c) of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal before the Additional District Judge who allowed the appeal holding that the tax could be assessed on the gross annual rental value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The High Court in second appeal held that the Municipal Tax was not leviable on the net annual letting values at 7%. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant Corporation was entitled to levy the house tax at the rate of 7% on the annual letting rent for the year 1952 53 and 1954 54 under section 4 of the 1958 Act. [131 B] (2) The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the strength of which the tax is assessed is for each such official year. The tax levied under the old Act and the rules framed thereunder on the footing that it has to prepare a fresh assessment list every year, that the Corporation therefore can and in fact have adopted the said list for the two years in question and that being so, the list so adopted was not correct. [132 E F] (3) The tax imposed on the appellant Corporation is not a tax on its annual letting Value but only a tax which has been levied under section 7% and therefore the rate fixed by the Municipal tax cannot be said to have been made under the 1954 Act. Therefore, to the extent that it was inconsistent with the provisions of section 73 of the 1959 Act, it is neither saved nor deemed to have become so made under section 73.

The assessee company was carrying on manufacturing and selling chemicals and other raw materials. The assessee company sold the chemicals to its buyers and the sales were made by the assessee company in liquidation. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the sale was not a realisation sale after the Company had been wound up but had the characteristics of a trading sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transaction was not for the purpose of carrying on the business and even if it be assumed that there was a profit other than what results from the appreciation of capital, the assessee could not be said to be a realisation of the profits and that the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the transactions were not for carrying on any business or even for the purposes of carrying out the business. [966 B] (ii) The assessee Company was wound up at least in so far as its match manufacture was concerned. It is a trading activity which would be carried on by the buyer till the entire consideration was paid, makes no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the assessee Company had kept the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf Of the buyer. [936 B] In the instant case, the sale of the chemicals and raw materials was nothing more than a winding up sale. The sale could not therefore be regarded as a realisation in the course of business or that the profit was earned by it. [948 C D] (iii) The fact that the appellant company was woundup at least for the time during the accounting year did not make any difference because, the agreement itself indicated that it was the assessee 's trading activity. It was impossible to infer that the chemicals were sold in the ordinary way of business and that there could be no profit other except a windingup sale.
